News.title: UK weather live: Met Office 'stay indoors' warning as Storm Boelo brings 80mph winds
News.content:
The Met Office has issued 'danger to life' amber weather warnings for Storm Boelo, which arrives just after Storm Austen caused serious damage in the South West

Storm Boelo is set to bring 80mph winds and 'widespread travel disruption' to the UK this weekend, with forecasters warning of potential flooding, power cuts and problems on the roads.

One amber warning for wind, two yellow warnings for wind and a yellow warning for rain will cover different areas across the UK this weekend, with the Met Office advising people 'stay indoors as much as possible' to avoid potential injury from high winds.

It comes after Storm Austen led to airports being closed, flights cancelled and even Brighton's iconic West Pier partially collapsing.

An amber weather warning is in place across Scotland today, along with the north of England down to Carlisle and the north-east of Northern Ireland, with a yellow weather warning stretching further down across the North West to North Wales and Yorkshire in the east.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned on Friday that the UK could face “a winter of greater flooding” and said we are living in a world where “unexpected events” are “more and more common”.

More than 100 flights have been cancelled across the UK as Storm Boelo brings up to 80mph winds to the country

Dozens of flights have been cancelled across the UK this weekend as Storm Boelo continues to batter the country.

‌

Six wind and rain weather warnings have covered the country, with some of them still in place, bringing "damaging gusts" and "danger to life" from flying debris and leaving thousands without power. Travel has also been severely disrupted by the storm, which followed Storm Austen just hours later, as up to 100 flights have been cancelled.

‌



This comes as the most powerful gusts so far have been recorded in Scotland, with 84mph winds. Among the affected airports are Heathrow, Manchester, Belfast International Airport and Edinburgh Airport.

‌

News.title: Inside Britain's multi-million car parking industry as PM announces clampdown
News.content:
Inside Britain's multi-million car parking industry as PM announces clampdown

EXCLUSIVE: Parking guru Tony Taylor, 66, has helped almost 13,000 motorists overturn fees in his battle against the 'lucrative' industry - as it emerged a record 16.9 million tickets were issued last year

View 2 Images A record 16.9 million parking tickets were issued by private firms last year (file photo) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A former whistleblower has shared the ways the 'lucrative' car parking industry tries to catch out motorists - and how to beat them.

‌



‌



Tony Taylor, 66, once worked as a team leader for the private parking firm UKPC, but has dedicated himself to helping almost 13,000 motorists overturn their parking charges since becoming a consumer champion 12 years ago.

‌



The parking guru has explained exactly what you should do if you find yourself issued with a ticket, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised the 'end of rip-off charges' through a raft of new rules.

‌



Mr Taylor said that many of the government's changes, such as the £100 cap and the five and ten-minute grace periods, were already included in the industry's code of practice, but the new private parking code of practice will turn those guidelines "into law".

View 2 Images Ignoring a parking ticket can lead to a county court judgement - causing potential damage to your credit rating (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham promises to end rip-off parking charges with new rules to challenge fines READ MORE :

His first bit of advice to anyone who receives a Parking Charge Notice in the post from a private company is 'don't panic' - but don't ignore it either, as that could prove costly.

‌



Under current guidelines, the maximum you can be charged for a single ticket is £100, with that typically reduced to £60 if paid within 14 days. But if the fee goes unpaid, private firms usually pass it onto debt collectors, beginning a process that can wreck your credit rating.

Mr Taylor said: "Do not ignore it. Before 2013 it was more or less okay to ignore them, but that year a case went to the Supreme Court, and they ruled in favour of the parking company.

‌



"When I see people on Facebook groups saying, 'Oh, ignore it, there's nothing they can do, it's only the police and the council who can fine you' - no, they're wrong. Parking companies can send it to a debt company."

"I've seen people ignore them, and suddenly they get a county court judgment by default. When you get one of them, you often can't even get a phone contract. I've seen people being refused mortgages because of a parking ticket issued three years ago."

‌



Much of his success in beating the private parking firms comes in identifying common loopholes and errors - such as faded white lines, operators ignoring grace periods, or poor onsite signage that doesn't explain the rules properly.

"Parking companies have been getting away with a hell of a lot for many, many years", he said. "A lot of people will see a letter mentioning court and they will pay straight away, they'll break themselves just to pay the parking ticket".

‌



To date, he has won nearly 13,000 cases, and claims to have a more than 90% success rating in getting tickets overturned.

Despite more guidelines coming in over recent years, the private parking sector continues to be a "highly lucrative" business, Mr Taylor added.

‌



Britain's largest parking company, ParkingEye, turned over about £60million last year. Rival Excel Parking meanwhile reported pre-tax profits this year of £5.5m on a record £21.1m turnover, while CitiPark had operating profits of £2.5m.

According to the government's latest figures, a record 16.9m parking tickets were issued across the industry last year by private firms. Drivers should be aware that any fines issued by a private company can only be pursued as a civil matter - but if you're sent a parking charge by the police or the council, it could result in prosecution.

‌



"When it's private, they're not penalties and they're not fines, they're Parking Charge Notices", he said. "The actual tickets on the cars, they're dressed up to look like fines and penalties in the yellow, just like the council issues. But theirs is a penalty charge and the private are a parking charge notice. Private parking tickets are only a civil matter.

"Only the council and the police issue fines and penalties. A private parking company issues a parking charge notice, which can only be pursued through the county courts through a civil action."

‌



What is the government doing about car parking charges?

Under the new Private Parking Code of Practice announced by the Prime Minister, drivers will be given stronger legal powers to challenge "unfair" charges by parking firms.

The changes, expected to come into force by the end of this year, include:

Woman raped near historic city centre landmark as man, 40s arrested

The incident reportedly took place on Walmgate in York near the city walls, which date back to the Roman times. A man was arrested at the scene

View 2 Images (Image: Getty Images)

A woman has allegedly been raped near a historic landmark in York. The incident reportedly took place on Walmgate in York near the city walls, which date back to the Roman times.

Officers received a call following the incident, North Yorkshire Police said, at around 10.45pm on Thursday. On arrival, they arrested a man in his 40s who has since been released on conditional police bail.

The woman, who is aged in her 40s, is receiving support from specialist agencies.

View 2 Images Walmgate in York city centre (Image: Wikipedia)

A statement from North Yorkshire Police reads: "A man has been arrested on suspicion of rape following an incident on Walmgate in York near the city walls. Police received a call at around 10.45pm on 22 October following the incident.

News.title: People 'feel stupid' after discovering what AM and PM actually mean
News.content:
People 'feel stupid' after discovering what AM and PM actually mean

People have been left feeling pretty silly after only just learning the origin of the terms AM and PM. While some people consider this common knowledge, others have admitted they had no idea what the terms meant

View 2 Images Do you use AM and PM when telling the time, or are you more of a fan of the 24-hour clock? (Stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

People have been left feeling dumb after only just learning what something they say almost every day means. Unless you're a fan of the 24-hour clock, you're probably used to referring to times in the morning with the suffix 'AM', along with 'PM' for the afternoon and evening.

‌



‌



But what exactly does it mean? Some people might consider the origins of the terms to be common knowledge, but others admit they have no idea what they mean.

‌



Writing on X, formerly Twitter, one user asked: "I might be called stupid after this, but WTF does 'AM' and 'PM' stand for?" Fortunately, people were swift to provide clarification.

‌



What do AM and PM mean?

As with much in the English language, the origins lie in Latin. AM is short for "ante merīdiem, meaning "before noon/midday".

PM, on the other hand, means "post merīdiem". This means – you've guessed it – "post noon/midday".

View 2 Images Have you ever thought about what AM and PM mean? (Stock image) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



Lots of people have admitted they had never even thought about this. One user commented: "I've never in my life thought to ask this question... lmao."

Another chuckled: "Haha, my wife just said, 'almost morning and past morning?'" And a third remarked: "I bet 5,000 people got the answer to that question from this post, when they didn't even have the question in them before this post. That makes it a great post. It made people think and answered the question."

‌



While some people were genuinely amazed by the discovery, others took a more cynical view of the revelation. One person responded sarcastically: "Wow, this gives me a great idea!

"What if there was some way on the internet that you could search for answers without having to ask specific people? I think a site that could do that might do very well!"

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

What is the origin of AM and PM?

The application of AM and PM as components of the 12-hour clock format can be traced back to ancient times. The 12-hour timekeeping method itself originates from ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, where sundials and water clocks were employed to separate the day into distinct segments.

‌



The Romans similarly operated on a 12-hour day, splitting daylight into 12 hours and night time into 12 hours, with lengths that fluctuated according to the seasons. The use of AM and PM became increasingly standardised alongside the formalisation of contemporary clock and timekeeping mechanisms.

The broad acceptance of mechanical clocks during the medieval era and the later standardisation of time throughout the Industrial Revolution helped establish these abbreviations in daily use.

News.title: Mum says phone call from hospital 'felt like I’d been handed a death sentence'
News.content:
Mum says phone call from hospital 'felt like I’d been handed a death sentence'

Charlotte Curnow is now trying to make the most of her time

View 3 Images Charlotte Curnow on her first day of radiotherapy (Image: Charlotte Curnow/Brain Tumour Research)

A mum felt she’d been “handed a death sentence” when she had a phone call from the hospital with her test results.

‌



‌



After facing two brain tumour diagnoses nearly 20 years apart, she is now calling on the Government to increase investment in research to help improve treatment options and outcomes for patients. Charlotte Curnow, 56, from Nottingham, was first diagnosed with a low-grade glioma in 2004 after an MRI scan for hearing problems unexpectedly revealed the brain tumour on the right frontal lobe of her brain.

‌



Following three years of monitoring, she underwent surgery in 2007 to remove the mass. After years of stable scans, doctors suggested discharging Charlotte, but she requested to continue having MRI scans every two years.

‌



Brain-infecting fungus on rise, ‘zombie’ cells hide from immune system, hidden Alzheimer’s culprit overlooked, and crisps and frozen meals raise risk of brain damage - all this and more in our science newsletter

Scans showed regrowth

In 2023, those scans revealed the tumour had started growing again, but this time it was an aggressive and incurable glioblastoma – a brain cancer with a poor prognosis. Although just one-third of people diagnosed with glioblastoma will survive beyond a year, there have been no new treatments approved since 2005, according to Brain Tumour Research.

View 3 Images Charlotte Curnow with her son Elliott on his graduation day (Image: Charlotte Curnow/Brain Tumour Research)

‌



Last week, the Government made a historic commitment to improving survival rates for brain tumour patients, following a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the Commonwealth swimmer and brain tumour patient Archie Goodburn. Brain tumours kill more children and adults under 40 than any other cancer, yet funding remains critically low.

Just 1% of the national spend on cancer research was allocated to brain tumours between 2002 and 2021, the charity said. New analysis from Brain Tumour Research has shown that nearly three-quarters (74%) of research funding into brain tumours comes from the charity sector, compared to just 26% from the Government. Now, Charlotte joins the charity’s call on the Government to support increased investment of at least £45 million a year in research in order to improve survival rates and patient outcomes in line with other cancers such as breast cancer and leukaemia.

‌



'I was dumbstruck'

Charlotte said: “Before my diagnosis, life was busy but ordinary. I’d worked in financial services for most of my career and was looking forward to returning to work after maternity leave. My son, Elliott, was still a baby and, like any new mum, my world revolved around him. I’d experienced some problems with my hearing, so my consultant arranged an MRI scan before I was due back to work.

“I felt completely well and had no reason to think anything serious was wrong, so when the scan showed a mass on the right frontal lobe of my brain, I was completely dumbstruck. I didn’t have any symptoms at all. One moment I was planning my return to work and the next I was being told I had a brain tumour. It felt like I was carrying a time bomb inside my head.”

‌



Charlotte was initially placed on a watch-and-wait programme, undergoing regular MRI scans for three years. When the tumour grew, she underwent a craniotomy in 2007 and a biopsy confirmed it was a slow-growing grade 2 glioma. She continued to have regular MRI scans after surgery.

Requested continued monitoring

Around 10 years later, Charlotte said, her consultant believed changes visible around the surgery site were scar tissue rather than tumour regrowth and suggested she could stop having scans and be discharged. Charlotte didn’t feel comfortable ending the monitoring and agreed to a compromise with her consultant to continue having an MRI every two years.

‌



Charlotte said: “Six years later, an MRI scan showed the tumour had started growing again. Around that time, I also started experiencing seizures. My hearing and vision would become strange before my heart started racing – giving me just enough time to lie down if I could.

“In August 2023, I underwent my second craniotomy. Because the tumour was deep within my brain, my surgeon carried out a partial debulking rather than attempting to remove all of it, as preserving my quality of life was incredibly important to me.

‌



"The surgery went well and, after six weeks recovering at home, I was preparing to start radiotherapy and chemotherapy when I received a phone call with the biopsy results. When I heard the words ‘grade 4 glioblastoma’, it felt like I’d been handed a death sentence. I went downstairs to tell Elliott the news.”

The charity said brain tumours are indiscriminate; they can affect anyone at any age and nearly 13,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour every year. Six weeks after surgery, Charlotte began radiotherapy alongside chemotherapy, followed by a further six months of chemotherapy. She completed treatment in June 2024, but it took another six months before she began to regain her physical strength.

‌



View 3 Images Charlotte Curnow ringing the bell following her treatments (Image: Charlotte Curnow/Brain Tumour Research)

'Scanxiety'

Charlotte said: “One of the hardest things to live with is ‘scanxiety’. I try not to let the worry consume every day leading up to the appointment and instead remind myself that, although my diagnosis is devastating, I do at least know what I’m dealing with. I know the warning signs to watch for, such as seizures or weakness and numbness in my left leg and I know when to seek help.

‌



"There are so many people who don’t have those answers yet, and reminding myself of that helps me stay grounded. No matter how positive you try to be, waiting for MRI scans and then sitting in the clinic waiting for the results never becomes easy. Over time, though, I’ve learned to manage it better.”

Since finishing treatment, Charlotte has reduced her working hours and is determined to make the most of her time with family and friends. One milestone she feared she would never see was Elliott’s university graduation, but she was able to watch him graduate last year.

‌



Raising awareness

Charlotte has now turned her attention to raising awareness and funds for research into brain tumours. She completed the Brain Tumour Research 88 Squats A Day in July challenge to support vital research such as that taking place at the Brain Tumour Research Centre of Excellence at the University of Nottingham. Scientists at the centre are using artificial intelligence, advanced brain imaging, and genomic techniques to better understand glioblastoma recurrence and accelerate progress towards improved treatments.

Charlotte said: “One thing I feel incredibly strongly about is the need for more research. Brain tumours remain desperately underfunded compared with many other cancers, and yet the impact they have on people’s lives is devastating. Better research means better treatments and more hope for families like mine.

‌



“If I could leave anyone with one message, it would be not to be frightened of asking questions or speaking up for yourself. I truly believe continuing my MRI scans saved my life and I’m so grateful I trusted my instincts all those years ago.

"I also want people to know that statistics don’t define you. None of us knows exactly what the future holds, so I’ve chosen to focus on making memories, spending time with the people I love and saying yes to every opportunity that comes my way.”

‌



Dr Karen Noble, director of research and policy at Brain Tumour Research, said: “Charlotte’s story is a powerful reminder of the devastating impact a brain tumour can have, not only on the person diagnosed but on everyone around them. One in three people knows someone affected by a brain tumour and nearly 13,000 people are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour each year.

"The Government has seized the opportunity to place research at the heart of transforming outcomes for brain tumour patients. We are optimistic that this renewed focus will help ensure discoveries in the laboratory actually make it to the patients who so desperately need more options.”

Article continues below

Brain Tumour Research funds sustainable research at dedicated centres in the UK. It also campaigns for the Government and larger cancer charities to invest more in research into brain tumours in order to speed up new treatments for patients and, ultimately, to find a cure. The charity is the driving force behind the call for a national annual spend of £45 million in order to improve survival rates and patient outcomes in line with other cancers such as breast cancer and leukaemia.

News.title: Slimming World woman 'couldn't play with grandchild' but has now lost 5st without jabs
News.content:
Slimming World woman 'couldn't play with grandchild' but has now lost 5st without jabs

Emma Artemiou was classed as obese

View 4 Images Emma Artemiou before her weight loss (Image: Slimming World/SWNS)

A woman who struggled with weight gain during the menopause says she can finally get on the floor to play with her granddaughter after shedding five stone without using jabs.

‌



‌



Emma Artemiou weighed 13st 6lbs (85 kg) in September 2021 - which, due to her 5ft stature, classed her as obese. Emma, 51, previously found it difficult to walk and impossible to get up and down off the floor with Margo, her two-year-old granddaughter, due to the extra weight she was carrying.

‌



Alongside weight gain, Emma said she experienced low energy, hot flushes and mood changes because of the menopause – all while also dealing with grief following the death of her father. But she now weighs a healthy 8st 6lbs (53 kg) and she lost the weight without using jabs, instead seeking out help from her local Slimming World weight loss support group.

‌



Brain-infecting fungus on rise, ‘zombie’ cells hide from immune system, hidden Alzheimer’s culprit overlooked, and crisps and frozen meals raise risk of brain damage - all this and more in our science newsletter

View 4 Images Emma Artemiou when she was younger (Image: Slimming World/SWNS)

'Incredible' difference

Emma said: "The difference has been incredible. The pressure on my joints has reduced significantly, I have more energy, more confidence and a much more positive outlook on life."

‌



Previously working as a school cook, Emma found losing weight difficult as she was ‘constantly surrounded by food’, all while raising her daughter. On an average day, she would skip breakfast and eat shop-bought sandwiches, crisps and chocolate at lunch – before tucking into a frozen pizza with chips, or a takeaway curry at dinner, followed by two glasses of wine and a share-size bar of chocolate.

Emma, who works as a pet sitter, now has a more balanced diet and batch cooks her meals on the weekends. On an average day she now eats overnight oats for breakfast, tucks into a jacket potato for lunch and has roast chicken for dinner – with sugar-free or low-fat desserts instead of chocolate.

‌



The grandmother-of-two, from Portsmouth, Hants, said: “I wasn’t looking after myself, I’d grab whatever was convenient. Takeaway pizza, ice cream, chocolate and red wine. Even though I cooked healthy meals for other people, I wasn’t taking care of me.”

View 4 Images Emma Artemiou now weighs a healthy 8st 6lbs (Image: Slimming World/SWNS)

‌



Weight caused pain

Emma said her weight caused pain in her knees, with even short walks leaving her struggling and everyday tasks becoming more difficult. She lost 9lbs (4kg) of weight in her first month with the Slimming World group alone. Her husband Jamie even joined up in June 2024 to focus on his health.

Emma said: “I feel healthier, stronger and more in control of my wellbeing than I have in years. I now enjoy regular walks by the sea, cycling with Jamie and I’m thinking about taking up tennis again – I used to love playing when I was 40.

‌



“Most important of all, it’s the time I spend with my gorgeous two-year-old granddaughter, Margo, that means the most. Being able to get up and down off the floor with Margo is a huge win.

“I can take her to the park, play on the equipment with her, go down the slide and run around soft play. If I was still carrying almost five extra stone, I wouldn't be able to do those things. Those moments are priceless.”

‌



View 4 Images Emma Artemiou now (Image: Slimming World/SWNS)

Emma's diet before weight loss

Breakfast: Often skipped

‌



Lunch: Shop-bought sandwich with crisps high in fat and salt, chocolate and a low-calorie cola

Dinner: Frozen pizza with chips, homemade spaghetti Bolognese, a rich béchamel sauce, full-fat steak mince and full-fat cheese or a takeaway curry

‌



Dessert: Share-size bar of chocolate or ice cream

Snacks and drinks: One or two glasses of wine per evening, full-fat crisps

‌



Emma's diet after weight loss

Breakfast: Overnight oats with plenty of fruit and low-fat yoghurt or Slimming World's full English breakfast - two slices of lean bacon with the fat trimmed off, Slimming World sausages, grilled tomatoes, spinach, two poached eggs and mushrooms – most items cooked in the air fryer

Lunch: Jacket potato with salad, tuna and low-fat cheese or a lunch bowl such as Bang Bang Chicken and rice from the Slimming World Food Range at Iceland

‌



Dinner: Slimming World roast chicken dinner with fresh vegetables and low-fat homemade gravy

Dessert: Sugar-free jelly, low-fat yoghurt and fresh fruit or a low-fat mousse

Article continues below

Snacks and drinks: Fruit, high fibre cereal bar, water, de-caffeinated coffee, gin with slimline tonic

News.title: Andy Burnham's 'resurgent' Labour secures poll boost over Reform and Tories ahead of crunch week
News.content:
Andy Burnham's 'resurgent' Labour secures poll boost over Reform and Tories ahead of crunch week

Ahead of a crunch week for the government, two polls found Andy Burnham's Labour party now has a clear eight-point lead over Conservative and Reform rivals

View 2 Images Andy Burnham will mark 100 days in office on Tuesday (Image: Temilade Adelaja/Press Association)

Andy Burnham's "resurgent" Labour has secured a boost in the polls - as the Prime Minister prepares to mark his 100 days in office.

‌



‌



According to two surveys published this weekend, Mr Burnham's party now has an eight-point lead over Tory and Reform rivals. Pollsters Ipsos said it was the largest lead it had recorded for Labour this Parliament.

‌



It comes ahead of a crunch week for the government, with Mr Burnham set to mark 100 days in Downing Street on Tuesday - 24 hours before Chancellor John Healey delivers the Budget.

‌



Ipsos found 32% said they will vote Labour at the next general election - a 5-point increase on last month - compared to 24% for Kemi Badenoch's Tories. The survey also shows Nigel Farage's embattled Reform trailing in third place on 20%.

Director of politics at Ipsos in the UK, Keiran Pedley, said: "Whilst the headline figures do show a striking change, they confirm a pattern we have been seeing in the underlying data for some time.

View 2 Images Ipsos found Nigel Farage's embattled Reform trailing in third place behind Labour and the Tories on 20% (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"The Labour Party under Andy Burnham is resurgent, consolidating voters on the left behind them. On the right, the tectonic plates have been shifting recently and now this is reflected in the Conservatives - not Reform UK - being in a clear second place."

But he added: "We should be mindful against overreacting to one poll.

‌



"The Government faces a challenging budget this coming week and the lesson of the last year is the British politics is volatile. The picture today is very different to six months ago and it could be different again in six months' time too."

Meanwhile pollsters Opinium also found Labour had an eight point lead on 30% with Nigel Farage's embattled Reform trailing in second place on 22% and the Tories on 20%.

‌



It also found the Greens on 10% and the Liberal Democrats on 9%.

Mr Burnham has repeatedly ruled out the prospect of an early general election. But if Labour continues to improve its position in the polls it will reignite speculation over an early vote.

‌



Asked by ITV Calendar in September whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: "Well, yes, that's when the next election will be.

"All of this speculation on an early election - I can knock that dead.

Article continues below

"You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we've discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I'm not going to do that."

News.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.

The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.

On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement.

"I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

News.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
News.content:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants to pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.

"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external

"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."

He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.

In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.

However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.

The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".

Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."

Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".

"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

News.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
News.content:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around Â£24bn to as low as Â£11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.

News.title: Who are the candidates in Brazil's presidential election?
News.content:
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday to vote for their next president.

They are choosing between Brazil's current left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva and the right-wing Senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin.

As Americas correspondent Ione Wells reports from Rio de Janeiro, voters are choosing between two very different candidates.

News.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
News.content:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic â the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

News.title: Moment of jeopardy as King embarks on Caribbean tour
News.content:
The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

News.title: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists
News.content:
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

News.title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
News.content:
Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.

The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (Â£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.

Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

News.title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
News.content:
Under the plans for the regions, an initial Â£285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new Â£1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the Â£285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.

She told the Sunday Times, external, that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

News.title: Murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

News.title: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband says
News.content:
"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post.

"I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together.

"My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."

Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".

In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".

He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
The first part of the parade was followed by a series of speeches, mainly from members of the Orange Order.

This was very much an Orange Order event and not a political rally but inevitably there was a political tone to many of the comments.

There was explicit criticism of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, the secretary of state and the first minister, but also implicit criticism of the leaders of the two biggest unionist parties - the DUP and Ulster Unionist Party.

Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister was applauded but by far the loudest cheers were for the Orange Order's legal adviser Jamie Bryson and the local MP Lockhart.

She was invited on to the stage and presented with a special gift for her support of the Orangemen.

Lockhart was the only politician to take to the stage, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go.

"That's where I stand, and this lady is not for turning."

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson warned politicians that they could face consequences at the next election over the Drumcree dispute.

"Politicians need to remember that we put them into office and we can take them out of office," he said.

He added that the Orange Order had won the right "to return home via our traditional route and Portadown District intends to exercise that right on a date and time of our choosing, and if necessary, without further recourse".

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said Drumcree must not be allowed to divide unionism.

"It should not be used by parties to attack each other publicly over differences of opinion," he added. "We need to stand united."

News.title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding
News.content:
More than Â£1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

The Scottish government funding will support habitat, species and river restoration, control of invasive non-native species and deer management across Scotland.

It includes Â£150,100 for recovery and nature restoration work following the Abernethy wildfire in the Cairngorms in July, to restore damaged habitats, help wildlife recover and reduce the risk of future wildfires.

Further funding will be provided to a range of other projects.

News.title: Reward offered over murder in flat used as brothel
News.content:
A Â£20,000 reward is being offered by Crimestoppers in connection with the murder of a man who was found dead in a Birmingham flat in 2022.

Jinming Zhang had been stabbed multiple times before he was found in the property, which police said was being used as a brothel, in Moseley Street in Digbeth.

West Midlands Police previously released CCTV of a suspect, while a DNA sample from the suspected killer found at the scene did not produce a match on the national database.

The case was featured in the BBC series of Forensics: The Real CSI last year, which revealed police believed the murder suspect may have sustained a hand injury in the frenzied attack.

Jenny Birch, who has been overseeing the investigation, urged anyone with information "no matter how small" to contact police.

"Someone out there knows something, and we won't give up until we have answers," she said.

News.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
News.content:
Sam Fender has said he has removed a ticket category from sale after being unhappy with pricing for his upcoming tour.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician now appears to have lowered the prices and said the "costs are astronomical compared to two years ago" but he could not control the venue or ticketing fees.

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

Fender initially said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

News.title: Wind-up radios selling out after government advises public to stockpile for crisis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Wind-up radios are flying off the shelves after the government advised the public to start stockpiling to prepare for a crisis.

At least seven models sold out at four outlets on Saturday, two days after the government listed battery and wind-up radios on the checklist for households to prepare for emergencies.

The 'Be Ready' campaign marks the beginning of a three-year drive to boost household emergency preparedness, as defence secretary Wes Streeting unveiled updated advice for threats such as flooding and wildfires.

UK households are advised to take simple steps in case everyday services are disrupted, such as keeping a three-day supply of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home.

Maplin said its torch sales had risen by 284 per cent in the last few days, while sales of its power bank were up 106 per cent, The Telegraph reported.

Mr Streeting previously called for a "whole society approach" to strengthen national resilience, though he insisted people should remain "alert not alarmed" regarding potential risks.

open image in gallery UK households are advised to take simple steps in case everyday services are disrupted ( AFP/Getty )

According to new research from The Prepared Household, Scotland has the UK's highest search interest in extreme-weather and emergency-preparedness supplies relative to its population.

Marcus Clarke, founder at The Prepared Household, said: “Scotland stands out clearly in the data, with more preparedness-related searches per person than anywhere else in the UK. People are searching for everything from emergency kits and blackout supplies to flood equipment and backup power.

"The West Midlands also records particularly strong interest, especially around practical items such as emergency torches, power banks and power-outage kits. It suggests people are looking for straightforward ways to prepare for disruption at home."

open image in gallery Britons advised to prepare for emergencies in new government guidance ( Gov.uk )

A new government website has also been launched with an emergency kit checklist that can be downloaded.

The checklist includes:

News.title: Angela Rayner sympathises with Meghan Markle over family rift: 'I can understand the difficulty'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Angela Rayner says that she sympathises with the Duchess of Sussex over the furore surrounding her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr.

Authorities in the Philippines are investigating allegations that Mr Markle kept a hoard of child sex abuse images at his former home there.

Mr Markle has denied the claims, calling them a “bunch of lies”.

On Saturday, it emerged that the Metropolitan Police received a letter in January 2019 featuring claims of Mr Markle’s alleged offending.

The force admitted that it passed the letter to Meghan and her husband Prince Harry, but did not share details with other law enforcement agencies.

open image in gallery Meghan has been estranged from her father Thomas for a number of years ( Instagram )

On Sunday, Ms Rayner, the housing secretary, told Sky News that the matter was an “operational issue”.

She said: “The police have a very robust system in place of independence, where they will act to ensure that where they need to share information, it’s appropriate, they will do that.

“That is an operational issue for the police. They’re independent, I’m sure that they’re making those decisions based upon people upholding the law and especially protecting children.”

Meghan said this week that she kept a distance from her father after learning of the alleged offending, and chose not to allow him to have contact with her children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in order to protect them.

It has also been reported that Meghan wrote to her father in 2025, telling him that she knew of the sex abuse claims against him and that she would never allow him to meet his grandchildren.

open image in gallery Angela Rayner says that Meghan has faced ‘a tremendous amount of intrusion’ into her family ( AFP/Getty )

The letter was understood to have been sent while Mr Markle was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

Sources close to Meghan told the BBC that she wrote it was the last time she would contact him.

Ms Rayner, asked on Sunday if she felt sorry for the duchess, said: “Meghan Markle has faced a tremendous amount of intrusion into her family. It must be difficult as as a daughter to have all this out in the open.

“She’s made a statement and she’s been very robust in that statement.

“As a mother myself, I can understand the difficulty that that is for Meghan, and for it to be all over the news every day.

“Her estrangement from her father has been something that’s been in the press for some time. But she’s been really clear now, I think, on the reasons, some of the reasons, why that is the case.

“But at the heart of this, you’ve got a mother who is trying to raise her children and protect them, and to have a great family life, and that is obviously very difficult when you’re in the public eye.”

News.title: Reform UK’s support collapses in major boost for Burnham, new poll shows
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Support for Nigel Farage’s Reform UK has collapsed, giving Kemi Badenoch’s Tories their biggest lead over them since the general election in 2024 and a major boost for Labour, according to the latest Ipsos poll.

The survey has put Reform on just 20 per cent with the Tories four points ahead on 24 per cent – but it also suggests that Andy Burnham’s Labour could win a large majority if there were a general election.

In a boost to the prime minister, Labour has its biggest poll rating since the last election, on 32 per cent.

According to political consultancy Electoral Calculus, this would give Labour a large majority of 134 MPs, slightly down on the 167 majority they won in July 2024.

open image in gallery Support for Nigel Farage’s Reform has collapsed ( Reuters )

Research director Keiran Pedley said: "Whilst the headline figures do show a striking change, they confirm a pattern we have been seeing in the underlying data for some time.

"The Labour Party under Andy Burnham is resurgent, consolidating voters on the left behind them."

Looking at the collapse of Reform’s support, he suggested that the “tectonic plates” are shifting.

He said: “On the right, the tectonic plates have been shifting recently and now this is reflected in the Conservatives – not Reform UK – being in a clear second place.

“However, we should be mindful against overreacting to one poll.”

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham is on course to winning a general election (Temilade Adelaja/PA) ( PA Wire )

He added: “The government faces a challenging Budget this coming week and the lesson of the last year is that British politics is volatile. The picture today is very different to six months ago and it could be different again in six months' time too.”

A year ago Reform was polling at above 30 per cent and Mr Farage was favourite to become prime minister at the next election. The Ipsos findings followed a YouGov poll last week which showed voters no longer consider Reform to be a “main party”.

But even before Labour ditched Sir Keir Starmer in the summer, Reform's support had been sliding.

Since Mr Burnham became leader, Reform support has continued to drop, while Labour has opened up a bigger lead, taking advantage of a collapse in support for the Green Party on the left.

Reform has been hit with a number of scandals including a standards commissioner investigation in parliament over a £5m donation Mr Farage received from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Meanwhile, there are police investigations into deputy leader Richard Tice and Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick.

A Channel 4 investigation on receiving illegal donations saw chief of staff Dan Jukes and policy director James Orr forced to step down and in recent weeks, an ITV investigation revealed racism among candidates and councillors in the party.

However, Raheem Kassam, a key ally of Mr Farage, lashed out at the poll, warning the UK that money would be pulled out of the country if Reform fails to win.

Commenting on the Ipsos poll, he said: “I suspect this isn’t actually very good data but on the off chance that it is accurate, I will have no sympathy for the Britons who vote for the uniparty and then endure the worst decade they’ve ever experienced between now and 2036. The capital flight will be astounding. You’ll be begging for foreign aid in rather than dishing it out.”

Meanwhile, Zack Polanski’s Greens registered just 8 per cent of support – less than half the high point it enjoyed when it won the Gorton and Denton by-election in February and appeared to be eating into Labour’s vote.

Meanwhile, with questions continuing on Sir Ed Davey’s leadership the Lib Dems came up with just 9 per cent which would see them lose almost half their seats at the next election.

News.title: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes deep beneath Pacific near Japan, country’s meteorological agency says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has struck deep beneath the Pacific Ocean near Japan's remote Ogasawara Islands, about 1,000km (620 miles) south of Tokyo, with no threat of a tsunami, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.

The preliminary magnitude was recorded at around 11.10am local time (2.10am GMT) on Sunday, in waters west of the island chain and at a depth of about 470km (290 miles), the agency said.

The quake measured 3 on Japan's seismic intensity scale, which runs from 0 to 7, on the islands of Chichijima and Hahajima, the two inhabited islands of the group. The Ogasawara Islands, also known as the Bonin Islands, are administered by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government.

Earlier, European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) said that a magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck the Bonin Islands.

There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Despite the distance, the tremor was felt across a wide area of eastern and north-eastern Japan, Kyodo News reported, because seismic waves are believed to have travelled through the Pacific plate, one of the large slabs of the Earth's crust.

The islands lie in the seismically active Izu-Bonin-Mariana region of the western Pacific, where the Pacific plate moves beneath the Philippine Sea plate.

Japan sits where four tectonic plates meet, and about 10 per cent of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6 or higher strike in or around the country. The magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami of March 2011 left 22,303 people dead or missing, including deaths from disaster-related causes. In July, an earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture in the southwest killed at least 30 people.

Deep earthquakes off the Ogasawara Islands can be felt far away.

A magnitude 7.9 quake at a depth of 664km in 2015 was felt across almost all of Japan and stopped elevators in Tokyo, though it killed no one. The government has warned there is a 70 to 80 per cent chance of a magnitude 8 to 9 earthquake on the Nankai Trough, a subduction zone off the south coast, within 30 years.

News.content:
