World.title: Obama’s Ohio, Michigan speeches: Key takeaways on Trump, Iran war, midterms
World.content:
The former US president warns of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values ahead of the November 3 vote.

Former President Barack Obama has railed against the Trump administration on a range of issues, including dragging the United States into “an unnecessary war” against Iran, as he campaigned for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Speaking at rallies on Saturday, Obama accused President Donald Trump of “chaos and corruption”, as he urged voters to reject Republicans.

The speeches came just 10 days before the elections, with Senate and gubernatorial races taking place in both states.

Here are the key takeaways:

Obama blames Trump’s Iran war for rising fuel prices

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

“Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said.

The former president defended the 2015 nuclear agreement reached under his administration, which restricted Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief.

“Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged kept them from getting nukes, and I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy,” Obama said.

“He pulled out of it, starts this war.”

Obama blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases, American casualties and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

“Our allies and our bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed, hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where oil goes through to the world market,” he said.



The disruptions in oil flow through the strait, located between Iran and Oman, have pushed up energy prices worldwide. Before the war, a fifth of global oil and gas passed through the strait, which Iran has used as leverage in the war.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up … This is the reason the price of diesel is up.”

The spike in diesel and petrol prices will likely cost the Republican Party, as the majority of Americans hold Trump responsible for starting the war and the subsequent increase in prices.

Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his focus on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

“These are not serious people,” Obama said.

Tariffs are making life more expensive for Americans

Obama criticised Trump’s tariffs, saying Americans were paying more for goods, including products made in the US using imported parts.

“When you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” he said.

“It’s not just the goods that you use directly that have been imported … It’s also the car you build here in America. They might need a part from somewhere else, and now suddenly there’s a tariff on it.”

He questioned Trump’s trade dispute with Canada, a major US trading partner.

The two countries have been locked in a trade dispute, with Trump threatening 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027.

“And the big trade war he’s starting now is with that well-known evil empire Canada,” Obama said sarcastically.

“Canadians are the nicest people … they’re like our friendly neighbours to the north, and he’s like picking a fight with them.”

Obama also pointed to the growing US national debt, which has reached $40 trillion.

“Instead of bringing down deficits like he said with these tariffs, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.”

The figure refers to the total federal debt, which has accumulated over successive administrations, rather than the annual budget deficit.

Charges of corruption and enriching the wealthy

Obama accused the Trump administration of favouring wealthy Americans while common households struggled with rising costs.

“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”

He pointed to Trump’s 2025 tax and spending legislation, which extended tax cuts while reducing federal spending on programmes including Medicaid and food assistance.



“The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefitted the richest Americans,” he said.

Obama also took aim at Trump’s White House renovations, including plans for a ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked.

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”

Obama condemns Trump’s immigration crackdown

The former president said the US needed secure borders but criticised the methods used by immigration agents under the Trump administration.

“I believe that we do need to make sure that our border is orderly and secure and that people who want to come here do so lawfully,” he said.

“But I don’t recall anybody campaigning on sending masked agents running through our streets. I don’t recall anybody talking about law-abiding citizens being arrested, detained, or shot.”

“That’s not what we have to do to get our borders under control,” he added.

Obama attacks Ramaswamy over controversial Amy Acton 

In Ohio, Obama criticised Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over a campaign  featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

The  features Acton’s mother questioning her honesty and her account of her childhood, without mentioning the allegations of sexual abuse that led to their separation decades ago.

It has drawn criticism from Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, although Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended it.

Obama condemned Ramaswamy’s decision to use Acton’s family history in the campaign.

“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said.

He also praised Acton’s career in public service and urged Ohio voters to support her on November 3.

Obama urges Michigan voters to back El-Sayed and Benson

In Detroit, Obama campaigned for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial contender Jocelyn Benson.

He praised El-Sayed’s Michigan roots and criticised his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, over his support for the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s trade policies.

“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said, referring to his upbringing in the state, his family’s ties to the auto industry and his involvement in school sports.

Obama also spoke about attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim identity, comparing them with false claims about his own religion and birthplace during his presidential campaigns.

“Unlike Mike Rogers, Abdul hasn’t spent months cheerleading the Iran war … or called these tariffs ‘masterful’.”

The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.

Obama also praised Benson for standing by Michigan’s 2020 election results despite threats and protests outside her home.

“When armed protesters showed up outside her home in 2020, demanded she overturn Michigan’s fair and free election results, Jocelyn stood her ground, stood up for you and your rights,” he said.



Obama calls midterms a ‘circuit breaker’ against Trump

Obama said the midterm elections offered voters a chance to limit Trump’s power during the remaining two years of his presidency.

“This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said. “It’s the circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker.”

He also warned that dishonesty, intimidation and bullying were becoming accepted in US politics.

“We are not going to fix the economic system or the political system … so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes and where people in the highest offices in the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully,” he said.

“What we are missing in our public discourse is just basic decency.”

World.title: UFC 333: Volkanovski knocks out Evloev to retain featherweight title
World.content:
Alexander Volkanovski secures a technical knockout in the closing seconds of round two at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi, UAE.

Australia’s Alexander Volkanovski has retained his featherweight title after making short work of Russia’s Movsar Evloev in the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) 333 main event in Abu Dhabi.

Volkanovski secured a technical knockout (TKO) with a right hand, followed by a ground-and-pound move in the closing seconds of the second round of their scheduled five-round fight on Saturday.

The official time was 4:54, as the fight was called off with six seconds left to the jubilation of the Etihad Arena crowd in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

It was Evloev’s first professional loss, and he remained classy in defeat.

“Like I said, Alex is a great champion, and it was an honour to share the cage with him,” Evloev said after the loss.

Meanwhile, Volkanovski said he wants to keep stacking wins for as long as he can.

“I’m choosing to do [fight]; I don’t have to. I said if I didn’t take too much damage, we will probably keep going. So maybe we keep going,” Volkanovski said.

In the co-main event, Petr Yan won his three-fight series against Merab Dvalishvili in a Russia vs Georgia showdown as he swept the scorecards 48-47, 48-47, 48-47, using a gruelling pace and a mix of wrestling and dirty boxing while keeping Dvalishvili at a distance to defend his UFC bantamweight title.

Yan beat Dvalishvili last December to regain the title for the second time, having previously won it in July 2020 against Jose Aldo at UFC 251.

The finishes kept coming, but this time in the flyweight division. England’s Lone’er Kavanagh secured a TKO stoppage against Uzbekistan’s Ramazan Temirov with an uppercut, followed by strikes, at 4:28 of Round 1.



At heavyweight, Russia’s Alexander Volkov won a unanimous decision over Rizvan Kuniev, utilising dominant wrestling and top control to earn his third straight win. Volkov called for a title shot at Thursday’s presser, seemingly stumping UFC CEO Dana White when Volkov addressed him.

Kuniev had his two-fight winning streak snapped.

In the opening fight on the main card, Aaron Pico needed just over a minute to TKO Losene Keita of Guinea in their featherweight fight. Pico has won back-to-back fights, while Keita has split his last four.

World.title: Why is Egypt so wary of getting involved in Yemen’s conflict?
World.content:
As Egypt considers defending Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks, memories of its war in Yemen in the 1960s loom large.

Share Why is Egypt so wary of getting involved in Yemen’s conflict? on social media

Egyptian forces arrived in Yemen in the thousands, backing the country’s government in a civil war against rebels that threatened to overthrow it.

But this is not today’s war – this is 1962, and the Egyptians were supporting republican forces in North Yemen against the country’s royalists. The intervention came after Yemenis who were friendlier to the Arab nationalist ideology propagated by Egypt under President Gamal Abdel Nasser led a revolution that overthrew Zaidi Imam Mohammad al-Badr – a theocratic monarch.

Although the republican side was ultimately successful in the war against the Saudi-backed royalists, Egyptian forces withdrew in the wake of their defeat in the 1967 war against Israel, and after also suffering heavy losses in Yemen.

Suggestions of a new military intervention by Egypt in Yemen today, after comments by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, are therefore bringing back memories of that period for Egyptians.

Following some backlash against the suggestion of direct military intervention, el-Sisi emphasised on Wednesday that any military deployment would be focused on defending Saudi Arabia, and would not involve any direct aggression against Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

And on Thursday, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for a political solution to the conflict.

What has the Egyptian government said it will do?

After Saudi Arabia came under more intense attacks from the Houthis, including a strike on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh which killed 13 people, including one Egyptian, earlier this month, it appears that the kingdom expects support from its longtime allies, including Egypt.



Some countries, including Turkiye, Pakistan, France and the United Kingdom, have already deployed forces to Saudi Arabia in defensive operations or have indicated they are willing to do so.

Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks as the war in Yemen escalated over the past few months, particularly after a Saudi-backed Yemeni government counteroffensive against the Houthis began in early October. Saudi Arabia has supported a counteroffensive by forces allied to the internationally recognised government, with air raids against the Houthis.

Egypt’s National Defence Council said on October 18 the country was ready to provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”.

While much has been made of the possibility of an Egyptian deployment, Cairo has repeatedly made it clear that it has no intention of involving itself in direct attacks against the Houthis.

But even a defensive combat mission would involve the deployment of Egyptian forces outside the country’s borders, so it requires approval from the Egyptian parliament. A vote is scheduled for Monday, after a weeklong delay to allow reticent lawmakers to deliberate on this move.

Why is Egypt wary of becoming involved in Yemen?

This apprehension over military involvement in Yemen is largely related to the Egyptian government’s desire to avoid foreign military entanglements and direct involvement in the US-Israel war on Iran and its allies.

Active participation in attacks against the Houthis could open Egypt up to retaliation by the group or Iran. The Houthis have already shown they are capable of pinpoint attacks on vital civilian and military targets in Saudi Arabia.

An expansion of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping – both Egyptian and otherwise – would also be highly damaging to Egypt’s economy, as the country controls its northern entry point, the Suez Canal, and is heavily reliant on this waterway for trade.

Fewer ships passing through the Red Sea means fewer fees paid to the Egyptian government for their passage through the Suez Canal. El-Sisi has said Egypt has already lost $20bn in potential revenues over the last few years due to regional instability, including previous attacks on ships in the Red Sea and the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.



Disruptions to energy supplies via the Bab al-Mandeb now, which the Houthis effectively control, would likely lead to higher oil prices and knock-on effects for net consumers such as Egypt.

There is also the historical aspect. While Egypt can argue that its intervention in Yemen in the 1960s was an overall success, with the Republican side eventually emerging victorious, the campaign in mountainous northwestern Yemen was brutal. Thousands of Egyptian soldiers were killed in the campaign, and this was blamed by some for the Egyptian military’s lack of readiness in confronting Israel in the 1967 war.

“There is the memory that [Egypt] went to Yemen and faced forces supported by Saudi Arabia, and Egyptian troops were killed there,” said Ahmad Dahshan, the editor-in-chief of the Center of Arabic Eurasian Studies. “Then [the mentality is] that Egypt will send troops to Yemen once again, where they would also be killed, but this time on behalf of Saudi Arabia.”

How could Egypt support Saudi Arabia?

While Egypt has not detailed what “defensive” military assistance it could provide, judging by the support supplied by other countries aiding Saudi Arabia, this could include operating air defence equipment and interceptors to protect the kingdom from missiles and drones or guarding sensitive sites.

Even this could lead to the deaths of foreign soldiers, as Houthi strikes have so far targeted sites in Saudi Arabia they perceive to be strategically important, including those that Egyptian personnel could be deployed to.

There is also potential for naval assistance in the Red Sea to protect shipping, and forces stationed on the Saudi-Yemeni border to reinforce security there, which have also been targets.

“These troops would only be deployed, if they are deployed at all, to contribute to the protection of Saudi territory,” Dahshan said. “The discussion this time may be taking place because there is a possibility of ground troops being deployed to protect the Saudi border against any attempted Houthi incursion.”

How important is foreign support for Yemen?

Egypt was officially part of the Saudi-led coalition to restore the Yemeni government in 2015, but played only a limited role in operations. However, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have played decisive roles during the war, with other countries such as Sudan at times contributing fighters on the ground.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE not only conducted heavy bombing campaigns against the Houthis, but also had forces in the country coordinating with the Yemeni military and anti-Houthi groups. This exposed both countries to Houthi attacks.

But some Yemenis on the anti-Houthi side blame foreign forces, in particular the UAE, for undermining the independence of the Yemeni government. The UAE was allegedly a major supporter of the Southern Transitional Council, and was eventually forced out of Yemen at the start of the year following a Saudi-backed Yemeni government push to defeat southern secessionists.



While Saudi air support has been a huge advantage for Yemeni government forces over the Houthis, many observers say that the pro-government side does not need additional manpower on the ground.

“The Yemeni government just needs political support and economic support, and that has been the case since the war started,” said Mohammed al-Qadhi, an independent Yemeni political and conflict analyst. “The Yemeni government has enough fighters … it lacks weapons and economic support, as well as logistical and technical support. It needs better coordination and command and control for the forces on the ground.”

As for the prospect of any Egyptian involvement, al-Qadhi said many Yemenis remain indebted to Egypt for the support it has provided the republic in the past.

“Yemenis still cherish the Egyptian role with pride and respect … Without the Egyptian role and Nasser’s support, the republic would not have existed,” al-Qadhi said. “The Houthis recall history and how the Egyptian support in defending the republic was vital … though I dismiss a similar role for the Egyptian army today.”

World.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
World.content:
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France, which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.

After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.

But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.

The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.

World.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
World.content:
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.

World.title: Voters in Brazil to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
World.content:
Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.

Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts.

He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s.

"The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video.

"There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years."

He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health.

In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours.

"Brazil needs change, and FlÃ¡vio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.

Another said that what she most liked about FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

World.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
World.content:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.

Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".

Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.

The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.

"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."

He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."

Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90km/h and do not work on Russian territory.

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.

World.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
World.content:
Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say.

There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.

The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.

Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.

Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.

The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its north-east that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.

Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.

The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday.

"We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.

He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.

Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece.

"They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."

World.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
World.content:
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.

Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.

There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.

Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.

The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.

Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.

He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.

World.title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
World.content:
Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.

Trump, 48, who has five children with US President Donald Trump's eldest son, said that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free", in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account.

Vanessa and Kai Trump then released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention.

Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.

"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.

"I sat down with my mum and Dr Nicole Saphier to talk about my mum's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection."

Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from US singer and media personality Mary Millben.

Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour.

"It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results.

"You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you."

Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.

She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said.

The average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, it says.

Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some cancer cells remain, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.

Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

World.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections.

"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America".

The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.

Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members while speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough'," the former president said in Cleveland.

Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.

"If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".

World.title: Why African economists aren’t winning Nobel Prizes, By ‘Tope Fasua
World.content:
There are many observations around the subject of economics that African economists are better suited to understand. We could write about informality, for instance, for we have the world’s largest informal economies, products of past dislocations and distrust of imported systems of government. We could write and research around the impact of history on economies, or the paucity of data to make economic decisions. What about the calculation of domestic investment in informal economies, where capital formation at the informal level is more rapid and exceedingly more robust but largely ignored?

I had it in mind to question why there have been no Nobel Prize winners in Economics from Africa, ever. Is it because most of the economies in Africa are underdeveloped, going by the standards set by top global economies and so the Nobel committee thinks we have nothing to offer? Is it because the economies of Africa are mostly not industrialised? Or are they considered not to be complex enough? Just what does it take for economists in Africa to get noticed, and for some of their work to be taken seriously? Perhaps African economists themselves are not doing enough intellectual work, which they can put out there in top journals. Another problem could be around the fact that those same journals are involved in hard gatekeeping, which can sometimes be termed as discriminatory. African economists themselves must be daring, and articulate. They must be proud of their work too and depend less on foreign funding. A lot can even be done with little local funding in the field of Economics. I believe that what matters for global recognition, whether at the level of the Nobel Prize or other genuine platforms, is the profundity of the work that economists do.

Or maybe Africa and the global South may create their own equivalents of the Nobel Prize that recognises their work and encourages economists – we could even include other sciences – along the lines of impact and excellence. I believe we have enough private sector entities that can take this opportunity and etch their names in the annals of history just like Alfred Nobel and – for the purpose of Economics – the Sverige Riksbank (Swedish Central Bank) have done. We have successful banks, mining and oil companies in Africa – even Nigeria – that can occupy this space if, as it now seems, African scientists, and economists are not considered worthy of the Swedish Prize. But that could be termed reactionary. Let us stick to the 131 years old Nobel Prize for science, and the 58 years old Swedish Central Bank prize for economics, for now. I hope we know the importance of Economics in Africa? It affects everything. Like Lord Maynard Keynes once wrote, no field of human endeavour is beyond the contemplation and influence of an economist. So, creating awards that recognise the profundity of thought and research that inches the continent forward, or that makes a case for recognition at extant platforms, is no waste of time at all.

These thoughts came rushing back to me recently at the Bank of Industry annual economic lecture when Professor Asad Alam presented Robert Solow’s Total Factor Productivity function, which explains the part of an economy’s output that is not explained by labour and capital. I was quick to point out the fact that Nigerian scholars should be interrogating Solow’s formula to see how we can decompress the residual that is known as Total Factor Productivity – which is a larger residual for countries like Nigeria, where so many interactions and activities that lead to growth go uncaptured because of our large informal economy, and cultural differences that Solow and other Economic greats may not have contemplated. Now, this takes us back to the four factors of production that we were taught in secondary school – land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship – and which is still being taught the same way today, up to university level. In fact, some PhDs in Economics will swear by that formula till today. In previous articles, I had challenged this theory developed in the times of Adam Smith and proposed that there are other productivity functions in today’s world, which can stand on their own, and which are often more powerful than the usual land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship. These include factors such as technology, information, data, knowledge, and even now, AI. Some of these could stand alone, in terms of their impact. So, the understanding of factors of production in economics must change.

The above example is just one instance in which we can successfully challenge some economic theories using African peculiarities and experiences. There are many other instances where the kind of complexity that adds to the body of knowledge will come from Africa, and among the deluge of economists that saturate Africa, I believe there are many notable, hardworking, and smart ones who have dedicated their researches to such good causes. We have an overhang of economic shock (the sudden shift from our traditional systems to the modern system via colonisation), we have the phenomenon of slavery that emptied our population into the Caribbeans, the Americas and elsewhere (who knows what we could have been without that happening), we have our abundant resources, which has often been blamed for our legendary complacency, we have our cultures, we have espionage, the Cold War, etc, as well as geopolitics (the China-Western play), to analyse as variables when we discuss our economies and project into the future. Some of these factors are difficult to quantify and this is what makes them more fascinating and tough to explain. And if we don’t write about what makes our economies peculiar and our honest challenges at advancing our economies, certainly nobody will.

We could even research about how relatively low levels of literacy and underdeveloped political systems affect economics or conduct new research around resource dependency. The point is that we must never assume that all the research work relevant to our situation and to the study of economics have already been done, or that only non-Africans are better suited to think and postulate about peculiar issues. That will be the worst defeat that we would have conferred upon ourselves. African economists must be bold, must be articulate, and daring.

We had an example in the health sector of what I am talking about. The biggest tragedy of the COVID-19 era was how African scientists and African opinions were totally rejected, minimised, silenced, ignored, denigrated, pooh-poohed. The other day I ran into videos of African leaders fearfully agonising about how we were going to find vaccines to prevent whole populations from dying. In the beginning of the pandemic, what we had were Western scientists and leaders projecting that poverty-laden Africa was going to be the worst hit continent, after all, in their heads, we were already disease-ridden. The few who thought differently, who tried to think through the pathology of the flu or postulated about local remedies or lifestyle advantages that Africans had, were labelled as conspiracy theorists, crazies, and frauds. But by the time the world was tired and needed to move on, Africa had the lowest numbers of casualties in all the continents. A country like Nigeria had less than 5,000 deaths, even though I saw with my own eyes on TV when Mrs Bill Gates said we would have so many deaths, such that we will have to leave corpses on the streets! Did the world learn from that episode or did we treat it like it was nothing? Were there things we did in Africa that made us less-susceptible to dying from COVID-19? Are there African remedies that could benefit the world? Or is there subtle racism or classism involved in these matters?

Another recent example came from geography but was also profoundly linked to economics. Flemish geographer Geraldus Mercator developed a map of the world in 1569, which was convenient and suitable for navigational purposes. But it minimised the size of the African continent especially. I recall a young white American guy speaking about that matter on social media about three years ago. I shared his video on my social media timelines. But he was ignored and made to look like a fraud. Until Togo took the matter up, pursued it through the United Nations, and got the World Map rightsized. Still a lot of African analysts said it doesn’t matter. That victory itself was another opportunity for self-deprecation, self-minimisation, and the heaping of blame on ourselves in what has now become ‘learned helplessness’.

Some asked if that was going to help us manage our resources better. Others answered that it was not, since we were destined to be this way. In their minds, everything could be explained away with corruption and our relative backwardness. They ignored the principle behind it. They justified the miseducation that has defined our thinking and destinies so far. They would rather work with wrong information in all spheres, in all disciplines, rather than take the effort to research the truth about ourselves and the world, or support and affirm those who do. The simple questions are: Would Africa have been taken more seriously if the true size was known since 1569? Would we have fought colonialism more stridently if we knew the true size of the land annexed? Could we have a bigger say in world fora like the United Nations? Could our own understanding of our own potentials be more enhanced? And why teach the untruth to our children for so long? It is this same type of tragedy that has us relying on economic theories propounded by Adam Smith, with Scottish data and realities in 1776, or David Ricardo’s Comparative Advantage theory of 1820, till today. We must think for ourselves!

There are many observations around the subject of economics that African economists are better suited to understand. We could write about informality, for instance, for we have the world’s largest informal economies, products of past dislocations and distrust of imported systems of government. We could write and research around the impact of history on economies, or the paucity of data to make economic decisions. What about the calculation of domestic investment in informal economies, where capital formation at the informal level is more rapid and exceedingly more robust but largely ignored? We could even research about how relatively low levels of literacy and underdeveloped political systems affect economics or conduct new research around resource dependency. The point is that we must never assume that all the research work relevant to our situation and to the study of economics have already been done, or that only non-Africans are better suited to think and postulate about peculiar issues. That will be the worst defeat that we would have conferred upon ourselves. African economists must be bold, must be articulate, and daring. The earlier we start along these lines, the earlier we will get the required recognition, but more importantly, our economies and people will be most positively impacted.

For the year 2026, Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford won the Sverige Riksbank Prize for research that generated a paradigm shift in ‘stabilisation’ policy. New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world. The achievements of Nigeria’s Central Bank under Olayemi Cardoso should be documented along these lines and it was a practical deployment in real time, not of Hall and Woodford’s ideas but our own organic thinking, which repositioned our economy.

Let us now look at those topics which have earned people around the world the best prizes in economics, with a view not to denigrating any, but to draw inspiration that we too can do this. I will select just a few:

For the year 2026, Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford won the Sverige Riksbank Prize for research that generated a paradigm shift in ‘stabilisation’ policy. New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world. The achievements of Nigeria’s Central Bank under Olayemi Cardoso should be documented along these lines and it was a practical deployment in real time, not of Hall and Woodford’s ideas but our own organic thinking, which repositioned our economy. In 2025, Joel Mokyr, Phillipe Aghton and Peter Howitt got the Nobel in Economics for demonstrating how innovation and new technology drive sustained economic growth and counteract historical stagnation. This should be an African story, really. And should not be so difficult for a bunch of African economists to put together. I believe it piggybacks on Joseph Schumpeter’s ideas of Creative Destruction and Innovative Entrepreneurship, which were the bedrock of my PhD dissertation.

In 2024, Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson got the Nobel in Economics for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity. Their chunky book, Why Nations Fail, is a testimony to their world. I personally find the book onerous and cumbersome, and many economists around the world have now criticised their logic. In 2023, Claudia Goldin received the Nobel for ‘advancing our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes.’ I believe we have female economists in Africa that could have a lot to say about female contributions to the GDP, to entrepreneurship, to the family unit and general development of nations, even from a historical angle. I conclude that the world now suffers from a deficit of African opinions.

Other awardees include Ben Bernanke, Philip Dybvig and Douglas Diamond in 2022 for research into banks and financial crises; David Card, Joshua D Angrist, and Guido W Imbens in 2021 for contributions to labour economics and the analysis of causal relationships; Paul R Milgrom and Robert B Wilson in 2020 for improvements to auction theory and new auction formats; Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, and Michael Kremer in 2019 for research into experimental approach to alleviating global poverty; Richard H Thaler in 2018 for contributions to behavioural economics, and so on. I don’t think any of these topics upon which the prizes were given were esoteric. I think they all tell human stories around the discipline, and by now, Africa has more human stories to tell. African economists, rise up, speak up, and boldly showcase your work. Our time is now!

‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

World.title: NPFL Preview: Rivers United face Bendel test as Ikorodu City, Shooting Stars clash in Lagos
World.content:
The 2026/2027 Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) season enters another crucial phase, with Matchday 10 serving up a stern test for unbeaten leaders Rivers United. A fiercely contested Southwest derby between the Oga boys, Ikorodu City, and Ibadan landlords, Shooting Stars, plus several key battles that could reshape the standings, are also on the cards.

Port Harcourt-based Rivers United will test their impressive defensive record against Bendel Insurance in Benin City, while former champions Enyimba face a tough trip to Nasarawa United. In Umuahia, Abia Warriors welcome Niger Tornadoes, with both sides seeking valuable points as the campaign gathers momentum.

The matchday has already produced its first result, with Katsina United and Plateau United sharing the points in a 2-2 draw in an all-northern encounter. The result leaves both sides with reasons to reflect on a contest that offered goals but denied either team maximum points.

With several clubs separated by only a handful of points, Sunday’s fixtures could prove significant in the race for the top positions and the struggle to establish consistency.

Rivers United face their biggest test yet

Rivers United head into Matchday 10 at the top of the NPFL table, level on 17 points with Enugu Rangers, who have two games in hand and have played one game fewer. The Port Harcourt club, however, remain unbeaten after nine matches, with four wins, five draws, and only two goals conceded.

That defensive record has made Rivers one of the most difficult teams to beat this season, but their tendency to share the points means Finidi George’s side cannot afford to become complacent.

Their latest outing ended in a goalless draw against Barau FC, extending their unbeaten run but also representing another opportunity to collect maximum points that slipped away.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Standing in their way this time are Bendel Insurance, who will welcome the league leaders to the Samuel Ogbemudia Stadium with ambitions of delivering a statement victory on home soil.

The Benin Arsenal have been inconsistent, alternating between wins and defeats, but their attacking threat makes them a dangerous opponent. With 14 goals scored in their opening eight matches, Bendel possess the firepower to test even the league’s most disciplined defence.

For Rivers, the challenge will be to maintain their defensive organisation while turning possession and chances into goals. Another draw would preserve their unbeaten record, but a win could strengthen their grip on top spot and warn their title rivals.

Bendel, meanwhile, have the opportunity to end Rivers’ unbeaten run, climb the log as a result, and announce themselves as serious contenders for a place among the leading teams.

Ikorodu City, Shooting Stars renew Southwest Rivalry

The Southwest derby between Ikorodu City and Shooting Stars at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena in Lagos promises another intriguing encounter, with local bragging rights and crucial league points at stake.

Both teams will be eager to build momentum, although their recent fortunes have differed.

Ikorodu City have struggled for consistency, falling 2-1 to Niger Tornadoes in their last league outing. They will be determined to respond in front of their supporters and avoid allowing another result to derail their campaign.

Shooting Stars, on the other hand, head into the contest after ending their winless run with a 3-1 victory over Ranchers Bees in Ibadan. The Oluyole Warriors had gone five matches without a win before that result, and the victory should provide a timely boost ahead of their trip to Lagos.

The Oluyole Warriors will hope the win marks a turning point in their season, but an away trip to Ikorodu City presents a different challenge.

For Ikorodu City, the derby offers a chance to restore confidence and climb the standings. For Shooting Stars, it is a chance to build on their recent recovery and prove their victory over Ranchers Bees was more than a reprieve.

Nasarawa United, Enyimba battle for crucial points in Lafia

Enyimba will travel to Lafia to face Nasarawa United in a fixture with important implications for both clubs’ ambitions this season.

The People’s Elephant have endured an inconsistent campaign at best, and will be keen to collect points on the road as they attempt to establish themselves among the leading sides.

Their last league outing ended in a goalless draw against Warri Wolves, leaving them with work to do up front. Enyimba will need a sharper edge in front of goal if they want to leave Lafia with maximum points.

Nasarawa United, meanwhile, will look to make the most of home advantage. Their 2-0 victory over Inter Lagos in their previous match provided a positive result, and they will be eager to maintain that momentum against one of Nigerian football’s most decorated clubs.

The hosts have an opportunity to strengthen their position with another victory, but Enyimba’s experience makes them a difficult opponent to underestimate.

For both teams, the encounter represents more than a routine league fixture. It is an opportunity to build consistency and avoid losing further ground as the table begins to take shape.

Abia Warriors host Niger Tornadoes in Umuahia

Abia Warriors will welcome Niger Tornadoes in another fixture that could shape both clubs’ campaigns.

The Umuahia side will look to capitalise on home advantage and take all three points, while Niger Tornadoes arrive with confidence after defeating Ikorodu City 2-1 in their last league outing.

That victory gave the Ikon Allah boys a much-needed boost, and they will hope to carry the momentum into another challenging away fixture.

Abia Warriors, however, will be determined to make life difficult for their visitors. Home performances could prove crucial to their ambitions this season, especially as the competition for points intensifies.

Niger Tornadoes have already shown they can hurt opponents, but maintaining that attacking threat away from home will be essential if they want to leave Umuahia with a positive result.

Warri Wolves, Kano Pillars Seek Consistency

Warri Wolves will host Kano Pillars in the “Sai Masu Gida”, a contest between two sides looking to strengthen their positions and build momentum.

The Sai Masu Gida will be hoping to return to winning ways after their recent results, while Warri Wolves will look to make their home advantage count.

The fixture offers both teams a chance to secure valuable points, but the side that manages the key moments better could come away with the advantage.

Kano Pillars possess the experience to make the contest uncomfortable for their hosts, but Warri Wolves will be determined to avoid surrendering points on home soil.

Barau FC welcome Kwara United

Barau FC will take on Kwara United in another important encounter, with both sides looking to improve their standings.

Barau have shown they can compete with the league’s leading teams, as shown by their goalless draw with Rivers United. They will now look to turn that defensive resilience into a winning performance against Kwara United.

The visitors, meanwhile, will be eager to bounce back after Abia Warriors held them to a 1-1 draw in Ilorin. Dropping points at home would have been frustrating, and they will hope to respond with a stronger away performance.

The contest could come down to which team makes better use of its opportunities, particularly if both sides approach the game cautiously.

Kun Khalifat, Inter Lagos search for a breakthrough

Kun Khalifat FC will welcome Inter Lagos in a fixture that offers both clubs an opportunity to improve their fortunes.

Kun Khalifat have shown flashes of competitiveness this season, but they will need greater consistency to move away from the lower reaches of the standings.

Inter Lagos, meanwhile, travel in search of a response after losing 2-0 to Nasarawa United in their previous outing.

Both teams will recognise the fixture’s importance, with a positive result potentially providing the momentum needed to improve their positions in the coming weeks.

Home advantage could be significant for Kun Khalifat, but Inter Lagos will be determined to make amends for their recent setback.

Postponements alter Matchday 10 Schedule

The Matchday 10 programme has also been affected by rearrangements.

Ranchers Bees’ scheduled meeting with Doma United has been postponed. Meanwhile, the encounter between Sporting Lagos and Enugu Rangers has also been moved to a later date due to Rangers’ continental commitments. New dates are to be confirmed.

The absence of those fixtures means the two clubs involved will have to wait to add to their points tallies, while the remaining teams can take advantage of the situation.

Rangers, who remain among the early pacesetters despite having played fewer matches than some rivals, will monitor the results closely as the top-of-the-table race intensifies.

Matchday 10 Fixtures

Saturday’s result

Katsina United 2-2 Plateau United

Sunday’s fixtures

Bendel Insurance vs Rivers United

Warri Wolves vs Kano Pillars

Abia Warriors vs Niger Tornadoes

Ikorodu City vs Shooting Stars

Nasarawa United vs Enyimba

Barau FC vs Kwara United

Kun Khalifat FC vs Inter Lagos

Postponed

Ranchers Bees vs Doma United

Sporting Lagos vs Enugu Rangers

The race for NPFL supremacy intensifies

Matchday 10 arrives as early standings begin to reveal which teams can sustain a challenge and which still have significant work to do.

Rivers United have established themselves as a difficult side to beat, but their trip to Bendel Insurance will provide a stern examination of their unbeaten run. The People’s Elephant, Enyimba, face a demanding assignment in Lafia. Meanwhile, the Southwest derby between Ikorodu City and Shooting Stars offers both teams a chance to claim local bragging rights and valuable points.

With Katsina United and Plateau United already sharing the spoils, attention now turns to Sunday’s fixtures, where the leading sides will look to strengthen their positions, and those lower down the table will be desperate to avoid falling further behind.

As the 2026/2027 NPFL season gathers momentum, every point matters, and Matchday 10 could provide another important twist in an increasingly competitive title race.

World.title: Hunters kill 14 bandits in Bakori attack, two residents die
World.content:
The Katsina State Government says community hunters killed 14 suspected bandits during an attack on travellers in Bakori Local Government Area on Friday.

Two people, including a hunter and a traveller who was reportedly burnt to death inside his vehicle, died during the incident. Another hunter sustained gunshot injuries.

The Commissioner for Internal Security and Home Affairs, Nasir Mu’azu, disclosed this in a statement issued on Friday, 23 October.

According to the commissioner, security authorities received intelligence at about 1:28 a.m. that 26 armed men on 13 motorcycles were moving toward Dawan Laila forest in Bakori.

He identified the suspected leader as Isiya Kwashen Garwa. He said security personnel in the local government area were placed on alert over intelligence suggesting a planned mass abduction in neighbouring communities.

Mr Mu’azu said the authorities subsequently received reports at about 1:31 p.m. that the armed men had attacked travellers from Kakumi Ward who were heading to Illela market in Sokoto State.

The attackers reportedly set ablaze a private vehicle belonging to Jamilu Lawal, 50, who was travelling with three other people.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The commissioner said hunters from Gidan Wawo village, Kakumi Ward, mobilised to confront the attackers, resulting in a gun battle.

He said 14 suspected bandits were killed during the confrontation, while three of the travellers were rescued.

However, Mr Lawal was burnt inside the vehicle, according to the statement.

A 29-year-old hunter, Mohammed Jidda, was also killed, while another hunter, Usman Sunday, 25, sustained minor gunshot injuries and was receiving treatment.

The government did not explain how the traveller became trapped in the burning vehicle or whether the reported deaths of the suspected bandits had been independently confirmed by security agencies.

The casualty figures could not be independently verified by PREMIUM TIMES.

Government warns of possible reprisal attack

Mr Mu’azu said intelligence reports indicated that the armed group might launch a reprisal attack following the confrontation.

He said the state government was working with security agencies to prevent further attacks in the area.

The commissioner did not disclose the specific security measures introduced, but assured residents that the authorities were responding to the reported threat.

He commended the community hunters for confronting the attackers and urged residents to provide security agencies with credible information.

The government also appealed to residents to remain calm.

World.title: Kano ACF chair resigns, three-member interim leadership team appointed
World.content:
The Arewa Consultative Forum (ACF), Kano State Chapter, has appointed a three-member interim leadership team to steer its affairs alongside the remaining executive committee members after its chairman, Goni Umar, resigned.

The ACF’s spokesperson in Kano, Nasiru Ibrahim, said in a statement to PREMIUM TIMES that the interim team comprises Isyaku Tofa, Bala Sani and Rabia Adamu.

The appointments were announced by Haliru Akilu during a joint meeting of members of the ACF Board of Trustees representing Kano State and the chapter’s executive committee, held on Saturday at the Late Amina Habib ACF Secretariat in Kano.

Mr Akilu, a retired army general, said the three members would manage the chapter’s affairs for the remainder of the current executive committee’s tenure, pending the election of a new chairman.

He explained that the decision was intended to restore understanding, promote reconciliation and strengthen cooperation among members following disagreements that had affected the chapter.

He urged members to set aside their differences and work collectively in the forum’s interest, stressing that the meeting aimed to resolve outstanding issues rather than revive past controversies.

“The spirit that should guide every one of us is the same: consultation before decision, integrity before convenience and service before self,” Mr Akilu said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He called on members to embrace patience, humility and constructive dialogue, adding that every contribution should help the chapter find lasting solutions to its challenges.

Mr Akilu also acknowledged receipt of Mr Umar’s resignation letter, in which the outgoing chairman cited the demands of his busy schedule.

He expressed appreciation for Mr Umar’s service to the chapter, commending his time, energy and commitment to the forum. He also wished him well in his other responsibilities and hoped he would continue to offer advice and support.

Mr Akilu further commended Assistant Controller-General of Narcotics Abubakar Ahmed for serving as acting chairman for approximately four months during the outgoing chairman’s absence.

He praised Mr Ahmed’s dedication and contributions to the chapter, noting that his service had helped sustain its activities during the period.

In their separate remarks, the three newly appointed interim leaders expressed appreciation for the confidence reposed in them and pledged to justify the trust through dedicated service.

Mr Akilu said a united and purposeful ACF Kano Chapter would be better positioned to contribute to the development of Kano State and northern Nigeria, particularly in addressing challenges relating to insecurity, poverty, education, youth empowerment and peaceful coexistence.

World.title: SERAP sues Nigerian govt at ECOWAS Court over ₦78.8bn cash transfer
World.content:
The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has filed a lawsuit against the federal government over “the alleged diversion, irregular expenditure and failure to account for over ₦78.8 billion in public funds involving the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO) and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO).”

The allegations are documented in the Auditor-General of the Federation’s 2024 Annual Report, published on 7 August 2026. According to the Auditor-General, the findings cover various periods between January 2023 and 31 December 2024.

In the suit number ECW/CCJ/APP/42/26 filed last week at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, Abuja, SERAP is seeking: “a declaration that the failure of the Nigerian government to account for over ₦78.8 billion in public funds allocated for federal cash-transfer and social-protection programmes is unlawful and a violation of Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.”

SERAP is seeking a declaration that “the government’s failure to ensure the lawful administration of public funds allocated for cash-transfer programmes intended to benefit vulnerable households undermines the enjoyment of the rights protected under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights.”

SERAP is also seeking “an order of perpetual injunction restraining the government from administering or disbursing cash-transfer and social-protection funds without adequate financial accountability, beneficiary verification, auditing and oversight mechanisms consistent with Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.”

In the suit, SERAP is arguing that “the government has violated, and continues to violate, the rights to social security and an adequate standard of living, including food, clothing and housing, by failing to properly administer social-protection funds and ensure access to benefits intended to meet basic needs.”

SERAP is also arguing that “the failure to account for substantial public funds allocated for social protection, and to investigate and remedy deficiencies, undermines the socio-economic rights of millions of affected Nigerians.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to SERAP, “The funds were intended to benefit over 3.2 million households across 35 states, whose access to financial assistance has been affected by the allegations made by the Auditor-General.”

The suit filed on behalf of SERAP by its lawyers, Kolawole Oluwadare and Kehinde Oyewumi, read in part: “The failure to investigate the ₦78.8 billion cash-transfer scandal, account for the questioned funds and recover any unlawfully spent amounts violates Nigeria’s obligations to protect the human rights of vulnerable households.”

“SERAP brings this public-interest case to protect the interests of affected households and ensure accountability for public funds allocated for their benefit.”

“SERAP submits that failures to account for public funds allocated to socio-economic rights, coupled with a failure to take effective corrective action, engages the State’s human-rights obligations. Cash-transfer programmes help address extreme poverty and enable vulnerable people to meet their basic needs.”

“The suit relies on the Auditor-General’s 2024 Annual Report, published on 7 August 2026, which identified financial irregularities in federal institutions, including the National Cash Transfer Office and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office.”

“The Auditor-General questioned approximately ₦33.751 billion reportedly transferred to over 3.2 million households across 35 states in 2023, as adequate records to verify the payments and reconcile beneficiary records were not provided.”

“The report also identified ₦36.744 billion in payments made without prepayment audits, ₦4.616 billion in unsupported expenditures, and other questioned payments, including ₦350.182 million for enrolment, ₦89.511 million for store purchases and ₦17.422 million in diesel advances.”

“SERAP brings this public-interest case under Article 9(4) of the ECOWAS Court Protocol to protect the interests of affected households and ensure accountability for public funds intended for social protection.”

“The issue is whether the government has discharged its obligations under applicable human-rights treaties to safeguard resources allocated for social protection, investigate documented financial irregularities, provide effective remedies and ensure that those resources are applied for their intended purposes.”

“The Auditor-General is constitutionally responsible for auditing and reporting upon the public accounts of the Federation and the offices and agencies of the Federal Government. His findings are recorded in annual reports submitted to the National Assembly and constitute important official records concerning public expenditure.”

“The obligation to recognise and give effect to the rights protected under the African Charter, guaranteed by Article 1 of the Charter, include the obligation to adopt legislative or other measures necessary to give effect to protected rights.”

“The right to equality and non-discrimination, under Article 2 of the African Charter and the corresponding obligations, would be violated where there are failures in administering or verifying social-protection programmes which result in discriminatory exclusion or unequal access to benefits.”

“The Nigerian government has the obligation to take effective measures to prevent and address corruption and related misuse of public resources. The government has failed to take appropriate measures in response to the allegations made by the Auditor-General.”

“The right to social security cannot be effectively realised merely by establishing a formal cash-transfer programme where the State fails to maintain reasonable systems for identifying beneficiaries, maintaining records, reconciling disbursements, monitoring expenditure, investigating irregularities and remedying losses.”

“Following publication of the Auditor-General’s Report, SERAP issued a public statement and, in a letter dated 5 September 2026, urged President Bola Tinubu and relevant authorities to account for the questioned funds, publish audit records, investigate irregular expenditures, recover any funds unlawfully spent or diverted, and take appropriate action against those responsible.”

“SERAP also requested payment and beneficiary records, verification documents and an explanation for the missing REMITA records.”

“The deadline given to the government to address the Auditor-General’s findings had elapsed without adequate action.”

“The financial irregularities and the government’s failure to address them raise human rights concerns, particularly the rights to social security, an adequate standard of living, and the right to economic, social and cultural development.”

“The government must properly manage public funds allocated for social protection in accordance with its human rights obligations and take reasonable measures to ensure that vulnerable households receive their intended benefits.”

“The Auditor-General’s findings on beneficiary verification, prepayment audits, supporting documents and financial reconciliation raise serious questions about whether these funds were properly managed and reached vulnerable households.”

“Articles 1 and 21 of the African Charter, alongside Article 9 of the UN Convention against Corruption, require effective measures to protect people’s rights and resources, ensure transparent public financial management, investigate irregularities and recover public funds where losses or improper expenditure are established.”

“SERAP relies on Kolawole Olaniyan’s Corruption and Human Rights Law in Africa (Hart Publishing, 2014) and Ownership of Proceeds of Corruption in International Law (Oxford University Press, 2023) as persuasive academic authority on the impact of corruption on human rights, public resources, victims’ rights, accountability and international legal remedies.”

“These works support principles grounded in applicable human rights treaties and jurisprudence.”

“SERAP accordingly submits that the Auditor-General’s findings cannot be treated merely as administrative irregularities where public funds allocated for social protection may have been lost, improperly spent or left unaccounted for, and the government fails to take effective corrective action.”

“The failures in public financial management that impair protected human rights may engage the right to an effective remedy. The government’s failure to adequately investigate, account for and recover misused funds, and provide appropriate remedies, may constitute a continuing failure to meet its human-rights obligations.”

SERAP is therefore asking the ECOWAS Court for the following reliefs:

1. A DECLARATION that the failure to take effective measures to investigate and remedy the financial irregularities identified in the 2024 Annual Report of the Auditor-General of the Federation, insofar as those failures impair or risk impairing access to intended benefits, violates the Respondent’s international human rights obligations.

2. AN ORDER directing the Respondent, through the National Cash Transfer Office (NCTO), the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO) and other relevant agencies, to provide a comprehensive and verifiable account of the questioned funds, including relevant payment, beneficiary, verification and reconciliation records.

3. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to conduct an independent, prompt and effective investigation into the identified irregularities; recover public funds improperly spent, diverted or lost where established; and take appropriate legal or administrative action against persons found responsible, in accordance with due process.

4. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to strengthen financial accountability, beneficiary verification, auditing, reconciliation and oversight mechanisms to prevent the recurrence of irregularities in federal cash-transfer and social-protection programmes.

5. AN ORDER directing the Respondent to take effective measures to ensure that eligible vulnerable persons and households receive the social-protection benefits intended for them and that any established adverse effects on their protected rights are appropriately remedied.

No date has been fixed for the hearing of the suit.

Kolawole Oluwadare

SERAP Deputy Director

25/10/2026

Lagos, Nigeria
