MAINEVILLE, OHIO — A mosque rising amid rural homes and farmland in southwest Ohio has become a focal point in the community’s growing concerns over an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies and trucking fraud, with a Fox News Digital review revealing significant financial ties between the mosque, trucking companies and the government of Uzbekistan.

Roughly one mile north of the main intersection in Maineville, a small Warren County village with about 1,400 residents, sits the Islamic Center of Maineville, which has been under construction for the past four years following its approval by Hamilton Township in April 2022.

Fox News Digital found that the mosque received substantial donations from trucking companies that government records show were cited for serious safety and compliance violations, while the mosque’s own Telegram channel displayed associations with people identified as current or former Uzbek officials.

For years, the Islamic Center of Maineville has posted on Telegram to its 3,600 members, courting donations, acknowledging partnerships with trucking companies, and even sharing screenshots of donations from local trucking companies, owned by Uzbeks, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars.

HOW AN UZBEK TRUCK DRIVER’S FATAL CRASH EXPOSED TROUBLING FRAUD TREND IN MIDDLE AMERICA: ‘CHAMELEON CARRIERS’

Buraq Limited, a Springboro trucking company associated with Rukhshona Sultonova, donated at least $28,000 to the Islamic Center across 28 gifts, according to Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital.

A review of the company’s records found dozens of reported violations, including multiple English-proficiency violations, four ELD (electronic logging device) violations, three invalid-CDL violations, four expired medical cards and four hours-of-service violations.

Premier Trucking Group Inc., owned by Sam Avazov, has received over 100 total violations, including for unsafe driving and invalid CDLs. In September, the Islamic Center posted a screenshot of a $1,000 donation from Premier Trucking Group, which has donated at least $25,000 to the mosque.

OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’

Foko Logistics LLC, owned by Abubakr Olimov and based in Hilliard, donated $20,000 in a single gift to the mosque, and had 52 violations across 37 inspections in FMCSA’s current 24-month record. The company had vehicle-maintenance violations involving damaged brake hoses, an inoperable tractor-protection valve and severely underinflated tires. Ten of its 24 vehicle inspections resulted in an out-of-service designation, a rate of 41.7%.

Maca Transportation and Services LLC, based in Dayton and owned by Muminkhuja Kholkhujaev, donated at least $7,000 across eight gifts. FMCSA’s records show 120 violations across 72 inspections, including an English-proficiency failure and multiple false or incomplete hours-of-service records. The company also had serious brake, tire, and other vehicle-maintenance violations, with 14 of 36 vehicle inspections resulting in an out-of-service designation, or 38.9%.

One trucking company that gave $150,000 to the mosque and helped organize the overall fundraising effort , Phoenix Cargo, told Fox News Digital the mosque approached the company multiple times asking for donations but said the $150,000 figure the company ultimately donated "represents only a fraction of the mosque's total construction budget" and that "Phoenix Cargo is not even among the project's top 100 donors."

Phoenix Cargo has been cited hundreds of times for safety violations, including English proficiency, ELD tampering, and unsafe driving violations.

Fox News Digital reached out to the mosque for comment but did not receive a response. Earlier this month, the Islamic Center said it is "committed to operating responsibly and in accordance with applicable law."

"The fundraising for the Islamic Center concerns me because a large percentage of the Uzbek truck companies that donate have been repeatedly cited for the same kinds of serious inspection violations," Nodawolf, an online researcher who lives in the area and has been documenting alleged trucking fraud in southwest Ohio for months and was granted anonymity due to death threats he's received, said. "Those violations suggest a pattern of non-compliance with our laws and regulations among the donors, which is troubling given the community’s concentration in the freight industry in Maineville."

Fox News Digital also asked the mosque if an administrator for their Telegram channel with the name "Bek A" is Bekhzod Asrarov, an Uzbek truck driver living in Maineville who authorities say struck and killed 21-year-old Ohio soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe earlier this year. Asrarov was unable to communicate effectively in English at the scene, according to authorities, and has been accused of removing and concealing his dashcam after the crash.

ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

The mosque did not provide a response.

The Islamic Center’s website says it does "not solicit donations from any foreign government, organization, association, partnership or individual or any agent thereof" and that "any such attempt" should be reported to the mosque immediately. However, the organization's Telegram account suggests close ties with the government of Uzbekistan, specifically when it comes to trucking companies.

Hamkor Uz Cincinnati Association is a nonprofit organization established in 2020 to unite Uzbeks in the Cincinnati area and support community projects, including the construction of religious and cultural centers. Hamilton Township records identify Hamkor as the owner of the roughly 6.7-acre property where the Islamic Center of Maineville is being built.

Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital show the organization’s ties to former Uzbek government officials. One image shows the Mason office of Erkinbay Abdulla, with an accompanying message describing him as a former Uzbek official who "creates the trucking companies."

Another screenshot contains a community statement attributed to Sukhrob Norbekov, whom an accompanying message identifies as another former Uzbek official who represents the mosque. The material places officials linked to Uzbekistan alongside an organization involved in the mosque project and individuals involved in creating local trucking companies.

Current Uzbek officials also appear to be involved with the mosque and local trucking industry via the central Asian nation’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, according to photos posted on the mosque’s Telegram.

The screenshots show a list of a six-member Uzbek delegation that traveled to the United States in April 2025, including Ambassador Furqat Sidiqov, regional government officials, and three officials from the Ministry of Digital Technologies. Separate posts invite entrepreneurs and truck-company managers to an April 19 IT conference hosted by Hamkor Uz Cincinnati at a banquet hall in Loveland, Ohio.

TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES

Additionally, a review of the Hamkor Uz Telegram channel, with current and former Uzbek government officials as administrators, showed s for local trucking companies, removable truck signs, English courses for truck driving school, and legal counseling. Other posts include the owner of the mosque providing guidance on how to understand "Shariah compliant banking" and a post on "speaking English with the police" and how to "learn on the road."

Nodawolf said the ties to the government of Uzbekistan are troubling to him "because these Uzbek trucking companies appear to be tightly organized, with patterns that look almost like a shared blueprint."

"Given the documented safety and compliance problems in many of these companies, it’s reasonable to ask whether gaps in U.S. regulations are being systematically exploited," he added.

Several locals who spoke to Fox News Digital said they have expressed their concerns about the rise in Uzbek trucking companies and potential safety gaps that could come along with it to their elected officials but have largely been ignored.

"They're scared, I think they recognize that they could be called names, they can recognize they could be called out for, you know, like, Islamophobic or racist or things, but it's not that at all," a resident from nearby Middletown, Ohio, which has also experienced an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies, who posts information about trucking companies online under the name GHOSTOPSUZ, told Fox News Digital.

One lawmaker who has taken action against trucking fraud is Ohio Republican state Rep. Michelle Teska, who represents most of Warren County, including Maineville, and has introduced legislation to strengthen commercial-driver licensing requirements, including a measure requiring driver examinations to be administered in English, which she told Fox News Digital addresses the "low-hanging fruit of the problem."

"I did some research and basically found out that you can get your driver's license and your CDL license in the state of Ohio and you can have that test in 10 different languages," Teska said. "So that, to me, common sense says that's insanity."

Teska says she has seen the problem "firsthand" while driving around her district, calling it "rampant."

"This past weekend, I was at an event in Warren County and I was at an event that is right across the street from the BMV and I was just kind of observing a gentleman pulling in a semi truck cab into the parking lot on a Saturday at the BMV taking up four spaces, clearly had no idea how to drive the truck," Teska explained. "So I walked over to the BMV and spoke to this person and kind of confronted him and said, hey, do you speak English? He replied, no, I don't speak English. Asked him where he was from. He was from Uzbekistan. So it was crazy because I was watching it all take place live."

Authorities in Warren County have been ramping up their presence in the trucking industry and on the roads in recent weeks, including a crackdown over the last week.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The Hamilton Township Police Department actively monitors traffic safety concerns within our jurisdiction and works with our public safety partners to address violations and unsafe driving behaviors when identified," a spokesperson for Hamilton Township said. "In fact, our officers recently participated in a targeted traffic enforcement initiative focused on commercial motor vehicles, working alongside partner agencies to identify safety violations and improve roadway safety. We will continue to enforce applicable laws and take appropriate action when circumstances warrant."

Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell stressed there is nothing inherently wrong with mosque fundraising and he has not received any information that any laws have been broken. He told Fox News Digital, however, that clearly "there’s something going on" within the Uzbek community in southwest Ohio that "warrants at least awareness on the part of law enforcement."

"It's disproportionate to what we see with any other immigrant community," Fornshell said.

Since 2021, Fornshell said the area has seen an "influx of cases involving Uzbeks" that has prompted the need to hire more court interpreters and city employees who speak the language, particularly in the lower courts that deal with traffic offenses.

"I would say hardly a week goes by where we don't have some felony case involving an Uzbek, it's pretty frequent at this point," Fornshell said.

Census data from 2024 shows that roughly 1,500 people born in Uzbekistan live in Greater Cincinnati, while about 3,800 Uzbekistan-born residents live across Ohio. Uzbek community leaders say the actual population is significantly higher, estimating that roughly 4,000 Uzbek families live in southern Ohio, including U.S.-born children.

"This is our motherland now, from now on," Hamkor Uz board member Nodirjon Ernazarov told the Cincinnati Enquirer through a translator last week in a story highlighting the Uzbek population’s efforts to become part of the community. The article explains that the influx of Uzbeks was driven, in part, by the area’s proximity to the trucking industry.

"Uzbek people are very hardworking people," Ernazarov added. "So this mosque is (being built) by the help of all Uzbeks."

The article does not mention that Ernazarov also owns a trucking company, Ray Cargo Corp., which has donated tens of thousands of dollars to the mosque and has been cited for numerous safety violations, including unsafe driving and driver fitness.

Fox News Digital reached out to every trucking company mentioned in the article for comment.

"The president is defiant, and he always is optimistic," Leavitt said this week in a Fox News Digital interview in her home state of New Hampshire.

Republicans also face a challenging campaign climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

KAROLINE LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP NEEDS A 'FIGHTER' AS SHE WEIGHS IN ON HER SUCCESSOR'S QUICK DEPARTURE

He's been everywhere this week from North Carolina to South Carolina. Be in Michigan again this weekend."

Republicans are also facing a low propensity problem in the midterms - MAGA supporters who don't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot.

"The president is getting out there and reminding voters what's at stake in this election and why it's so important to get out and vote in the midterms," Leavitt noted. "He's being frank and honest with his voters that 'I know you don't turn out in midterm cycles, but we need you to this time."

World.title: Iran’s oil lifeline is drying up. The biggest pain may fall on ordinary citizens
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Iran is approaching a financial reckoning as a U.S. naval blockade threatens to wipe out its seaborne crude oil revenues by mid-December — but the economic pain may fall more heavily on ordinary Iranians than on the military Washington is trying to constrain.

Iran’s trackable floating oil inventory outside the U.S. blockade zone has fallen to zero, according to energy intelligence firm Kpler, which projects that Tehran's crude revenues could dry up by the middle of December as outstanding payments are settled.

But the loss of oil revenue would not necessarily translate into an immediate military funding crisis. Tehran could shield military spending while cutting civilian programs, allowing inflation to erode purchasing power and drawing on alternative revenue sources.

BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP

That complicates Washington's pressure campaign: The blockade may deprive Tehran of one of its biggest sources of cash without immediately starving the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the money they need to operate.

Oil directly accounts for roughly 30% of Iran's government budget, according to Gregory Brew, a senior Iran and energy analyst at Eurasia Group, and Miad Maleki, an Iran sanctions and financial expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Iran entered the year expecting to export about 1.7 million barrels per day at roughly $54 per barrel, Brew said. Actual exports have fallen short of that target, though higher oil prices allowed Tehran to build some financial cushion.

Maleki estimated that oil and refined petroleum products account for between 50% and 60% of regime revenue when indirect income is included.

Still, the December deadline is not a date on which Iran suddenly runs out of money.

"The December timeline is more of a cash flow kind of disruption, and not really a collapse state," Maleki told Fox News Digital.

Tehran has so far allowed inflation and the weakening rial to absorb some of the pressure rather than abruptly stopping government salaries or allowing widespread shortages to develop.

"The purchasing power of Iranians incrementally declines," Maleki said.

Losing a revenue stream that covers roughly 30% of the government budget would nevertheless force increasingly difficult choices. Tehran can cut spending, borrow more or run larger deficits. Deeper cuts could hit subsidies, pensions and other government programs, while deficit spending risks fueling already high inflation.

"There's already expectations that government spending next year is going to be greatly reduced," Brew said . "A bigger chunk of the budget is likely going to be met through borrowing and deficit spending, which is of course going to add to inflation."

IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS

Military spending, however, could prove more resistant.

"There is a broad expectation that non-military spending is going to be slashed significantly, while military spending is going to be maintained and might even increase because of the overall war footing that the Iranian regime has been put on," Brew said.

Iran is already spending resources to rebuild missile production facilities and other military infrastructure, expand underground facilities and repair damage to its nuclear program, Brew said.

Iran's armed forces also have a direct connection to the country's oil trade.

US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS

The Treasury Department said last year that Tehran was allocating roughly 200,000 barrels of crude per day to its armed forces, with the value of planned allocations expected to exceed $10 billion annually. Military organizations can sell allocated oil abroad and use the proceeds themselves.

Maleki said those sales have helped finance equipment, chemicals and weapons components and support Iran-backed groups including Hezbollah and Hamas.

The IRGC also draws revenue from smuggling, black-market commerce and sanctions-evasion networks outside the formal state budget. Brew said its economic influence has expanded as sanctions have squeezed Iran's private economy.

"If the IRGC is the single most important institution in the country, and if it largely benefits from sanctions and blockades and various forms of U.S. economic pressure, then there's a world in which it benefits from this new environment rather than being squeezed like the overall government budget," Brew said.

Iran's oil squeeze has been months in the making.

Tehran held roughly 135 million barrels of crude in floating storage before the war began in February, providing a stockpile it could continue selling after U.S. forces restricted new exports. That offshore inventory has now been exhausted.

U.S. Central Command estimates the blockade has already denied Tehran at least $25 billion in oil revenue.

Buyers of Iranian crude typically settle payments one to two months after delivery, creating the lag between the disappearance of Iran's floating inventory and Kpler's projected revenue cutoff in December.

Even if that projection broadly holds, however, Iran is unlikely to stop earning money from hydrocarbons altogether.

Smaller quantities of oil can still move overland by truck and rail and across the Caspian Sea, while refined petroleum and petrochemical products can travel through routes outside the seaborne crude trade targeted by the blockade.

"While the amount of Iranian oil that can be tracked has fallen to zero, it's unlikely Iran's oil exports completely fall to nothing," Brew said. "The amount will likely be fairly small, but it won't be completely zeroed."

Both experts said an agreement with Washington allowing Iranian tankers to resume leaving the Persian Gulf could reverse the trajectory . Without a deal or relaxation of the blockade, the financial pressure is expected to build into next year.

The bigger test may arrive in March, when Iran begins its new fiscal year and must reconcile its spending plans with dramatically lower oil income.

"There's going to be a fiscal squeeze, and there's going to be pressure around the release of the new budget," Brew said. "There's going to be economic unrest, potentially even economic turmoil as the government rolls out spending cuts."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

By then, Tehran could have gone months without its traditional seaborne crude income, forcing the regime to decide how much of the financial squeeze it is willing to pass on to its population while preserving spending elsewhere.

World.title: Democrats ask judge to dismiss Trump administration’s challenge to Alaska Senate race
World.content:
Attorneys for Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and Senate Democrats filed a motion Friday urging a federal judge to drop the Trump administration’s lawsuit that seeks to block the results of the upcoming election if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses.

The motion, filed on behalf of Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, called the lawsuit filed by the Justice Department “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections.”

“This case directly threatens both Proposed Intervenors’ interests by demanding that defendants refuse to certify the election if, and only if, Peltola wins,” the filing said. “It is part of a nationwide attack on free elections by the federal government, which the DSCC has fought at every turn.”

The Trump administration filed suit against election officials in Alaska Thursday, arguing that candidate Dan J. Sullivan Jr.’s appearance on the ballot could mislead those who wish to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election.

The lawsuit came after President Donald Trump repeatedly complained about both the incumbent being threatened by a man with the same name and the state’s use of ranked-choice voting.

“I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM.”

The DOJ’s lawsuit asks the court to block the Alaska Senate results from being certified if Dan S. Sullivan does not win the election, and if “had all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

The filing from Peltola and Senate Democrats pushes back against this request, stating that “the Department of Justice’s assumption that every voter who casts a vote for Dan J. Sullivan really meant to vote for Senator Sullivan is insulting to voters and irreconcilable with Alaska’s ranked choice voting procedures and the ballot’s clear differentiation between the two candidates.”

“Alaskans for Mary and DSCC are entitled to intervene as of right to defend against the Department of Justice’s extraordinary assault,” the motion said. “And there is reason to doubt that the existing defendants will vigorously defend against DOJ’s demands, given their effort to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot earlier this year.”

After Dan J. Sullivan Jr. was removed from the ballot in June after election officials decided his candidacy was “not in good faith,” a judge in Alaska overturned the decision later that month, validating his campaign.

Trump has claimed that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. is only running because “Democrats put him up as a matter of confusion,” calling his candidacy “corrupt.” Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has denied the allegations.

NBC News reported in July that federal and state investigators were looking into whether Dan J. Sullivan Jr. could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters, according to two people who had knowledge of the situation.

The DOJ’s lawsuit comes less than two weeks ahead of Election Day and after the state has begun early voting. The court has not yet set a hearing date for the suit.

Legal and election experts told NBC News that the DOJ’s case is on shaky ground.

As U.S. elections are run and certified by state and local officials, rather than the federal government, the law limits the Justice Department’s role in elections.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the Alaska Senate contest as a “toss-up.” The race marks a critical opportunity for Democrats to take a seat from Republicans as they vie for control of the Senate.

World.title: How Democrats could win the House, how the GOP could hang on, and where to look for a wave
World.content:
Districts to watch: NC-14, KY-6

Another way to estimate the possible size of November’s swing is to look at the partisan shifts in elections held in 2025 and 2026, ever since Trump took office. These races include the 2025 governor’s elections in New Jersey and Virginia, other high-profile statewide elections and several special elections for the U.S. House.

Although Trump lost Virginia and New Jersey, the other recent elections have tended to occur in places that supported Trump in 2024. Averaging across all of these states and districts, Trump won them by an average of about 3.5 percentage points in 2024. In the 2025 and 2026 elections, however, those states and districts supported the Democratic candidate by an average of about 11 points. This amounts to a shift of 14.5 points in the Democrats’ favor.

If the Democrats are able to shift the vote in every district by such a historically massive margin in 2026, they could win as many as 263 seats to the Republicans’ 172. That would be the largest majority that either party has held in the U.S. House since the 1990 midterm elections.

Such a shift could put into play districts like Florida’s 27th District, represented by GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar. Republicans in Florida left this district nearly unchanged when they redrew the state’s congressional map, believing that a district that Trump won by 14.6 points would be out of reach for the Democrats.

But it appears the race in this heavily Hispanic district is tightening, as polls show Latino voters nationwide turning against Trump and Republicans, with economic concerns weighing heavily on their minds. These voters were critical to Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, and indications that they are moving back toward Democrats are helping drive the party’s competitiveness in Republican-leaning, heavily-Hispanic districts in states like Texas, too. Salazar outran Trump’s win margin by nearly 6 percentage points in 2024, and her survival in the 2026 election may require a similarly strong overperformance.

A 14.5-point national swing toward Democrats could also make North Carolina’s 14th District competitive. Republican Rep. Tim Moore’s district is one that North Carolina Republicans did not bother changing when redrawing their maps last year. Trump won the district by 15.1 points, and Moore himself won it in 2024 by 16.1 points.

Another district to watch is Kentucky’s 6th District. This open Lexington-based seat has been held by Republican Andy Barr since 2013, and was carried by Trump in 2024 by 15.0 points. Barr is running for the U.S. Senate this year. Republican and Democratic-aligned groups are spending heavily here, reflecting the importance of the race, as Republican Ralph Alvarado faces off against Democrat Zach Dembo.

The NBC News Decision Desk rates this race as lean Republican. In 2024, this district reported almost 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. ET. If Democrats are on track for a massive national shift, this district may provide one of the best pieces of early evidence.

National trends don’t mean every district shifts the same amount

To be sure, all of these scenarios assume that the partisan shift in 2026 will be the same in every district. This may be true on average, but some districts will have a larger shift than the national average and others will have a smaller one.

Demographics of a specific district may play a role in the size of the shift. For example, if Hispanic voters shift more dramatically toward the Democratic Party than non-Hispanic voters, then districts with higher concentrations of Hispanic voters will vote more favorably for the Democrats than the underlying partisanship of the district would predict.

Incumbency can also play a large role in causing a district to shift more or less than the national average. In 2024, the incumbent members of Congress outperformed their party’s presidential candidate by an average of 2.5 percentage points.

This year, there are slightly more Democratic incumbents seeking re-election than Republican ones. This means that the Democratic Party as a whole stands to gain more from the benefits of incumbency compared with the Republican Party.

On the other hand, there are more Republican incumbents who represent districts with an evenly divided underlying partisanship. For example, an “incumbency bump” matters a lot more to a Republican in a district Trump won by 5 points than to a Democrat in a district Harris won by 25 points.

Finally, redistricting has also played a key role in this year’s midterms. By redrawing districts in several states, Republicans stand to win as many as 10 more seats than if the map remained unchanged after 2024.

Redistricting impacts the role of incumbency, too. When the lines for a district are redrawn, incumbents are now fighting for the votes of people whom they’ve never represented, and who may be less familiar with their record. This tends to diminish the size of the incumbency advantage. Republican incumbents in Texas and other red states and Democratic incumbents in California must lean heavily on the “D” or “R” next to their name when they try to win the support of their new potential constituents.

World.title: 12 injured, including several minors, in shooting near Florida A&M University stadium
World.content:
Twelve people, including several minors, were injured in a shooting near Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium, where homecoming celebrations included a football game Saturday.

The Tallahassee Police Department said in a statement that 11 of the 12 were shot and that three victims had serious injuries, with one minor in serious condition. The others, it said, were in stable condition.

Six of the injured are under 18 years old and the youngest is 11 years old, Chief Lawrence Revell of the Tallahassee Police Department said at a press conference early Sunday morning.

“Our preliminary information shows that an altercation occurred between individuals,” he added, describing it as “an isolated incident between two or three individuals.”

Revell said that no arrests had yet been made, nor anyone taken into custody, but that police believed one shooter was involved.

“Our priority is to determine what happened and why it happened, and to bring the people that are responsible for this to justice,” he added, asking any witnesses to come forward.

The violence unfolded about 8 p.m. at an intersection adjacent to Bragg Memorial Stadium, it said. Early in the evening, Florida A&M’s Rattlers hosted the Arkansas-Pine Bluff Golden Lions for the historically Black university’s annual homecoming game.

After the shooting took place, the university issued a statement on X asking members of its campus community to stay away from the area.

It described the shooting as having taken place “near campus,” which it said was safe.

“Our hearts are with the victims and everyone affected by tonight’s incident on Perry Street,” the university said.

Florida State University, about a mile away from Florida A&M, issued an emergency alert about the violence and said it didn’t appear anyone from its school community was involved.

“As a precaution, students, faculty and staff in the Tallahassee area are advised to remain indoors this evening and stay alert,” it said.

Revell offered condolences to the victims and their families, and also praised officers who he said ran without hesitation “into the middle of this, still not knowing where the shooters were, still not knowing how many victims we had.”

“We had officers that were picking up victims and carrying them in their arms to transport victims because they couldn’t get through the mass of people,” he said.

The investigation into the violence was ongoing, and police asked witnesses to come forward.

World.title: At least 12 injured, including 6 children, in Tallahassee shooting
World.content:
At least 12 people were injured, including six children, in a shooting Saturday near a football stadium in Tallahassee on homecoming weekend for Florida A&M University, authorities said.

Tallahassee police said in a statement at least three of the shooting victims have sustained serious injuries, while nine others are reported to be in stable condition.

The preliminary investigation indicates that a fight broke out prior to the shooting, according to police. It followed a football game in a crowded area.

Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell told reporters that no arrests had been made.

"Tonight, our thoughts are with the victims and their families as they face the devastating impact of this violence," said Revell. "It is especially heartbreaking to know that children are among those injured."

The university said on social media that the shooting happened near its campus and that it remained safe.

World.title: Kim Jon-un visits China to open new bridge, reaffirm ties
World.content:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and vowing to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor.

Kim's visit to China, the first in a year, is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a "new Cold War."

Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry and China's official Xinhua News Agency.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, alongside Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, during a see-off ceremony at the new Yalu River Bridge, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (Rao Aimin/Xinhua via AP) Rao Aimin

In Dandong, Kim visited a memorial marking China's support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War and met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China's Communist Party.

At the memorial, Kim said that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) will "firmly carry forward the invincible DPRK-China friendship forged at the cost of blood all the time," according to the North's official Korean Central News Agency.

During their meeting, Kim reaffirmed a resolve to develop bilateral cooperation, while Wang conveyed Chinese President Xi Jinping's greetings and said Kim's visit to the memorial was "of great significance" in carrying forward the friendship between the two countries, KCNA said.

Kim Jong Un, left, visits Dandong, China Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government.

The two toured a car factory as well, before Wang accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to KCNA and Xinhua.

While returning home via the bridge, Kim said "the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries," KCNA reported.

Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. China, for its part, has sought to restore its unique influence over North Korea.

North Korea has sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.

Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.

World.title: Man's murder, wife's death feed into local legend of "cursed" mansion
World.content:
The lake country straddling the Kentucky-Tennessee border has a quiet, majestic beauty. But in September 2022, that vast landscape seemed to have swallowed up Mike Harding, a California transplant who disappeared without a trace.

JULIE HARDING (phone call): Hi Captain, this is Julie Harding with the California Highway Patrol …

Mike's wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol, began to place urgent phone calls to the Kentucky State Police from her home in Sacramento.

JULIE HARDING (phone call): I can't get any information. And I just, I need your help with this … My concern right now … is where he is. Is he OK? … and what's the status of this investigation?

The calls led her to a sheriff she knew — Brandon Boone of Clay County, Tennessee, whose office was spearheading the missing person's case. But the answers were few and far between and Boone says Julie Harding grew frustrated.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: She got very angry with a couple of — of my people, uh, because we wouldn't disclose certain information to her …

Within days, Julie was there in person on Sheriff Boone's doorstep.

JULIE HARDING (bodycam): Hi.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE: How are ya?

JULIE HARDING: I'm good, how are you? Well …

Bodycam video of Julie Harding with Clay County, Tennessee, Sheriff Brandon Boone. Clay County Sheriff's Office

In a moment recorded on a body camera, she immediately apologized for being rude.

JULIE HARDING (bodycam): Let me first apologize. My tone was inappropriate I was very irritated, umm, and I should have been more calm. My assumptions, umm, and my emotions in this, umm, killed my reasonableness so I apologize for how we spoke the other day.

OFFICER: Yes ma'am.

JULIE HARDING: OK. So, from now on, I, I hope it's calm. I hope it's cooperative. Umm, because all I want is Mike to come back in and go … I was in wherever fishing.

Boone sent her to a sheriff in Kentucky who had taken over the investigation.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE (bodycam): Cumberland County Sheriff's Office has called us. They need you there.

JULIE HARDING: OK.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE: That's all I can tell you.

JULIE HARDING: OK.

A grisly discovery

Just hours earlier, David Hammersley and his family were house hunting in nearby Burkesville, Kentucky. They went room to room at a vacant, three-building property — unaware of what lay ahead.

David Hammersley: … the rest of the party had gone to this building here …

Hammersley wandered into the garage and was surprised that there was a large pickup truck parked inside.

Peter Van Sant: The rest of the family has moved on to this cottage. What do you hear from the garage?

David Hammersley: Well, as they're attempting to open the door, I hear this awful screech and, "Oh, it's — it's terrible. There's something dead over here!"

Hammersley says his family figured some sort of animal must have wandered in and never got out. David walked over and stopped just inside the cottage's front door.

David Hammersley: It was over 100 degrees at the time, I believe … and I was just attacked, if you will, by flies. … And the odor was just so overpowering.

The Kentucky property that became a crime scene. CBS News

What he then saw was far worse.

David Hammersley: I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched … obviously, dead from gunshot wounds … (sighs) Ah, sorry. … his life is gone under violent circumstances and just left there. It — it — it was devastating.

The dead body was Mike Harding, says prosecutor Ann Marie Gordon Anderson.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: It seemed like he had probably been there for a week, from September 19th [to] the 26th.

The Cumberland County Sheriff immediately called in the Kentucky State Police. Detective BJ Burton was assigned to lead the investigation. He learned that Mike Harding had been shot four times, twice in the torso and twice in the head.

Detective BJ Burton: It kind of looks like somebody that wants to be a professional hit man — but is not quite there.

Burton said the killer removed evidence from the scene, including the murder weapon and three shell casings. But the assassin left behind one distinctive shell casing; investigators determined it was from a Hornady Critical Defense bullet.

Back in Sacramento, Mike's son Steven Harding, from Mike's first marriage, was told his father had been murdered.

Peter Van Sant: And can you put into words the horror of this news for you?

Steven Harding: There's really no words for it other than your best friend is gone (crying).

Mike Harding Cleary Family

For Steven's older sister Heather Cavalieri, also from Mike Harding's first marriage, news of their father's murder came from a friend.

Heather Cavalieri: I didn't want to believe it, you know. I loved my dad … So, all of it's just hard … it's been hard. It's been really hard.

At the crime scene, investigators were trying to figure out why Mike was at this seemingly random location. His cellphone was about to shed some light.

Detective BJ Burton: Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls … it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house.

The phone revealed texts from a realtor named James Fraser. He asked Mike — who owned an HVAC business — to check out the house.

Detective BJ Burton: He thought he was going there for … what he thought was a heating and air service call. … You see the text messages when Michael Harding is on his way there …

Around 4 p.m., Mike Harding texts James Fraser that he is "35 minutes out." Fraser texts, "No worries." Mike asks, "Is that good for you?" and Fraser tells him "Yes." The final exchange Mike texts, "See ya soon." Fraser replies "Perfect."

While those texts gave investigators a solid timeline, the investigation hit a roadblock early on: they could not find a realtor named James Fraser.

Detective BJ Burton: So, it was probably just a made up name.

But they did have some potential leads. When investigators later contacted the phone company of the number used to text Mike Harding, they discovered that number came from a prepaid cellphone used only to arrange Mike's murder.

Detective BJ Burton: It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone. …

Peter Van Sant: And for those who don't know, what is a burner phone?

Detective BJ Burton: Somebody … goes and buys a burner phone, they'll put in like John Doe, any town USA just they … think it's untraceable at which to some degree it is.

And remember that pickup Hammersley saw in the garage? Burton said it was Mike Harding's.

Detective BJ Burton: My thought is … whoever murdered him and then pulled the truck in the garage, there's a very good chance that their DNA may also be in the truck.

Burton tried to call Mike's wife, Julie, but she didn't pick up. Burton had been told she was heading his way — to the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office, so he waited there to give her the bad news face to face.

The local legend of the "cursed" mansion

Steven Harding: When you see your hero get taken from you … you know you're not untouchable …

After delivering the devastating news about Mike Harding's death to his children, Detective Burton was desperate to reach Mike's wife Julie, who indicated she was on her way to a local sheriff's office.

Det. BJ Burton: Myself and another detective waited there for some period of time. … She never showed up.

A few days later, Burton located her at a neighbor's house in Celina.

Detective BJ Burton: I introduced myself to her, uh, you know, try to talk to her. …

She referred all questions to her lawyer, which Burton thought was unusual for someone in law enforcement and the spouse of a murder victim.

Detective BJ Burton: She didn't want to talk to me …

Burton and his team began investigating the Harding's personal lives. They learned the two met online in 2018. Julie, 44, and Mike, 48, had both been through divorces. They married in 2019 and within months, Burton says they bought that spectacular house in Celina where they planned to live after retirement.

Mike and Julie Harding Kathleen Rourke/Facebook

Julie's close friend, Kathy Rourke says Julie was over the moon in love with Mike.

Kathy Rourke: She thought she had something that she — she wanted more than anything else … A man to come home to, a man to hug her, to comfort her, to make her feel like a woman.

Kathy Rourke: … she was so proud to be married, she was so proud …

When she turned 50, Julie would be eligible to retire from the California Highway Patrol — an iconic agency known around the world.

Kathy Rourke: Wearing her uniform was the greatest joy in her life.

Detective BJ Burton: I think early on in their marriage … the decision was made … Mike would go ahead and move to the lake house in Celina, Tennessee, so he could get his HVAC service repair business started there.

Julie planned to join Mike full time when she retired. But she was a frequent visitor, and the couple made the house a home, complete with Julie's dog Chippy the Chihuahua and Mike's boxer Charlie.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: The one thing that would always put a smile on Captain Julie Harding's face were her dogs.

Julie and Mike Harding became friendly with the locals — including Sheriff Brandon Boone.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: … uh, very nice couple, talked about couldn't wait to retire to get here full time.

Peter Van Sant: She seemed like a pleasant woman when you met her?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Yes, she did. Very pleasant … They seemed like a, a wonderful couple together

Mike Harding's children understood how their father felt about Julie but thought he was making a mistake.

Heather Cavalieri: I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her … So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her.

Cavalieri says Julie Harding was arrogant and made her feel uncomfortable.

Peter Van Sant: Did the two of you ever go out and visit, uh, at the house in Tennessee?

Heather Cavalieri: No, I didn't think that I would be welcome there.

Locals say the Harding's dream home overlooking Dale Hollow Lake was cursed. CBS News

Steven and Heather said they stayed away from the mansion, as did many locals. The house, Boone says, had a reputation for being cursed.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: There was a divorce that happened here that, that got pretty nasty. … We've had calls in the past of uh, gunshots that happened here that later ended up being a murder right in Burkesville. Uh, the gentleman who lived here shot the person up there.

Peter Van Sant: Now, is it true that a realtor actually brought some sort of spiritual person out here to try to purge the evil spirits from the house?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Yes, that's what the realtor advised me and told me — that he had, he had brought a guy here to uh, get the spirits to go away.

Peter Van Sant: And you're serious?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: I'm serious.

And then there's the legend of Dale Hollow Lake, which was created when the Army Corps of Engineers flooded a small town that became known as "the town that drowned." Even today, the eerie foundations of the long-ago town are visible when the lake is low.

But Mike and Julie Harding ignored all the country rumors. And their long-distance marriage seemed to work.

Preston Cleary: Mike seemed pretty happy. He always bragged on her, how smart she was … he really cared about her. He'd do anything for her.

Sergeant Brian Wittmer worked side by side with Captain Julie Harding for several years.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: They looked like a very cute couple.

But Wittmer said sometime in 2022 he noticed a change in Julie.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: So for the first several years … I had never seen her consume any alcohol.

But then she began drinking.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: … she was going to Napa Valley and having drinks, having wine, going to — to vineyards on weekend trips.

Wittmer said it was almost like someone flipped a switch.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: … she was … hyper. Uh, she would talk a lot. She, um, was anxious.

Mike Harding's friend Preston says that Mike also noticed the stark change in Julie's behavior.

Preston Cleary: Mike was mad because she didn't want to spend time with him …

Mike Harding revealed to Preston that he believed Julie Harding was cheating on him.

Peter Van Sant: Did Mike suspect there was another man in Julie's life?

Preston Cleary: He, he did.

Mike Harding had noticed lingerie purchases in their Amazon account.

Preston Cleary: And she … had no plan to be here to see him.

Those Amazon purchases, coupled with Julie Harding's drinking and the way she avoided spending time with Mike Harding, bruised his ego, Cleary says. But the biggest blow came when Julie told Mike she wanted to postpone her retirement for five years.

Preston Cleary: It was at that moment I seen a shift in their relationship and Mike … he had a different outlook toward her. … He was just crushed that she would choose to work five more years … he's just like, this is, this isn't going to work out.

Preston says Julie Harding filed for divorce in May 2022.

Preston Cleary: He was blinded. …he really, really loved her.

Sheriff Boone says the emotional turmoil took its toll on Mike Harding, who sensed Julie saw him as her enemy.

Peter Van Sant: Did you notice a change in Mike's attitude? Did you notice kind of a paranoia?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Oh, absolutely.

After a break-in at his home, and fearing for his safety, Mike Harding wrapped chains with a padlock around his patio doors. Clay County Sheriff's Office

Mike Harding told Boone that someone had broken into his house one night while he was sleeping and he reported one of his guns had been stolen. After that, he made it a habit of wrapping chains with a padlock around his patio doors.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: And after seeing the locks and the chains around the door, you really think, whoa, you know, he was, he was afraid of something.

At the same time, Julie told friends and colleagues that she was afraid of Mike and feared he was engaged in some dangerous activities.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She said that Mike … was potentially dealing ghost guns, drugs … was taking money from her bank accounts.

Mike Harding feared his wife, say family and friends

In May 2022, soon after Julie Harding filed for a divorce, Mike Harding told friends and family that he feared for his safety.

Steven Harding: There was solid steel chains wrapped around my dad's front door and as well as his back doors … he would do that so that no one would come in while he was sleeping. Or if it was Julie, the dogs aren't going to bark if you know the person.

Peter Van Sant: And so you're telling me that your father feared Julie?

Steven Harding: Yes.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton.

Jesse Stockton: …he told his friends that … If he ever was murdered or disappeared or something nefarious happened to him, that they needed to make sure somebody looked at Julie Harding.

Mike Harding's friend, Preston Cleary, knew Mike also was worried about his savings, and he gave Mike some advice about the pending divorce.

Preston Cleary: … whoever gets to the bank first, you know, that's their money. So, Mike, if you want to be fair, you go take half the money out of the bank. He goes, "no." … He goes, "I'm going to do this in court."

Around the same time, Sgt. Brian Wittmer says Julie Harding called him to announce that she was going to raid the family funds.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She said that she was driving from Sacramento to Tennessee and she was going to withdraw money from her bank accounts before Mike Harding did.

Mike and Capt. Julie Harding Preston and Crystal Cleary/Cumberland County Justice Center/CHP

At that point, Julie Harding was telling friends that Mike was involved with illegal weapons and narcotics.

Peter Van Sant: Did she think about turning in her own husband if he's selling ghost guns and dealing drugs, for goodness sakes?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Well, that's what you would expect from somebody … with her rank and her knowledge. And she would tell me that she had a friend working out in Tennessee law enforcement … that was potentially looking into things.

Peter Van Sant: Were you ever able to confirm that?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: I was not.

Authorities say there is no evidence Mike Harding sold drugs or ghost guns or was involved in any other type of criminal activity.

Heather Cavalieri: I want people to know that he was a good man, he loved his family and he loved life. Any other narrative you hear is not the real narrative … We want the truth to be told, and that's why we're here.

Not long after telling Cleary he was not going to transfer any money out of the couple's bank accounts, Mike Harding got a call from the bank.

Preston Cleary: The bank … had told him, "Julie Harding was just here, and she cleared out almost all your savings in your accounts" …

Julie Harding reportedly withdrew around $360,000 from various bank accounts, according to what Mike Harding told his divorce attorney. Julie's friend Kathy Rourke says at least part of that money belonged to Julie.

Kathy Rourke: She didn't need his permission.

Peter Van Sant: So she's taking that money to do what with it?

Kathy Rourke: Bring it back here to California … She gave most of the money to her mom 'til she figured out what she was gonna do.

But Mike Harding's son Steven says a lot of that money belonged to his father.

Steven Harding: My dad was a very smart, well-educated man. He was very good with stocks. … He was very good with his finances.

Peter Van Sant: In the days prior to his disappearing, he'd heard all this bad news. Money had been taken … There's no reconciliation coming his way … How did that change him? …

Preston Cleary: It destroyed uh, the friend that I had … there was no more fishing for Mike … Mike was strictly business, trying to rebuild his life and get back to where he was.

Mike Harding Kathy Rourke

And Mike Harding would rely on his HVAC business to rebuild his life — which is why friends say he responded so quickly to the call from the mysterious "James Fraser" asking him for a repair estimate at that empty house in Burkesville, Kentucky. Investigators strongly suspected there was a connection between Fraser and Julie Harding.

Det. BJ Burton: It was obvious that really the only main conflict he had going on in his life was this contentious divorce involving property and money with — with Julie Harding.

Peter Van Sant: In other words, if somebody had a motive, it was her.

Det. BJ Burton: Correct. Yes.

Burton says investigators soon learned that Julie Harding was in California at the time of Mike's murder, but they suspected her just the same.

Det. BJ Burton: She contacted three different people involved in law enforcement during this time frame. And every one of them that she talked to … walked away with a feeling of suspicion that she was involved.

Lacking any cooperation from Julie Harding, Sheriff Boone, warrant in hand, led his armed deputies into the Harding mansion where Julie was staying after Mike's death.

The deputies went room to room looking for clues.

Investigators say taunting notes written by Julie Harding on Post-its were found around the home during their search. Cumberland County Justice Center

No one was home, but the deputies found yellow Post-it notes that investigators say were handwritten by Julie Harding when Mike Harding was still alive. They read: "0 $ Here," "0 $ here either," and "Whatcha lookin 4?"

Detective BJ Burton: So there's these little sticky notes when we did the search warrant down there that would say something like "no money here." "Nope, no money here."

Peter Van Sant: Taunting him.

Det. BJ Burton: Yeah, taunting.

Investigators began executing additional warrants — specifically for the call log of Julie Harding's cellphone in the months before Mike's murder. That's when something caught Burton's eye.

Det. BJ Burton: It jumps out that she's calling this one number, that they're talking almost every single day.

Peter Van Sant: … there were 194 calls made between her number and this other number, correct?

Det. BJ Burton: Yes, yes.

Peter Van Sant: That's a lot of calls.

Det. BJ Burton: Yes.

Investigators traced that number to a man named Thomas O'Donnell, a former car salesman from Houston, Texas. He had recently relocated to the wine country of Napa, California — a place Julie Harding was known to visit.

Did Julie Harding hire a hit man to kill her husband?

After investigators discovered Julie Harding was talking incessantly to a man named Thomas O'Donnell, they explored that connection and learned the two likely met on a dating website that catered to self-described millionaires.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton: … they had, uh, an extensive and significant relationship. Whether it was romantic or not, I cannot say, but they communicated with each other by phone for months …

For prosecutors Jesse Stockton and Ann Marie Gordon Anderson, the math did not add up. Two months of constant calls — 194 of them — stopped cold only days before Mike Harding was murdered.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: I think based on that … can probably speculate that there — there may have been some type of conversation … about what was going to happen.

Peter Van Sant: A conspiracy in other words.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: Conspiracy.

Investigators already knew the texts used to lure Mike Harding to his death came from a burner phone. They pulled the phone's locational data from its service provider.

Detective BJ Burton: And the first thing you notice is … the phone is first turned on when it's … in the Houston, Texas … area.

Houston, Texas—Thomas O'Donnell's hometown. To investigators, that was too coincidental to be a coincidence.

Jesse Stockton: I don't think Mister O'Donnell got out here by accident. … The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding.

Investigators developed a theory that Julie Harding had paid Thomas O'Donnell to kill Mike Harding. And they thought it likely that O'Donnell was the fictional "James Fraser" who had lured Mike to that empty house. The next step in their investigation was securing the call log from O'Donnell's personal cellphone.

Det. BJ Burton: When you start looking at the locational data from his personal phone and comparing it to the locational data with the burner phone, it — it matches up perfectly.

The FBI created maps that showed O'Donnell's phone and the burner phone.

The FBI map shows the prepaid burner phone (red) and Thomas O'Donnell's cellphone (black) were traveling together in the weeks before Mike Harding's murder. Cumberland County Justice Center

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: … the red on the screen, it is the burner phone, that's what it's showing. Anything that you see that's black, that is Thomas O'Donnell's personal cellphone.

Investigators noted that the two phones were traveling in lockstep through the south in the weeks before Mike Harding's murder.

Peter Van Sant: We know the burner phone is involved in the murder.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: That's … it's only purpose.

Background checks showed that, years earlier, O'Donnell had been arrested for stalking a girlfriend. He eventually received probation. But what really struck Detective Burton was how "irresponsible" O'Donnell was with money. He was no millionaire; O'Donnell appeared to be a man desperate for cash, Burton said.

Det. BJ Burton: It seems like his whole life, like he's always just looking for the … next big thing that's going to make him be able to afford the lifestyle that he wants to — to lead …

And Julie Harding, who admitted raiding the couple's bank accounts, was loaded with cash after withdrawing hundreds of thousands of dollars from the couple's bank accounts.

Peter Van Sant: Authorities think she took out that cash so she could pay Thomas O'Donnell to murder Michael.

Kathy Rourke: Absolutely not. That's the most ludicrous thing. That's what kills me about this whole story …

Peter Van Sant: Were you ever able to make a connection from all this cash that she took out and any sort of payment for Thomas O'Donnell?

Det. BJ Burton: No … it's impossible to track. I mean if someone walks up and hands you a stack of cash … it's untraceable …

But it wasn't only money that Julie was after. Investigators say she wasn't leaving Tennessee without Mike's beloved dog Charlie.

Heather Cavalieri: I think she deemed Charlie hers. But that wasn't her dog, that was my dad's dog …

Police say Julie Harding was determined to get the dog back from a friend of Mike's who'd been caring for Charlie since Mike went missing.

Steven Harding: … she knew I wanted the dog after we knew that my dad was dead.

Doorbell camera video shows Julie Harding taking Charlie the boxer from the home of a friend who was caring for the dog after Mike Harding's murder. CBS News

But Julie Harding wasn't in the giving mood, Mike Harding's children say. Some two weeks after Mike's body was found, Julie simply took Charlie for herself. She is captured on a Ring doorbell camera, boldly opening the front door and stealing Charlie from the friend who was taking care of him. Steven says he never saw Charlie again.

Steven Harding: I would have taken that dog in a heartbeat. I just, I feel like it would be better under my hands because I — I am my father. … I — I would have loved it like my dad did. I would protect it.

The friend who cared for the dog wanted to press charges against Julie Harding, but at that point, Burton says the focus was on processing evidence from the murder scene.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton: … people from the Kentucky State Police lab come to the scene … and then they take a lot of swabs from Michael Harding's truck because they also believe that whoever killed him moved his truck.

Peter Van Sant: Are they able to get a – a usable DNA sample?

Jesse Stockton: Yes …

That sample was found to be consistent with Thomas O'Donnell's DNA.

Det. BJ Burton: So, we got to a point where there was just so much overwhelming locational data coupled with other evidence … where we felt like we had enough to make an arrest …

In early December 2022, two months after Mike Harding's murder, investigators learned that O'Donnell was going to be at the Sacramento airport.

Det. BJ Burton: … most people aren't going to fly or travel without having their phone on them. So, the thought was … we can catch him in the airport … we can also seize his phones at the same time.

A still from video of Thomas O'Donnell's arrest at Sacramento International Airport. Kentucky State Police

Police searched O'Donnell's truck and say they found one of Mike Harding's guns. It was the same gun that had been stolen from Mike's house. Also in the truck was a box of Hornady Critical Defense bullets, the same type of ammunition used in the murder.

Burton says there was not enough evidence to charge Julie Harding with murder but on the same day of O'Donnell's arrest, Julie's dognapping of Charlie came back to bite her. She was arrested and charged with criminal trespass.

Burton was hoping either Julie Harding or O'Donnell would flip on the other, but neither did. O'Donnell was held on the murder charges, while Julie was released on her own recognizance. The next day, Dec. 9, 2022, Julie's superiors at the California Highway Patrol called her in Tennessee to inform her that her status as a peace officer was revoked.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She's a normal citizen at that point.

Peter Van Sant: Does she have to turn in her badge and her gun?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Yes, she would have –

Peter Van Sant: She's disarmed.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Correct.

Peter Van Sant: Once she got released, did she give you a call?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: I did not hear from Captain Julie Harding that evening.

Kathy Rourke: I think she was losing control … I think that anybody that wants to stand in her shoes needs to go and let themselves be booked into jail as a woman and go through what she went through. That broke her in two.

Julie Harding, the once proud captain of her own fate, was alone with her own thoughts in her supposedly cursed home overlooking Dale Hollow Lake.

An eerie fog descends on the supposed "cursed" mansion

It's the morning of Dec. 10, 2022. An armed deputy, wearing a body camera, makes his way toward the Harding house—shrouded in an eerie fog—searching for a potential killer.

DEPUTY (bodycam): Are you the mailman?

DAVID OGLETREE: I am.

Just minutes before, mail carrier David Ogletree and another man had made a tragic discovery — what looked like a body at the base of that distant tree. They called 911.

911 OPERATOR: What's going on honey? DAVID OGLETREE: OK, this, this is David Ogletree, I'm the mailman up here and we may have a body laying up here. 911 OPERATOR: OK … We'll get you someone up there in just a second OK.

Peter Van Sant: Hey David.

David Ogletree: Hello, how are you?

Peter Van Sant: Peter Van Sant, "48 Hours" CBS News. Nice to meet you.

David Ogletree: Nice to meet you.

What Ogletree saw that day is burned into his memory.

David Ogletree: She was, she was laying right up here beside this tree here face down.

Blood can be seen around the woman's body.

DEPUTY (bodycam): Until uh, we get her turned over and see if there's a gun, this could be a murder.

Sheriff Boone arrived at the scene. When investigators rolled the body over, they saw that it was Julie Harding. Her right hand was gripping a gun. An investigator concluded she took her own life.

The blood-stained note found in a bag next to Julie Harding's body. Clay County Sheriff's Office

Investigators also saw a bag next to Julie. Inside, note to Mike, stained in blood, which read:

"I lived a good life until a year ago. Mike, you win! You got what you wanted, me in a coffin…"

Det. BJ Burton: It was just bizarre … almost like she was obsessed with somehow trying to get back at Michael Harding or —I don't know, didn't really understand it.

But Burton had a theory, and it involved Thomas O'Donnell.

Det. BJ Burton: She knows her co-conspirator has been arrested. … She's been suspended in California Highway Patrol … she saw the writing on the wall, what the future looked like, and wasn't going to stick around for it.

But what role did Julie Harding play in her husband's death? Investigators hoped they'd learn something when Thomas O'Donnell agreed to talk.

DETECTIVE BJ BURTON (police interview): So let — let me ask you this. When or how — when did you first meet Julie or how do you know Julie?

THOMAS O'DONNELL: I don't know, Julie.

DETECTIVE BJ BURTON: Julie Harding?

THOMAS O'DONNELL: Doesn't ring a bell.

After 20 uneventful minutes, O'Donnell requested an attorney, immediately terminating the interview. Seven days later, he was indicted by a grand jury.

O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge. Three years later, on April 27, 2026, he went on trial at the Cumberland County Justice Center in Burkesville, Kentucky for killing Mike Harding.

PROSECUTOR ANN MARIE GORDON ANDERSON (in court): This case is about the murder of Michael Harding.

PROSECUTOR ANN MARIE GORDON ANDERSON (in court): According to Julie Harding's phone records, between July 1st and September the 8th, of '22, there were over 100 phone calls between her and the defendant, Thomas O'Donnell.

Gordon Anderson said Julie and O'Donnell used those calls to meticulously plan Mike's murder. Why? Julie realized she'd likely lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in a divorce, said Detective Burton.

Peter Van Sant: One possible solution for Julie in this financial war is to do what?

Det. BJ Burton: Get rid of him.

Prosecutors believe O'Donnell posed as a realtor to get a key to gain access to the property in Kentucky. They told jurors the data from the burner phone puts him at the scene of the crime. And believe it or not, O'Donnell's attorneys agreed O'Donnell, they said, was at the scene of the crime. It was a new admission that caught the prosecutors off guard.

Thomas O'Donnell Kentucky Department of Corrections

Remember, after his arrest, O'Donnell told investigators he did not know Julie. Now, his lawyers said he not only knew Julie, O'Donnell worked with her to lure Mike to that house in Kentucky, but he never pulled the trigger.

Prosecutor Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: I was really shocked … they point-blank just said he was at the scene, he opened the door, but he let someone else in.

That "someone else," says defense attorney Sara Zeurcher was the real killer. The defense claimed a neighbor saw two men at the property the day Mike was murdered.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY SARA ZEURCHER (in court): A neighbor told police exactly what he saw on September the 19th. Two men at the scene.

Investigators could find no evidence to back up the neighbor's account. The defense also criticized the investigation itself and pointed out its shortcomings. The burner phone prosecutors talked about was never recovered. Neither was the murder weapon. And there was no evidence that Julie paid O'Donnell to kill her husband.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY SARA ZEURCHER (in court): If this case were a mystery novel … you'll never hear the final chapter that explains what actually happened because the Commonwealth doesn't know.

After five days of testimony, O'Donnell decided not to testify. The jury needed just two hours to reach a verdict.

JUDGE DAVID WILLIAMS (in court): We, the jury, agree by a unanimous vote that defendant Thomas O'Donnell is guilty of the offense of murder.

Jesse Stockton: … for the family, they finally got justice for their father … all I can do is take satisfaction that the proper thing was done.

Julie Harding's close friend, Kathy Rourke, says Julie played no role in the murder of Mike Harding.

Kathy Rourke: If you knew her, you would know that she would never do anything cowardly or anything illegal, let alone try to kill this guy.

Steven Harding: She was the true monster of all of this … she was the one that executed every move, other than physically pulling the trigger on my father.

Heather Cavalieri: My dad was the victim in this case, not Julie.

Mike Harding Kathy Rourke

Steven Harding and Heather Cavalieri said the victory at trial, while satisfying, will never temper their sense of eternal loss.

Steven Harding: He died before my 30th birthday and 29 years isn't enough. I mean, people think 29 years is a lot, but it's not …

Heather Cavalieri: I was close with my dad for a long time. … Just not having a dad, you know, someone to call, like he was a jokester, you know. He was fun with my kids. (crying) … It's hard not having him here.

Thomas O'Donnell was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.



Produced by Paul LaRosa. Jordan Kinsey and Cindy Cesare are the development producers. Nancy Bautista is the associate producer. Wini Dini, Eric Modena and Greg Kaplan are the editors. Anthony Batson is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.

World.title: Security cameras upend man's story of finding wife fatally shot in his car
World.content:
It was Tuesday, Nov. 15, 2022, and a small strip mall in Huntsville, Alabama, was teeming with police activity.

The frantic scene was captured on police body cameras and dashcam video in the moments after police discovered 37-year-old Savannah Tolbert shot dead in the front seat of a red Tesla.

Moments before police arrived, her husband David Tolbert was captured on video from security cameras in the store where he had been working -- after he found her lifeless body. He appeared shocked and upset and is seen walking briskly with his hand covering his mouth.

David Tolbert, seen upper right, crouched on the floor after apparently discovering his wife dead in his car. Huntsville Police Department

Moments later, David Tolbert is seen crouching on the floor. When police arrived at the scene, the store's owners said they observed David with tears in his eyes and his hands in his pockets.

Red flags appear early in Savannah Tolbert's death investigation

Jeff Kreiter and Greg Hayden, investigators with the Huntsville Police Major Crimes Unit, were assigned to the case.

Investigator Greg Hayden: We wanna know … who saw what happened … because … information is the most important thing that … we can get out there.

When Hayden arrived at the scene, it appeared that Savannah Tolbert had taken her own life.

Investigator Greg Hayden: She's sitting up … in the passenger seat with her head tilted … to the left side ...

Anne-Marie Green: Where is her hand and where is the gun?

Investigator Greg Hayden: The gun is in … her right hand. And it's actually laid across her lap.

First responders said they had found Savannah Tolbert's fingers curled around the gun when they got there. It was a red flag for investigators.

Investigator Greg Hayden: It didn't match up to a suicide … her gun was in her right hand … and the bullet hole was on her left side in the back of her head.

Savannah Tolbert Savannah Tolbert's family

None of it made sense to Savannah Tolbert's sisters, Holly and April Hancock.

April Hancock: No way.

Anne Marie Green: — your sister did this to herself.

April Hancock: Never. No.

Anne Marie Green: Why so sure?

April Hancock: She wouldn't do that. …

Holly Hancock: She wouldn't leave her daughter.

April Hancock: She knows – she — no.

In addition to the gun that police determined belonged to her, authorities discovered a shell casing on the rear seat, behind the driver. The Tesla was seized as evidence and taken by police for testing.

Anne-Marie Green: Who do you want to talk to next?

David Tolbert NoblePhoto

Investigator Greg Hayden: Our most important person is … her husband.

Anne-Marie Green: David is handcuffed and put in a patrol car. … he's a grieving spouse. Why was he handcuffed?

Investigator Greg Hayden: Our policy … is that whenever we transport somebody, if they are in … a scene, we always handcuff … for officer safety.

David Tolbert, 47, hadn't been arrested, but he was a person of interest. He was taken to the police station. Once the handcuffs were off, investigators began questioning him.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: What we had to work with at that point is — who was around her.

Kreiter was joined by Investigator Julian Johnson, who had met David Tolbert at the scene.

INVESTIGATOR JULIAN JOHNSON (police interview): Hey David.

DAVID TOLBERT: Hey.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Remember me?

DAVID TOLBERT: Yes, sir.

On that day, David Tolbert, a retired corrections officer, was helping the owners of a new store prepare for a health inspection. After investigators read David his rights, he started talking.

Anne-Marie Green: What does David tell you happened that day?

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He was at the store … Savannah shows up, wants to talk to him.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): I didn't know she was gonna come up there today. And I told her I had to go into work.

The store had four security cameras.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): We were going over the stuff for the inspection and she came in and ...

Savannah Tolbert is seen on security video just after entering the store at 1:48 p.m. on Nov. 15, 2022. Huntsville Police Department

Police say Savannah Tolbert had driven her blue Kia Sorento to the store that day. She was sporting a new, short hairstyle and is seen on camera arriving at the store shortly before 2 p.m. David Tolbert, wearing a black baseball cap and a hoodie, greets his wife with a hug. Moments later, they leave the store together.

You can't hear the audio, but you can see David and Savannah talking outside the store.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He tells her to wait. It'll be about 30 minutes before the inspection is done.

David Tolbert walks back to the store, alone. Then, one of the cameras from inside the store captures a glimpse of Savannah Tolbert walking across the parking lot. Investigators believe she was walking to the Tesla and that it was the last time Savannah was seen alive.

Then, about 20 minutes later, David Tolbert grabs a Yeti-style coffee mug and is seen leaving the store.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He goes out to the … Kia that … she drove there in, she's not there. He says she must have went to the Tesla maybe to watch a movie.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): My car has a screen. You can go in and watch TV on it and stuff like that. … I went over there and hit the thing to get in my car and just sat down and looked over and she was there.

Investigators quickly learned everything they could about the couple. After almost two years of marriage, they had been living apart for several months. And according to David, Savannah had been struggling with mental health issues.

INVESTIGATOR KREITER (police interview): What is this she is diagnosed with?

DAVID TOLBERT: She had depression, anxiety.

Investigators had been told by first responders that the gunshot wound was in the back of Savannah Tolbert's head, near the left side, but the gun had been discovered in her right hand.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): Is she right-handed or left handed?

DAVID TOLBERT: She's right-handed.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: She's right-handed. OK.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Did you see a gun on her when you got in the car?

DAVID TOLBERT: I saw it in her — in her lap.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: If she was right-handed … why would she do this to shoot herself?

DAVID TOLBERT: Why would she shoot herself to begin with?

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: That's what we're trying to find out.

Investigators started talking to David and Savannah's friends and soon learned about a woman named Chelsea Finch.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: In talking, uh, to everybody … David himself, Chelsea's brought up.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): Who is Chelsea?

DAVID TOLBERT: Chelsea is one of my friends. I installed a Tesla charger at her house.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: We end up calling her … and she agreed to come up and meet. And it just so happened she ended up being there at the same time … David was in the interview room … 'Cause we kind of wanted to see that reaction when she got the news.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): … we're here to talk to you about David and his — his wife, um, Savannah.

CHELSEA FINCH: OK.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Well, she's deceased.

CHELSEA FINCH: Gotcha.

Investigators say Finch, an aerospace missiles engineer, appeared calm when she learned Savannah Tolbert had died. She told investigators she had met Savannah a few times at a vape shop where David Tolbert worked.

CHELSEA FINCH (police interview): And then I — he was my go-to person for Tesla because he had a Tesla and I was given no tutorial on how to operate my Tesla.

Investigators soon learned David Tolbert and Finch had been doing a lot more than talking about their Teslas.

CHELSEA FINCH (police interview): We said I love you and stuff like it's — it was definitely —

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Intimate.

CHELSEA FINCH: Yes.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: OK … you understood that he was still married. Did you press him to get a divorce?

CHELSEA FINCH: No.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: … she said that they were in love, uh, that David was gonna leave, uh, Savannah for her …

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): Do you — do you love him?

CHELSEA FINCH: Yeah, I do.
