Police say it is unclear whether Savannah Tolbert knew her husband was having an affair. Finch revealed in her police interview that David had told her his wife might be moving back to their home.

Chelsea Finch: So, if she moved back in, in my mind, that's my hard cutoff.

Even if Savannah Tolbert had moved back home, David Tolbert, it seems, had already decided to end their marriage. He had given her divorce papers, but she had not signed them. Three days later, those papers were found in the red Tesla where Savannah was discovered.

Savannah Tolbert's husband says she was depressed; her sister says she was scared

After Savannah Tolbert's death, her sisters were still reeling from the devastating news they had learned from investigators: their sister may have taken her own life.

Holly Hancock: it really wasn't a question in our mind. We knew she didn't kill herself.

April Hancock: We know Savannah wouldn't do something like this.

Savannah was the eldest of three sisters in a close-knit southern family. Holly Hancock is the middle sister.

Holly Hancock: Growing up we were thick as thieves until somebody stole a hair bow or a T-shirt … when you think about the kind of family dynamic with sisters, I would say we fit that to a T. We always had each other's backs unless we were at each other's backs.

Savannah and her sisters suffered a life-changing loss as children when their mother took her own life.

Anne-Marie Green: What sort of impact did that have on your family?

Holly Hancock: I would say that brought us closer together as sisters and it really put Savannah in the spotlight for that older sister role who also assumed kind of the lead female in the family.

And Savannah shared her story on social media.

SAVANNAH TOLBERT VIDEO: Today is, um, world suicide prevention day … this is a really personal topic for me. As some of you, most of you probably know, my mom passed away by suicide when I was 16 …

According to her family, Savannah had a keen sense of awareness and understanding when her family and friends were going through a rough patch. April Hancock is the youngest sister.

April Hancock: She's always a listening ear. … If you're having a hard time, if you're going through something talk about it … Don't bottle it up, don't hold it in. Like, I'm here. I'll take the time.

Savannah Tolbert and her daughter, Avery Foster. Savannah Tolbert's family

And time with her family was a priority for Savannah. She doted on daughter Avery, from a previous marriage.

Avery Foster: She loved to craft. She got me into crafting, um, she liked to go on walks. She liked to spend time outside.

Anne-Marie Green: She liked to make videos too …

Avery Foster: … she just liked to video everything …

Anne-Marie Green: What do you think Savannah saw in David?

Holly Hancock: I think that he knew how to say the right words.

David Tolbert told investigators he met Savannah in 2013. The couple got married in 2020.

Savannah and David Tolbert on their wedding day in 2020. NoblePhoto

Holly Hancock: She did a 1920s — roaring 20s-themed wedding … she had down to the tiniest little detail planned out …

Anne-Marie Green: What was David like at the wedding?

April Hancock: Cloud nine.

Anne-Marie Green: Were you all happy that she was getting married?

April Hancock: We were happy that she was happy.

After the wedding, the newlyweds started a food truck selling mac and cheese. The business fizzled out after seven months.

In May 2022, April and Holly Hancock, who lived in Tennessee, noticed a change in Savannah Tolbert's demeanor in their phone conversations.

Holly Hancock: She seemed a lot more flighty to me …

She didn't seem like herself, they say, but they didn't know why.

April Hancock: … more on edge.

Holly Hancock: Skittish. Yeah, on edge … she didn't have as much to say.

Savannah's ex-husband Andy Foster, Avery's dad, knew Savannah's mom had taken her own life. He gave Savannah his word that he would keep an eye on her mental health.

Andy Foster: I always made her a promise … if I ever noticed any shifts that I would step in and intervene … and I did that …

He lived in the Huntsville area and when he observed Savannah was struggling —

Andy Foster: I called her sister and I called her dad … and I'm like hey, this is what I've noticed with Savannah. Something needs to happen. She needs to go somewhere. I'm — I'm not related to her, so I can't send her anywhere. I need help from you guys.

Savannah's sisters later learned she had voluntarily checked herself into a Birmingham, Alabama, hospital around July 2022. They say they don't know why she was admitted, but she stayed three days. It was something David claims Savannah didn't want to share with her sisters.

Anne-Marie Green: David's not calling you?

Holly Hancock: No. … We proceeded to call Dave after that and asked him for well-being and also why he hadn't told us any of this and his response was that Savannah wanted him to keep it a secret, um and that he was trying to honor her wishes.

At the time, Savannah's daughter Avery was living with her dad. After Savannah was discharged from the hospital, she was readmitted to another hospital in early September for a longer stay.

Holly Hancock: Dave brought her to Nashville where I live and I met him at the hospital to help check her in together,

Anne-Marie Green: What was she like at that point?

Holly Hancock: Very childlike, very timid. … She was scared. She did not want to stay there.

David Tolbert told investigators during his police interview about Savannah Tolbert's behavior at the time, including how, he says, she avoided going anywhere near their home.

DAVID TOLBERT (police interview): … she thought there was black mold at the house and the house was haunted, and uh, there was a lot of stuff wrong with the house and she couldn't stay there … with me not being there because it was either too loud or too quiet and both of them were terrible for her.

Savannah was discharged from the hospital, moved out of the marital home, and moved in with her grandparents. On Nov. 15, 2022, the day she died, investigators learned Savannah had an appointment with her therapist.

Anne-Marie Green: Was Savannah depressed?

Holly Hancock: Honestly, I would say no. What … I observed from her was not depression. It was — she was scared.

Back at the police station, David Tolbert was tested for gunshot residue, known as GSR, in the interview room .

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (police interview): You told me you didn't wash your hands, right?

When investigators got the results –

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Those GSR tests, they pop blue for GSR on your hands.

DAVID TOLBERT: I don't know what GSR is.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Gunshot residue.

DAVID TOLBERT: Oh.

While investigators waited for Savannah's autopsy report, they learned there was no gunshot residue found on her hands.

David was free to leave after his interview. But before he left the police station, investigator Kreiter presented a hypothetical scenario.

INVESTIGATOR JEFF KREITER (police interview): So there's — the investigator that is out there right now, looking at the cameras, the surrounding buildings, not gonna find footage.

DAVID TOLBERT: Not a bit.

INVESTIGATOR KREITER: Of — of you —

DAVID TOLBERT: Doing nothing.

INVESTIGATOR KREITER: — shoot — shooting your wife.

DAVID TOLBERT: I did not shoot my own wife.

Investigators Kreiter and Hayden showed us what they had discovered — another valuable clue to learn what really happened that day.

Anne-Marie Green: So you're looking for some camera, something to see what happened with Savannah. What do you guys discover as you look around?

Investigator Greg Hayden: We searched the entire area … and luckily we were able to find this camera right here on Valley Pools.

The security camera was perched near the roof of the Valley Pools store – about 100 yards away from the scene.

Anne-Marie Green: The Tesla is parked all the way over there.

Investigator Greg Hayden: That's correct … The camera's pointing directly at us in front of the business right there.

Investigators believe David Tolbert didn't know about that camera. It was far away, but close enough to capture video of his red Tesla.

Multiple cameras provide clues. What will the Tesla tell investigators?

In the days following Savannah Tolbert's death, her sisters Holly and April Hancock, continued to cope with their grief. But David Tolbert never reached out to them. Their relationship with their brother-in-law was strained from the beginning.

Anne-Marie Green: How did David kind of interact with your family?

April Hancock: Very boastful … always bigger and better and can outshine and outdo …

Holly Hancock: He did always have a better story. He had a better car than you.

Avery Foster: So, I never really saw him a lot … unless it was like, like a weekend and it was really late.

Savannah's daughter Avery first met David Tolbert when she was about 5 years old. She said her new stepdad was somewhat strict – especially about what she watched on TV.

Avery Foster: … and he'd be like … "well this is not a kid show. You can't watch it with us. You gotta go to bed" … and I was like alright … feel like I'm being pushed off because I don't — like I don't get to hang out with y'all. … I feel like a family is supposed to watch TV together, even if it's a little late on a Saturday night or something.

The family says David Tolbert made an impression, wearing three-piece suits and carrying a wad of cash.

Anne-Marie Green: Was he wealthy?

April Hancock: … no. I think he just liked to portray that.

He also liked luxury cars — especially Tesla, says investigator Jeff Kreiter.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: He- — he loved that Tesla … probably — it was probably his prized possession.

And that Tesla – where David said he found Savannah's body – would become a focus for investigators, as would that parking lot security video from the Valley Pools store.

Investigator Greg Hayden: I went back to when he first pulled that Tesla up and we watched from when he got there …

Anne-Marie Green: The thing with this Valley Pools video is that it's far away and it's really grainy and even kind of … when you zoom in, it almost becomes more obscured.

Investigator Greg Hayden: It pixels out.

Despite the poor quality, investigator Greg Hayden had a hunch it could provide another valuable clue – adding to the video police had gathered from the store where David worked.

Investigator Greg Hayden: You can clearly see his face, what he has on which is a dark sweatshirt …

When the store video was synced up with that grainy parking lot footage of David's car —

Investigator Greg Hayden: An entire scene is put together.

— it provided a video timeline for investigators to follow from the moment Savannah arrived at the store.

Security cameras show Savannah and David Tolbert hugging inside the store at 1:48 p.m. on Nov. 15, 2022. Huntsville Police Department

Investigator Greg Hayden: Right here you'll see Savannah walking … and you'll see her walk over to the edge of the counter where she greets, uh, David at and they hug here.

Anne-Marie Green: And then what happens?

Investigator Greg Hayden: Then he'll eventually walk her back outside, which will be to her car.

David returns to the store. Then, shortly after 2:15 p.m., the Valley Pools video shows an unidentified person standing near the Tesla just as Savannah is seen approaching the car's passenger door.

Investigator Kreiter points to Savannah Tolbert standing outside the passenger side of David Tolbert's red Tesla as an unidentified person dressed in black is seen far left just after 2:15 p.m. Huntsville Police Department

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: You see this black blur right here … This is Savannah. You see the door open. And then she will get inside the passenger side seat of the Tesla … We know this because … there's no other blurs or blobs or whatever you want to call it get near that passenger door. You never see that passenger door open again.

The unidentified person walks away, and about 20 minutes later another person approaches the driver's side of the Tesla.

Investigator Greg Hayden (pointing to security camera video): That's him right there.

Investigators say the figure who appeared about 20 minutes later, dressed in dark clothing and standing at the driver's side of the Tesla, is David Tolbert. Huntsville Police Department

There's a tree partially blocking the view, and you can't see a face, but investigators say that's David Tolbert near the car.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter (pointing to security camera video): … which is this pixel-y type blob at the car.

David Tolbert told investigators when he opened his car door, he discovered Savannah dead in the front passenger seat. But investigators didn't believe he was telling the whole story.

Investigator Greg Hayden: I think that when he opened that door … pulled out that weapon and she moved away from him and he shot her.

Investigators say David Tolbert moves away from the car. A short time later the Tesla's taillights flashed on and off.

By now investigators were highly suspicious David had something to do with Savannah's death, so they called him in for a second interview.

He arrived at the police station with Chelsea Finch. She is by his side, rubbing his back.

Anne-Marie Green: Why was Chelsea there in the interview room?

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: She gave him a ride.

Investigator Greg Hayden: Yeah.

When Finch left the room, the interview started.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (second police interview): Alright Dave, how you been doing man?

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: Trying to absorb everything?

DAVID TOLBERT: I'm lost.

Anne-Marie Green: So what happened in the second interview?

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: That's when he brought up this, uh, toy cannon or whatever.

After David Tolbert's car was seized for evidence, authorities discovered a mini cannon, a collectible for hobbyists, in the trunk.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: … It would fire off like small projectile-type stuff. … it's something that could have — would've had gun powder on it.

Investigators already knew the retired corrections officer had tested positive for gunshot residue on the day Savannah died.

Investigator David Kreiter: He was smart enough to know that was … you know, an issue of course he had a law enforcement background, um, so he needed to come up with a way to explain it.

David Tolbert claimed the cannon had fallen off the seat in his car and that he had moved it to the trunk. Kreiter believes David cooked up that story to justify the gunshot residue on his hands.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: The problem would be when we got the video from Valley Pools, you can see him pull in ... At no point does he go to passenger side or go to the trunk ...

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (second police interview): When did you go to the trunk of that car?

DAVID TOLBERT: I want to say I did it as soon as I pulled up because that's when it fell.

What would the exterior cameras on David Tolbert's Tesla tell investigators about what happened? Huntsville Police Department

Police believed David Tolbert's Tesla could provide additional evidence, especially when they discovered the car's exterior cameras – a feature known as Sentry Mode – where a series of cameras can record and monitor what's happening outside the vehicle.

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: So obviously we're interested in that …

David Tolbert was asked about it during his initial interview.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (first police interview): Does your car automatically record?

DAVID TOLBERT: It does if I had my jump drive in it.

According to investigators, David Tolbert was an ardent user of Sentry Mode.

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He wanted Sentry Mode to always be active.

We wanted to know how Sentry Mode works, so we asked Rich Benoit an electric vehicle specialist and the host of the YouTube channel "Rich Rebuilds." He demonstrated on a Tesla similar to David Tolbert's car.

Anne-Marie Green: So how many cameras are on, say, a Tesla like this?

Rich Benoit: On this specific Tesla, it has eight cameras, but only four are used for Sentry Mode …

Anne-Marie Green: OK, and it's recording now?

Rich Benoit: It's recording right now, yes.

Benoit showed us where the cameras are located.

Rich Benoit: This is the first camera for Sentry Mode right here.

Anne-Marie Green: Mm-hmm.

A feature known as Sentry Mode can record what's happening outside the car. Here, a backup camera captures Rich Benoit and "48 Hours" correspondent Anne-Marie Green during a demonstration. CBS News

Rich Benoit: And then we have one at the back where the backup camera would be. So, right there.

Anne-Marie Green: Oh, yeah.

Rich Benoit: Yeah, there it is.

When the camera detects motion, it starts recording.

Anne-Marie Green: How much do the cameras see? Can it — can they see all around the vehicle?

Rich Benoit: You see the entire 360 view around the vehicle. So you see from both sides, you see from the rear, and the cameras in the front.

Anne-Marie Green: Where is the data stored?

Rich Benoit: That's a very good question. So for this specific car and how this is set up, the data is stored locally on the vehicle on a USB drive.

Prosecutor Ben Gibbons says David Tolbert was known to have his car's Sentry Mode turned on.

Asistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He would tell people you know this is to save you, this is to protect you. Keep Sentry Mode active.

But on the day of Savannah's death?

Investigator Jeff Kreiter: Unfortunately, uh, David, um says he doesn't have a memory card in, uh, in the car to keep any data on there. … so this car that he was so proud of and has all these features, he was choosing not to use any of them, um, at least on this particular day.

Investigators believed they had a lot of the evidence that could prove Tolbert had murdered Savannah – but what they needed was the autopsy report from the medical examiner.

Anne-Marie Green: When you locate the wound in her head, tell me what's going through your mind?

Dr. Jonrika Malone | Medical examiner: What's going through my mind is, this is not right.

Was David Tolbert's mistress a motive for murder?

The circumstances surrounding Savannah Tolbert's death were highly suspicious, but to make a case for murder, authorities needed the medical examiner's report.

Savannah Tolbert Savannah Tolbert's family

Dr. Jonrika Malone: The circumstances were suggestive of a possible suicide based on the fact that she is sitting in the car with the gun in her hand. …

Dr. Jonrika Malone is a state medical examiner for the Alabama Department of Forensic Sciences.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: I had to actually find the gunshot wound, which was in the back of her head, in her hairline … and so that did not ring normal to me and made me a little suspicious.

Remember, Savannah was discovered in the front passenger seat with a gun in her right hand. So, the location of the wound, in the back of her head, raised even more questions for Malone.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: It's very difficult, especially seated in a car, considering there's a headrest behind you, to be able to get your arm and hand back around there in order to do the gunshot wound to yourself.

Malone learned from investigators that there was no gunshot residue found on Savannah — so her next discovery was telling. There was no imprint from the gun's muzzle on Savannah's head.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: The barrel of the gun was not directly in contact with the skin nor was it very close to the skin.

Anne-Marie Green: Could you estimate how far the gun was from her head?

Dr. Jonrika Malone: Well, taking into consideration the different characteristics that you see in a gun .. the lack of gunpowder stippling suggests that …the gun should have been at least three to four feet away from her head at the time of discharge.

That means the gun was fired at a distance and not at close range. Malone determined Savannah had not taken her own life.

The autopsy report concluded Savannah had died from a gunshot wound to her head. The manner of death: homicide.

Anne-Marie Green: Why are you so confident that this is a homicide?

Dr. Jonrika Malone: The reason for my confidence in this is that there is no feasible way that she could have done it.

On Dec. 9, 2022, less than a month after Savannah's death, David Tolbert came into the station for a third police interview.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (third police interview): You haven't been back to work?

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: So, you've been doing no work?

DAVID TOLBERT: I've just been trying to make it.

Just like the two previous police interviews, David was read his rights and agreed to answer questions without a lawyer present.

Investigator Greg Hayden: When we talk to him, David, in my opinion, was all matter-of-fact … I think he was very confident … that I got these guys wooed over. They even let me go twice.

Anne-Marie Green: And what was the purpose of the third interview?

Investigator Greg Hayden: Third interview was we was gonna break a little bad news to him …

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON (third police interview): And we talked to, uh, the district attorney … and we — we told them everything, we — we showed them the videos – we — we did all this stuff, man.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: … and their conclusion was that — to arrest you.

INVESTIGATOR JOHNSON: To arrest you for capital murder.

Tolbert appeared stunned. Madison County assistant district attorneys Shea Keller and Ben Gibbons would prosecute the case against David Tolbert.

Anne-Marie Green: Why is this a capital murder case?

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: So, in Alabama, capital murder is a murder plus something … and there are a whole list of the somethings that can, uh, aggravate a murder into capital murder. … In this circumstance, it was because Savannah was sitting inside of a car … the facts are that she was inside of a car when he shot her so it's capital murder.

Tolbert was patted down and checked for weapons.

Before investigators left the room, they asked David Tolbert if he had anything to say.

DAVID TOLBERT: I don't believe this is happening.

DAVID TOLBERT: I tried so hard to get her mental health help for months and months.

Moments later, Chelsea walked into the interview room. She had driven David Tolbert to the police station in his Tesla. Investigators do not believe she had any knowledge or involvement in Savannah's death.

DAVID TOLBERT: They're arresting me.

DAVID TOLBERT: They're arresting me for murder.

CHELSEA FINCH: … I know you didn't do it.

CHELSEA FINCH: I got you. OK?

David Tolbert and his girlfriend Chelsea Finch in the police interview room after his arrest for murder. Huntsville Police Department

Chelsea, holding Tolbert's hand, continued to comfort him.

CHELSEA FINCH: Babe. Hey.

CHELSEA FINCH: I need you to stay strong, OK?

CHELSEA FINCH: You pinky promised me.

CHELSEA FINCH: I got you. You didn't do this. I know this.

David Tolbert was handcuffed and taken to jail where he was held until his murder trial.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: So I love trying a case with Ben, because Ben is like science and facts. And I'm like what's the juice here? … Why did he do this?

Prosecutors say David Tolbert had manipulated everyone around him and wanted them to believe Savannah, who had been struggling with mental health issues, had taken her own life.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: This is not a case about mental health…. This is about a man murdering his wife.

And Tolbert's motive for murder?

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He wanted Savannah out of the way so that presumably he could be with his mistress.

No witnesses heard the gunshot the day Savannah Tolbert died and, despite the hours of video investigators had collected in this case, there was no video that could prove David Tolbert had fired the gun that killed her.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: As a prosecutor, your job is to seek justice from the smallest thing on a traffic ticket, all the way up to a capital murder like this case. Rarely do you have a truly innocent victim. … And that's what Savannah was.

Two-and-a-half years after Savannah Tolbert's death, a jury would have to decide if Tolbert had killed his wife in broad daylight without a single witness while she sat in the passenger seat of his red Tesla.

The case against David Tolbert

David Tolbert went on trial in May 2025 in Huntsville, Alabama. There were no cameras in the courtroom. We spoke with two first-time jurors selected to decide Tolbert's fate.

Andrea Mendoza | Juror: My name's Andrea Mendoza … I am a mom. I'm 26 years old. I'm currently a college student who is studying vet medicine.

John Grzybowski | Juror: My name is John … I'm a retired rocket scientist.

Anne-Marie Green: The setup in the Huntsville courtroom is a little different than it is in a lot of other places … the jury's kind of like in the middle of the room.

Andrea Mendoza: Yeah.

John Grzybowski: Yes … I had not heard about this shooting previously before the trial, so it was all new to me. So, I was just kind of … surprised that something this tragic had happened so close to where I live.

The case against David Tolbert would be argued by assistant district attorneys Shea Keller and Ben Gibbons.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: This case is about a master manipulator.

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: I think the real him showed himself … in the Tesla when he pulled the trigger.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: David Tolbert was somebody who wanted out of the circumstances of his life. … He wanted out of his marriage … it's about someone using … the fact that they're suffering … mental health issues, their darkest days against them, trying to make that the scapegoat for a murder.

The prosecution's case centered around security camera video — particularly, the grainy footage of Tolbert's red Tesla.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: Some of the worst evidence we've ever put in in a trial …

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: It did what it, you know, what we needed … in showing that the only two people to ever even approach that car … were Savannah, because she never left the car, unfortunately, and David, because he walks to the car presumably to find her body and then walks back in the store.

Prosecutors say David Tolbert shot Savannah Tolbert in cold blood before he walked back inside the store. And, because the Valley Pools camera was about 100 yards away from the Tesla —

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: … you can't definitively say you can see David open a car door on the driver's side. You can't tell if it's the front door or the back door. … I think that he opened the back door and kind of ducked down and shot her.

And they believe David Tolbert had been hiding the gun in the pouch of his hoodie – and that Savannah Tolbert saw it before he pulled the trigger.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: I think she saw, she turned, and that's why the bullet lodges where it lodges.

David Tolbert's defense case was based on Savannah Tolbert's struggles with her mental health. Defense attorneys said she had taken her own life. And they zeroed in on medical examiner Malone's own words in her report to make that case: that because it was an active investigation, suicide cannot be completely ruled out. Dr. Malone defended her findings.

Dr. Jonrika Malone: At the time that I closed my report, there were ongoing investigations … it's easier for me to explain it in the courtroom to say, yes, that's what I said, but it doesn't change the fact that it's a homicide.

Prosecutors also called Chelsea Finch, the woman they believed was the motive for the murder, as a witness. Chelsea told the court David Tolbert wanted a future with her.

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: … he lied to her as well.

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: That's true.

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He lied to everyone about everything. She wanted to believe him.

Finch testified that she broke up with Tolbert a few months after his arrest. Prosecutors learned that after David Tolbert's Tesla was processed for evidence, it was returned to him. Before he was arrested, he took a road trip with Chelsea.

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: He took her to Disney in that Tesla.

Anne-Marie Green: In the Tesla that Savannah died in?

Assistant D.A. Ben Gibbons: Yes.

The defense did not call any witnesses, and David Tolbert did not testify. He did not respond to our request for an interview. After three days of testimony, the jury got the case.

Andrea Mendoza: We wanted to all go through the evidence, but we were all pretty much on the same page.

They deliberated for about 3 hours.

John Grzybowski: We found him guilty.

Guilty of capital murder.

David Tolbert is led out of the courtroom after he was found guilty of capital murder. WHNT

Andrea Mendoza: I made it, uh, a thing to look at him directly as it was happening … they were putting him in handcuffs is when he kinda like … turned a little red and looked like he was a little wobbly in the lip … it's kind of like he knew it was coming is what it felt like in my opinion …

Savannah Tolbert's family still struggles with her death. For sisters, April and Holly, her loss is also a life lesson.

Holly Hancock: I think as a family member, a lesson that we have learned is that, like, you should speak up when you're uncomfortable and things don't seem right … And even if you're afraid that you're going to hurt your family member's feelings … your intuition is something that you should trust.

Savannah's daughter Avery lives with her dad and stepmom.

Anne-Marie Green: Do you see Savannah in Avery?

April Hancock: Yes.

Holly Hancock: So much so.

Anne-Marie Green: Tell me what you see.

April Hancock: Man, all her spunk, her intelligence, charisma.

Savannah Tolbert and daughter Avery Foster Savannah Tolbert's family

Today, she is finding her way and reaching for the stars.

Avery Foster: I hope to work for NASA and … join the astronaut program by taking that stepping stone of being a Naval pilot. … and I wanna show that there's women that can go through hard things and still make their dreams come true. … I think that drive really did come from my mom.

For Savannah's sisters, the jury's guilty verdict was bittersweet.

Holly Hancock: It wasn't a positive feeling, you know? … It's like, it doesn't bring her back …

Anne-Marie Green: Did you look at David?

April Hancock: Oh, most definitely … pay the piper. May you rot. May you rot.

David Tolbert is serving a life sentence without the possibility of parole. The prison where he's locked up is a place he knows all too well.

Anne-Marie Green: David Tolbert is a retired corrections officer. … Where is he now?

Assistant D.A. Shea Keller: Limestone Correctional Facility, the exact correctional facility where he was a corrections officer. … justice for the family and justice from our perspective is different. And that is just rich. … that is the cherry on the top for the two of us. Yes.

If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, contact SAMHSA'S National Helpline at 1-800-622-HELP.

Produced by Marcelena Spencer. Iris Carreras is the field producer. Michael Vele, Grayce Arlotta-Berner and Marcus Balsam are the editors. Anthony Batson is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.

World.title: In the Venezuelan stronghold of Doral, some voters discouraged by Trump's policies
World.content:
Latinos voted in record numbers for President Trump in 2024, but polling shows that voting bloc is up for grabs in the midterms.

And one region that reflects that shift is Florida's Miami-Dade County, where Latinos and Hispanics make up more than 70% of the population.

In January, CBS News met Andrea Ramos and her husband in Doral, Florida, as they were celebrating and closely following the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Ramos, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Venezuela, told CBS News that she credited President Trump with Maduro's capture. Doral has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.

"I had such big admiration for him," Ramos told CBS News about her sentiments for the president following Maduro's arrest and extradition to the U.S.

But about nine months later, her feelings have changed.

"I feel disappointed," Ramos said. "I feel, in a way, betrayed."

While disappointed with the economy, it is the Trump administration's immigration crackdown that has led Ramos to sour on Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

"Overall, I'm not feeling like the law is being respected," Ramos said.

According to a CBS News Battleground Tracker poll released earlier this month, 60% of Hispanic likely voters said they were likely backing congressional Democrats in the upcoming midterms, compared to 39% who said they were likely backing Republicans.

That marked a considerable shift from 2024 CBS News exit polls, which found that 51% of Hispanics voted for Democrats, compared to 46% who voted for Republicans.

In the same new poll, 59% of Hispanic likely voters found that the Trump administration was trying to deport more people than they had expected, compared to 51% of all likely voters.

Asked in the poll about the Trump administration's focus on deportation, 59% of Hispanic likely voters responded that it was too much, compared to 49% of all likely voters.

Stephanie Caro's family-owned coffee shop in Doral is among many local businesses that have seen a decrease in foot traffic and sales as masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have been photographed on the city's streets.

"I'd say there is a heightened sense of fear," Caro said.

Some local business owners have said they're concerned they'll have to close their doors.

"It really impacts the entire community," Caro said. "People are scared to leave their houses. They're changing their daily routines."

Doral voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, driven by Venezuelan Americans who fled Maduro's socialist regime.

But ICE has increasingly targeted asylum seekers who have pending cases and active work permits, and Mr. Trump's close relationship to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez has impacted his support in Doral.

When CBS News asked Doral's Republican Mayor Christi Fraga three times if she still supported Mr. Trump, Fraga refused to give a direct answer.

"There is a lot of things that I support, and there's also questions that I've raised," Fraga told CBS News.

Ramos remains undecided on who she will vote for in the upcoming midterms. On that question, Fraga also declined to advise her constituents to vote for Republicans.

Said Fraga, "Vote your conscience."

World.title: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protesters and police clash
World.content:
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.

Nuñez said the number of arrests is expected to rise significantly. He said marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.

He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.

A protester waves the French flag near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026. Aris MESSINIS /AFP via Getty Images

Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week.

Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.

Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march

Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."

Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.

Protesters march during a demonstration in Paris, Saturday, on Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP

The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.

As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."

Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said.

The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.

A protester clashes with police near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026. Aris Messinis /AFP via Getty Images

Protesters march against far-right gathering

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

A crowd marches along a sunken roadway during the cross-party protest against the National Rally in Orleans, France, on Oct. 24, 2026. Romain Gautier / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.

French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.

Protesters and police clash in smaller cities

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.

A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.

French policemen during a demonstration in Lyon, France on October 24, 2026. Mathieu Prudhomme/Anadolu via Getty Images

Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city.

Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details.

In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured.

Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.

A protester faces police officers in Toulouse, southwestern France on October 24, 2026. Matthieu Rondel /AFP via Getty Images

In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.

Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.

A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Strasbourg, France, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Jean-Francois Badias/AP

More protests spread across Europe

Other protests took place across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italian police said in a statement that they carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement said. Police on Saturday also said they had arrested a 30-year-old man suspected of being the figure behind the "October 17 Movement," a group which had called for the protests.

Soldiers were deployed to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, ahead of fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Others remained defiantly open after a call by the city's mayor Giuseppe Sala not to "panic."

"We want to give the message that we are not scared by these kids," said Alessandro Buhne, 30, who works at the Philipp Plein menswear shop. "Tourists are scared of this situation so we want to give the signal that you are safe if you enter our store."

Italy Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.

In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites.

Some protesters briefly broke into the Colosseum, officials said.

Police "managed to isolate and contain the violent fringes, with balance and professionalism," Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, according to Italian news agency ANSA.

"In Italy there can be no room for those who delude themselves that they can act with impunity," he said.

Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

Five hundred soldiers have been deployed to patrol Milan, Italy, on Oct. 23, 2026. Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu via Getty Images

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.

In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.

Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

World.title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
World.content:
A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.

Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.

The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.

Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

Still from a webcam of the Kehlsteinhaus early on Oct. 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out in the southern German state of Bavaria. Berchtesgaden /AFP via Getty Images

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.

There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Smoke is seen at the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, which once was Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, after a large fire had broken out. KERSTIN JOENSSON/AFP via Getty Images

Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.

"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

World.title: DOJ demands that some California counties set aside alleged noncitizen ballots
World.content:
Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Trump's Justice Department, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted L.A. County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of more than 20,000 people who it alleges are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the L.A. County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They were given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.

The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including Social Security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

However, the California attorney general's office said the letters contained errors. For example, Mendocino County officials received a list of people who were not residents there, according to a court filing by the state.

Department of Justice spokeswoman Kiersten Pels emphasized in a statement on Saturday that the department is explicitly "not requesting a purge, cancellation of registrations, or any programmatic action."

Instead, Pels wrote, federal officials are asking for collaboration to "ensure the most secure election in California history."

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.

"All of this is simply meant to raise huge doubts about the integrity of this election," said John Tuteur, the registrar of voters for Napa County in California's wine country.

Tuteur said that two uniformed Department of Homeland Security officers delivered a letter to his office late on Friday afternoon. The letter included the names of 42 people whom the federal government accused of being noncitizens illegally registered to vote. There are roughly 86,000 people registered to vote across the county of over 130,000 people, Tuteur said. Approximately 11,000 people had already cast a mail-in ballot as of Friday.

Tuteur and other election officials who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday said they have already started to count ballots that have trickled in from the state's 23 million registered voters.

"We're not changing anything we're doing. We're proceeding with the election," he said.

He said his employees and his relatives were worried about what could come next.

"My family's upset, worried about what's going to happen to me," he said.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

"This is NOT A DRILL: Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said in a statement Friday. "Trump's DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They've admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere."

World.title: When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?
World.content:
When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?

Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images

How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?

That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.

Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.

Sponsor Message

Impact on youth body image

For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino, the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.

Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.

"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."

Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.

The problem with 'subtle' editing

However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.

Sponsor Message

Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.

It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.

"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."

Tech guardrails vs. moving targets

Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.

The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems. Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.

Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.

Evolving beauty standards

They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Sponsor Message

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.

Technological changes

While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

Legal and regional challenges

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.

Sponsor Message

Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.

In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.

Teens want to be heard

Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"

Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

World.title: More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are
World.content:
More dads taking paid family leave for a new baby, sometimes as much as moms are

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Karlo Campana is usually outnumbered these days. He has three young kids under age 4.

On a recent Saturday, he played a mini-game of basketball with his two older kids in their Southern California home, shooting a ball into a hoop on the door, while his baby boy watched from his bouncy chair.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Campana took paid time off in May after the birth of his son — just as he did for his daughters.

It's sometimes called "bonding" or "family" leave, to distinguish it from the paid leave ("maternity" or "disability" leave) that mothers can take to physically recover from childbirth.

"You need that adjustment period," he said. Campana, who works at an ad agency, said having the time off not to think about work — or worry about losing income during that time — was crucial for him and his family during a sleep-deprived period.

Sponsor Message

"My wife isn't doing it on her own," he said. "She doesn't feel like she's alone on this journey. She feels like she has support." He jokes that by kid No. 3, he thought he had nailed diaper changes without too much mess — but he was wrong.

"The benefits are I get to spend time with each of them when they were in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers," he said. " It's like the funny moments of, like, being a parent, like, 'This is it right here, you're in the thick of it.'"

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Campana is among a growing number of fathers who take leave to bond with a new child in the states that offer paid family leave programs — and are part of a larger cultural shift that has seen dads handle more caregiving duties.

In California — as in several other states — men make up about half of bonding claim applications. Last year, men even surpassed women — as in Colorado and Washington — for the first time in the state's history. This trend comes at a time when the federal government has said it wants Americans to have more babies, and families report affordability is an obstacle in raising them.

Sponsor Message

There's no federal law guaranteeing paid parental leave, but California is one of 14 states, plus Washington, D.C., that have passed legislation to enact paid family leave programs — and in many of those places, more dads are opting in.

"We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20-plus years ago," said Molly Weston Williamson, policy director at Paid Leave for All, an organization that advocates for paid family leave policies.

California's program offers, within a year, up to eight weeks of paid bonding leave for parents after a birth, adoption, or foster care placement. That's on top of six to eight weeks of paid disability leave that moms get to recover after birth.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

Campana said he initially wasn't sure if he should take paternity leave because of lingering gender stereotypes.

" I felt guilty, for sure," Campana said. " I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working."

Campana said that when he was growing up, his father worked three jobs. "It was hard for him to be present, and I think that's the one thing now — it's like, 'No, be present. Be there for your kids.'"

Research has shown that paternity leave confers benefits beyond allowing a father extra time to bond with a new child: It has positive effects on the whole family, including better health outcomes for both parents.

Paid parental leave has also been linked to lower odds of postpartum depression and a decrease in infant mortality rates.

In California, men accounted for 51% of bonding claims filed in 2025. It's a massive shift from when the state program started in 2004, and men made up about 18% of claim applications.

Sponsor Message

States fund their paid family and medical leave programs with different combinations of employer and employee contributions; California is among six states where family leave is entirely funded by employee payroll deductions.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

In addition to changing gender norms, Williamson said other factors are likely contributing to the increase in claims by men in the state: greater awareness about the program, and recent changes to the benefit.

In 2025, the state boosted the amount of income a worker can recoup while on family leave. Now, in California and in other states, the leave benefit can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.

"That makes it a realistic option for a lot more families, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change," Williamson said. Still, she said, there's a lot the new data about dads isn't telling us.

"We're getting one particular vantage point into this data, which is useful and valuable, but it's only telling us sort of part of the story, and we'd need other kinds of information to better understand the full picture," Williamson said.

"Is it that more dads are working and therefore are potentially eligible for these benefits? Is it that women are deciding not to take leave?"

While private employers can offer their own paid leave as a benefit, this data also reflects only people who took leave through California's paid family leave program.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

A spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department, which administers the state's family leave program, said the department couldn't provide definitive reasons for the increase in male bonding claims.

One thing is clear: The growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically.

President Trump has said, "We want more babies," and has promoted policy initiatives like expanding access to in vitro fertilization and offering investment accounts for newborns.

Sponsor Message

"People really are very worried about the affordability of kids," said Jeremy Pope, a professor of political science at Brigham Young University, and a principal investigator of the American Family Survey.

toggle caption i Dania Maxwell for NPR

According to the latest survey in 2025, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children had become unaffordable, according to the survey. It was the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago.

"I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids," Pope said. "But they worry a lot about how much it costs and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs."

The Pew Research Center found in a recent survey of full-time working parents who are not self-employed, 84% said paid parental, family, or medical leave would be "extremely or very helpful" to them, but only half said it was available to them.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with LAist and KFF Health News.

World.title: In Arkansas, Democrats see an opening at the edge of the competitive midterms map
World.content:
In Arkansas, Democrats see an opening at the edge of the competitive midterms map

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

HOPE, Ark. — For Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner, the most important political label she wears isn't that she's a Democrat. Or that she's not a Republican. Instead, it's that she is an Arkansan.

As a lunchtime crowd ate at Tailgater's Burger Company Friday, Shoffner decried what she called a historically unproductive Congress driven by extreme voices in each party and pitched herself to receptive — if skeptical — voters as a candidate who would better serve their needs.

Arkansas is one of the most conservative states in the country, with nearly two out of three voters supporting President Trump in 2024 and Republican Sen. Tom Cotton in 2020.

Sponsor Message

But in the final days of the 2026 midterm election, Shoffner and other Arkansas Democrats are crisscrossing the state with a message that seeks to capitalize on the Trump administration's unpopularity, stubbornly high prices and anti-incumbency vibes.

"We're the sleeper race," Shoffner told NPR. "I mean, we're the race that no one's noticed and that no one is going to see coming."

Republicans have taken some notice, pre-emptively pouring millions of dollars into the Senate race, the Little Rock-based 2nd Congressional District and robust get-out-the vote efforts to try and stem the rising tide of dissatisfaction with the party.

But even in a midterm cycle where Senate races in states like Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are viewed as tossups, and where the landscape of potentially competitive House races stretches deep into conservative territory, Arkansas seems a bridge too far for election forecasters.

Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District is considered "Likely Republican," according to the Cook Political Report, and its Senate race is "Solid Republican."

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

Arkansas First

At an outdoor coffee shop in Arkadelphia, Vanilla Hannah said she was there to support Shoffner and talk about her own reelection bid to be a local justice of the peace. She said it's possible that Arkansas could elect Democrats this year because the crop of candidates seems willing to work with people to meet their needs — and there are a lot of them.

Sponsor Message

"When it comes down to basic needs or whatever, the 'D' or the 'R' after your name don't mean a thing, because we're all suffering and all having the same issues and everybody's ready for a change," she said. "And running for an election is not just running specifically on the Democratic policies or the Republican or the libertarians or whatever. It's just what you believe in, and it seems like more and more people are having a common belief now."

Later, Shoffner visited a small family farm in nearby Bierne where several members of the Hatley family cooked sorghum to make syrup and talked about why they were supporting her campaign.

Shoffner is a multigenerational farmer who decided to shut down her family's operation in 2025, citing financial headwinds from rising input costs and Trump administration tariff and trade policies. That in turn inspired her Senate run and influenced much of her campaign's focus.

Sliding behind the wheel of a side-by-side utility vehicle, Shoffner takes off across the property and recounts her life story that led her away from the farm, into nonprofit work and back home when her dad got sick.

She doesn't buy the argument that her chances are low to win.

"This race isn't about Democrats or Republicans or independents or any of that," she said. "This isn't some kind of weird political alignment, this is a values alignment. This is reorienting representation in Arkansas based on common sense, based on compassion and based on showing up."

She said national Republicans — and Democrats — have made the mistake of ignoring the needs of Arkansas residents, especially with agriculture and trade policies.

"I come from a place, a community, that died in my lifetime," she said. "I was the last one left and I felt left behind. I felt like no one was really talking to me or talking about me. I felt like folks were making decisions about me, but without me, and ultimately they were rewriting the rules."

Sponsor Message

Now, with record diesel prices, the war in Iran and tariffs, Shoffner said she believes that Arkansas voters of all stripes want something different. She's also glad that the race hasn't seen an influx of outside air support from national Democratic groups.

"I don't need them, I really don't," she said. "This is an Arkansas First campaign, and I'm an Arkansan, and I want to talk directly to Arkansans, and I want them to know that when I go to D.C., the only letters that will mean anything next to my name are the "A" and the "R."

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

'Folks are hurting'

On the flip side, Chris Jones has the backing of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee as one of dozens of "Red to Blue" flip targets.

At an outdoor jazz night held at a brewery in Little Rock, Jones worked the crowd between visits to polling sites and a high school football homecoming game on a campaign that has seen millions of dollars in outside spending by Republicans.

"They understand that people are in pain," he said. "Folks are hurting. They can't afford gas. They can't afford groceries. And our campaign has always been about affordability and accountability for all. So prices are way too high."

Jones also ran for governor against Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in 2022 and lost, so he started off with higher name recognition as a serious challenger to Rep. French Hill.

He knows it's a tall task, even in a national environment more favorable to Democrats. Hill is a longtime incumbent whose district only became more conservative after the last Census-led redistricting in 2021.

But he also knows that Democrats, Republicans and independent voters alike are open to looking for something other than the current leadership.

"Here's what's so fascinating: a lot of folks here voted for the president and this administration because they wanted lower prices, they wanted to end foreign wars, and they wanted to end corruption, particularly with the Epstein files," he said. "None of that has happened, so they're super frustrated."

Sponsor Message

Like many states that have seen the potential for close races next week, Arkansas has a longer history of single-party control that has led to anger and frustration at the status quo and incumbency in a way that extends beyond typical partisan labels or voting history.

"One of the things that we forget, because there's so much that comes out of this administration: It wasn't but 15 years ago that the entire federal delegation of Arkansas was Democrat," he said. "So it's not that long ago. The reason they got in office was because of the conditions that existed, the economic anxiety and pain that people feel — and folks feeling like what they wanted to happen out of Washington was not happening. We're in that same place now."

In addition to the DCCC support, Jones has had campaign visits from former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear have both endorsed his run. And he's heard from people who don't normally support Democrats saying they'll back his campaign.

"Folks are literally hurting, and it's to the point where they're saying, 'my life is so bad that I don't care about party anymore'," he said.

Black voter turnout surges

Another factor working in Democrats' favor this election cycle is a surge in Black turnout following a Supreme Court decision that weakened part of the Voting Rights Act.

Multiple states across the South rushed to redraw House maps to gain a partisan advantage, with many of the new districts crafted in a way that minimized Black voting power. Arkansas lawmakers did not redraw their maps — the state has an entirely Republican congressional delegation — but after the 2020 Census did split Little Rock up in a manner that made Hill's district more Republican.

In primaries following the ruling, and early voting this month ahead of the midterms, there has been sustained higher Black turnout in states like South Carolina, Georgia and Louisiana in ways that could affect the outcome in key races across the region.

Sponsor Message

"I think part of it is that folks realized that there was an imminent threat to their right to vote," Jones said. "And people realized across the country that if we don't show up now, and Black folks realize if we don't speak up now, then our ability to do it later might not be there."

Marcus Hatley, one of the people who met with Shoffner at his family farm, said the increased turnout seemed like a "course correction."

"People are dissatisfied with the way that that happened, and some are crossing sides and voting in a different direction," he said. "And a lot of it has to do with removing, in some of those states, the ability for people of color to have equal representation in their districts. So it looks like to me there's going to be a course correction. I could be wrong, but I believe there's going to be a change."

World.title: Independent candidates sense a moment in the West. Democrats are hoping they're right
World.content:
Independent candidates sense a moment in the West. Democrats are hoping they're right

toggle caption i Austin Johnson/AFP via Getty Images
