World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

World.title: 20 years of ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’: 5 facts about Del Toro’s masterpiece
World.content:
Two decades after its theatrical release, “El Laberinto del Fauno” (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) remains Guillermo del Toro’s magnum opus and a timeless classic of popular culture. What began as a modest, independent project between Mexico and Spain ended up breaking records and conventions on a global scale: It moved the Cannes Film Festival with a legendary 20-minute standing ovation, grossed over US $80 million worldwide at the box office, and cemented its critical success by winning three Oscars and numerous awards at national and international ceremonies.

Set in the postwar period of 1944, this R-rated film follows Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), a young girl sent to an oppressive military camp controlled by her violent stepfather, Captain Vidal (Sergi López), a Francoist officer obsessed with eradicating the guerrilla resistance. In this hostile environment, Ofelia discovers a labyrinth where an ancient faun (Doug Jones) reveals a delicate truth to her: She is Princess Moanna, ruler of the underground kingdom, and must complete supernatural tasks to reclaim her throne.

Weaving historical horrors with fantasy, “El Laberinto del Fauno” serves as a profound allegory about the loss of innocence and the importance of ethical disobedience in the face of injustice and oppression.

To mark its 20th anniversary and re-release in theaters, we’re delving into the depths of this legendary labyrinth to bring you the most amazing and unexpected behind-the-scenes facts: from its original conception and its connection to “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”), to how the story managed to make Stephen King himself squirm in his seat.

1. The original script was darker and more sexual

Little Ofelia’s journey — forced to overcome dangerous, fantastical challenges after moving to a military setting — did not always have the tone or the ending that we have come to love and admire. Few people know that, in its early stages of development, “El Laberinto del Fauno” did not feature a young girl as the protagonist, nor was it set in postwar Spain.

In the original version, Guillermo del Toro wrote a much rawer, darker and more erotically charged draft set in the Victorian era. The protagonist was an adult, pregnant woman who discovered the labyrinth after moving with her husband into an old mansion. There she met the faun, but instead of undertaking fantastical tasks to reclaim her throne, she became entangled in a dark, passionate relationship with the creature.

In the official DVD commentary, the director shares details of this concept: “They made passionate love, she fell in love with him, and he asked for the blood of the firstborn in return for the labyrinth to open and for her to go to the magical kingdom with him.”

By shifting his focus to childhood, Del Toro transformed that idea of adult horror into the fascinating gem of innocence, resilience and rebellion that made it to the big screen. Fortunately for the history of cinema, the Mexican director changed his mind just in time.

2. Two films connected

“El Laberinto del Fauno” was conceived by Del Toro as a companion piece to his 2001 film “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”). Although they lack a direct narrative connection or shared characters, the director has formally defined them as “mirror films” due to their profound parallels. Together, they function as a diptych that explores the horror of war through the vulnerable and unspoiled eyes of childhood.

Beyond the historical context — with “El Espinazo del Diablo” set in 1939 during the Spanish Civil War and “El Laberinto del Fauno” in 1944 during the postwar Franco era — the closest connection between the two films is that neither uses horror in a superficial way.

The supernatural appears in Del Toro’s films from a profound and metaphorical dimension to help us process social tragedies and shed light on the darkest corners of the human condition. As the filmmaker explained to Voices of Monterey Bay: “In fairy tales, monsters exist to be a manifestation of something we need to understand, not just a problem we need to overcome.”

Like its predecessor, “El Laberinto del Fauno” demonstrates that true monstrosity does not stem from the supernatural realm — symbolized by the faun and the creatures of the underworld — but rather from the cruelty of human beings.

In both stories, the authentic villains are bloodthirsty, heartless men — such as Jacinto and Captain Vidal — who are obsessed with money, weapons and absolute control. It is in the face of these oppressors’ brutality that the child protagonists use their imagination and sensitivity to come to terms with the world they find themselves living in, defy the tyrants and defend their very existence.

3. The origin of the faun

Long before becoming an iconic figure in modern fantasy, the faun was already haunting Guillermo del Toro’s mind. During his childhood, the director used to have intense lucid dreams in which this creature came to life, emerging from the back of an old family wardrobe.

“I used to sleep at my grandmother’s house … And every night, right at midnight, in my bedroom, a faun would come out of the armoire. It must have been lucid dreaming, but for a child, it was as if it were real,” he told The Guardian. “I would see the faun’s human hand emerge from the armoire, then the smiling face of a goat, and then the hairy leg of a goat. I could clearly see him pulling his body out of the armoire, and I would start screaming.”

For Del Toro, bringing the monster that made him scream at night to the big screen was his way of coming to terms with his childhood fears. Although the faun we see in the film underwent countless changes in appearance, the idea was born from that peculiar childhood experience. Who would have thought that those terrifying sleepless nights would be the origin of the fantastical universe that would ultimately establish him as an international star?

4. The bold rejection of Hollywood that preserved the film’s identity

When the major studios read the story of “El Laberinto del Fauno,” they tried to entice Guillermo del Toro by offering to double the budget, on the condition that he relocate the story to the U.S. market.

However, true to his artistic vision, the filmmaker flatly refused. He believed that if he accepted the change in language and setting, the story would lose all its political power, its historical context and its authentic identity.

During an interview with KPBS, he clarified the direction the film would have taken under the industry’s commercial demands: “I never would have attempted to make ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ in Hollywood because we would have audience-tested it, and we would have had a super-happy ending with dancing little creatures.”

5. The movie terrified the ‘master of horror’ himself

Sharing your work with an icon like Stephen King is a dream come true for any filmmaker, but to make the master of horror himself squirm with fear at your own movie is an achievement reserved for very few. That’s exactly what Del Toro experienced in New England during a special screening of “El Laberinto del Fauno.”

During the iconic scene where the unsettling Pale Man comes to life to chase Ofelia, the Mexican director noticed that the celebrated writer began shifting uncomfortably in his seat, completely overwhelmed by the tension.

As you can imagine, witnessing the obvious unease of one of his greatest artistic influences was one of the most significant moments of recognition in his entire career.

As Del Toro explains in the film’s official commentary: “I must say, it remains the single best screening experience of my life — sitting next to Stephen King and watching him squirm during the Pale Man sequence. That, for me, is an Oscar. That’s absolutely the best thing that ever happened to me in my life.”

Disobedience as a legacy

Two decades have passed since Ofelia first entered the labyrinth, and the good news is that this dark fairy tale retains its ability to delight and unsettle us. Beyond its global box office success and a historic awards season — in which it won three Oscars (art direction, cinematography and makeup), three BAFTAs, seven Goya Awards, and nine Ariel Awards, among others — the deepest impact of Guillermo del Toro’s masterpiece lies in its power to engage with the challenges of modern times.

Far from being a childish escapist fable, this film stands as a manifesto on individual sovereignty and civil disobedience in the face of the dangers of blind, mechanical and unconditional submission. The lesson the film continues to impart to us today is that, in the face of overwhelming and dehumanizing authority, dissent is not an act of immature rebellion, but rather a moral virtue and an indispensable tool for survival.

As Dr. Ferreiro so aptly put it before his execution: “To obey just like that, for the sake of obeying, without questioning … That’s something only people like you can do, Captain.”

Twenty years later, that call to think for oneself and to challenge tyrants — both on and off the screen — remains more alive and urgent than ever.

Carolina Alvarado is a Venezuelan journalist who has devoted much of her career to creative writing, university teaching and social work. She has been published in Lady Science, Latina Media, Global Comment, Psiquide, Cinetopic, Get Me Giddy and Reader’s Digest, among others.

World.title: Mexican Americans are Mexico’s untapped opportunity: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Being married to a woman born in India, I have watched in amazement over the years at the level of engagement and activity that the Indian American community has with India. I think a lot of that starts with a deep-rooted sense of pride. Despite the country’s economic and other challenges, India’s education system instills a sense of pride in its history, culture and contributions to the world — a pride that people carry with them when they move abroad. You often see a similar sense of pride among immigrants from other countries. Many Indian businesses in the United States, despite the geographical distance from India, stay closely connected with the country. They look customers to grow, for suppliers to source from, and for talent to staff their teams. They look to create businesses that can operate in both countries and take advantage of the strengths of each country.

Just as importantly, the Indian government has worked hard to keep Indian Americans informed and educated about modern India — motivating them to stay engaged with the country. India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, has taken 10 trips to the U.S. since he was first elected prime minister in 2014. On these visits, he often focuses on the business community. He has done rallies in Madison Square Garden in New York City, met with technology executives in San Francisco, and on his “Howdy Modi” tour in 2019, even gave a speech to over 50,000 people in a football stadium in Houston, Texas. His messages to the Indian American community — urging them to remember and invest in India — are crystal clear. He is aware that the Indian American community, estimated to be 5.6 million people, less than 0.4% of the Indian population in India, is vital to the success of his country. He has leveraged their cultural pride and inspired them to turn it into action. It’s about more than a community remembering its roots; instead, he has turned it into a recognition of the diaspora’s central role in India’s future.

By comparison, an estimated 38 million Mexican Americans live in the United States, equivalent to almost 30% of the Mexican population actually living in Mexico. A recent study by the Latino Donor Collaborative estimated the GDP of Hispanic Americans (of whom over 60% are Mexican) to be US $4.4 trillion, which would make it the fourth-largest economy in the world.

Despite the geographic proximity of Mexico to the U.S., the significant trade between the two countries, and the massive Mexican diaspora in the U.S., Mexican presidents have rarely spent much time in the U.S. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Sheinbaum’s predecessor, came to the U.S. just five times in his six years in office, each time to attend a large global conference like U.N. Security Council meetings or the APEC summit. Sheinbaum, in over two years, has gone just twice: once to attend the FIFA World Cup draw and the other time to attend the FIFA World Cup final. Neither president spent significant time engaging the Mexican American community or the business community in the U.S.

Think about that for a moment: India’s Prime Minister has come to the U.S. more frequently over the past decade than Mexico’s presidents have. For some further perspective, Canada’s Prime Minister, Mark Carney, has been to the U.S. seven times already in just his first 18 months in office. Other members of Sheinbaum’s cabinet do travel more often to the U.S. Her economy minister, Marcelo Ebrard, frequently travels to the U.S., usually to Washington, D.C., for trade negotiations. Her foreign minister, Roberto Velasco, has also gone several times in his first few months in office, but does not yet have the experience or gravitas of la presidenta.

So what is going on here? Does it matter that Mexico’s presidents for the past eight years have spent so little time in the U.S.? And if it does matter, why?

I think Mexico is missing out on a huge opportunity. It’s extremely important to understand that, despite the significant Mexican American population in the U.S., net migration of Mexicans to the U.S. has been essentially flat for nearly two decades. What that means is that many, if not most, Mexican Americans living in the U.S. today have an increasingly outdated perspective on modern-day Mexico. Many are second or third generation, and as a result have few direct ties to the country. Many others know little more about the country than what they hear from family members back in their hometowns. Still others have never been to Mexico, or perhaps haven’t been there for decades. Most can’t fathom doing business in Mexico, let alone moving back there someday.

I have seen this firsthand countless times. I have had hundreds of conversations with Mexican Americans throughout the U.S. who often know shockingly little about Mexico. They know where their family is originally from. They are, of course, connected culturally through language, religion, food and music. But they often recite the same generic, outdated and negative soundbites about the country that a typical non-Mexican American would have. When asked, they almost always focus on the violence, the cartels, the drug problems, etc. Both the U.S. and Mexican media are in part to blame for this, but it goes beyond that.

As our team was developing MND Kids and was speaking to dozens of Mexican American school administrators from majority Mexican American school districts, we were constantly amazed at how many of them had never been to Mexico. Sadly, when asked why, many of them cited violence and didn’t even express a desire to visit. I have been equally shocked at how many Mexican American businesspeople I’ve met who haven’t considered Mexico as a place to grow their businesses with new customers, to expand their supplier base, or to build a bi-national business that taps into the talent of Mexico. There are many tens of thousands of medium and small businesses that could benefit from doing business in Mexico. Let me be clear: I am not saying that Mexican Americans should engage with Mexico out of obligation, but rather see engagement as an opportunity for their own business or family.

It’s also important to point out that millions of Mexican Americans send remittances (over US $60 billion in 2025) back to family members in Mexico each year. As Sheinbaum has often said, these people are quite literally modern-day heroes for the sacrifices they make by working hard abroad, away from family and friends, while sending money back to support their communities.

Failing to build stronger ties with the diaspora is a huge missed opportunity, and the Mexico News Daily team is certain that we can and must play an important role in further engaging this community. I personally have been working very hard to actively find ways for us to do so, including attending the national conferences of the U.S.-Mexico Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C., and the U.S. Hispanic Chamber of Commerce in Fort Worth, Texas, in just the past few months. I have also met with Ana Valdez of the Latino Donor Collaborative to explore collaboration with her organization, and I just recently met with the newly formed American Mexican Leadership Council to find out how we can work with them.

The following is a summary of what the MND team has been working on, as well as a preview of what is coming soon:

Preparing a bi-weekly business newsletter for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Mexico – Active Preparing a monthly business newsletter for the U.S.-Mexico Chamber of Commerce chapters of California, Houston and Miami, with more chapters to come – Active Creating more business newsletters with other U.S.-Mexico organizations – Coming soon Publishing weekly MND Intelligence reports that educate and inform about Mexico with data, not opinions – Active Publishing MND Kids as a tool to educate, inform and engage Mexican American kids in the U.S. about Mexico. – Active Launching MND en Español to reach a broader audience of Mexican Americans who might prefer to read in Spanish – Coming soon Engaging with the Mexican government to inspire them to leverage our platform to connect with both Mexican American communities and foreign commuities in Mexico – Coming soon Launching a new podcast targeting the Mexican American community – Coming soon Publishing a deep-dive series on Education in Mexico to highlight problem areas, as well as opportunities for engagement and improvement – Coming soon

We are certain that both countries can achieve massive benefits from a more actively engaged Mexican American diaspora. The team at MND will do our part to educate and inform the Mexican American community, and to inspire leaders to increase the engagement between the two countries. We have no doubt that a more actively engaged diaspora can accomplish great things.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ breaks down the state of public education in Mexico
World.content:
Many foreigners have a positive impression of the private education system in Mexico. I have written about it several times, and we even did an entire season of our Confidently Wrong podcast on what it is like for foreign kids to go to school in Mexico. We interviewed kids, parents, teachers, and administrators about what they have experienced and what they would recommend to families considering making the move.

In this new episode of Confidently Wrong, we focus on the public education system in Mexico. Several weeks ago, the international standardized testing results of PISA were released for 15-year-olds across the globe. The results were troubling in most countries, but especially bad in Mexico, which saw its results continue to deteriorate across the board. I reviewed the disastrous results in a recent article here: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO.

The test results show that nearly half of Mexican 15-year-olds cannot read at the most basic level. This means that they cannot even read at a level that permits them to learn. Imagine what awaits these kids in an economy that increasingly requires knowledge of AI and robotics for what used to be entry-level manufacturing jobs.

Mexico News Daily recently wrote a deep-dive report into the Mexican public education system. We looked at key metrics across the educational spectrum, and looked at the country’s progress (or lack of) in each. You can check it out here: The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 2: Education.

Tune into this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong as we break down the problems and implications of the public education system in Mexico.

World.title: Mining Tech Chief Calls Chile Underexplored
World.content:
Mining and mineral-processing sites in the Antofagasta Region of northern Chile, including green evaporation ponds, seen from the International Space Station on 7 July 2023. Illustrative image, not a copper exploration site and not linked to KoBold Metals. Photo: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

CHILE · MINING · COPPER EXPLORATION

Tom Hunt, chief technology officer of the artificial-intelligence explorer KoBold Metals, told Chile’s Diario Financiero that the country is “definitely under-explored” for copper, although his company has no project there yet.

Key Facts — The claim KoBold’s chief technology officer calls Chile “definitely under-explored” and points to copper deeper underground.

— The company KoBold uses artificial intelligence to find mineral deposits and has no project in Chile yet.

— The ranking Chile leads world copper exploration spending with US$669.6 million in 2025, or 20.5% of the total.

— The US link Chile supplied 68% of US refined copper imports from 2021 to 2024.

— The gap Only 2 of 94 exploration companies counted in Chile in 2025 were from the United States.

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

Tom Hunt, chief technology officer of the mineral-exploration company KoBold Metals, told the Chilean business daily Diario Financiero in an interview dated Saturday 24 October 2026 that Chile is “definitely under-explored” for copper. KoBold, which uses artificial intelligence to choose where to drill, has no project in Chile yet, and Hunt said it has not found the right partner.

For US readers the claim touches a supply line, since Chile provided 68% of US refined copper imports from 2021 to 2024, according to the US Geological Survey, and copper joined the official US list of critical minerals in November 2025. It is also the view of an interested party, because Diario Financiero reports that KoBold earns no revenue until a mine it helped find starts producing.

In Plain English KoBold Metals: an exploration company founded in 2018 that uses data, sensors and machine learning to pick drilling targets.

an exploration company founded in 2018 that uses data, sensors and machine learning to pick drilling targets. Under-explored: an area where many ore bodies are thought to be undiscovered because few drill holes have reached deep enough.

an area where many ore bodies are thought to be undiscovered because few drill holes have reached deep enough. Porphyry copper: a large copper deposit that forms deep underground; Hunt says the first Chilean mines were found where such deposits had eroded to the surface.

a large copper deposit that forms deep underground; Hunt says the first Chilean mines were found where such deposits had eroded to the surface. Cochilco: the Chilean Copper Commission, the state agency that advises the government and publishes mining statistics.

What Hunt Told Diario Financiero

Hunt argued that Chile’s first mines were the easy finds, because porphyry copper formed at least three to five kilometres (about two to three miles) down and only bodies that rose and eroded left surface clues. “All those deposits have already been found,” he said, but about 1,000 metres (about 3,300 feet) further down he sees “an equivalent distribution” of ore bodies that are far harder to find, since each sample needs a US$1 million drill hole.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

“I guarantee you they are there in Chile, because of how the ore formed,” Hunt said, adding that it is “a matter of putting up the money and the brains” to find them. This is a geological opinion, and the interview offers no Chilean drilling or survey data to back it.

“Definitely under-explored.”

Tom Hunt, KoBold Metals, Diario Financiero, 24 October 2026 (our translation)

KoBold is not active in Chile “yet”, Hunt said, stressing the word because “we know Chile has world-class rocks”, though the best ground already has an owner. It wants a joint venture with a partner such as Codelco, Chile’s state copper company, that would supply the land while KoBold supplies its models, sensors and, depending on the partner, operations.

Who KoBold Metals Is

KoBold was founded in 2018 by Kurt House, now its chief executive, Josh Goldman, now its president, and Jeff Jurinak, and says its goal is to turn exploration into a “repeatable science”. Diario Financiero reports that it has about 50 projects at different stages, in Zambia, Congo, Namibia, Sweden, Finland, Canada, the United States and Australia but none yet in South America.

Diario Financiero reports that KoBold pools satellite images, geophysical surveys, old drill logs and hand-drawn maps into one database, and Hunt says its sensor reads about 500 colours where a phone camera reads three, with geologists deciding where to drill. The company asks governments for concessions or forms joint ventures, sells no software and, the paper says, expects revenue only when one of its mines produces.

Its flagship, the Mingomba copper project in Zambia, broke ground on Wednesday 29 April 2026 with Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema present, KoBold says, and the company puts the investment at more than US$2 billion, with about 300,000 tonnes of copper a year targeted and first output expected in the early 2030s. We covered the project in our earlier report on the Mingomba mine.

What Chile’s Own Data Shows

The Chilean Copper Commission, known as Cochilco, counted US$874.7 million of exploration spending in Chile in 2025, which put the country fourth in the world with 7.1% of the US$12.4 billion global total. In copper alone Chile ranked first, with US$669.6 million, or 20.5% of world copper exploration, ahead of the United States at US$398.3 million.

Chile Exploration in 2025 Budget: US$874.7 million, up US$80.7 million from 2024.

US$874.7 million, up US$80.7 million from 2024. Who pays: large miners 78.9%, junior explorers 14.8% (US$129.1 million).

large miners 78.9%, junior explorers 14.8% (US$129.1 million). Where it goes: 51.4% inside operating mines (US$449.3 million), US$206.5 million to initial-stage exploration.

51.4% inside operating mines (US$449.3 million), US$206.5 million to initial-stage exploration. Prospects: 235 in all, with 158 active and 77 stalled.

235 in all, with 158 active and 77 stalled. Copper in the ground: 731.9 million tonnes of reserves and resources, the most of any country.

Cochilco says the challenge is to turn that spending into discoveries and developable projects without relying too heavily on work next to existing mines. It adds that more than 80% of active prospects lie in the northern regions of Atacama, Antofagasta and Coquimbo.

What It Means for You

The real stake for US readers is dependence on Chilean metal. Chile supplied 68% of US refined copper imports from 2021 to 2024, the US Geological Survey says, and it estimates that net imports covered 57% of US copper use in 2025, up from 45% in 2024.

Copper joined the US List of Critical Minerals on Friday 7 November 2025, a list the Interior Department says guides strategies to secure the nation’s mineral supply chains. Cochilco counted only 2 US companies among the 94 firms exploring in Chile in 2025, against 48 from Canada and 18 from Australia.

Cochilco says Chile allows accelerated six-year depreciation of exploration spending and sets its corporate tax rate at 27%. The interview itself announces no deal, project or investment, so it is a signal of intent, not a business event.

What to Watch Whether KoBold names a Chilean partner or a project.

Hunt’s appearance at Mining MAS Pitch, an event organised by DF MAS and ME Elecmetal on Wednesday 4 November.

Whether Codelco or other Chilean operators answer the joint-venture idea.

Whether Cochilco’s next exploration catalogue, after the November 2025 edition, shows more early-stage work.

What Is Not Known

No Chilean project, partner, concession or budget has been named. “Under-explored” is Hunt’s opinion, and we found no Chilean government measure that says so.

A 2021 Cochilco study found that new copper discoveries did not measurably change early-stage exploration budgets, a sign of balance between new information and lost ground, and called Latin America balanced for copper and gold. It covers regions, not Chile alone.

KoBold has one large discovery so far, and Hunt will discuss its hit rate only “when we have five discoveries”. Diario Financiero reports that a Berkeleyside profile quoted the mining executive Mike Anglin saying Mingomba extends ore bodies already mapped, and the consultant Mothusi Pahl saying KoBold underestimated its cost, claims we could not check.

Diario Financiero’s headline says KoBold is backed by Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos and Sam Altman, but KoBold’s website shows only logos of funds and companies such as Andreessen Horowitz and BHP Ventures. We could not confirm the Bezos and Altman stakes at any KoBold or investor page, so we attribute the claim to the newspaper.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Tom Hunt and what did he say about Chile?

Tom Hunt is chief technology officer of KoBold Metals, an exploration company that uses artificial intelligence. He told Diario Financiero, in an interview dated Saturday 24 October 2026, that Chile is “definitely under-explored” for copper.

Does KoBold Metals operate in Chile?

No, Hunt said the company is not active in Chile yet and has not found the right partner. Diario Financiero lists its projects in Zambia, Congo, Namibia, Sweden, Finland, Canada, the United States and Australia.

Is Chile really under-explored?

That is Hunt’s opinion, and we found no Chilean government measure that says so. Cochilco does show Chile first in world copper exploration spending, at US$669.6 million in 2025.

Why does Chilean copper matter to the United States?

Chile supplied 68% of US refined copper imports from 2021 to 2024, according to the US Geological Survey. Copper has also been on the US List of Critical Minerals since November 2025.

Who backs KoBold Metals?

Diario Financiero describes it as backed by Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos and Sam Altman. KoBold’s website shows logos of funds and companies, including Andreessen Horowitz and BHP Ventures, but no individuals.

World.title: Chile’s Kast and UK Talk Falklands and Trade
World.content:
The Chilean Navy frigate Almirante Condell, a former Royal Navy Type 23 frigate, leaving the port of Valparaíso on 19 March 2019. File photo; it is not linked to the 23 October call. Photo: Gordon Leggett, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

CHILE · UNITED KINGDOM · FALKLANDS

Chile’s conservative president, José Antonio Kast, spoke by phone with Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Friday 23 October about defence, trade and the Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas.

Key Facts — The call Chile’s President José Antonio Kast and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke by phone on Friday 23 October.

— The Falklands Britain raised the islanders’ right to decide their future; Chile has formally backed Argentina’s sovereignty claim.

— Defence Both leaders agreed that Chile and Britain should work together to modernise defence capabilities.

— Trade The leaders agreed on the need for closer trade; the UK-Chile association agreement has applied since 2021.

— What next The leaders look forward to speaking again; no date has been given.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives about 4.3% to the UK announcing a Falklands transfer to Argentina in 2026 (25 October, 5:16 a.m. ET).

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

President José Antonio Kast of Chile and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke by phone on Friday 23 October, and the UK government’s readout says they covered defence, trade and the Falkland Islands. Burnham, the Labour prime minister since Monday 20 July 2026, raised the islanders’ right of self-determination, while Chile has formally backed Argentina’s claim to the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas.

For US readers the call matters because Chile sits next to the dispute: it formally backs Argentina’s claim, a Chilean shipping company plans a cargo route from Punta Arenas to the islands, and its government is now talking defence and trade with London. On the same Friday Burnham raised the Falklands with President Donald Trump, according to the UK readout of that call.

In Plain English Falklands or Malvinas are South Atlantic islands that the United Kingdom governs and Argentina claims.

are South Atlantic islands that the United Kingdom governs and Argentina claims. Self-determination is the principle Britain cites: the islanders themselves should decide their future.

is the principle Britain cites: the islanders themselves should decide their future. A readout is the short official summary of a leaders’ call; this one is published by the UK government on gov.uk.

is the short official summary of a leaders’ call; this one is published by the UK government on gov.uk. The association agreement is the UK-Chile trade deal that has applied since January 2021.

is the UK-Chile trade deal that has applied since January 2021. Sea Lion is an oil discovery about 220 km north of the Falklands, Navitas Petroleum says; Argentina opposes it.

What the UK Says Was Discussed

The readout, published on gov.uk on Friday 23 October, says the leaders began by setting out shared ambitions to strengthen relations on defence, security, science and trade. It says they agreed that the UK and Chile need to work together to modernise defence capabilities.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

On the Falklands, the readout says the prime minister raised the UK’s interest in ensuring that the islanders keep the ability to exercise the right of self-determination. It does not record Kast’s reply, and the Chilean outlets La Tercera and Radio Agricultura, which reported the call on Saturday 24 October, relied on the British statement.

The readout adds that the leaders discussed growing cultural, scientific and people-to-people links and the effect they have had on investment and infrastructure. It says they recognised “untapped trade opportunities” and “agreed on the need for closer trading”, and that both look forward to speaking again.

Burnham, a former mayor of Greater Manchester, became prime minister on Monday 20 July, the UK government says. Kast, a conservative, took office on Wednesday 11 March, and Argentina’s foreign ministry calls his April trip to Buenos Aires his first international journey as president.

Chile’s Position on the Falklands

Chile has long backed Argentina’s claim, and on Monday 6 April Kast repeated that support in Buenos Aires, according to a joint communiqué that Argentina’s foreign ministry published. It says Kast reiterated Chile’s support for Argentina’s “legitimate sovereignty rights” and for a resumption of talks between Argentina and Britain, and that President Javier Milei thanked him for Chile’s “traditional support”.

Chile’s defence minister, Fernando Barros, complicated that line in late September, when he told a Punta Arenas radio station that Chile backs the claim but that there is “a de facto situation”, with “a friendly country” exercising sovereignty for about 200 years, a phrase that Ámbito and Radio Polar both applied to Britain (our translation). Radio Polar reported on Monday 28 September, citing government sources, that the foreign ministry had made its view known to the presidential palace informally.

Then government spokesman Máximo Pavez replied that the president and the foreign minister set foreign policy, and Radio Polar added that he did not rule out a clarifying note on the islanders’ self-determination. Whether the Friday call changes anything is unclear, because the readout records only what Burnham raised.

Argentina’s foreign ministry says the United Nations Decolonization Committee renewed its call in June for Argentina and Britain to resume sovereignty negotiations. Britain’s argument rests instead on the islanders’ right to decide, which is why the readout’s wording matters.

Why the Call Comes Now

On Monday 19 October, after meeting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Chile’s foreign minister, Francisco Pérez Mackenna, said it was time to raise relations to “a new level of strategic partnership”, Radio Polar and El Mostrador reported from a ministry statement. The minister listed critical minerals, investment, foreign trade and regional geopolitics among the topics.

British ambassador David Concar had visited Punta Arenas the week before, meeting the navy and regional officials to promote Antarctic science cooperation, El Mostrador reported. The minister’s trip came five weeks after ChileDay, when Chilean ministers met British officials and investors in London, the UK government says.

Chile and Britain, Recent Contacts — Week of Mon 14 Sep ChileDay in London brings Chile’s finance and public works ministers to British officials and investors.

— Mon 19 Oct Foreign ministers Pérez Mackenna and Miliband meet in London.

— Fri 23 Oct Burnham speaks to Kast, and the same day to Trump.

— Tue 27 Oct Argentine congressional committees are due to meet on the Falklands bill.

— Tue 10 Nov The Law of the Sea tribunal opens a two-day hearing on Argentina’s request over Falklands oil.

The Falklands Link and Argentina’s Bill

The Falklands sit beside all of this. A Chilean shipping company plans a monthly cargo route from Punta Arenas to Stanley, the islands’ capital, and Radio Polar’s reports give the first voyage as November or December.

Argentina’s foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, told broadcaster A24 that Argentina does not intend to stop the ship, though he did not rule out blocking it if it served the Sea Lion oil project, Radio Polar reported on Thursday 15 October. By Saturday 17 October Argentine opposition deputies had asked to summon Chile’s ambassador over the route, and Chilean lawmakers called that interference, Radio Polar reported.

The UK readout of Burnham’s call with Trump says the two discussed the Sea Lion project and what Britain calls Argentina’s “coercive measures”. The Rio Times has covered the US concern over Argentina’s Falklands bill, and Infobae reports that the government redefined the scope of the bill’s sanctions after US officials raised it.

Argentine committees are due to meet on Tuesday 27 October on the bill, Infobae reports, and the government hopes to take it to the floor on Wednesday 18 November. Infobae reported that Washington’s concern centres on penalties that could reach companies linked to the oil operators.

Trade and Defence Between the Two Countries

The UK government lists £2.28 billion (about US$3.05 billion) as total UK trade with Chile in 2025, under the association agreement that has applied since January 2021. Chile’s foreign ministry puts bilateral trade at US$1.196 billion for 2025, Radio Polar reported, citing Cooperativa, a figure the Rio Times could not reconcile with the British one, and pound amounts here convert at the 23 October close in house market data, US$1.3375 per pound sterling.

Chile’s ministry says it wants to combine the association agreement with the CPTPP, the Trans-Pacific trade pact that both countries belong to, and to attract British investment in technology and infrastructure, Radio Polar reported. At ChileDay in London, the UK government says, Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz met Latin America minister Chris Elmore and Public Works Minister Louis de Grange held discussions with UK Export Finance.

On defence, Chile’s navy already runs three Type 23 frigates that it bought from the Royal Navy, the Almirante Cochrane, the Almirante Condell and the Almirante Lynch, the Chilean Navy says. The readout names no equipment, and El Mostrador reported that Babcock International proposed in early October to build Arrowhead 140 frigates in Chile, a plan the Rio Times could not confirm.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, where users bet real money, gives about 4.3% to the UK announcing a transfer of Falklands sovereignty to Argentina in 2026, as of 5:16 a.m. ET on Sunday 25 October. Only about US$27,300 has traded in total, so one trade can move the price, and the contract is about the islands, not about Chile.

Polymarket Falklands Contract — Question Will the UK announce a transfer of Falklands sovereignty to Argentina by the end of 2026?

— Yes price About 4.3% on Sunday 25 October.

— Volume About US$27,300 traded in total.

— Before Thu 22 Oct About 1.75%, flat for almost two weeks.

The price jumped to a peak of about 4.95% on Thursday 22 October, the day US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau spoke in Buenos Aires about Argentina’s Falklands bill, and then settled between 4.2% and 4.35%. It showed no visible reaction when the call readout appeared at 2:42 p.m. ET on Friday 23 October, and these are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

If you hold shares tied to Falklands oil or to companies exposed to Argentina, the call changes little for you. The legal risk comes from Argentina’s proposed sanctions law and the tribunal hearing on Tuesday 10 and Wednesday 11 November, not from Chile and Britain talking.

If you plan to travel in southern Chile, nothing in the readout touches flights, borders or entry rules, and the Punta Arenas link is a cargo route, not a passenger service. If you follow US policy in the region, note that Burnham raised the islands with both Trump and Kast on the same Friday, while US officials have told Argentina’s government that its bill worries American firms, Infobae reported.

If you work in shipping, defence or energy, the details to watch are the first sailing of the Punta Arenas ship and any Chilean equipment decision, because the readout announces neither. The Rio Times found no announced purchase, and the Babcock frigate offer is a company proposal that El Mostrador reported.

What Is Not Known

Chile’s own account of the call is the biggest gap, because the readout is British and Chilean outlets repeated it. The Rio Times could not find a Chilean government account, so Kast’s reply on the Falklands and on defence is unknown.

Open Questions — Kast’s reply The readout does not say whether Kast accepted or answered the self-determination point.

— Chile’s line The Rio Times could not find a Chilean statement on whether the April backing of Argentina’s claim is unchanged.

— Defence What defence work the leaders agreed to, and whether it involves equipment, is not stated.

— Trade The British and Chilean trade totals for 2025 differ, and the Rio Times could not explain the gap.

— The ship The first Punta Arenas voyage is given as November or December in different reports.

— Argentina No Argentine government reaction to the call had been published by Sunday 25 October, as far as the Rio Times found.

The date of the next conversation between the two leaders has not been given. The Argentine bill faces a committee meeting due on Tuesday 27 October, and the tribunal hearing follows on Tuesday 10 November.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the British prime minister who spoke to Kast?

Andy Burnham, who became prime minister on Monday 20 July 2026, the UK government says. He was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 and returned to Parliament as the member for Makerfield in June 2026.

Did Chile change its position on the Falklands?

Not publicly. A joint communiqué with Argentina on Monday 6 April backs Argentina’s claim, and the Rio Times could not find a Chilean statement on the call or on any change of line.

What did Britain ask of Chile on the Falklands?

The readout says Burnham raised the UK’s interest in ensuring the islanders can exercise the right of self-determination. It does not say he asked Chile to do anything or that Kast agreed.

What trade deal covers UK and Chilean trade?

The UK-Chile association agreement has applied since January 2021, and both countries also belong to the CPTPP, a Trans-Pacific trade pact. The UK government lists £2.28 billion (about US$3.05 billion) in total UK trade with Chile in 2025.

Will the Punta Arenas ship to the Falklands sail?

A Chilean shipping company plans a cargo route to Stanley, and Radio Polar’s reports give November or December for the first voyage. Argentina’s foreign minister said Argentina does not plan to stop it, but did not rule out blocking it if it served oil work.

What happens next in the Falklands dispute?

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds a public hearing on Tuesday 10 and Wednesday 11 November on Argentina’s request against Britain over Falklands oil. Argentine committees are due to meet on Tuesday 27 October on the Falklands bill.

World.title: Ecopetrol Plans Recovery Under New Chief
World.content:
The oil pier at Coveñas on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, with the Ecopetrol name visible on the pier edge. File photo, January 2018. (Photo: Yair Alfonso Murillo Rincón, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · ECOPETROL · OIL AND GAS

Colombia’s state-controlled oil company has a new chief, a rebuilt management team and a government that wants a “rebirth”, but we found no published numerical targets.

Key Facts — The chief Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero, a business administrator, has led Ecopetrol since Monday 28 September 2026.

— The aim The government wants a “rebirth of Ecopetrol”: more exploration, new contracts including fracking, and new managers.

— Profit Third-quarter net income is guided at about US$1.3 billion to US$1.6 billion, down from US$1.9 billion.

— The rating Fitch affirmed Ecopetrol at BB with a stable outlook on Tuesday 20 October 2026.

— The shares Ecopetrol’s New York shares (NYSE: EC) closed at US$17.80 on Friday 23 October, up 4.6%.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Ecopetrol, Colombia’s state-controlled oil company, is being rebuilt around a new chief, Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero, and a government plan that President Abelardo de la Espriella calls the “renacer”, or rebirth, of the company. What has been decided so far is the chief, a new team of vice presidents and a policy of reopening exploration and fracking, while we found no published production, investment or profit targets for the Ecopetrol recovery plan itself.

For US investors the stake is a stock that trades in New York as the American depositary receipt NYSE: EC and closed at US$17.80 on Friday 23 October 2026, up 4.6% on the day, in Rio Times market data. Dollar values in this article use 3,158.43 pesos per US dollar, the official market rate (TRM) in force from Saturday 24 to Monday 26 October 2026, as published on Colombia’s open-data portal.

In Plain English Ecopetrol: the oil and gas company that Colombian officials call the country’s most important, owned 88.49% by government entities and led since 28 September by Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero.

the oil and gas company that Colombian officials call the country’s most important, owned 88.49% by government entities and led since 28 September by Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero. NYSE: EC: the American depositary receipt, a certificate that lets US investors hold Ecopetrol shares in dollars on the New York Stock Exchange.

the American depositary receipt, a certificate that lets US investors hold Ecopetrol shares in dollars on the New York Stock Exchange. Renacer: Spanish for rebirth, the word the president and the company use for the turnaround after allegations of corruption.

Spanish for rebirth, the word the president and the company use for the turnaround after allegations of corruption. mboed: thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day, the measure that adds oil and gas output together.

Who Runs Ecopetrol Now

Ecopetrol’s board chose Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero unanimously on Thursday 24 September 2026, and he took office on Monday 28 September, the company’s release says. Infobae adds that the board had been renewed at an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on Tuesday 15 September, which replaced six of the names on a nine-member board.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Gutiérrez is a business administrator with three specializations, in telecommunications project management, telecommunications law and health-services management, and the company describes a career in law, health, construction, farming and cattle. Infobae reports that he managed De la Espriella’s presidential campaign and has no earlier experience in hydrocarbons, and before his appointment El Colombiano reported that workers and people close to the company questioned his profile.

Ecopetrol’s release gives him the mission of building “bridges of trust” with the state, workers, regions, communities, investors and partners. It adds that he will start a recovery process to straighten the institutional course after what it calls alleged acts of corruption that harmed the company’s reputation and management.

“Ecopetrol does not belong to the president, nor to the government, much less to a political party.”

President Abelardo de la Espriella at the swearing-in in Santa Marta on 25 September, as quoted by Infobae (translated from Spanish)

What the Government Has Set Out

At a ceremony called Renacer de Ecopetrol on Friday 25 September 2026 at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino in Santa Marta, De la Espriella said his government “fully reopens the path of exploration and of signing new contracts, including fracking”, with “absolutely all criteria of environmental responsibility”. Infobae reports that he gave the company two tasks, to keep the hydrocarbons business going by replacing reserves and guaranteeing supply, and to find new energy sources and businesses that can pay their own way.

Gutiérrez told the same ceremony that Ecopetrol will advance conventional and unconventional projects, “implement responsible fracking” and keep exploring offshore, and that Barranquilla will get a new alternate headquarters. Infobae adds that he named exploration, adding reserves, gas supply and tax disputes as his priorities.

Ecopetrol reported proved reserves of 1.944 billion barrels of oil equivalent at the end of 2025, Valora Analitik reported in February, and Infobae puts their average life at 7.8 years, with gas at 6.3 years. The president says these indicators force Colombia to find new resources instead of importing energy it could produce, while Fitch put reserve life at 7.1 years at the end of 2025, Valora Analitik reported.

The Management Team Is Being Rebuilt

On Wednesday 30 September 2026 the board approved three vice presidents, who were to join by Tuesday 6 October, Blu Radio reports: Mónica Jiménez González for legal affairs and the secretary-general post, Mauricio Gutiérrez for corporate strategy and new businesses, and Camilo Rojas for administration and services, which covers contracting and procurement. Jiménez held the legal post from 2016 to 2022, and the company said the changes aim to strengthen key capabilities for its new stage.

Portafolio reports that the board then named José Eduardo Barreneche Ávila corporate compliance director on Thursday 15 October, replacing Rodolfo Mario García, who left on Tuesday 13 October by mutual agreement. On Wednesday 21 October it named Armando José Cuello Navarro, a former vice minister of energy, executive vice president for energy transition, with gas supply and energy security in his brief, as part of what Ecopetrol calls its “Nueva Era”, or new era, strategy.

Ecopetrol’s Turnaround So Far Thursday 24 September: the board names Gutiérrez Caballero.

the board names Gutiérrez Caballero. Friday 25 September: swearing-in in Santa Marta; he takes office on Monday 28 September.

swearing-in in Santa Marta; he takes office on Monday 28 September. Wednesday 30 September: three vice presidents approved.

three vice presidents approved. Thursday 15 October: a new compliance director is named.

a new compliance director is named. Wednesday 21 October: a former vice minister of energy is named to run energy transition.

a former vice minister of energy is named to run energy transition. Thursday 22 October: De la Espriella calls Gutiérrez to the Casa de Nariño.

De la Espriella calls Gutiérrez to the Casa de Nariño. Friday 23 October: the US Embassy announces its first official meeting with him.

What the Third-Quarter Outlook Shows

Ecopetrol’s preliminary update for the third quarter, which ended on 30 September, points to output of 740 to 750 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day (mboed), up from 705.8 mboed in the second quarter. The range includes all of Brava’s output from the acquisition date, and Brava is the Brazilian producer in which Ecopetrol bought a 51% stake and which made about 78.8 mboed in the first half of 2026, Valora Analitik reported in August.

The same update projects lower profit than the second quarter, with EBITDA, which is operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation, and net income both below the earlier levels. Ecopetrol calls the figures preliminary and says they may change before final results.

Ecopetrol by the Numbers Production: 705.8 mboed in the second quarter, down 6.6% from a year earlier; outlook for the third quarter 740 to 750 mboed.

705.8 mboed in the second quarter, down 6.6% from a year earlier; outlook for the third quarter 740 to 750 mboed. EBITDA: COP 17.7 trillion (about US$5.6 billion) in the second quarter; outlook COP 14.0 trillion to 16.5 trillion (about US$4.4 billion to US$5.2 billion).

Net income: COP 6.1 trillion (about US$1.9 billion) in the second quarter; outlook COP 4.0 trillion to 5.0 trillion (about US$1.3 billion to US$1.6 billion).

COP 6.1 trillion (about US$1.9 billion) in the second quarter; outlook COP 4.0 trillion to 5.0 trillion (about US$1.3 billion to US$1.6 billion). Revenue outlook: COP 33.0 trillion to 36.0 trillion (about US$10.4 billion to US$11.4 billion).

COP 33.0 trillion to 36.0 trillion (about US$10.4 billion to US$11.4 billion). Capital spending outlook: US$1.64 billion to US$2.0 billion.

Why Output Fell and Where Debt Stands

The second-quarter report ties the 49.7 mboed fall in output from a year earlier mainly to 33.3 mboed less from the Permian Basin in the United States, which it says matched the investment plan, and 13.7 mboed less gas and natural gas liquids. Expected growth in domestic oil was delayed by external disruptions and electrical incidents, including blockades in the department of Meta that cost an estimated 1.3 million barrels in the first half.

Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra, the acting chief executive at the time, signed that report, and Gutiérrez took office only two days before the third quarter ended, so both quarters mostly reflect the previous management. His first full quarter is the fourth, which ends on 31 December.

At the end of June the group held COP 11.3 trillion (about US$3.6 billion) in cash and cash equivalents, and its gross debt was 2.0 times EBITDA, below the company’s 2026 ceiling of 2.5 times. On Tuesday 20 October 2026 Fitch affirmed Ecopetrol at BB with a stable outlook, and Ecopetrol says Fitch also kept its stand-alone profile at bbb- and does not expect difficulty in refinancing the debt due in 2027.

What It Means for You

Ecopetrol’s American depositary receipts closed at US$17.80 on Friday 23 October 2026, up 4.6% on the day and up from US$17.01 on Thursday, in Rio Times market data. Ecopetrol’s own register shows JPMorgan Chase Bank, which holds shares for holders of the receipts, with 2.77% of the company on 8 September, while Colombian government entities held 88.49%.

That makes US holders minority investors beside a government that has set the direction in public, from reopening exploration to allowing fracking. Fitch’s BB rating is one outside signal so far, and it sits below investment grade even though Ecopetrol says Fitch rates its stand-alone profile at bbb-, which is investment grade.

Brent crude traded above US$110 a barrel on Friday, in Rio Times market data, well above the US$91.0 average price that Ecopetrol assumed for the third quarter. Higher prices help revenue, but production is the weaker part of the story, so the output figure in the full results will matter more than the oil price.

What Is Not Known

We found no document from Ecopetrol or the ministries that sets production, investment or profit targets for the recovery, and El Diario’s report of Saturday 24 October names no ministers and gives no production, investment or profit figures. The aims it lists, more production and more capital, are its own summary because it credits them to no speaker.

It is also not known how much of the third-quarter production gain comes from Brava, or when Ecopetrol will publish its full third-quarter results. The company says its preliminary figures remain subject to review and may be adjusted.

The US Embassy said on Friday 23 October that it discussed American investment opportunities with Gutiérrez, but neither the embassy’s post nor Portafolio’s account names any amount, project or financing. Infobae reports that the Council of State and the Inspector General’s Office have objected to fracking, so whether it can proceed is not settled.

What We Could Not Verify The reserve-life figures (7.8 years for oil and gas, 6.3 for gas) come from Infobae alone and differ from the 7.1 years Fitch is reported to use; we did not open Ecopetrol’s reserves report.

The US Embassy’s post on X could not be opened, so its wording comes from Portafolio.

Ecopetrol’s own filings on the appointments could not be read, so details come from Blu Radio, Portafolio and La República.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Ecopetrol’s new chief?

Joaquín Gutiérrez Caballero, a business administrator, took over on Monday 28 September 2026 after the board chose him unanimously. Infobae reports that he managed President Abelardo de la Espriella’s campaign and has no earlier oil-industry experience.

What is the Ecopetrol recovery plan?

The government calls it the “rebirth of Ecopetrol” and has said it will reopen exploration and allow fracking. We found no document with production, investment or profit targets.

How can US investors follow Ecopetrol?

Ecopetrol’s American depositary receipts trade in New York as NYSE: EC and closed at US$17.80 on Friday 23 October 2026. Holders are minority investors, because Colombian government entities own 88.49% of the shares.

Is Ecopetrol investment grade?

No, Fitch rates Ecopetrol BB with a stable outlook, which is below investment grade, though Ecopetrol says Fitch rates its stand-alone profile bbb-, which is investment grade. Fitch affirmed the BB rating on Tuesday 20 October 2026.

What did Ecopetrol forecast for the third quarter?

Its preliminary outlook expects output of 740 to 750 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day, including all of Brava’s output since the acquisition. It also expects net income of about US$1.3 billion to US$1.6 billion.
