World.title: Rosado Got To Go: House Speaker calls for removal of Alexis Rosado — ‘Unconscionable form of gaslighting’ for complainant; ‘Powerful men are protected, they matter more’
World.content:
Rosado Got To Go: House Speaker calls for removal of Alexis Rosado — ‘Unconscionable form of gaslighting’ for complainant; ‘Powerful men are protected, they matter more’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: In an extraordinary public statement that puts her directly at odds with Prime Minister John Briceño and Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, Speaker of the House of Representatives Valerie Woods has made a forceful case for Ambassador Alexis Rosado’s removal as Belize’s Co-Agent before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), arguing that his continued appointment while facing serious sexual offence charges compromises the country’s credibility and inflicts further distress on the complainant.

Woods, a longtime member of the People’s United Party (PUP), has publicly challenged the position of her own party’s leadership, questioning whether Rosado’s continued appointment represents an exception being made for a powerful individual.

In her statement titled “The Co-Agent Exception,” Woods writes:

“If, at this stage, there is still an insistence on his keeping the position, it raises the question whether the high-profile title is being used as a kind of unspoken influence.”

She goes further, stating:

“The message to anyone who is observing is that Mr. Rosado is an extremely important person in the eyes of the state and exceptions should be made for him.”

Her remarks follow Prime Minister Briceño’s public defence of Rosado earlier this week, when he declared that removing the ambassador at this critical stage would not be in Belize’s national interest.

“The ‘existential’ nature of Belize’s ICJ case cannot be used to justify keeping him as Co-Agent,” Woods counters.

She maintains that removing or replacing Rosado, based on the information publicly available, would not prejudice Belize’s territorial case against Guatemala.

Woods also directly challenges Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca’s explanation that the Government is following the advice of Belize’s lead agent, Assad Shoman, who considers Rosado vital to the ongoing preparation of the case.

“Whatever value Mr. Rosado brought to the preparation of the case is largely spent. He is not the lead Co-Agent and will not argue the case,” Woods states.

She argues that Belize’s written submissions have already been filed, hearing dates have been established, and responsibility for presenting the case rests with experienced international lawyers.

She consequently describes claims that Rosado is indispensable to the country’s case as exaggerated.

But perhaps the most striking aspect of the Speaker’s intervention is her defence of the complainant and her criticism of the message being sent to women and girls by the Government’s continued support for Rosado.

“For the complainant, this must be an unconscionable form of gaslighting that is unfolding publicly and compounding the distress of the proceedings,” Woods declares.

She warns that retaining Rosado in such a prominent position undermines the country’s efforts to confront sexual violence.

“It sends troubling messages, particularly to women and girls, that high ranking, powerful men are protected, they matter more, they are shielded from institutional consequences.”

Woods also invokes Belize’s commitments under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, the 2022 national parliamentary Domestic Violence in Belize Motion, the 2026 Blue Teddy Bear campaign and the annual 16 Days of Activism to End Gender-Based Violence.

She questions how the Government can reconcile those commitments with its decision to maintain Rosado in his prominent international assignment while he faces serious criminal charges. Her argument raises questions about the consistency of Belize’s commitments rather than establishing a legal violation of any convention.

The Speaker further points out that Rosado resigned from his diplomatic postings after being charged in April 2022, arguing that the same considerations that justified protecting the integrity of those offices should apply to his continued ICJ appointment.

Woods acknowledges that Rosado remains innocent until proven guilty, but maintains that the presumption of innocence does not prevent a public official from stepping aside while criminal proceedings are pending.

The intervention comes just hours after Breaking Belize News raised this very issue in a public discussion on Saturday morning, comparing Rosado’s continued professional appointment with the situation involving Pastor Kevin Tzib, founder of Dunamis Ministries, who was recently charged with seven sexual offences and subsequently released on bail.

BBN asked whether Tzib should similarly be allowed to continue his ministry if Rosado can remain in his ICJ role with the support of the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, and questioned what distinguishes the two situations. Dunamis Ministries has announced that it will take administrative measures, although the precise restrictions on Tzib’s ministerial duties have not been publicly established.

Woods’ statement addresses the broader questions of the presumption of innocence, public accountability and whether individuals facing serious criminal allegations should remain in positions of trust.

The statement is especially significant because it places the Speaker of the House in direct public disagreement with the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister on a matter involving Belize’s most consequential international legal proceedings.

Woods concludes by rejecting the suggestion that the importance of the ICJ case should shield any individual appointment from reconsideration.

“No individual appointment is beyond recall,” she declares.

“The importance of Belize’s case before the ICJ is not a reason to tolerate the avoidable reputational risk of retaining Mr. Rosado in the position of Co-Agent.”

She maintains that, as Belize prepares to present its case before the ICJ, it is precisely the importance of those proceedings that demands a rethink of Rosado’s continued appointment.

World.title: Mayor of Belmopan, councilors complete Good Governance Training at Galen University
World.content:
Mayor of Belmopan, councilors complete Good Governance Training at Galen University

By Zoila Palma: Belmopan Mayor Pablo Cawich and councilors of the Belmopan City Council have completed a 14-week Good Governance Training programme at Galen University, in collaboration with the U.S. Embassy.

The training focused on strengthening leadership and governance as the council continues its work to serve residents and advance development in the capital.

The council emphasized that leadership carries a responsibility and commitment to public service, noting that continued learning and growth are essential to improving governance and moving Belmopan forward.

World.title: International News: Thousands rally for Lula and Bolsonaro as Brazil braces for tight Presidential runoff
World.content:
International News: Thousands rally for Lula and Bolsonaro as Brazil braces for tight Presidential runoff

By Zoila Palma: Thousands of supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro took to the streets today as the candidates made their final appeals ahead of a closely contested presidential runoff election. Lula supporters filled Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach with the red colours of his Workers’ Party, while hundreds of bikers and other supporters rallied behind Bolsonaro in Belo Horizonte.

The rallies capped a bitter campaign that has deepened political divisions in Latin America’s largest country, AFP reports.

Lula, who turns 81 next week, waved a large Brazilian flag from a campaign truck as he addressed the crowd in Rio de Janeiro. He urged voters to choose between someone who respects Brazil’s national flag and someone who embraces the American flag.

Meanwhile, Bolsonaro’s supporters expressed confidence in his chances after he secured 47 percent of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula’s 45 percent.

A Datafolha Institute poll released during the week showed the candidates tied at 50 percent of voting intentions.

The election has drawn attention across the region as Brazil considers whether to continue under left-wing leadership or join a broader political shift toward the right.

World.title: BDF’s Lt. Col. Kenroy Smith receives prestigious Brazilian military aviation honour
World.content:
BDF’s Lt. Col. Kenroy Smith receives prestigious Brazilian military aviation honour

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Belize Defence Force officer has been honoured by the Brazilian Air Force.

Lieutenant Colonel Kenroy Smith, Commanding Officer of the BDF Air Wing, was awarded the Order of Aeronautical Merit in the grade of Grand Officer.

The award was presented by Brazil’s Ambassador to Belize, His Excellency Olyntho Vieira, during a ceremony at the Embassy of Brazil in Belmopan on Friday, October 23, as part of Brazilian Aviation Day.

The Order of Aeronautical Merit is a distinguished decoration of the Brazilian Air Force, recognizing outstanding service and exceptional contributions to military aviation and aeronautical development.

The BDF says the honour reflects Lt. Col. Smith’s significant contributions to military aviation, regional cooperation and stronger ties between the BDF and Brazil’s armed forces.

The Commander and members of the BDF congratulated him, saying his dedication and professionalism continue to bring distinction to the Force and to Belize.

World.title: International News: Vance becomes 11th Pacific hurricane this season
World.content:
International News: Vance becomes 11th Pacific hurricane this season

By Zoila Palma: Hurricane Vance became the 11th major hurricane of the 2026 central and eastern Pacific hurricane season on Friday, as meteorologists monitored its movement toward Mexico’s west-central coast.

According to AccuWeather, the storm briefly reached Category 3 status on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, with maximum sustained winds of at least 111 miles per hour. Forecasters are tracking multiple possible scenarios, including one in which the hurricane remains offshore and another in which it turns toward the Mexican coast.

Vance developed after an area of disturbed weather strengthened into a tropical depression on Wednesday before becoming a tropical storm four hours later. It intensified into a hurricane early Friday, with sustained winds reaching 90 miles per hour by 9 a.m. Friday.

AccuWeather Hurricane Expert Alex DaSilva said the storm could remain over open waters but warned that a northeast turn toward Mexico’s west-central coast could result in more dangerous conditions.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard cadet Elvis Solis completes major milestone in Mexico
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard cadet Elvis Solis completes major milestone in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Coast Guard (BCG) is congratulating Cadet Elvis Solis on successfully completing four years of academic and military training in Naval Nursing at the Centro de Estudios Navales en Ciencias de la Salud (CENCIS), under Mexico’s Naval University. The achievement marks a significant milestone in his journey toward becoming a qualified naval nurse.

Solis’s accomplishment reflects the Belize Coast Guard’s continued investment in developing its future leaders and specialized personnel. The training equips cadets with the academic knowledge and military skills necessary to support healthcare services within the naval force.

Following the successful completion of this phase of training, Solis will be commissioned into the Belize Coast Guard at the rank of Lieutenant Junior Grade before proceeding to his fifth and final year of professional training.

Upon successfully completing the final year, he will qualify for a Bachelor’s Degree in Naval Nursing.

The Belize Coast Guard commended Solis for his dedication, perseverance and commitment to excellence.

The Belize Coast Guard also expressed appreciation to the Government of Mexico and the Mexican Navy for their continued partnership and support in advancing the professional development of Belizean personnel.

World.title: BDF officer cadets participate in selection process for U.S. Army Officer candidate school
World.content:
BDF officer cadets participate in selection process for U.S. Army Officer candidate school

By Zoila Palma: Belize Defence Force (BDF) officer cadets have participated in a selection process for the opportunity to attend the United States Army Officer Candidate School (OCS), marking an important step in their military careers and professional development.

The process provides aspiring officers with an opportunity to demonstrate their readiness for the responsibilities of commissioned service.

The selection process is intended to identify candidates prepared to meet the demands of military leadership and serve with dedication. For the participating cadets, the opportunity represents more than selection, as it also involves preparing to lead with integrity, accept responsibility and uphold the professional standards expected of a BDF officer.

The Commander of the Belize Defence Force commended all participating officer cadets for their dedication and willingness to undertake the challenge of pursuing professional development through OCS. The Commander noted that their ambition reflects the importance of developing capable leaders who can contribute meaningfully to the Force and the country.

The BDF Force Headquarters and Training and Doctrine Battalion extended their best wishes to the candidates as they continue their journey toward commissioned service.

World.title: Belize Defence Force Air Wing commander receives Brazilian Order of Aeronautical Merit
World.content:
Belize Defence Force Air Wing commander receives Brazilian Order of Aeronautical Merit

By Zoila Palma: Lieutenant Colonel Kenroy Smith, Commanding Officer of the Belize Defence Force (BDF) Air Wing, has been awarded the Order of Aeronautical Merit in the grade of Grand Officer (Grande Oficial) by the Government of Brazil.

The award was presented by Brazil’s Ambassador to Belize, Olyntho Vieira, during a ceremony at the Brazilian Embassy in Belmopan on October 23, 2026, as part of the observance of Brazilian Aviation Day.

The Order of Aeronautical Merit is a distinguished Brazilian Air Force decoration that recognizes outstanding service and exceptional contributions to military aviation and aeronautical development.

Smith’s recognition highlights his contributions to advancing military aviation, strengthening regional cooperation and building professional ties between the Belize Defence Force and Brazil’s armed forces.

The BDF congratulated Smith on the achievement, commending his dedication, professionalism and commitment to excellence.

The BDF also expressed appreciation to the Government and people of Brazil for their longstanding support in defence, security, training and military professional development.

World.title: Heartless!
World.content:
HAVANA, Cuba — A woman carries water containers during a blackout in Havana, on July 7, 2026. Cubans were gradually getting power back on July 7 after the third nationwide power outage since the start of the year, causing mounting despair in the face of an energy collapse precipitated by a US fuel blockade. (Photo: AFP)

Ten former Caricom leaders are urging the global community to support the upcoming United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) resolution that calls for an end to America’s embargo against Cuba, denouncing the long-running sanction as inhumane and contrary to international law.

“The unilateral, coercive actions of the USA against Cuba represent the law of the jungle and can in no way be justified by the Charter of the United Nations or any other source of international law and justice,” the former Caricom heads of State and Government argued in an open letter to all nations of the world dated October 24, 2026.

They pointed out that every year since 1992, the UNGA has been “adopting overwhelmingly” a resolution on this subject. “Yet the USA has been ignoring the clear voice of the international community, the requisites of international law, and the most elemental of civilising principles.”

The 10 leaders are Freundel Stuart, former prime minister of Barbados; Dean Barrow and Said Musa, former prime ministers of Belize; Keith Mitchell and Tillman Thomas, former prime ministers of Grenada; Donald Ramotar, former president of Guyana; Bruce Golding and PJ Patterson, former prime ministers of Jamaica; Kenny Anthony, former prime minister of St Lucia; and Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines.

Noting that the vote is scheduled for October 28, the 10 leaders said they were “strongly and unequivocally” urging all nations to vote in favour of the resolution as the imposition of the embargo is contrary to “every civilised precept of life and living”.

Their appeal came a day after the US Government, in its latest bid to increase pressure on the Cuban Government, urged Cubans to make “discreet” contact with America’s Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).

“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA,” Rubio added.

French news service Agence France Presse (AFP), in its report on the development, said the unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is currently active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations, including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

According to AFP, Rubio’s call was mocked by Cuban officials.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

AFP reported that the CIA later uploaded a video to X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official US installation in person if they can safely travel to one.

For those hoping to contact the CIA online via the cia.gov website, the agency instructed users to access the Internet on a secure network, like a VPN, using a private browser and a ‘burner’ e-mail account unassociated with any personal details.

Those sharing information should be prepared to include their city, job, level of access, and contact information with their message, AFP reported.

For months, US President Donald Trump and other senior officials of his Government have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political, and legal pressure on the Spanish-speaking country.

Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

“Those beautiful [US military] ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast,” he said. “They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump’s threats.

“Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination,” he posted on social media.

In another move against the Cuban leadership, Florida’s top prosecutor last week announced an arrest warrant for former President Raul Castro on State murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Castro, 95, is wanted in connection with the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from Brothers to the Rescue, an organisation assisting Cubans fleeing to Florida by sea.

“Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said in a statement.

Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela’s then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.

Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has “no legal basis” and was an attempt “to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba”.

The US indictment has also been denounced by China and Russia, which both have close ties with Cuba.

On Wednesday, Beijing urged Washington to cease “all forms of coercion and pressure against Cuba”.

“China has consistently opposed the abuse of judicial measures to exert pressure on Cuba, and firmly supports Cuba in safeguarding its national sovereignty and resisting foreign interference,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference.

“Comrade Raul is a highly respected leader of the Cuban Revolution who enjoys great prestige internationally,” she added.

A day earlier, Russia said in a statement that it “categorically” rejected and “strongly” condemned the Florida arrest warrant, and reaffirmed Moscow’s “unwavering solidarity” with Cuba.

“Bringing a baseless and contrived accusation more than 30 years after the events can only be seen as an act of vengeance by the anti-Cuban lobby in Miami,” Russia’s foreign ministry charged.

In January this year, Trump began imposing a crippling fuel blockade on Cuba, intensifying the island’s severe economic crisis. Washington has since piled more sanctions on Cuba, cutting off nearly all its sources of revenue.

The island of just over nine million people has endured constant power cuts due to the poor state of its ageing thermoelectric plants. That has worsened significantly since the US action in January in its bid to pressure Havana’s communist Government.

A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba’s power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.

In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.

The cuts have also affected the island’s water supply and mobile phone network, adding to extremely tough general living conditions for residents.

Havana blames the crisis on the array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.

The embargo was first imposed in 1962 by then US President John F Kennedy, who invoked the Trading with the Enemy Act, which allows Washington to restrict trade with countries it considers foes.

Since 1978 every single US leader has renewed the provision annually.

In August this year the US extended the trade embargo by another year, drawing fury from the Cuban Government.

Foreign Minister Rodriguez called the embargo “a genocidal policy” and accused Washington of being “intent on suffocating an entire nation”.

“This extension comes at the cruellest moment of the US offensive against Cuba in recent years,” he said in a post on X.

Trump has claimed that Cuba, located 150 kilometres (90 miles) off Florida’s coast, represents an “extraordinary threat” to US national security.

However, the former Caricom leaders, in their open letter on Saturday, stated that “Cuba is not a threat to any nation or any person on planet Earth”.

They argued that the embargo “continues to be a threat to hemispheric and international peace and security…is a brazen violation of Cuba’s right to sovereignty and independence, [and] derogates from the most elemental human rights of a people established and declared by international law.

“The vote on this UNGA resolution this year is more urgent and important than ever before. In recent months, the US Government has further ramped up its illegal embargo against Cuba in an attempt to starve the Cuban people into submission through the imposition of third-party sanctions against any Government or entity which grants, sells, or transports energy products, including gasoline and diesel, to Cuba. Surely, such US conduct is inhumane, and undoubtedly contrary to international law,” the 10 leaders wrote.

“Accordingly, it is imperative that the blandishments and pressures currently being deployed by the USA to derail and defeat the proposed UNGA resolution must be resisted,” they added.

“Let us all contribute to the healing of the hemispheric fracture between the United States of America and Cuba by supporting the UNGA resolution on October 28, 2026. Let us all stand with Cuba and humanity on this matter,” the leaders said.

World.title: Shake-up ahead for underperforming hospital management
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton is speaking with patients waiting to see a doctor at the Noel Holmes Hospital outpatient area on Friday. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

FORT CHARLOTTE, Hanover — Strong action will be taken against the management teams of non-performing public health institutions warns Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton following a national patient complaints report showing that long wait times remain a primary grievance across the island’s hospital network.

“I am just giving a notice that we are going to be taking stronger action around throughput and the quality of throughput, and Noel Holmes is not going to be an exception. All institutions are going to have that,” stated Tufton during a press conference at the Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover on Friday afternoon.

Before the press briefing, the minister toured the Type-C facility, which is currently being rehabilitated following Hurricane Melissa last October. During the tour, several patients raised concerns about lengthy wait times.

“Coming here and hearing that five people are waiting at an outpatient area from 9:30 or 10:00 this morning until 12:00, and the doctor has not yet seen the patient — the five or six people — not a good thing. Nobody should wait three or four hours and you haven’t seen one patient yet. Sorry. We are going to have to call these things out when they happen,” stated Tufton.

The minister highlighted that staff numbers at Noel Holmes Hospital increased significantly from 189 before the hurricane to 270, including specialist doctors. He stressed that this expanded workforce must translate into enhanced service delivery, improved throughput, and shorter wait times.

Moving forward, the ministry will closely evaluate staff counts against productivity and patient throughput across the entire public health sector.

Tufton added that the recently completed national patient complaints report will be released publicly within three weeks.

“The number one reason why people complain is access to service — timely access to service. And I know that there’s a default mode that says, ‘It’s because we don’t have this,’ or, ‘We don’t have that.’ But if we hire more doctors, the least that can happen is that the doctor must turn up and deal with the patient on time. Patients are not supposed to wait long if you have more doctors working. I can’t put it any plainer,” said Tufton.

Tufton warned institutional and regional leaders that they will be held accountable for administrative and operational failures.

“Hiring more people means greater levels of productivity, more efficient throughput, and less wait time. People see their doctors more on time. Management, leadership, and supervisors must ensure that it happens, and they must be at their posts to ensure that it happens.

“And I’m charging the regions — this regional [acting] director [Deveta McLaren] is on the line now because I’m here in Noel Holmes, but when I go to the other places I do the same thing — they must ensure that their reports reflect that, because we’re ranking institutions now on levels of performance and on complaints. And if you fall below the satisfactory rank, a team is going to come in and they’re going to start with leadership: Are you the suitable person to run this institution or to provide leadership? Because, ultimately, the buck stops with leaders,” warned Tufton.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer what specific administrative actions could be taken, Tufton explained that measures would range from performance warnings to removal from leadership posts.

“It starts with appraisal; it starts with the board. The board is going to put the region under pressure, and the region will have to relate to your parish managers. Parish managers will have to look at the key performance indicators at the level of the institutions, and people will have to be spoken to,” argued Tufton.

He cited a recent example in which a non-performing hospital chief executive officer (CEO) was removed from his post, two weeks ago, following a written directive to the board.

“The board was told to find another place to put him, because he was not providing leadership in the hospital. And we’re going to get more of that. The board has the authority to do it. I appoint the board, and you know, the truth is I appoint or remove them at my discretion. They, ultimately, have responsibility, and they must ask for these reports,” stated Tufton.

To avoid the perception of a totalitarian regime, Tufton said training and technology will be used to provide support to employees.

“Where we need to train and retrain, it has to be a critical part of the culture going forward, and technology is an important thing — using technology to give support. Things like registration, follow-ups, those sorts of things have to be a critical part. It’s not just about the human component; it’s about the ecosystem that you build out around them,” he explained.

World.title: Legendary Derrick Harriott ‘checks out’
World.content:
Derrick Harriott (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Derrick Clifton Harriott, who excelled as a singer, producer, and record label owner, died at his St Andrew home on October 24.

He was 87.

Lorna Thomas, his friend of over 60 years, confirmed his passing in an interview with the Jamaica Observer. She said he died just after midnight, less than one week after leaving Medical Associates Hospital in St Andrew.

Thomas disclosed that Harriott had been ailing for some time, but his condition deteriorated since August when he was hospitalised twice.

The youngest of six children, Harriott was born in Kingston and attended Excelsior High School. He got his start in music during the late 1950s as a member of The Jiving Juniors, a harmony quartet that recorded mainly American-inspired ballads.

That was followed by a successful solo career that produced songs like Walk The Streets, Solomon, The Loser, Born to Love You, and the 1984-released Checkin’ Out.

Harriott also established himself as a producer with his Crystal label, which released hit songs by Keith and Tex (Stop That Train, Tonight), The Kingstonians (Singer Man), The Federals (Penny For Your Song) and Dennis Brown (Lips Of Wine, Silhouette).

Lips Of Wine, released in 1968, was Dennis Brown’s first song. Harriott also directed Brown on a 1973 album that includes covers of Glen Campell’s Wichita Lineman and Let Me Down Easy, originally done by Van McKoy.

Since the early 1970s, Harriott operated the Chariot record store in Twin Gates Plaza in Ha;f-Way-Tree, St Andrew. It was a hub for fans seeking hard-to-find vinyl records, as well as dances, shows, and roots plays on VHS.

One of the artistes whose careers Harriott impacted was singer McAnuff. He produced Pick Hits to Click, McAnuff’s first album, which was released in 1977.

“Derrick was like mi father, one of di nicest people yuh could ever meet. Him was a lesson in humility,” said McAnuff.

For his contribution to Jamaican music, Harriott was honoured by the Jamaican Government with an investiture into the Order of Distinction in 2009.

Minister of Culture and Entertainment Olivia Grange said that with the death of Harriott, Jamaica, sadly, has lost another of the icons who helped to shape the trajectory and reach of the country’s musical genres.

“Derrick was a true pioneer of Jamaican music, and it is interesting that February 6, his birthday anniversary, is the same as that of reggae legend Bob Marley,” she shared. “Through his music and his record store, he nurtured talent and preserved our music over many years.”

He is the latest entertainment industry stalwart to die in 2026. Drummer Sly Dunbar, guitarist Stephen “Cat” Coore, singer Stranger Cole, guitarist Rupert Bent II (who played on Lips of Wine), and bass guitarist Jackie Jackson predeceased him.

Derrick Harriott is survived by his 97 year-old sister, Loy Shegog; eight children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren.

World.title: 80 years for one, retrial for second in 2015 family massacre
World.content:
A Jamaica Observer file photo of inside a courtroom at the Court of Appeal building in downtown Kingston.

AN appeal from two men serving life behind bars for the “brutal execution-type slaying” of six members of one family and the arson of the family home, which left four survivors severely burnt, has resulted in one felon losing his bid to overturn his conviction and his 80-year pre-parole period being affirmed, while the other is heading to a retrial for the six murders. The Appeal Court, however, affirmed the sentences for that man on five other counts.

The men, Mikhail Campbell and Errol Clarke, had been jointly charged, tried, and convicted on an indictment containing 11 counts for the offences of arson (count one), murder (counts two to seven), and causing grievous bodily harm with intent (counts eight to 11) before Supreme Court Judge Justice Martin Gayle and a jury in the Hanover Circuit Court in November 2018. The jury convicted both men on all 11 counts, unanimously in the case of Campbell and by a majority of five to two in the case of Clarke.

Campbell and Clarke were sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment for arson and 20 years’ imprisonment for each count of causing grievous bodily harm with intent. Campbell was sentenced to life imprisonment on each of the six counts of murder, with the stipulation that he would not be eligible for parole until after serving 43 years for the first three counts of murder and 40 years for the remaining three. Clarke was also sentenced to life imprisonment for each of the six counts of murder; however, it was stipulated that he should serve 40 years before becoming eligible for parole on each count. For both men, Justice Gayle ruled that counts one to four and counts five to 11 were to be served concurrently, while counts five to 11 were to be served consecutively to counts one to four, resulting in a total minimum sentence of 80 years’ imprisonment before eligibility for parole.

In what was described by the court as “an unimaginable act of cruelty and brutality” on the night of October 8, 2015, perpetrators forcefully entered the home — which had just hours before been the scene of a celebration to welcome the mother and daughter who had returned from an overseas visit — and despite desperate pleas, shot and killed a 62-year-old matriarch, a pregnant 36-year-old woman, two men in the prime of their lives (40 and 29 years old), a young woman who had just attained the age of majority, and a minor aged 15 years.

They then set the house on fire, resulting in the deceased being burned beyond recognition and the four survivors being left with thermal injuries affecting 13 to 25 per cent of their bodies during their desperate fight to escape the flames.

The crime, according to prosecution witnesses, was premeditated and motivated by revenge on the part of Campbell, described as a “close, trusted family friend of the deceased” who had been present at the homecoming celebrations earlier in the day. Campbell, the court was told, took men to the house to exact vengeance on one of the family members for “disrespecting” him. After the family members failed to disclose the whereabouts of the man who was being sought, they were executed by Campbell and Clarke.

Ironically, that family member, who was one of the six Crown witnesses to testify during the trial, had taken refuge under a bed in one of the rooms in the house.

The men, following their convictions, appealed.

Campbell challenged his convictions and sentences, arguing, among other things, that the prosecution’s case against him should have been thrown out since it hinged entirely on voice identification evidence which he contended “was inconsistent, insufficient, and unreliable”.

Campbell did not challenge the sentences imposed for the offences of arson and causing grievous bodily harm with intent, but insisted that the sentences for the murders were “manifestly excessive”.

Clarke, on the other hand, in appealing his convictions, maintained that the jury was deprived of its statutorily mandated time for deliberating the six counts of murder against him, as such rendering the murder convictions “unsafe” and the trial a nullity.

According to the court’s record, on November 30, 2018, the seven jurors retired at 12:16 pm to deliberate and reach a verdict for Clarke and returned 58 minutes later at 1:14 pm; the foreman indicated that they had not arrived at a unanimous verdict. The trial judge directed them to continue deliberating. The jury retired again at 1:18 pm and returned 40 minutes later at 1:58 pm to announce their majority verdict. The total time of deliberation was one hour and 38 minutes. Section 44 of the Jury (Amendment) Act, 2016 stipulates that a jury deliberate for two hours before returning a majority verdict.

The Appeal Court, in considering the argument that the sentences for the murders were “manifestly excessive”, said “it cannot be denied that this matter could be regarded as an exceptional case and represented…‘the worst of the worst’ for this type of offending”. In fact, the Appeal Court said it was “worth recognising…that the prosecution could have, at the very least, sought the death penalty with respect to the second and subsequent murders”.

It, however, said, “In light of the errors identified in the learned trial judge’s approach to sentencing…it is fair to say that his sentencing approach lacked the required structure and clarity essential in a case of this magnitude, thereby entitling this court to embark on its own sentencing exercise.”

The judges of the appeal, while declaring that “the magnitude of the brutality and callousness surrounding the killing of all six deceased cannot be overemphasised”, admitted that “the learned trial judge did not employ the structured methodology that has since become well established for determining appropriate minimum pre-parole periods, nor did he otherwise demonstrate how he arrived at those periods”.

“In the absence of comparable cases to provide guidance, it was especially important for the basis of those periods to be apparent from his reasoning. The learned trial judge also failed to consider each count separately, and he imposed lesser sentences on the latter counts of murder,” they stated.

The Appeal Court panel, however, following a resentencing exercise for Campbell, said there actually was an increase in the aggregate minimum pre-parole period he was to serve. It, however, said since based on case law there can be no increase in a convicted person’s sentence on appeal without notice to him and/or his counsel of the court’s intention to do so, and given the absence of any such notice, “Campbell shall serve an aggregate minimum term of 80 years’ imprisonment before eligibility for parole, as ordered by the learned trial judge”.

“The learned trial judge did not err in rejecting the submission of no case to answer that was made on Mr Campbell’s behalf. The quality of the evidence was sufficient for the learned trial judge to determine that it merited the jury’s consideration. He also gave the jury all the appropriate directions on voice identification and on inconsistencies and discrepancies. It was for the jury, the judges of credibility, having heard the evidence and being properly and adequately directed, to determine the weight to be attached to the evidence and arrive at the verdicts they considered appropriate. It is pellucid from their unanimous verdicts that they were convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr Campbell was guilty as charged. The application for leave to appeal conviction is, therefore, refused,” the judges of the appeal ruled.

In respect of Clarke, the judges of the appeal said the trial court was obliged to observe and uphold the law which mandates that a majority verdict in a murder case may be received only after “the lapse of two hours from the retirement of the jury”.

“As a result, Mr Clarke’s trial, conviction, and sentence on counts two to seven of the indictment amount to a nullity. Therefore, the convictions on those counts will be quashed and the sentences set aside…a retrial of those counts of the indictment will be ordered in the interest of justice,” the judges of the appeal ruled.

In the meantime, however, the court said, the aggregate sentence of 40 years’ imprisonment — comprising two 20-year terms ordered to run consecutively — was neither manifestly excessive nor disproportionate, and did not breach the totality principle in Clarke’s case even though the learned trial judge erred in failing to deduct the three months Clarke spent in pre-sentence remand.

“In accordance with the authorities, this period will be deducted from the sentence imposed on count one of the indictment. This will result in a sentence of 19 years’ and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour. This is the only basis for interfering with the sentences imposed by the learned trial judge,” the Appeal Court said in allowing the appeal against the sentence, in part.

“The sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment at hard labour on count one of the indictment is set aside and substituted therefor is a sentence of 19 years’ and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour, with three months spent on pre-sentence remand being fully credited. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are affirmed. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are to run concurrently but consecutively to the sentence on count one as imposed by the learned trial judge. The appellant shall, therefore, serve an aggregate term of 39 years and nine months’ imprisonment at hard labour,” the judges of the appeal ruled in respect of Clarke.

“The sentence on count one is to be reckoned as having commenced on December 14, 2018, the date on which it was imposed. The sentences on counts eight to 11 are to commence after completion of the sentence on count one,” the court said further.

World.title: WHO WANTS IT?
World.content:
Colorado Murray of Waterhouse celebrates after scoring against Molynes United in their Jamaica Premier League match played at Constant Spring Sports Complex on Wednesday, March 18. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The lead in the Legend Jamaica Premier League will be up for grabs on Sunday, with Montego Bay United not playing until Monday and Racing United, Waterhouse FC and Tivoli Gardens all having a chance to move ahead of the leaders.

Three points separate the top five teams in the standings. Montego Bay United lead with 14 points from six games, followed by Racing United on 13, Waterhouse FC on 12, and Tivoli Gardens and Tru-Juice FC on 11 each.

Racing United, who are unbeaten in their last three games and have scored 10 of their 14 goals over that period, will start favourites to extend Humble Lion’s winless run to seven games. Racing are away to the bottom-placed team, who have yet to win this season.

Despite being held 0-0 by Waterhouse on Monday, Racing United remain one of the competition’s top-scoring teams. They will face a Humble Lion defence that has conceded 17 goals, five more than the next-worst team, Molynes United, with 12.

Nickyle Ellis and Tajay Grant have combined to score seven of Racing United’s goals, with each having scored more goals than Humble Lion’s entire team.

Waterhouse FC have drawn their last three games after opening the season with three wins. They will host Dunbeholden FC, who are 12th in the standings with three points.

Waterhouse have scored just two goals in their last three games, a sharp decline from the 13 they netted in their first three matches. They will hope to rediscover their scoring touch against Dunbeholden.

Colorado Murray and Mario Simms have scored three goals each for Waterhouse.

Tivoli Gardens could also move ahead of Montego Bay United on goal difference. They travel to face Cavalier FC, who are winless in their last three games and are coming off a loss to Molynes United.

Tivoli have scored 13 goals this season, with Leaunghn Williams leading the way with three. Steve Clarke and Ajuma Johnson have scored two each.

Tru-Juice FC will be looking for back-to-back wins when they visit winless Treasure Beach at the STETHS Sports Complex. It will be the first meeting between the teams in the Jamaica Premier League.

Tru-Juice are coming off a 4-0 win over Humble Lion, while Treasure Beach have scored just four goals in five games.

Defending champions Portmore United, who have played just three games because of their Concacaf Caribbean Cup commitments, will host Chapelton Maroons at the Ferdie Neita Sports Complex.

Portmore are ninth with five points after drawing their two most recent games and will be looking for a win. Chapelton, however, will be seeking back-to-back victories after edging Treasure Beach 1-0 last weekend.

World.title: Beenie Man faces Trinidadian backlash again, seeks to clear air
World.content:
Dancehall artiste Beenie Man

For the second time in just under two years, dancehall superstar Beenie Man is seeking to clear the air after offending the people of Trinidad and Tobago.

The Girls Dem Sugar deejay stirred controversy earlier this week when, during an interview on New York’s Hot 97, he suggested that Jamaica started carnival celebrations before Trinidad and Tobago, attributing its origins to late Jamaican music pioneer Byron Lee.

Carnival has deep historical roots in Trinidad and Tobago and several other Caribbean islands, with the celebration originating during the period of slavery. In contrast, Jamaica only began celebrating carnival on a national level in the early 1990s.

Against that background, Beenie Man has been chided across social media since his remarks surfaced online.

On Saturday, in a post on social media, he apologised for his comments, indicating that he got his “history wrong”.

Trinidad and Tobago, let me clear this up with love. I got the carnival history wrong, and I apologise. I confused my memories of Byron Lee’s contribution to carnival in Jamaica with the wider history,” Beenie man said, adding “Your carnival has its own rich history, and I respect that. I never intended to disrespect your people or culture, but I understand why my comments caused offence.”

In February 2025, the dancehall icon apologised to Trinidadians over comments he made on ‘doubles’, a popular food item in the twin island republic.

READ: Beenie Man gives heartfelt apology to Trinidadians in ‘doubles’ spat

In an interview on popular US podcast Drink Champs, the Who Am I singer said that a soca artiste had told him that stray dogs won’t eat doubles and he decided to try a little behavioural experiment to test the hypothesis with the channa-and-bara favourite. But the stray dog declined.

World.title: Security forces reacted to deadly force at Sligoville – McKay
World.content:
Jason McKay

Criminologist Dr Jason McKay has warned against “Monday-morning-quarterbacking” in the wake of the deadly shootout involving members of the security forces last week, which resulted in the death of two policemen and three alleged gunmen in Sligoville, St Catherine.

McKay, a trained hostage negotiator and serving member of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) assigned to the St Catherine South Special Operations team, pointed to questions raised in the media by former commissioner of police, Rear Admiral Hardley Lewin, and Security Consultant Robert Finzi-Smith.

Addressing the deadly standoff in which a 10-year-old girl was shot and injured, allegedly used as a human shield by the occupants, Rear Admiral Lewin questioned whether “there was an alternative way of dealing with this?”, suggesting the security forces had enough time to coax a possible surrender.

“There was, available to the operation, some 12 hours of daylight,” Rear Admiral Lewin remarked, referring to the firefight sparked by a 5:15 am attempt by the security forces to apprehend “criminals and wanted persons” in the Five/Six Mile area of Sligoville.

“It’s not something that was dusk. There are things that would have to be looked at, in any hot-washer that the police would do, to look at whether there was an alternative way of dealing with this. Did the men have a chance of escaping? Who was in that room that might be innocent?” Rear Admiral Lewin asked, questioning the tactics employed by the security forces.

However, McKay, who stood by as an International Cricket Council-required JCF hostage negotiator for any eventuality that might have arisen at the 2007 Cricket World Cup staged in Jamaica, pointed to specific circumstances under which a negotiator would be called in as opposed to additional support from tactical teams.

“Hostage negotiators generally get involved if there is a lull during a shooting. There was no lull. It was either constant or sporadic gunfire coming from the house, even during what appeared to be conversations between the occupants and the security forces, creating a high level of distrust among the police during which two of their own were shot and killed.

“Hostage negotiations do not take place in the middle of shootouts. Once there is sustained or sporadic shooting, it is the tactical operators who handle active shooting scenes,” McKay pointed out.

A widely-circulated 18-minute long telephone conversation involving two men engaging members of the security forces, indicating their willingness to leave the house, while claiming there was only one shooter, has been the subject of widespread debate.

One of the men was overheard encouraging the 10-year-old to scream, which, McKay said, could have been coercion to deceive the police, pointing out that even while the men were engaging the security forces a shot rang out from inside the house, triggering gunfire from what was by then a joint military-police team.

Finzi-Smth, former senior director, safety and security, at the University of Technology, alluded to the number of rounds fired by the security forces while there were “non-combatants in the house”, an assertion McKay called out as being not from an informed position.

“It became obvious that there were non-combatants in the house,” said Finzi-Smith. “You fire aimed shots. You don’t fire shots that find wherever they want to find, especially when there are non-combatants in the way,” he stated.

McKay, however, pointed out that before such an assertion can be made, one would have to determine at which point the greater volume of firepower was laid down by the police, whether the gun battle intensified after the child was removed.

“It is difficult to determine whether the bulk of the police’s shooting was during or after the child was out of the house. There was a point in time that the situation would have become a subject barricaded with a high-powered firearm.

“It is easy to Monday-morning-quarter back but, it is my personal opinion that if you are not the one going through the experience, being mindful that two of your fellow officers were killed after the initial engagement, enough gunfire to wound other security-forces personnel, the rate of return-fire would have been unquestionably above average.

“It was a threatening situation that had already proven to be deadly,” McKay reminded, pointing to his experiences of being involved in high-risk entries as a member of a special-operations team for almost 25 years.

World.title: Holness signals imminent changes to tackle red tape
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness speaks during the official launch of the Jamaica Reconstruction and Resilience Oversight Committee (JAMRROC) at Jamaica House in Kingston, where he addressed the ongoing recovery of Jamaica’s education system and defended the use of outdoor spaces for learning while some schools undergo repairs following Hurricane Melissa. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Prime Minister Andrew Holness says in the coming days the government will be announcing measures aimed at increasing efficiency across Government, making the bureaucracy more functional and improving service delivery to Jamaicans post-Hurricane Melissa.

The prime minister says the changes are necessary to increase the capacity of the Government to respond to current challenges.

Holness gave the update when he addressed a group of private sector leaders who attended an event on Thursday at the Terra Nova Hotel in St Andrew. The event was hosted by Cabinet Minister Daryl Vaz.

“We are a free country socially, but we are not a free country economically,” Holness said. “If we are going to address the issue of poverty in our country, we must address the issue of our bureaucuracy.

“We can’t get rid of bureaucracy, but we must make our bureaucracy make sense, it must be efficient,” the prime minister said.

The prime minister pointed to red tape for the lengthy time it has taken for the delivery of modular homes to families impacted by Hurricane Melissa.

“We imported the modular houses almost six months ago, and we are still not able to have them rolled out and built quickly… between the logistics, the contracting, the permitting, procurement, it is as if no one cares that it’s an emergency,” Holness said.

He said it was critical that Jamaicans in need are able to receive assistance much more quickly to mitigate their distress and improve their well-being and welfare.

“In the coming days, the government will be making certain announcements which will signal a change in how we do business,” Holness said.

World.title: Leaked emails show AfD co-leader’s U-turn on ‘explosive’ nationalist colleague
World.content:
The revelations come from more than 420,000 emails and roughly 48,000 documents released by hackers this week, providing a rare glimpse inside Germany’s largest far-right party. An anonymous spokesperson for the hackers told Die Zeit the attack was not “politically” motivated “in the sense that [they] support another party,” but that they published the allegedly stolen material to promote “transparency and public accountability.”

The AfD confirmed the breach, saying hackers had attacked a hosting provider in late September. It condemned the leak as “an attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy itself.”

WELT, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, examined emails from one of Weidel’s accounts between 2015 and 2017, when she was a relatively junior figure in the party’s leadership.

Asked by WELT to explain the contrast between her warnings at the time and her present position, Weidel declined to comment through a spokesperson.

A spokesperson for Höcke did not respond to a request for comment sent by POLITICO on Saturday.

‘Deeply problematic’

The messages seen by WELT show a politician deeply alarmed by the growing influence of Höcke, who championed an ethnically defined German nationalism drawing on ideas associated with the Nazi era.

World.title: Security Sunday: Bringen Frankreichs Proteste Marine Le Pen an die Macht? – mit Martina Meister
World.content:
Brennende Mülltonnen, verbarrikadierte Schaufenster und eine unübersichtliche Mischung aus Gelbwesten, Anarchisten und Banlieue-Jugendlichen auf den Straßen. Was als Schülerprotest in Frankreich begann, hat sich an steigenden Energiepreisen zu einer radikalen Bewegung entzündet. Präsident Emmanuel Macron verliert zunehmend die Kontrolle und wirkt in der Krise wie ein Pilot ohne Cockpit.

Inmitten der Eskalation positioniert sich Marine Le Pen geschickt als Kandidatin der Ordnung, während die politische Mitte zerbröselt und eine erdrückende Staatsverschuldung den Handlungsspielraum raubt.

Was ein möglicher Rechtsruck für die europäische Sicherheitsarchitektur und das ohnehin angespannte deutsch-französische Verhältnis bedeutet, analysiert Welt-Korrespondentin Martina Meister im Gespräch mit Rixa Fürsen.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren.
