World.title: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion factory in US
World.content:
After Donald Trump made the announcement at an election rally in Georgia, the German carmaker confirmed plans for a factory in the US state, but noted car production would only start early next decade.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that German car producer, Audi, will build a $4 billion (€3.77 billion) assembly plant in the US state of Georgia.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, Trump said the plant will produce 200,000 SUVs annually.

"Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That's incredible," Trump said.

The US president credited his tariff policies for the company's decision to build the plant in the US.

Europe tries to sway Trump on vehicle tariffs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump focusing on manufacturing as midterms loom

The US leader has pressured foreign and domestic businesses to move production to the United States. His tactics included sweeping tariffs on car imports.

Last year, Trump's tariffs cost Audi €1.2-billion-euro ($1.4-billion).

The latest announcement comes as Trump tries to make a last ditch effort to boost Republican candidates in the battleground state by following through on his promise of reinvigorate American manufacturing ahead of the midterm elections.

The Republicans are bracing for losses in the November 3 vote amid rising prices and the ongoing war in Iran.

What did Audi say?

Audi, which is owned by Volkswagen, said the construction of the manufacturing plant is ‌scheduled ​to begin next year, with car production starting in the early 2030s.

How will US tariffs hit Germany's car exports and imports? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters news agency.

The company also said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs.

World.title: Un negocio con muy buen olfato
World.content:
Más de la mitad de los hogares españoles cuenta con una mascota, un indicativo de la pujanza de un sector que mueve a 15.121 empresas, da trabajo a 91.700 personas y que trata de atender el creciente interés de los dueños por la calidad de vida de sus perros y gatos

Los nuevos hábitos de vida de los animales de compañía ya no caben en una tienda de mascotas tradicional... Se extienden por las clínicas veterinarias, los laboratorios farmacéuticos, las carnicerías, incluso por las guarderías y los salones de belleza. Cada vez más propietarios, o tutores, como prefieren llamarlos en el sector, tratan a sus perros y gatos como miembros de la familia y ya no buscan únicamente cubrir las necesidades básicas, sino mejorar su bienestar. Y esto se traduce en un auge del sector, explica Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance y uno de los protagonistas de este capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen. Su compañía, que comenzó en 2020 con un pequeño local cerca de la estación de Joaquín Sorolla, en Valencia, se ha especializado en hamburguesas para perros que siguen la dieta BARF (por sus siglas en inglés, biologically appropriate raw food, que significa alimento crudo biológicamente apropiado), un modelo de nutrición a partir de ingredientes frescos y crudos.

La revolución en el cuidado animal ha comenzado por la alimentación. El pienso común ha dado paso a otros que no tienen saborizantes ni colorantes artificiales, con conceptos como el NøPienso®, de la propia Wild Balance, producto en el que se observan a simple vista los ingredientes, como la carne y las verduras, y a dietas alternativas sin cereales, hipoalergénicas o que replican la de los humanos. Y recientemente se ha extendido al campo de la cosmética, para incluir productos ecológicos y con formulaciones más respetuosas con las mascotas, señala Alba Ciordia, fundadora de The Doog Life, marca ecológica que comercializa champús, dentífricos, espumas de limpieza en seco y suplementos alimenticios para perros y gatos, quien comparte protagonismo con Domingo en el pódcast de Banco Sabadell.

Cuenta Ciordia que se inició en el sector gracias a una de sus dos perritas, Claire, a la que los productos convencionales le producían reacciones cutáneas debido a la presencia de determinados ingredientes sintéticos. Encontrar alternativas no era sencillo. Por eso, Ciordia se formó en campos como la nutrición para perros y gatos y la fitoaromaterapia, un tipo de tratamientos complementarios a partir de aceites esenciales y extractos vegetales. Con ese conocimiento se embarcó en el desarrollo de soluciones junto a laboratorios especializados. Lo que comenzó como una búsqueda personal terminó por convertirse en una marca que hoy comercializa más de 30 referencias.

La conversación entre los empresarios sirve como hilo conductor para explicar un sector que hoy representa el 0,38% del producto interior bruto (PIB) español, cuenta con 15.121 empresas y da trabajo a 91.700 personas, de acuerdo a las estimaciones de la Asociación Española de la Industria y el Comercio del Sector del Animal de Compañía (AEDPAC). Su secretario general, Ignasi Solana, celebra, en conversación telefónica, el éxito de esta industria que, según él “aún se encuentra dando sus primeros pasos”.

“El subsector de la alimentación natural y de los cuidados naturales ha crecido mucho más rápido que el resto” Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance, acerca del auge de las alternativas a las dietas habituales para perros y gatos

Las fortalezas Una industria que se expande y encuentra nuevos modelos de negocio

Un sector en expansión. El negocio del cuidado de los animales de compañía crece cada año, de acuerdo con el Informe sectorial 2026 de la Asociación Madrileña de Veterinarios de Animales de Compañía, que analiza su evolución a nivel nacional. La facturación de las clínicas veterinarias, los laboratorios farmacéuticos y los fabricantes de alimentación aumentó un 7,4% en 2025 respecto al año anterior. Una cifra similar a la que ofrece el informe Pet-money: la economía de las mascotas y su impacto en el hogar español, de EAE Business School, que cuantifica la expansión en el 8,3%. Además, el sector exporta cada año más, en 2025, el 30% del valor del mercado de la producción de alimentos fue a Europa, Magreb, América y Sudeste Asiático, destaca Santiago de Andrés, secretario general de la Asociación de Fabricante de Alimentos para Animales de Compañía (ANFAAC).

Basado en productos de primera necesidad. Se caracteriza por una demanda constante en artículos de alimentación y atención sanitaria, lo que genera actividades con ingresos recurrentes, como las suscripciones de alimentación para recibir la comida de la mascota en casa, los planes veterinarios y los seguros.

Diversificado y con enorme potencial para la innovación y la especialización. El sector se expande continuamente hacia nuevos modelos de negocio como la cosmética canina y felina, el ocio y los viajes. También está abierto al desarrollo de productos nuevos en campos como la nutrición especializada, la telemedicina y los dispositivos inteligentes.

Con consumidores que buscan lo mejor para los animales a su cargo. La cesta de la compra para perros y gatos cada vez se parece más a la de los humanos. A veces, incluso, la supera en calidad en determinados artículos, especialmente en los alimentos, explica Ignasi Solana, de AEDPAC. “El ejemplo más claro es que los responsables de perros y gatos apuestan por comida de marca antes que por las genéricas, conocidas como marcas blancas, porque la asocian a mayor calidad. Es un fenómeno que se extiende a otros campos como la cosmética y que nosotros denominamos como premiumización”, indica para describir la estrategia comercial que consiste en ofrecer productos o servicios que son percibidos por su presentación o su precio como de mayor calidad.

“Hay un potencial muy grande de dispositivos inteligentes para la prevención que buscan detectar cambios en la salud del animal y que ayudan al veterinario” Alba Ciordia, fundadora de The Doog Life, sobre las posibilidades de innovación dentro de la industria

Los desafios El reto de luchar contra la pseudociencia y multiplicar los espacios para mascotas

Luchar contra la desinformación. Internet y, en especial, las redes sociales han multiplicado la información que reciben los propietarios o tutores, lo que puede generar confusión y dificulta la capacidad para distinguir los contenidos basados en evidencia científica, en publicidad, en opinión o en pseudociencia. Santiago de Andrés, de ANFAAC, señala que aún hay margen de mejora en la comunicación entre veterinarios y tutores, con datos precisos y basados en ciencia.

Atender a la sostenibilidad. La fabricación de alimentos implica un gran consumo de recursos a través de la producción ganadera. Además, genera gran cantidad de emisiones contaminantes. Los piensos, aperitivos y productos de higiene requieren de envases plásticos muchas veces difíciles de reciclar. La industria ya trabaja en proteínas alternativas y en el aprovechamiento de productos de la industria alimentaria para desarrollar formulaciones de menor impacto. Igualmente, investiga nuevos métodos de almacenamiento y distribución de los productos que permitan reciclar y reutilizar envases.

Potenciar la digitalización. La modernización del sector requiere un avance en dos de sus patas, señala Solana, de Aedpac. Por un lado, las tiendas de artículos para mascotas, como las pajarerías, habitualmente negocios familiares, están hoy en manos de la segunda o la tercera generación de comerciantes que afrontan paulatinamente la digitalización de sus sistemas y el desarrollo de sus comercios electrónicos. Por otro, la irrupción de la telemedicina y los dispositivos inteligentes abren nuevas oportunidades en el sector sanitario, pero requieren de grandes inversiones.

Contribuir a la creación de espacios adaptados a las mascotas. En España, señala Solana, aún hay mucho recorrido para convertir los lugares públicos en sitios propicios para el acceso con animales de compañía. La Ley de Bienestar Animal establece que hoteles, bares y restaurantes, entre otros establecimientos, pueden permitir su entrada y, en caso de no admitirlos, han de indicarlo en el exterior de manera visible. Solana es uno de los promotores del certificado ITVET, un protocolo de inspección técnica organizado por una empresa privada que acredita las buenas prácticas para facilitar la presencia y el tránsito de animales de compañía en instalaciones que se definen como pet-friendly (aptas para mascotas).

“Europa es mucho más ‘pet friendly’ en general que España” Kike Domingo, fundador de Wild Balance, sobre la presencia de animales de compañía en comercios y en el transporte público

World.title: ¿Dónde y por qué se protesta en Europa? Las reivindicaciones de los jóvenes de cada país
World.content:
Estudiantes, sindicatos y vecinos han convocado más de 170 manifestaciones en poco más de un mes en todo el continente. Sus motivos a menudo coinciden

Media Europa vuelve a salir a la calle este sábado. Hay convocatorias desde Grecia hasta Bélgica, pasando por Albania, Francia, Portugal y España. Son las últimas de un otoño de movilizaciones: entre el 15 de septiembre y el 23 de octubre, 12 países europeos suman al menos 177 protestas o manifestaciones. La cifra es parecida a la media de 190 protestas mensuales entre septiembre y octubre de los otoños más intensos de la crisis del euro (2010, 2011 y 2012), según los registros de PolDem, un proyecto universitario que recopila protestas a partir de noticias de agencias. Francia, España, Italia, Portugal y Bélgica concentran la mayoría de las movilizaciones contabilizadas.

Las reivindicaciones cambian de un país a otro, pero tres se repiten de forma constante: la vivienda, la educación y el coste de la vida. Francia es ahora el centro de las concentraciones por la educación y el coste de la vida, y esas protestas se han extendido a Italia y Bélgica. En España, el foco es la vivienda: la primera gran manifestación del otoño se celebró el 26 de septiembre, tras el desahucio de Maricarmen, y reunió a al menos 25.000 personas en Madrid, según la Delegación del Gobierno (el Sindicato de Inquilinas contabilizó 300.000). Hasta esa fecha, fue la mayor protesta en una sola ciudad de este ciclo, y ha inspirado a manifestantes de Portugal e Italia. Al este del continente, los motivos son otros: la corrupción es el problema principal en Albania y en Serbia. En Alemania, las concentraciones son más pequeñas y se centran en la oposición al servicio militar y al rearme.

Images) Estudiantes se manifiestan contra la falta de recursos y personal en el sistema educativo, en la plaza de la República de París, el 4 de octubre de 2026. Veronique de Viguerie (Getty Images)

Los estudiantes han protagonizado buena parte de las protestas, pero se han ido sumando sindicatos, docentes y otros colectivos. Coinciden en el tiempo y comparten reivindicaciones, pero responden a conflictos nacionales distintos y no forman un movimiento coordinado. Que coincidan en otoño tiene una explicación en el calendario: “Los estudiantes vuelven a los centros, las redes organizativas se activan y los cambios en las tasas, las ayudas y las condiciones de estudio se vuelven inmediatamente tangibles”, explica Luka Lešić, de la Unión Europea de Estudiantes.

Los datos recopilados por EL PAÍS, a partir de agencias, medios y fuentes oficiales, incluyen las protestas contra medidas gubernamentales que reunieron al menos un centenar de personas y tuvieron cobertura en medios nacionales. Como se ve en el gráfico, los cinco países con más movilizaciones reúnen el 80% de las registradas.

La mayoría de las manifestaciones han sido pacíficas. Según los datos recopilados por este periódico, 49 protestas han terminado con detenidos y al menos 30 con agentes de la policía heridos. Ha habido episodios violentos en Italia, Albania y, sobre todo, Francia. Allí, la jornada del 17 de octubre reunió a 550.000 manifestantes en todo el país, según el Ministerio del Interior y terminó con más de 2.000 detenidos, casi 1.000 agentes heridos y destrozos importantes en varias ciudades, como el incendio del Ayuntamiento de Limoges. En Italia, el 18 de octubre, unos 2.000 jóvenes convocados por redes sociales, sin organización ni reivindicaciones políticas, irrumpieron en el centro de Milán para romper escaparates y saquear tiendas. La policía llevó a comisaría a 271, el 80% de ellos menores. Mientras, en Albania, más de 10 días de movilizaciones violentas han dejado el Tribunal Supremo, el Ministerio de Educación y otros edificios de la ciudad incendiados.

Manifestantes vandalizan un establecimiento durante unas protestas en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/Getty Images)

A continuación, repasamos las causas y las razones de las reivindicaciones más transversales entre las protestas del continente.

Educación

En Francia, las protestas empezaron a mediados de septiembre con bloqueos de institutos y se extendieron en tres semanas a todo el país. El 1 de octubre hubo cientos de centros bloqueados. Los alumnos piden que se cubran las plazas de profesores vacantes —al comienzo del curso faltaba al menos uno en el 53% de los centros, según el sindicato docente SNES-FSU—, menos alumnos por clase y edificios en mejor estado. Este malestar social, en parte provocado por la necesidad de Francia de hacer recortes presupuestarios para reducir un elevado nivel de endeudamiento, ha cristalizado en el mayor movimiento de protesta en décadas.

La furia de los estudiantes franceses también encendió la ira de sus compañeros de la Bélgica francófona, que protestan desde octubre contra la subida de las tasas y los recortes presupuestarios, sobre todo en Bruselas y en Lieja. En prevención de posibles nuevos disturbios este fin de semana, Bruselas emitió una prohibición de circulación de patinetes y bicicletas eléctricas compartidas entre las diez de la mañana del viernes y las 22.00 del sábado en el centro de la ciudad.

En Italia salieron a la calle el 16 de octubre, entre otros motivos contra la norma que limita al 30% la presencia de determinadas categorías de alumnos extranjeros en las clases de primer curso. En Madrid, los profesores de la enseñanza pública están en huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre, y en Atenas más de 10.000 personas, según la policía, secundaron el día 21 una huelga de maestros.

Vivienda y coste de la vida

En España, a la acampada de Sol le siguió el 3 de octubre una jornada de marchas en medio centenar de ciudades, un día después de que el Congreso tumbara los dos decretos de vivienda del Gobierno. Los sindicatos mayoritarios convocaron una huelga general para el 11 de noviembre. En Portugal, las acampadas de Lisboa y Oporto pedían retirar un proyecto de ley que facilita los desahucios: la policía las ha desalojado el 20 de octubre.

El combustible movilizó a los transportistas del sur de Italia, que bloquean carreteras desde mediados de octubre, con el gasóleo a 2,30 euros el litro. En 2018, la subida de su impuesto ya llevó a la calle en Francia a los chalecos amarillos. En Alemania, los sindicatos reunieron el 26 de septiembre a 175.000 personas, según los convocantes, contra los recortes en pensiones y sanidad. La inflación se ha moderado desde el máximo de 2022, pero desde entonces los precios han subido un 23,6% en la UE, según Eurostat.

Corrupción

En Albania, la protesta empezó en mayo como un movimiento pacífico, la llamada revolución de los flamencos, contra la cesión de una reserva natural a empresarios vinculados con Jared Kushner, yerno de Donald Trump. Con el comienzo del curso, el 13 de octubre, se sumaron los estudiantes y las protestas se volvieron violentas: el 14 ardieron los ministerios de Educación y de Finanzas, y hasta el 19 hubo 310 heridos, según Europa Press. Piden la dimisión del primer ministro, Edi Rama, en el poder desde 2013, y acusan al Gobierno de proteger a grupos mafiosos. Ningún tribunal lo ha probado, aunque la Fiscalía investiga a la exviceprimera ministra, Belinda Balluku, por corrupción y blanqueo y el alcalde de Tirana, Erion Veliaj, permanece en prisión preventiva desde febrero de 2025, acusado de los mismos cargos.

Manifestantes hablan con agentes de policía durante una protesta antigubernamental de estudiantes en Tirana, Albania, el 20 de octubre de 2026. Louisa Gouliamaki (REUTERS)

En Serbia, el movimiento estudiantil ha madurado a lo lago de dos años en las calles, después de la muerte de 16 personas en el derrumbe de la estación de Novi Sad, en noviembre de 2024. Sus demostraciones forzaron al Gobierno de Aleksandar Vucic a adelantar las elecciones, convocadas para este domingo. El movimiento se presenta como Lista de Estudiantes y es la segunda fuerza, según la última encuesta de Ipsos. El jueves, unas 150.000 personas se concentraron en Belgrado, según recuentos independientes.

La respuesta de los gobiernos

En Francia, el Gobierno decretó toques de queda en París y otras ciudades, y también anunció más de 3.000 profesores suplentes y retiró la subida de algunas tasas universitarias. Para este sábado, el Ejecutivo solo ha autorizado las marchas sindicales y ha prohibido las concentraciones en Lyon y Marsella, con un despliegue policial un 20% mayor que el del 17 de octubre.

En Italia, el decreto de seguridad ya castigaba la participación violenta en una manifestación con hasta cinco años de prisión, y de cara a la jornada de hoy las autoridades han blindado el centro de Milán y las estaciones de la periferia desde las que llegaron los jóvenes.

La policía lleva a cabo detenciones y arrestos de los manifestantes tras las protestas contra el alto costo de la vida en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/ Getty Images)

Las próximas citas llegan en noviembre: una jornada sindical en Francia el día 5, una jornada estudiantil en Alemania el 17, la huelga general del sindicato CGIL en Italia el 20 y, en Portugal, una manifestación de la CGTP ante el Parlamento portugués el 24. Además de la huelga general convocada en España para el 11 de noviembre.

Con información de Raquel Villaécija, desde París; Silvia Ayuso, desde Bruselas; Francisco Peregil, desde Tirana, e Íñigo Domínguez, desde Roma.

Artículo elaborado en el marco del proyecto ChatEurope, financiado por la Comisión Europea

World.title: Países Bajos no está hecho para los tanques
World.content:
Países Bajos, la quinta economía de la UE, suele presentarse como la puerta de entrada al continente debido a su ubicación junto a Francia, Bélgica y Alemania, y el mar del Norte. También, por la pujanza del puerto de Róterdam y el aeropuerto de

Ámsterdam-Schiphol, y por el servicio de trenes que conecta con Bruselas, Londres o Fráncfort en pocas horas. En caso de que hubiera una guerra en suelo europeo, sin embargo, ese emplazamiento privilegiado pasaría a convertirse en estratégico, y las rutas de tránsito militar (corredores, en lenguaje técnico) no cumplen con los acuerdos de la OTAN para grandes transportes. Se trata de una red de carreteras, puentes y ferrocarriles que necesitan una inversión de al menos 9.500 millones de euros para mejoras, según el Tribunal de Cuentas, que ha publicado este mes un informe a la vista del aumento de la inestabilidad geopolítica en Europa.

Sin un hipotético panorama bélico sobre la mesa, el Gobierno neerlandés afronta ya un déficit total de 80.000 millones de euros para proyectos de equipamientos a escala nacional, tal y como indica la carta remitida en marzo pasado al Congreso por el ministerio de Infraestructuras y Gestión del Agua. “No se puede hacer todo, ni se puede hacer todo al mismo tiempo”, dijo entonces su titular, Vincent Karremans, que hizo un llamamiento al Parlamento para “tomar juntos decisiones difíciles”.

De producirse un conflicto, gran parte de los recursos militares de la OTAN entrarían en Europa a través de los puertos neerlandeses, pero las carreteras, vías férreas y puentes que deberían usarse para ello no pueden resistir ese tipo de tráfico. Se trataría de tanques, vehículos más pequeños o sistemas de armamento, y entre los requisitos militares señalados por el alto mando de la OTAN “se incluyen, por ejemplo, las alturas de los viaductos o los puentes ferroviarios que soporten vagones con cargas pesadas”, según reza el informe del Tribunal de Cuentas. El cálculo de sus expertos cifra la inversión necesaria “en 4.500 millones de euros en mejoras de las que también se beneficiarían los ciudadanos”. Unos 5.000 millones de euros adicionales se destinarían a “cumplir con los requisitos militares”.

En 2023, la UE designó una serie de corredores en Europa destinados al transporte rápido de material militar. El Tribunal de Cuentas advierte de que algunos vehículos de grandes dimensiones no podrían circular por la parte neerlandesa de esas rutas especiales. Bien porque las carreteras son hoy demasiado estrechas, o porque los puentes no aguantarían el peso. En el caso del ferrocarril, el informe señala que como esta clase de material precisa de un transporte más ancho, “los trenes que circulen en sentido contrario no podrían hacerlo, o tendrían que desviarse”, con el consiguiente disturbio y retrasos para la ciudadanía.

Sin recursos para invertir

En tiempo de paz también hay transportes militares regulares, y el Servicio Nacional de Trafico colabora con el Ministerio de Defensa para adaptarse al estado diario del tráfico. En caso de conflicto, tener que cambiar de ruta puede suponer un problema si una pasarela es demasiado baja, un puente necesita reparaciones o unas traviesas están hundidas en algún tramo de la vía del tren. En su respuesta por carta al Tribunal de Cuentas, el ministro Karremans abunda en el hecho de que “gran parte de la infraestructura nacional está obsoleta y con necesidad de mantenimiento”, pero “no se dispone de recursos financieros suficientes para ponerla a punto al ritmo necesario”. De ahí que se esté llevando a cabo una “reordenación de las prioridades”, para el mantenimiento de las infraestructuras “que garanticen el transporte militar a gran escala a través del país”, y para mantener a su vez “el funcionamiento de la sociedad con la mayor normalidad posible”. Si bien el trazado exacto de los corredores militares es secreto por razones de seguridad, Defensa colgó en 2021 en su web una nota donde decía que “se habilitarán tres distribuidos geográficamente por Países Bajos”, que incluyen vías por carretera, ferrocarril y vías navegables, adaptadas al material más grande y pesado.

World.title: More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.

Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.

The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.

The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.

So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.

World.title: Egypt protests shut Dutch embassy over arrest of Sisi loyalist
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch embassy in Cairo has closed to the public until further notice after nine days of protests outside the building, during which staff had to be evacuated, the embassy has announced on social media.

The demonstrators are demanding the release of Ahmed Nasser, deputy head of a pro-government Egyptian youth group, who was arrested in the Netherlands on October 10.

He was reportedly detained on suspicion of threatening Anas Habib, an Egyptian activist who lives in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has been extended by 14 days, broadcaster NOS reported.

Habib drew international attention last summer when he filmed himself padlocking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague, in protest at the Egyptian government keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed.

His action sparked similar protests at Egyptian embassies in more than 16 countries, after which supporters of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi began gathering outside embassies to “protect” them.

Days after Nasser’s arrest, Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty called his Dutch counterpart to demand his release and better protection for Egypt’s embassy in The Hague.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said on social media that the two had “discussed the need for progress on the security of our respective embassies and consular affairs.”

It is unclear exactly how Nasser is alleged to have threatened Habib.

World.title: Getting home safely: ADE festivals step up protection measures
World.content:
With the Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE), the world’s biggest electronic music event, underway, extra safety measures have been put in place by festival organisers and the city to make sure, Amsterdam says, that everyone feels “safe in the nightlife scene – free from any form of harassment, violence, discrimination, or (sexual) misconduct.”

To that end, there is a host of initiatives at various festival sites where techno lovers can recharge or get help getting home safely.

Bike buddies, hosts and Check-Ins

At the DGTL festival on NDSM island, cycling buddies will be on hand to help people get safely back and forth to the ferries. They will be working in pairs to ensure their own safety.

A Safe Check-In on NDSM wharf will be open all night for people who need physical help, feel unsafe at night or just need a breather. Phones can also be charged there.

At Awakenings in Halfweg, a Goodbye Host will be stationed at the exit, keeping a watchful eye on partygoers leaving solo. Hosts can help with route planning, and phones can also be charged here.

Both locations will also feature an Awareness Crew, trained teams identifiable by badges or vests that offer support to those feeling uncomfortable or unsafe.

Taking back the night

Some of the safety measures are not new. Last year, following the August murder of teenager Lisa while she cycled home alone and the resulting Take Back the Night campaign, the biking buddies programme was set up.

“We’ve been running social safety measures at our events since Covid, through our awareness teams and social safety hub, so this is something we’ve prioritized for a long time already,” Nikki Schuurs, who deals with Social Safety at DGTL, told Dutch News.

“Bike Buddies, however, was indeed introduced in response to the Take Back the Night campaign, following the murder of Lisa. Safety doesn’t stop at the dance floor.”

Visitors can find the Bike Buddy meeting point just outside the event. Group rides depart every 30 minutes between 21:00 and 07:00, on the hour and half-hour.

Safety concerns have again risen in the city following the violent death of 29-year-old Hajar, whose body was found in a suitcase in the Amstel River last week. She had last been seen cycling with a man near the RAI convention centre. He has since been arrested in connection with her death.

World.title: Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
World.content:
You can’t have failed to notice that Dutch cycle paths are no longer the preserve of old-fashioned cyclists. E-bikes, fatbikes, scooters, snorfietsen, speed pedelecs, disabled vehicles – a seemingly never-ending stream of other road users have moved in. But what exactly are the rules and regulations?

Lesson 64: what is allowed on the cycle path?

Fatbike

The fatbike, with its characteristic thick tyres and frequently thick riders, has become wildly popular. It’s not surprising because at the moment, riders do not need a helmet, driving licence, or third-party liability insurance. The fatbike is officially an e-bike, and therefore there is no age limit, but measures are afoot to make helmet-wearing compulsory for riders up to the age of 18.

Fatbikes are allowed to travel at up to 25 kph. However, many are doctored to go faster – as you will notice when you see them whizzing past cars that keep to the 30 kph limit, mandatory for cars in some Dutch cities.

Electric bike

The electric non-fat bike, so to speak, is literally overtaking the person-powered bike, and that is partly due to its popularity among older riders – who are also well represented in the annual traffic death toll. The same rules of the road as apply to fatbikes apply to ordinary e-bikes – none. You will, however, see more and more elderly riders with a helmet.

Electric cargo bike

The cargo bike, or moedermobiel, deserves a separate mention because of the riders’ mistaken opinion that everyone has to make way for this space-hogging vehicle because it carries cute little toddlers. A good place to spot cargo bikes is outside primary schools at 3pm, when they cause a veritable jam of their own.

Speed pedelec

Speed pedelecs are electric bikes as well, but unlike normal electric bikes, they can legally reach speeds of up to 45 kph. This makes them motorcycles in the eyes of the law, with the rules that then apply, such as mandatory helmet-wearing, a driving licence and insurance. Speed pedelecs can travel on cycle paths, but only at a maximum of 25 kph.

Snorfiets, or moped

No pedalling is needed for this motorised bike or moped, which has a maximum speed limit of 25 kph and is allowed on cycle paths. Although snorfietsen have the same speed limit as electric bikes, they are technically considered to be motorcycles, and riders need a helmet, a driving licence and insurance.

The introduction of helmets for all types of mopeds several years ago led to the downfall of the snorfiets – after all, if you need a helmet, why not drive a proper motorbike – or a fatbike?

Scootmobiel

The motorised wheelchair or scootmobiel is possibly the most dangerous vehicle on the cycle path. According to statistics agency CBS, the traffic death rate among mobility scooter riders is over six times that of motorbike riders and over 20 times that of cyclists.

Users don’t need to pass any tests or learn the rules of the road, and they can go pretty much wherever they like – shopping centre, pavement, cycle path, ordinary road – just not the motorway.

The Canta

The Canta looks like a brommobiel – a small electric vehicle with four wheels – but because it is considered a mobility aid for people with a disability, it is treated in the same way as a scootmobiel.

The Canta is not supposed to go faster than 30 kph on the cycle path and 45 kph on the road, but is allowed to mount the pavement and annoy pedestrians at 6 kph. It can also park anywhere and does not need a number plate.

The minimum age is 16, and you’ll need to take out insurance, but you don’t need a driving licence. The Canta became popular with youngsters who could not be bothered to cycle and has since spawned a surge in far hipper micro cars.

Micro cars

The Birò and its ilk are small, fashionable and, according to many, extremely annoying electric vehicles which are banned from cycle paths but whose drivers use them anyway – particularly as a sneaky escape when faced with a traffic jam.

Popular with estate agents and PR people, micro cars have a maximum speed of 45 kph. If you want one, you will need a brommobiel driving licence and must be 16 or over.

Electric scooter

The step, or scooter, used to be a children’s plaything, but since the invention of the electric version, they have been taking over cities throughout Europe. Steps which have been officially approved have been allowed on Dutch cycle paths since July 1 this year. In Dutch terminology they are known as “light electric vehicles”.

The step has a maximum speed of 25 kph, and riders have to be 16 or over. You will need third-party liability insurance, and the base must have a number plate which is clearly visible.

The e-step is predicted to rival the fatbike in popularity and ability to provoke cycle-path rage – as long as helmets are not compulsory.

World.title: Amsterdam exploring single-use packaging ban
World.content:
Amsterdam is considering banning single-use packaging, including coffee cups, fast-food containers and other single-use plastics that it says make up 30% of the city’s litter.

“Litter is a persistent problem; it is a symptom of a ‘throwaway society’ that pollutes our beautiful city and costs millions every year,” said Amsterdam executive Lian Heinhuis, who is responsible for waste and sanitation, in a statement.

“Yet the solution is within reach: putting an end to the throwaway culture.”

To that end, the city has commissioned a study into what it can legally do to tackle the problem. According to CircuLaw, which provides legal information on circular transitions, such a ban could be implemented, but only after less restrictive measures have proven not to work.

A ban also works best alongside other measures, such as a reliable supply of reusable packaging and a well-established return system.

The city says it will work with business owners and residents and also look at how other cities are managing the problem, including Copenhagen and Lisbon, the latter of which has already implemented a single-use packaging ban.

“Single-use packaging is a major problem,” the city said. “The plastics used in these items take hundreds of years to decompose – if they ever do at all. They pollute the soil and groundwater for a very long time, despite being used for an average of only about seven minutes.”

World.title: Student union furious as minister says interest cap unaffordable
World.content:
Despite a coalition promise to cap student loan interest rates at 2.5%, education minister Rianne Letschert has told parliament that the government can no longer afford to stick to its pledge.

The minister said that capping the interest rate at 2.5% is risky and expensive, and that the €40 million annual budget the coalition had set aside to cover the cap is only a quarter of what it would actually cost – €160 million – and could lead to other cuts in the education budget.

“I understand the concerns of current and former students regarding the rise in interest rates on student debt, driven by global instability and an increase in long-term interest rates,” Letschert said in a statement on Thursday.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that it is not possible to implement a 2.5% interest rate cap with the €40 million per year that has been set aside. I find this very disappointing.”

Geopolitical costs

Since the coalition agreement was first presented at the end of January, the global landscape has significantly shifted due to geopolitical tensions and financial uncertainty. Long-term interest rates – to which student loan rates are linked – have risen from 2.7% to 3.3% and could climb higher.

“Recent shocks in the financial markets highlight just how unpredictable – and potentially financially risky – this interest rate policy is,” the ministry said.

But students aren’t buying it. “This effectively sends students out into the world burdened by an incredibly heavy backpack of debt,” LSVB, the national student union, told news service ANP. “The only certainty this cabinet offers students is the assurance that interest rates will rise even further in the coming years.”

Student union ISO added that once again, “students are the victims of empty promises.”

Letschert will discuss the issue with parliament later this month.

World.title: Cyber security centre warns PHP hacking situation could worsen
World.content:
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating the first signs of successful hacks on websites following the exposure of critical vulnerabilities on the web, and says the situation could “rapidly worsen”.

A spokesperson told the Volkskrant on Thursday that the signals came from the NCSC’s international network, and that there was no sign yet of abuse involving Dutch websites. The centre is still checking whether the reports are accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers, working with the help of AI, found that PHP, the programming language on which a majority of the web is built, had at least two serious vulnerabilities in its code.

Details of the weaknesses were leaked online on Monday, and the PHP developers announced they would issue an upgrade by Wednesday afternoon.

Hacking attempts began even before the leak, with Amazon reporting an attack attempt on October 17. US internet security firm Cloudflare said it saw hacking attempts run from thousands before the upgrade to millions afterwards.

Initially, the NCSC said that there were no signs of active hacks and the PHP developers said there were no indications of breaches.

Large amounts of government, healthcare and news sites were forced to go dark temporarily while awaiting the upgrade, including Dutch News.

The Netherlands was fast to act, closing a large amount of its sites and issuing warnings early on Wednesday, after which governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland did the same. The issue is now a global concern.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP said on Thursday it had not yet received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.

World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Protesters return to Poland’s streets demanding liberalisation of abortion law
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition. World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident

Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year. World.title: How will recent scandals affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.
