World.title: Court acquits Polish soldier who accidentally shot Syrian refugee at Belarus border
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier. The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence. ❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta. Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026 The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland. In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed. Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026 A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border. After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds. One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland. Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years. In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison. The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty. Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client. The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border. The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024 In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground. Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal. Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.” In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border. A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases. Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus. That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross. World.title: Poland condemns Ukrainian region for honouring figures associated with WWII massacres of Poles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland. Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026 On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice. The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander. While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw. “Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska. “Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves. Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”. The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News. Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”. Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine. Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.… — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026 Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”. It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.” However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN. The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M. Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026 Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession. However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory. But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018. World.title: Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis. To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok. Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC — Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026 When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws. However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday. One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life. That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law. The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era. In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem). Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table. Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill. In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term. However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected. All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm. Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law. President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026 Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him. However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”. He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”. .@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️ 🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026 A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS. Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year. Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Turn a Sleepover Into a Special Memory With atelier stories
World.content:
A sleepover with friends can be one of those childhood moments that children remember for years.

But for parents, organising one often means buying decorations, preparing bedding, rearranging furniture and dealing with the cleanup afterwards.

Prague-based atelier stories takes care of everything, bringing a fully styled teepee sleepover directly to the family home. Parents choose the theme, date and number of children, while the company handles the delivery, setup, styling and collection.

Founded by Jana Hrochová, who has a background in event production, organisation and guest services, atelier stories was created around a simple idea: making special moments for children without turning them into another project for parents.



The concept works for birthdays, but it doesn’t have to be a special occasion. A weekend with friends, a school holiday or simply an evening when children want to do something different can become a small adventure at home.

Families can choose from three themes: Mermaid World, Wizard Academy and SPA Night. Each setup features coordinated colours, soft textiles, fairy lights and themed accessories. The result is a playful sleeping space designed to appeal to children while remaining stylish enough to fit comfortably into the family home.

Every booking includes the equipment and styling, with teepees assembled and individual sleeping spaces prepared with mattresses, bedding, pillows, blankets, decorative cushions and other details suited to the chosen theme. Optional extras include creative kits, themed activities, photography and Instax memories.

The service is designed to make the experience as easy as possible for parents. There is no need to buy decorations, assemble teepees, wash bedding or find storage space for the equipment afterwards. Once the sleepover is over, atelier stories returns to dismantle the setup, pack everything away and collect it.

Quality, comfort and hygiene are central to the service. The equipment and textiles are cleaned and prepared between bookings, and each sleeping space is carefully arranged to ensure children have a comfortable place to settle in for the night.

Families can book a sleepover for one night or an entire weekend. Prices start at CZK 3,490 for two children for one night, or CZK 4,900 for two children for a full weekend, from Friday to Monday. Both options include the equipment, styling, setup and collection, with delivery within Prague included free of charge.

The service can also make a thoughtful gift from grandparents. Instead of another toy or physical present, a gift voucher gives grandchildren an experience to look forward to.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by atelier stories | tématické přespávačky pro děti (@atelierstories.cz)

Vouchers can cover a complete sleepover or contribute towards one, allowing the family to choose the theme and date later. They are valid for one year and delivered by email within 24 hours of payment.

While at-home sleepovers remain the main focus, atelier stories also creates children’s lounges and play areas for weddings and other events, giving younger guests a dedicated space to play and relax while adults enjoy the occasion.

World.title: Czechia Has the EU’s Lowest Poverty Risk Rate, Eurostat Finds
World.content:
Czechia has the lowest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the European Union, with 12% of its population affected, according to 2025 data from Eurostat.

The figure is well below the EU average of 21%, meaning that around one in five people across the bloc face the risk of poverty or social exclusion. Among children, the proportion rises to one in four.



The EU measure covers people whose incomes fall below the poverty-risk threshold, those experiencing severe material and social deprivation, and those living in households with very low work intensity.

Poland also records a relatively low rate, at 15%, followed by the Netherlands and Slovenia at 16%. Slovakia, Belgium, Finland and Cyprus each report 17%, while Austria stands at 19%.

At the other end of the scale, Bulgaria has the highest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, at 29%. Greece follows at 28%, and Romania at 27%. Lithuania and Spain each report 26%, while Latvia stands at 25%. Italy records 23%, Estonia 22%, and Germany, France and Croatia each match the EU average of 21%.

EU Moves to Strengthen Anti-Poverty Measures

The figures come as European institutions seek to strengthen measures to reduce poverty and social exclusion across the bloc.

Earlier this year, the European Parliament called for more decisive action, stressing that poverty undermines human dignity and that everyone should have access to basic necessities.

In May, the European Commission adopted the EU’s first-ever anti-poverty strategy, setting out measures intended to prevent and reduce poverty across member states.

The strategy addresses several areas, including access to affordable housing, employment opportunities and support for families raising children. It also seeks to remove barriers to employment and tackle in-work poverty, which affects people who have jobs but still struggle to make ends meet.

Housing exclusion and the availability of social and affordable housing are among its priorities. The strategy also focuses on child poverty, support for older people through adequate pensions and opportunities to remain in employment, and efforts to combat discrimination and stigma.

World.title: Internationally Acclaimed Chef Meir Adoni to Open New Restaurant in Prague
World.content:
An internationally acclaimed chef is preparing to open a new restaurant in Prague’s Old Town.

Samna, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant by Israeli chef Meir Adoni, will open at Ovocný trh on November 5, 2026.

The restaurant is being developed in partnership with the team behind SaSaZu and will combine Mediterranean cuisine with Middle Eastern and Moroccan influences.



Adoni has built an international reputation through restaurants in Tel Aviv, New York, Berlin, Singapore and Marbella. His cooking draws on Middle Eastern traditions, modern techniques and the flavors of his Moroccan heritage.

His previous projects include Catit and Mizlala in Tel Aviv, Nur in New York, Layla in Berlin and Aniba in Singapore. He has also appeared as a judge on television cooking competitions, including MasterChef and Game of Chefs, and mentored participants in the S.Pellegrino Young Chef competition.

Samna follows a concept already established by Adoni in Marbella, bringing together Mediterranean recipes, contemporary techniques and bold flavor combinations.

The chef’s approach draws on childhood memories and traditional home cooking, reinterpreted through a modern culinary perspective.

Further details about the menu and the restaurant’s opening arrangements have not been announced in the provided information.

World.title: Prague Airport Adds 20 Destinations to Winter Flight Schedule
World.content:
Prague Airport will offer direct flights to 145 destinations this winter, including 20 new destinations, as its winter flight schedule takes effect on Sunday, October 25.

The 2026/2027 winter schedule will run until March 27, 2027, with 69 airlines operating flights from Václav Havel Airport Prague.

Among the new destinations are Lille, Palermo, Turin, Venice and Bergen. Travellers will also have new options for reaching ski destinations, including Bolzano in Italy and Poprad in Slovakia.



The winter schedule also introduces new long-haul connections to Almaty in Kazakhstan and Hanoi in Vietnam, operated by Vietjet.

Charter flights will add further options, including Phuket in Thailand, La Romana in the Dominican Republic and Sihanoukville in Cambodia.

EasyJet will launch a new route to Marrakesh, Morocco, while Smartwings will introduce scheduled flights to Lisbon, Portugal.

Several routes previously operated mainly during the summer will continue into the winter season. These include easyJet flights to Newcastle in the UK and Wizz Air services to Vilnius in Lithuania.

More Flights to Popular Destinations

Several existing routes will see increased frequencies during the winter months.

Air Serbia will increase its Prague–Belgrade service from nine to 11 flights per week, while Pegasus Airlines will raise the number of weekly flights to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen Airport from 14 to 17.

TAP Air Portugal will increase flights to Lisbon from seven to eight per week. Korean Air will also add a weekly service to Seoul, bringing the total to four flights per week.

Jazeera Airways will operate flights to Kuwait during the winter season for the first time.

New airlines operating passenger services from Prague this winter include Vietjet, SkyAlps, Fly2Galicia, Jazeera Airways and STARLUX Airlines. TUI Airways and Enter Air will also operate charter flights.

More Routes Planned for Summer 2027

Prague Airport has also confirmed new routes for the 2027 summer season. Delta Air Lines will launch flights to New York in mid-April, while SkyUp Airlines will introduce a new connection to Chișinău, the capital of Moldova.

World.title: Prague Reopens Bobsleigh Track With a New Alpine Coaster
World.content:
Prague’s Prosek bobsleigh track has reopened after a CZK 100 million renovation, introducing a second alpine coaster and doubling the attraction’s capacity.

Located on Mahalka Hill in the Prosek district, the facility has operated for 22 years. It reopened on Wednesday, October 21, with two tracks supplied by German manufacturer Wiegand.



The original track, measuring 700 metres, features a stainless-steel trough in which wheeled carts travel along a concave surface. The new 650-metre track uses the Alpine Coaster 2.0 system, with carts running on a monorail.

Both tracks allow riders to reach speeds of up to 45 kilometres per hour. Passengers can regulate their speed using a manual handbrake.

The newer coaster also incorporates an automated safety system. Around 2,000 magnetic sensors positioned along the track monitor the location and speed of individual carts. If necessary, induction brakes are activated automatically to prevent collisions or carts leaving the track.

Unlike the original ride, the Alpine Coaster 2.0 requires passengers to wear seatbelts.

The renovation has also brought improvements to the surrounding facilities, including a new café and an observation deck. A children’s playground and a rooftop relaxation area are still under construction, with completion planned for spring 2027.

Prices and Opening Hours

The attraction is located at Prosecká 906/34b in Prague 9. Tickets can be used on either track, with visitors choosing which one to ride when they arrive.

Ticket prices

– One ride – CZK 99

– Five rides – CZK 400

– Ten rides – CZK 700

– Twenty rides – CZK 1,300

– Thirty rides – CZK 1,800

Tickets for one, five and ten rides are valid for three months from the date of purchase. Twenty- and thirty-ride passes are valid for one year.

Opening hours

– Monday to Thursday – 10 am to 10 pm

– Friday and Saturday – 10 am to 11 pm

– Sunday – 10 am to 8 pm

World.title: GALLERY: The Czech Republic’s Largest LEGO Store Opens in Prague
World.content:
The Czech Republic’s largest official LEGO Store opened on Thursday, October 22, on Na Příkopě.

The two-storey store covers 496 square metres and combines retail space with interactive attractions, creative activities and displays inspired by the Czech capital.

Among the features greeting visitors at the entrance are the words “Ahoj Praha” (Hello Prague), a model of a No. 23 tram, and figures depicting a lion, Emperor Charles IV and a traditional Prague lamplighter.



The ground floor houses shelves of LEGO sets alongside glass display cases showcasing models and figures. The displays were developed with the involvement of staff at the LEGO factory in Kladno, whose work is also reflected in the store’s custom-built models.

The first floor features a Christmas-themed play area where visitors can build their own decorations from LEGO bricks and hang them on a specially prepared Christmas tree. The activity is open to children and adults alike.

A separate wall made entirely of LEGO bricks gives visitors the freedom to create their own pictures without following instructions or predefined designs.

Visitors who take the stairs to the second floor will find another part of the store’s design. The staircase and surrounding walls feature murals inspired by Prague, including a city panorama and Prague Castle.

The second floor contains further interactive attractions and creative spaces. Its centrepiece is a three-metre-tall replica of Prague’s Astronomical Clock.

World.title: Prague’s Indian Community to Celebrate Navratri With Music and Dance
World.content:
The Indian community in Prague will gather for an evening of traditional music, dancing and food on Saturday, October 24, as Navratri 2026 returns to Top Hotel Prague.

Organized by Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj, the event will celebrate the cultural traditions of Gujarat, a state in western India known for its distinctive music, colourful clothing and energetic folk dances.

The programme will start at 5 pm and is open to people interested in Indian culture and traditions.



The celebration will feature Garba and Dandiya Raas, two traditional dances closely associated with Navratri festivities in Gujarat.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to enjoy Indian food, see traditional clothing and learn more about Gujarati culture.

Garba will be one of the main attractions of the event. The traditional Gujarati folk dance is performed in circles, with participants moving rhythmically to music and following a series of coordinated steps. The dance is closely associated with Navratri, a Hindu festival celebrated over nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga and the feminine divine.

Dandiya Raas is another traditional dance associated with the festival. Participants dance in pairs or groups while striking decorated wooden sticks together in time with the music. The movements, rhythms and colourful outfits make it one of the most recognisable features of Gujarati Navratri celebrations.

Beyond the dancing, the event will offer visitors an opportunity to explore different aspects of Gujarati culture, including traditional clothing and Indian food.

Traditional clothing is also an important part of the festivities. Women often wear colourful chaniya cholis, while men may dress in traditional kediyu outfits. Embroidery, decorative patterns and bright colours are common features of clothing worn for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

Tickets and further information are available on the Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj website.

World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.



She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: From the Ganges to the Danube: Why Mukesh Srivastava fell in love with Hungary – Exclusive interview
World.content:
From the Ganges to the Danube, Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s journey in Hungary became far more than a diplomatic posting. Having completed her tenure as director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest, he returned to India from Hungary – the country where his child was born – with unforgettable memories, lasting friendships and a deep personal connection. In an exclusive interview with Daily News Hungary, Dr Srivastava reflects on his love for Hungary, his experiences learning the Hungarian language, the growing cultural ties between India and Hungary, and why Budapest will always feel like a second home.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): As you have concluded your tenure as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and returned to India, how do you look back on your time in Hungary?

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava: I look back on my time in Hungary with immense gratitude, a deep sense of fulfilment and countless cherished memories. Serving as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre was both an honour and a privilege. For me, it was much more than a professional assignment; it was a beautiful journey of cultural exchange, lasting friendships, learning and personal growth.

What I will treasure most are the people I have met along the way. I have had the privilege of interacting with remarkable Hungarian artists, scholars, Indologists, students, cultural practitioners, Yoga enthusiasts, Ayurveda experts, journalists, and other countless friends of India, as well as the vibrant Indian community in Hungary. Their warmth, enthusiasm and genuine affection made my journey truly special. Through these interactions, I witnessed how culture has the extraordinary power to bring people together, transcending differences of language, geography and traditions.

Hungary also holds a deeply personal place in my heart, as my child was born in Budapest. The city will therefore always be part of our family’s story and most precious memories.

Now that I have returned to India, I look back with a sense of professional satisfaction, but also with the emotions that come from leaving behind a place that became so close to my heart. I have brought home enduring friendships, wonderful memories and a firm belief that the cultural relations between India and Hungary will continue to grow stronger in the years ahead.

DNH: What were your first impressions of Budapest, Hungary when you arrived?

Srivastava: My first impression of Budapest was of a remarkably beautiful and historic city. The majestic Danube, magnificent architecture, iconic Parliament Building, elegant bridges and rich cultural heritage captivated me from the very beginning.

What particularly struck me was the wonderful balance between old-world charm and modernity. Budapest is a cosmopolitan city with a vibrant cultural and social life, yet it retains a very strong sense of its history and traditions. I admired the respect Hungarians have for their heritage, culture and language, as well as their deep appreciation for arts.

Over time, however, Budapest became much more than a beautiful city. I began to discover its people, artistic traditions, intellectual life and sense of history. I also came to appreciate the warmth, resilience and creativity of Hungarians. Initially, I saw Hungary largely through the eyes of a visitor; gradually, I began to experience it as a home.

DNH: What was the first year like for you, both professionally and personally?

Srivastava: The first year was a period of adjustment, discovery, and learning, both professionally and personally.

Professionally, there was much to explore and understand—the Hungarian cultural landscape, the interests and perspectives of the local community, the institutional environment, and how best to present Indian culture in ways that would resonate with the Hungarian people.

Personally, adapting to a new country and a different rhythm of life brought learning experiences and rewarding discoveries. The warmth and hospitality of the Hungarian people made the transition much easier.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Looking back at your time in Hungary, how have you seen the cultural relationship between India and Hungary evolve?

Srivastava: During my tenure, I have witnessed a meaningful and encouraging evolution in the cultural relationship between India and Hungary. What has impressed me most is the growing sense of mutual understanding, appreciation and curiosity among people from both nations.

There has been increasing interest in Indian art, literature, classical music, dance and cinema. However, what stands out most is the remarkable popularity of Yoga and Ayurveda, particularly for their holistic health and well-being benefits. This growing interest is also reflected in the increasing presence of Yoga and Ayurveda institutions across Hungary.

I have also observed that cultural exchange is becoming more reciprocal and collaborative. Beyond showcasing Indian culture and traditions in Hungary, artists, institutions and communities from both countries are increasingly coming together to share ideas, celebrate their heritage and build lasting connections.

The cultural and community activities during my time in Hungary have reinforced that the strongest bonds between nations are often built through people-to-people connections; it is also about the friendships, shared experiences and mutual understanding that remain long after an event has concluded.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and the Liszt Cultural Institute in New Delhi have played significant roles in strengthening cultural relations between the two countries, providing continuity to cultural engagement and transforming programmes into enduring relationships.

DNH: Which event, programme or initiative organised during your tenure are you most proud of, and why?

Srivastava: It is difficult to single out just one programme, as every successful initiative was the result of collective effort, dedication and teamwork. What made these experiences truly special was the opportunity to bring people together, encourage cultural dialogue and strengthen the bonds of friendship between India and Hungary.

Several initiatives remain particularly close to my heart: India Knowledge Series, which introduced Hungarian audiences to India’s rich cultural heritage, philosophy and traditions through lectures and discussions in the Hungarian language; Yoga at Liberty bridge, unique experience of Yoga on a moving cruise along the Danube, Indian Film Festival at Budapest’s historic Puskin Cinema, 100+ Yoga events organised across Hungary as part of the International Day of Yoga (IDY) 2026; and the School and college Connect Programme, which brought Indian culture closer to young Hungarian students.

However, one initiative of which I am particularly proud is the proposed establishment of a statue of Swami Vivekananda at Széchenyi István University in Győr. I am deeply grateful that the University leadership graciously accepted the proposal of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, Embassy of India and extended its support for installing the statue at a prominent location on the University campus, continuing its longstanding support for our cultural initiatives.

I sincerely believe that, once realised, this initiative will not only honour the legacy of Swami Vivekananda but also serve as an enduring symbol of India–Hungary friendship, inspiring future generations and further strengthening the cultural and intellectual ties between our two nations.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Were there any moments when you felt that Hungarian audiences connected with Indian culture in a particularly meaningful way?

Srivastava: Absolutely. There were many unforgettable moments when I witnessed the genuine warmth and appreciation of Hungarian audiences for Indian culture.

One particularly touching experience was this year’s Indian Film Festival at Puskin Cinema in Budapest. After the final screening, the audience responded with such tremendous enthusiasm that the applause seemed endless. What moved me even more was that several people personally approached me to thank for the festival and share how much they had enjoyed the films. At that moment, I felt how beautifully Indian cinema could touch hearts and bring people together beyond language and borders.

Another memorable moment was the Yoga event at Budapest’s Liberty Bridge in 2024. Seeing the bridge filled with people practising Yoga together was extraordinary. I felt the same spirit during the IDY celebrations at Dr. Koltai Jenő Sportközpont at the Hungarian University of Sports Science, where people of different ages and backgrounds came together in a shared spirit of harmony and well-being. It was a powerful reminder of how an ancient Indian tradition has become an integral part of everyday life in Hungary.

What was most striking is the genuine love and respect that so many Hungarians have for Indian culture, Hindu philosophy and spiritual traditions. Their enthusiasm for Yoga, Ayurveda, Indian festivals, ancient wisdom and spiritual heritage is truly remarkable. Krishna Valley in Somogyvámos is a wonderful example of how Indian spiritual traditions and philosophy have taken deep root in Hungary, reflecting this profound cultural connection.

During my tenure, I met many Hungarians whose knowledge and understanding of Indian philosophy and traditions are extraordinary. One of my most meaningful experiences was the personal conversations after cultural events, when Hungarian audience shared their appreciation for Indian culture and often discovered similarities with their own values and culture.

DNH: How could cultural, educational and people-to-people ties between Hungary and India be strengthened further?

Srivastava: We should invest even more in sustained exchanges rather than one-time events. Artist residencies, University partnerships, student exchanges, joint research, translation projects, collaborations between museums and cultural institutions, and opportunities for young artists would all be valuable.

Hungarian Indologists, artists, and practitioners who have dedicated themselves to the study, preservation, and promotion of Indian culture, traditions, and heritage should also receive greater encouragement and support. Their invaluable contributions reflect the depth and vitality of the people-to-people ties that have long enriched relations between India and Hungary.

There is also considerable scope for greater engagement beyond Budapest and beyond the major institutions. Digital platforms can help connect audiences, but physical interaction remains extremely important. When students, artists, academics and people from all walks of life spend time in each other’s countries, they develop a deeper mutual understanding that cannot be achieved through formal diplomacy alone.

DNH: What was everyday life like in Budapest for you and your family?

Srivastava: Everyday life gradually developed its own rhythm. Budapest is a city where history and modern life coexist beautifully. We enjoyed walking along the Danube, discovering different parts of the city, visiting cultural institutions and simply observing everyday Hungarian life.

One of the things I particularly enjoyed was the Danube. Coming from Varanasi, where the Ganges River is such an important part of life and identity, looking at the Danube often reminded me of the Ganges in Varanasi. Of course, the two rivers are very different in their character and history, but both have a powerful presence in the life and imagination of the people living along their banks. That created a very personal connection for me.

Living abroad also teaches you to appreciate small things—local neighbourhoods, familiar cafés like Vaj at Hello Buda and Mandragora near Batthyány tér, public transport, seasonal changes, food and conversations with friends you meet regularly. Over time, these experiences become some of your strongest memories of a place.

During my tenure, I was fortunate to make wonderful friends who stood behind me like pillars of support. Their friendship and kindness made my life easier, happier and much more enjoyable.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: During your time in Hungary, you often expressed your deep affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their culture, frequently greeting audiences in Hungarian during your speeches and even delivering messages in the language at national celebrations, International Day of Yoga events and other cultural occasions. Given that Hungarian is widely regarded as a particularly challenging language for foreigners, how did you approach learning it, and what did the experience mean to you personally?

Srivastava: Learning Hungarian was certainly challenging, but equally rewarding. I have always believed that making an effort to speak the language of a country is not only a gesture of respect but also a genuine way to connect with people and understand their culture.

I approached it with patience, curiosity and determination, beginning with simple phrases and gradually gaining confidence. Over time, I realised that even a few words spoken sincerely in someone’s native language could create a special connection.

Speaking Hungarian on occasions such as Hungary’s State Foundation Day, International Day of Yoga celebrations, the Indian Film Festival and, finally, in my farewell video was my way of expressing my affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their language.

Although I am far from fluent, the response I received was overwhelmingly encouraging. For me, the Hungarian language became another beautiful bridge connecting me with the people and culture I deeply admire.

Simply put, I love Hungary and its language.

If you missed it: Youngest Indian diplomat Dr. Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s Hungarian farewell message draws widespread public appreciation

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Apart from your cherished memories and friendships, what is one thing you have brought back with you from Hungary to India?

Srivastava: Beyond the wonderful memories and enduring friendships, one of the most valuable things I have brought back from Hungary is a deep appreciation for the way Hungarians cherish their cultural heritage and the dedication with which they preserve and pass it on to future generations.

I have also been deeply inspired by the spirit of collaboration among Hungarian artists, scholars and cultural practitioners. My experiences in Hungary reinforced my belief that tradition and innovation are not opposing forces; rather, they can complement and enrich each other, keeping cultural heritage alive while embracing new ideas and perspectives.

DNH: How would you describe the Indian community in Hungary today and its role in preserving and promoting India’s rich cultural heritage?

Srivastava: The Indian community in Hungary is vibrant, diverse and deeply connected to its cultural roots. During my tenure, I witnessed a strong sense of preservation of Indian traditions while embracing Hungarian society and culture.

Festivals such as Holi, Diwali, Navratri and various regional celebrations bring families and younger generations together, keeping our rich cultural heritage alive. The community also enthusiastically shares these traditions with Hungarian friends.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre provided an important platform for such cultural exchanges, while community-led initiatives further strengthened the cultural bonds between India and Hungary.

DNH: Now that you have concluded your tenure in Budapest and returned to India, what message would you like to share with the people of Hungary?

Srivastava: My message is simple, but it comes from the bottom of my heart: Thank you for everything.

I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the Government and people of Hungary, my Hungarian friends and everyone who contributed to strengthening the cultural bonds between India and Hungary. Your warmth, generosity, support and friendship made my journey truly unforgettable.

Hungary was my first overseas posting, and it will always hold a special place in my heart. I arrived to share India’s rich cultural heritage and returned with something precious: lasting friendships, beautiful memories and a deep affection for Hungary and its people.

Although I have returned to India, the friendships and connections I built remain as meaningful as ever. I sincerely hope to return one day, not merely as a former Director, but as a friend.

I firmly believe that the cultural bonds between India and Hungary will continue to flourish, bringing our people even closer together.

In hindsight, my tenure in Hungary may have come to an end, but the bond I have built with this country and its people will last a lifetime.

Until we meet again – Viszontlátásra !!

World.title: Op-ed – The invisible transition: Hungary’s new government and Europe’s old rules
World.content:
Péter Magyar has inherited a luxury most European leaders can only dream of: a kétharmad, Hungary’s politically formidable two-thirds parliamentary majority. After sixteen years, Viktor Orbán is out of power, and Hungary’s new prime minister has the votes to rewrite much of the country’s political rulebook. Unfortunately for him, Brussels plays by another set of rules. Winning an election does not automatically come with the keys to the European treasury.

Guest post by Costantino Pistilli

On 23 September, the European Commission proposed lifting financial measures imposed on Hungary in 2022, potentially releasing €4.2 billion in cohesion funding and restoring access to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe for affected institutions. Brussels acknowledged progress on public procurement, anti-corruption safeguards and conflicts of interest. On 13 October, the Council approved the lifting of those measures. After years of disputes, Budapest finally had more than a promise: the restrictions were removed, although other financial conditions remain.

The European machinery has hardly slowed down. At the General Affairs Council in Luxembourg that same day, EU ministers examined Hungary’s position under Article 7 of the EU Treaty, the procedure launched in 2018 over rule-of-law concerns. Budapest outlined reforms already undertaken and further measures planned, while ministers also discussed the EU’s 2028–2034 budget. The meeting offered Magyar an early institutional test before his European partners. The financial breakthrough did not close the separate Article 7 procedure. Governments change. Brussels keeps its files.

For Magyar, the challenge is unusual. He has the parliamentary strength to dismantle much of Orbán’s institutional legacy, but must prove that the replacements will be independent of his own government. Replacing those in charge is relatively easy. Persuading them to respect limits on their power is another matter.

Some changes are already under way. In June, Parliament amended the Constitution to introduce an eight-year limit on the premiership. A broader constitutional amendment followed in July, addressing senior state institutions, the judiciary and the rules governing key legislation. These measures demonstrate Magyar’s willingness to use his supermajority. Whether they produce institutions less dependent on political power is a more demanding question.

If you missed it – Reuters: Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project

Consider the public-interest foundations established under Orbán, whose governance became a central issue in the dispute over European funding. Transparent appointments, independent audits and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules could help protect them from political interference. The same applies to public procurement: open competition and effective oversight would give Hungarian businesses a better chance of winning contracts without the right political connections. A two-thirds majority makes passing legislation easier. Earning public trust takes rather more than a parliamentary vote.

Poland offers a useful warning. Donald Tusk returned to government in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, only to discover how controversial the methods of institutional repair could become. Magyar faces a similar dilemma: how to dismantle a system of political control without building another one, merely changing who gives the orders.

For ordinary Hungarians, the consequences extend well beyond constitutional arguments. The Council’s decision has made €4.2 billion in cohesion funding available again, potentially supporting regional infrastructure and development. It has also reopened Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe opportunities for students and researchers at affected institutions. Yet other restrictions remain: approximately €3.5 billion in cohesion funding is subject to separate EU conditions. Unlocking one part of the money does not mean collecting the entire amount.

The next EU budget adds another complication. On 10 October, Ireland’s presidency of the Council presented a revised negotiating proposal for the 2028–2034 financial framework. Agriculture, regional development, competitiveness and security are competing for resources. Hungary will need practical allies, including countries such as Italy, which also have substantial interests in agricultural and cohesion funding. Political friendships help, but when billions are being divided, every capital reaches for its calculator.

Brussels, meanwhile, has its own credibility to defend. If Hungary meets the agreed conditions, its progress must be recognised regardless of who governs in Budapest. Otherwise, the suspicion that European funding depends partly on political sympathies will only grow. The standards applied to Orbán must also apply to Magyar. Equally, an electoral victory cannot erase unresolved legal concerns.

Hungary’s transition is therefore a test for both sides. Magyar can change institutions, while Brussels retains the authority to assess reforms and enforce financial conditions. The new prime minister must resist the temptation to inherit Orbán’s powers along with his office. The European Union must demonstrate that its rules remain consistent when the political landscape changes.

Magyar has achieved what once seemed improbable: replacing Orbán after sixteen years. His supermajority gives him the means to reshape Hungary, but also deprives him of a convenient excuse if reforms fail. The real achievement would be institutions capable of functioning independently when that majority is gone. Brussels, having demanded such independence for years, will have to demonstrate that it knows how to recognise it.



*Costantino Pistilli is an Italian geopolitical analyst and author. His work has appeared in the Daily Express, Comment Central and Defensa.com. He has also contributed research and analysis to New Direction.

World.title: More Chinese flights from Budapest cancelled as airlines suspend routes – what could be behind the cuts?
World.content:
More Chinese flights from Budapest are facing cancellations and temporary suspensions, raising questions about the profitability of long-haul connections between Hungary and China. Following changes to Hainan Airlines’ Shenzhen service, China Eastern Airlines and Shanghai Airlines are reportedly cutting flights to Ningbo and suspending their Xi’an route for several months.

Chinese flights from Budapest face further cancellations

According to information published by Hungarian aviation news outlet Budflyer and subsequently reported by Világgazdaság, several previously scheduled flights between Ningbo, a major commercial and industrial city in eastern China, and Budapest will not operate in November and December 2026.

The affected dates are:

November 2026: 5, 9, 12 and 16

December 2026: 3 and 14

The route is operated by Shanghai Airlines, part of the China Eastern Airlines group.

However, some third-party flight databases continue to display departures on certain affected dates. The cancellations should therefore be treated as reported schedule changes rather than independently confirmed cancellations of every listed service.

Xi’an–Budapest route reportedly suspended until February 2027

A more substantial interruption is expected on the Xi’an–Budapest route.

According to the same reports, the once-weekly direct service will be suspended from 7 November 2026 until 26 February 2027, leaving the two cities without their regular nonstop passenger connection for several months.

Xi’an, the capital of Shaanxi province and the historical starting point of the Silk Road, is an important cultural, educational and economic centre in north-western China.

The reported suspension could affect tourists, business travellers and passengers visiting friends and relatives. However, the precise duration of the interruption has not yet been independently confirmed through an official airline statement.

Hainan Airlines also reduces its Budapest operations

The latest developments follow significant adjustments by Hainan Airlines.

As AIRportal.hu reported on 16 October, Hainan’s Shenzhen–Budapest flights have been removed from booking systems between 16 and 30 November.

Services could resume on 4 December, although the airline’s schedules for the remaining winter months remain uncertain.

Hainan Airlines is also reducing or suspending services on several other European routes, including connections to Vienna, Brussels and Madrid.

These changes indicate that the adjustments extend beyond Budapest and form part of a broader revision of the carrier’s international operations.

If you missed it: Exclusive interview – Chinese Ambassador: Hungary-China ties on a ‘steady track’ as Budapest emerges as a potential robotics hub

Why are Chinese flights from Budapest being reduced?

Neither China Eastern Airlines nor Shanghai Airlines has publicly provided a detailed explanation for the reported cancellations. Hainan Airlines has also not officially confirmed the specific commercial reasons behind its latest schedule changes.

Nevertheless, several economic and operational factors could explain why airlines might reduce their long-haul capacity.

– High aviation fuel costs: Long-haul flights consume substantial quantities of fuel, making their profitability particularly sensitive to changes in global energy prices. Higher operating costs can make routes with limited margins less attractive.

– Insufficient passenger demand: If flights fail to attract enough paying passengers, or if average ticket revenues are too low, operating the service may become financially unsustainable. However, there is currently no publicly verified evidence that low booking numbers are responsible for these particular cancellations.

– Withdrawal of financial or marketing support: Some international air routes benefit from promotional agreements or financial incentives during their development. According to AIRportal.hu, earlier Chinese media reports linked previous Hainan Airlines route reductions to the withdrawal of support. Whether this directly contributed to the latest Budapest changes remains unconfirmed.

– Seasonal fluctuations in travel demand: Airlines frequently adjust capacity during the winter season, particularly on routes where leisure travel represents a significant share of passengers.

– Aircraft and network optimisation: Carriers may redeploy aircraft to routes offering stronger demand, higher yields or better connections through their main hubs.

Importantly, these are possible commercial explanations, not confirmed reasons for the individual route suspensions. No verified passenger load figures or route-level financial results have been published to establish whether the Budapest services were operating at a loss.

What does this mean for Budapest Airport and passengers?

Hungary has developed extensive direct air connections with China in recent years, supported by growing economic cooperation, Chinese investment and tourism.

Direct flights are particularly valuable for business travellers because they eliminate the need to transfer through other European, Middle Eastern or Asian hubs.

The reported reductions do not mean that direct air travel between Hungary and China is coming to an end. Nevertheless, they highlight how individual routes remain exposed to changing market conditions and airline commercial decisions.

Passengers booked on affected Chinese flights from Budapest should check their reservation status directly with the operating airline or travel agency. Where a flight has been cancelled, travellers should request information about alternative connections, refunds and any applicable passenger rights.

For now, the key question is whether the changes represent a temporary winter adjustment or the beginning of a longer-term reduction in capacity. The airlines’ subsequent schedule updates will provide a clearer picture.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: Matolcsy detained, 1956 anniversary and Russian energy dilemma
World.content:
Hungary’s political and economic landscape saw another eventful week, with a major development in the Matolcsy investigation, commemorations marking 70 years since the 1956 Revolution, and important questions surrounding the country’s energy relationship with Russia. Our latest Hungary Weekly Briefing brings together the stories that matter most.

The biggest development came in the investigation involving former central bank governor György Matolcsy, who was remanded in custody for 30 days. An international arrest warrant issued for his son, Ádám Matolcsy, has added another dimension to the case.

Meanwhile, Hungary marked the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution, with national commemorations, political speeches and messages from European leaders highlighting the uprising’s lasting significance.

On the economic front, Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government outlined its 2027 budget priorities, including tax cuts, pension increases and housing measures. Questions also emerged over the future of the Russian-backed Paks II nuclear project, while MOL pursued new energy interests in Serbia.

Beyond these headlines, this week’s edition covers Hungary’s diplomatic activity, business developments, international relations and the latest stories from Hungary Insider.

World.title: Court remands former central bank gov Matolcsy into custody
World.content:
The Budapest Central District Court on Friday remanded Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH), into custody for one month.

The court ordered the detention on suspicion of graft and use of forged documents, Anna Madarasi, a spokesperson for the court, said.

Madarasi said the court also ordered the 30-day detention of the representative who acted during the conclusion of the loan agreement – which forms the basis of the suspicion – as well as a lawyer involved in the securities transaction, Mihaly Valko and Tamas Sandor. She noted that György Matolcsy did not provide a statement, nor did the other two suspects.

The court found that there were well-founded concerns regarding the suspects — specifically the risk of them absconding, going into hiding, interfering with the proceedings, or reoffending — and concluded that no less restrictive coercive measure would be appropriate. The court also entertained no doubts regarding the well-founded suspicion that a crime had been committed or the financial loss that had been incurred, the spokesperson stated.

If you missed it – Prosecutors seek to arrest former Hungarian central bank chief Matolcsy – UPDATE: video of arrival at prison

She also said that the prosecutor’s office has requested the issuance of European and international arrest warrants for Adam Matolcsy, as well as for Gyorgy Stofa, the head of the companies managing the assets of the NBH foundations.

Following appeals filed by the suspects and their defence counsel, the court order for their arrest is not yet final, the spokesperson said.

Matolcsy was detained for questioning on Wednesday by the Central Chief Prosecution Office of Investigation (KNYF) on suspicion of financial fraud and the use of forged documents.

The KNYF said it had taken action regarding the attempted transfer of control, under a sham securities lending agreement, of assets in the central bank’s PADME Foundation to a group of people over whom Matolcsy would have influence after his mandate as central bank governor ended. The aim of the agreement, signed a day before the governor’s term ended, was to enable Matolcsy and his son to use the assets for investments for their own gain, it added.

The resulting financial loss cannot be precisely calculated at present, but is “well over” the HUF 500m threshold for a “particularly significant financial loss”, the KNYF said.
