World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: What can Asia do to avoid crossing crucial climate tipping points?
World.content:
Ambulance sirens blaring throughout cities amid deadly heat waves. Sustained wildfires that worsen cross-border air pollution and kill thousands. Weakening ocean currents that devastate crops and flood communities.

These are some of the signs of a planet approaching critical thresholds as a result of human-induced climate change. Beyond these climate tipping points, the Earth’s natural systems could undergo self-propelling, potentially irreversible changes.

How close are we to crossing the thresholds? And more importantly, what can Asia, home to about 60% of the world’s population, do to avert them? That was the central question at the four-day Global Tipping Points Conference held in Malaysia earlier this month. It was the third edition of the conference series, which was launched in Britain in 2022, and the first one to be held in Asia.

With global warming now set to breach 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, failing to meet the limit agreed upon by the 2015 Paris Agreement, scientists say the Earth’s systems are at risk of crossing multiple climate tipping points.

For one, coral reefs in warm tropical waters are dying at an unprecedented rate and scale, as their thermal tipping point of 1.2 C of warming has already been crossed. Nearly all of the world’s coral reefs may be gone by 2075, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned last week.

The Global Tipping Points Conference, attended by over 500 experts and stakeholders from across Asia and Europe, covered how to mobilize law, finance, health systems and religious communities more efficiently to catalyze positive changes for our environment. | Annice Lyn / Sunway Centre for Planetary Health

That means the diverse ecosystem that hosts over a million species of marine life, as well as a key revenue source for the fisheries and tourism industries, is being lost. Parts of polar ice sheets and some regional mountain glaciers may have also crossed tipping points, while the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, a giant ocean current that moves heat and nutrients to the north across the Atlantic Ocean, is at risk of collapse. If it continues to weaken, it would make Northwest Europe’s winters more severe while prolonging heat waves in the Southern Hemisphere.

“The fact is ... overshoot (of the 1.5 C target) is now inevitable,” said climatologist and conference co-chair Johan Rockstrom of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. He was referring to a United Nations Environment Program report in September that concluded that the only option left for humanity to avert catastrophic impacts of climate change is to take the “overshoot, peak and decline” scenario.

“The challenge is to go from linear incremental change at best to now find transformative, many times exponential, pathways towards a safe landing that can secure prosperity, but also equity and resilience for humanity,” he said.

The conference, held in a suburban township southwest of Kuala Lumpur, was also impacted by an ongoing environmental and health crisis: many attendees wore masks and complained of sore throats due to the transboundary toxic haze, caused by slash-and-burn agricultural clearing and peatland fires in Indonesia — a crisis that was made worse by climate change.

Speakers and participants stressed, however, that “positive tipping points” are already emerging in many sectors and regions.

The skies of Petaling Jaya, Malaysia, are covered with smog due to wildfires in the region on Oct. 15. | TOMOKO OTAKE

Tim Lenton, founding director of the Global Systems Institute at the University of Exeter and another co-chair of the conference, said that if we carefully craft a social and economic system that develops, adopts and amplifies zero-emissions technologies such as electric vehicles and solar panels, thus moving away from fossil fuels, we can tip the balance in the right direction.

In Norway, for example, the percentage of EVs in new car sales has grown over the past decade to reach almost 100%. Lenton credited the work of musician and environmentalist Morten Harket, who rigorously campaigned and won support for policies that incentivized the uptake of EVs.

“A very few people, but committed actors with a coherent plan, can tip a whole market and country,” Lenton said.

Another example is the recent solar panel boom in Pakistan, where, as a result of dramatic falls in solar panel prices, people who previously had no access to electricity are rapidly installing PV panels in off-grid or mini-grid settings.

Attendees from Pakistan said that rooftop solar panels are so popular in the country now that they are being used as wedding dowries.

According to Renewables First, a Pakistan-based think tank, and U.K.-based Ember, 27 gigawatts of distributed solar was deployed in Pakistan in just two years through June 2025, the same capacity as all coal, gas and oil plants that have ever been built in the country.

Paramedics treat a patient in an ambulance after he collapsed in the shower during a heat wave in Chestnut Ridge, New York, on July 2. | REUTERS

The country’s solar PV imports surged from under 1 GW in 2018 to over 51 GW by early 2026, which also drove a 40% drop in oil and gas imports between 2022 and 2024.

Apart from the energy transition, the conference, attended by over 500 experts and stakeholders from across Asia and Europe, covered how to mobilize law, finance, health systems and religious communities more efficiently to catalyze positive changes for the environment.

Toward the end of the conference, with British singer-songwriter Cat Stevens in attendance, a 260-page “faith-based toolkit” was unveiled to help faith leaders incorporate planetary health in their religious teachings, considering that over three-quarters of the world’s population identifies as religious.

Jemilah Mahmood, a gynecologist and executive director of Sunway Centre for Planetary Health who served as the conference co-chair, said the event was aimed at introducing tipping points science to people in Asia and giving them the opportunities to speak for themselves about the positive changes that are happening in this region.

“We do have a sense of urgency ... we don’t have time,” she told reporters after the conference. “We need to rapidly scale up what we’re doing (positively). And therefore we have to recognize that we can’t do it alone. We now need to build a coalition that will move forward together.”

Travel expenses for the Global Tipping Points Conference were paid by Sunway Centre for Planetary Health. No part of this article was shared with the organizers prior to publication.

World.title: How this long-term resident avoids the annoying tourist label in Japan
World.content:
Whenever I cross Tokyo’s famed Shibuya scramble intersection, the site of myriad acts of madness for the sake of social media footage, I try to broadcast that I am unimpressed. I confidently barrel forward in a direction that I hope is the correct one to show off that I am not a tourist or, worse, a content creator.

In reality, this probably doesn’t work, and more often than not, I am indeed going in the wrong direction.

But the point is that long-term foreign residents of Japan, including me, don’t like being lumped in with the growing crowds of foreign tourists.

World.title: U.S. Marine indicted in Okinawa robbery-murder case
World.content:
Public prosecutors in Okinawa Prefecture indicted U.S. Marine Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, on robbery and murder charges on Sunday after a 39-year-old woman was found dead in the prefecture earlier this month.

According to the indictment and other sources, Ballard allegedly strangled the woman with a telephone cord in a hotel room in Naha, approximately between 2:10 a.m. and 4:15 a.m. on Oct. 3 and took a backpack containing her wallet and other belongings.

The Naha District Public Prosecutors Office has not disclosed whether Ballard, who is stationed at the U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in the city of Ginowan, has admitted to the charges.

Investigative sources said that the woman checked in with a man at the hotel around 2:10 a.m. that day but she did not leave by checkout time. Around 4:15 a.m., a hotel employee entered the room and found her body.

Security camera footage showed a man with a backpack and features similar to Ballard’s, including tattoos on both arms, leaving the hotel. The backpack was found near the hotel.

Okinawa Prefectural Police found Ballard walking on a street in the city of Okinawa around 11:30 a.m. the same day and arrested him on suspicion of robbery and murder.

World.title: Opposition parties urge Takaichi to explain tax cut bill herself
World.content:
Opposition party officials demanded Sunday that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi clearly explain her government’s consumption tax cut legislation in parliament herself.

During a televised debate, opposition representatives questioned the lack of details about a planned benefit program included in the legislation, as well as the uncertain economic impact of cutting the tax rate for food to 1% for two years.

“It’s unprecedented that a bill to establish a new system lacks specific figures,” said Yasuhiro Nakagawa of Komeito. “We can’t hold a vote unless details are clarified.”

Nakagawa also argued that the temporary tax cut would be “very problematic,” referring to its potential impact on the agriculture and restaurant industries, as well as on households when the food tax rate is raised back to 8%.

“Nothing specific is stipulated in the legislation,” said Motohisa Furukawa of the Democratic Party for the People. “We want to ask during Diet deliberations,” Furukawa added, calling for the prime minister to attend House of Representatives Financial Affairs Committee meetings.

Yuichi Goto of the Democratic Reform Party pointed out that, given that business operators have not sufficiently reflected higher raw material costs in prices, “tax-included prices are unlikely to fall” even if the consumption tax is reduced for food. Goto said that the tax cut may not relieve consumers’ financial burdens.

Meanwhile, Hideki Murai of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party noted that the government is trying to explain the legislation in various ways, including by presenting figures from cases in other countries. “We seek further efforts by the government, so we can hold highly specific discussions in the Diet,” Murai said.

Regarding the opposition’s request for Takaichi to attend Diet deliberations on the legislation, Murai said, “We take it seriously.”

Takashi Endo of the Japan Innovation Party, the LDP’s coalition partner, called for concessions on measures against inflation to create “a system that allows people to feel secure.”

World.title: Brewers rally past Rays to take 2-0 lead in World Series
World.content:
Rookie Cooper Pratt made the most of his second opportunity.

Pratt singled in the go-ahead run to atone for a costly error, and the Milwaukee Brewers overcame a four-run deficit behind six scoreless innings from their lockdown bullpen for a 5-4 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday night and a 2-0 lead in the World Series.

The Brewers, who trailed 4-0 in the first inning, took their first lead of Game 2 in the seventh when Brice Turang doubled off Tyler Wells (0-2) and advanced on a flyout, and Pratt greeted Kevin Kelly with an RBI single to right to put Milwaukee up 5-4.

World.title: Quiet quitting comes to India. AI will make it worse.
World.content:
Doomsday predictions of artificial intelligence causing massive white-collar job losses haven’t come to pass. At least not yet.

There is, however, evidence that AI tools, while helping experts become more productive, are hollowing out the skills that young people acquire early in their careers. This divergence may be showing up as a big jump in “quiet quitting” — a lack of meaningful workplace connection — even in an economy like India’s, where youth are starved of decent employment.

A wave of emotional detachment is sweeping corporations. According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace survey, employee engagement declined for a second year in 2025 to its lowest level since 2020. India is mimicking the trend, with barely 23% of staff feeling invested in their roles. A staggering 59% are doing just enough to survive. The rest have switched off entirely.

World.title: A dramatic bear hunt in a midsize Japanese city could be a harbinger of what is to come
World.content:
Utsunomiya was on edge.

It was early June and a bear was running rampant in the Tochigi Prefectural capital, throwing the city of 500,000 into a state of paralysis.

Schools were closed, residents were frantically checking their gardens for any signs of the animal and specialists from the local zoo were deployed to bring the bear under control.

The three-day chase ended when a zookeeper shot the bear with a tranquilizer gun near a private residence.

The dramatic episode, which was widely shown on TV and the internet, was the latest in a growing number of conflicts between humans and bears in Japan.

Following last fiscal year’s record-breaking number of bear-related incidents — nationwide, 238 people were attacked and 13 were killed — Japan is bracing for another pre-hibernation surge in sightings, encounters and attacks this fall. So far, experts say the relatively rich acorn harvests this year would keep many bears sufficiently fed, likely preventing the recurrence of horrors played out across the Tohoku and Kanto regions last autumn.

But in the medium to long term, Japan’s challenges will continue, with incidents like the one in Utsunomiya being only a harbinger of what could happen in other communities.

Nationwide countermeasures

Last November, the central government compiled an emergency bear attack prevention plan aimed at actively reducing the number of bears in the country and increasing staff and resources for bear management and culling, including through the wider adoption of “government hunters.”

In March, the government followed up with a roadmap outlining steps to take by 2030, such as tripling the number of municipal officials in charge of capturing bears to 2,500 and doubling the number of bear traps to 10,000 across the nation.

A male bear that wandered into Utsunomiya, Tochigi Prefecture, in June is seen on a path after being shot with a tranquilizer gun. | COURTESY OF TOCHIGI PREFECTURAL GOVERNMENT

The government also set region-specific goals for the number of bears to cull, based on the assessment that the number of Asian black bears — long the target of conservation efforts and still classified as a vulnerable species by the International Union for Conservation of Nature — had become overpopulated in the Tohoku, Kanto and Chubu regions.

It aims to reduce the bear population in Tohoku, Kanto and Chubu to 62%, 67% and 63% of the current level, respectively, by fiscal 2030. In Hokkaido, home to an estimated 11,600 brown bears, the government aims to reduce the population of that species to 8,200 in fiscal 2030.

The government is planning a less drastic reduction in the number of bears in the Kinki and Chugoku regions, culling just enough — about 900 bears — to keep the current population level.

Under a new emergency culling system instituted last year, hunters can now shoot bears in residential areas with permission from local authorities. Guns have been fired 36 times under the system as of Oct. 12.

Evidence-based approach

But culling alone won’t solve longstanding problems.

Mayumi Yokoyama, professor of wildlife management at the University of Hyogo and a member of an expert panel on bear management measures under the Environment Ministry, advocates for a long-term, evidence-based approach. She says that while the series of new measures taken by the government is welcome, it will take years to nurture specialists and accumulate data.

A police officer holding animal capture equipment looks for a wild bear during a widescale search for the animal in Utsunomiya on June 9. | AFP-JIJI

Yokoyama has long called for wildlife management that takes into account the nation’s aging population and decline, saying not just bears but deer, boars and monkeys have grown rapidly and expanded their habitats in abandoned or less-monitored farm fields, intensifying crop damage.

In response to a request from the Environment Ministry, the Science Council of Japan in 2019 put together a list of proposals, calling for scientific monitoring of wildlife populations, community-based solutions for abandoned farmlands, utilization of wild meat and nurturing of wildlife management experts. But government efforts fizzled out soon after that, she recalls.

“This time, related ministries all responded and set aside budgets for various measures, which is a very big move,” she said. “But on the ground, the lack of data and specialists persists. They cannot be improved overnight.”

Municipal governments are now competing to hire the limited number of wildlife management specialists in the country, she said, noting that Japan needs to educate more of them so young researchers can envision a long-term career in this field.

Another major issue is that, because of the lack of data and human resources for continued monitoring in many prefectures, there’s no precise count of how many bears there are in the nation. In June, for example, the Niigata Prefectural Government announced it raised the estimated median number of bears in the prefecture from around 1,400 to 8,747 — a sixfold increase. As a result, local experts warned that the possibility of bears roaming Niigata cities could not be ruled out.

Some prefectures have done better than others. In Hyogo Prefecture, officials and researchers, including Yokoyama, have monitored the bear population for over 25 years.

In the late 1990s, Hyogo officials started a new program that involved capturing bears that ventured too close to human settlements, “punishing” them with bear spray and other methods, and releasing them back into the wild.

The released bears were tagged with microchips so researchers could track their behavior. The prefecture now has a database of some 3,000 microchipped bears, which it uses to estimate the bear population.

The prefecture decided to start culling if the number of bears exceeded 800.

The officials confirmed that the number hit the threshold in 2016 and that the bear population had grown at a rate of 15% a year. This prompted Hyogo to move from conservation to culling.

Furthermore, when the bears are culled, they are dissected so the officials can collect biological data such as age and nutritional condition. Over 700 bears have been analyzed this way in the prefecture, according to Yokoyama.

Urban bears

Meanwhile, bear management is being complicated by urban bears, or those who have become accustomed to human populations and frequently roam into residential neighborhoods to search for food.

Kazuhiko Maita, a former official at Akita Prefectural Government who now heads the Institute for Asian Black Bears, points to a possible surge in urban bears next year due to increased acorn production.

“When acorn production follows its natural cycle and the crop is abundant, more cubs are born,” he says. “Then the following year, if there’s a poor crop, mother bears with their cubs come down into human-inhabited areas.

“When the mothers are culled, their cubs, which are only about 50 centimeters long, are left behind. Having had no experience with life in the wild, these young bears remain in human settlements and gradually become what we call urban bears.”

Police officers prepare equipment as hunters and officials search for a wild bear in Utsunomiya on June 9. | AFP-JIJI

As this process repeats over time, we may see more cases of exceptionally large bears emerge in urban areas next April, Maita says.

While Utsunomiya grabbed many of the headlines, this spring also saw post-hibernation bears turning up in the cities of Akita, Sendai and Koriyama, Fukushima Prefecture.

Impact of climate change

A lot remains unknown about the effects of a warming planet on recent rises in Japan of bear sightings and attacks, both Yokoyama and Maita say.

Researchers at the Forestry and Forest Products Research Institute wrote in a 2019 paper that rising temperatures over the past 40 years may have disrupted this harvest cycle of acorns and shortened it to two years instead of three to four years previously.

Yokoyama says that bears in the Shiretoko Peninsula of Hokkaido, which have a salmon-heavy diet, may be affected by rising ocean temperatures and the resulting fall in salmon traveling upstream.

“But we have very little data to substantiate the effects of climate change; we don’t even know how many bears exist to begin with,” Yokoyama says.

The male bear in June that turned up in Utsunomiya was probably not out hunting for food, Maita says. It ventured into the city during the mating season, when male bears fight fiercely for female bears. Bears that lose are often driven out of the mountains and travel long distances to areas with few competitors, he says.

After a three-day hunt, it was zookeeper Tetsuo Iso who put an end to the saga.

As the drama unfolded, Iso, a 65-year-old worker at Utsunomiya Zoo, was asked by the prefectural government to help capture the bear. Because the bear traveled widely across town, often disappearing into bushes around homes, the first challenge for him and other officials was simply to locate it.

Tetsuo Iso, a worker at Utsunomiya Zoo in Tochigi Prefecture, recalls that June’s bear chase in downtown areas of the city involved several unique challenges. | TOMOKO OTAKE

When Iso, the zookeeper, finally came face to face with the bear on June 9, two days after being mobilized by the city, the animal seemed resigned to its fate, he says.

The bear was cornered into the narrow bushy area of a residential property, surrounded by a condominium, a parking lot, a 1.8-meter-high sheet metal fence and a garden shed. Visibility was poor.

“Police officials asked me if I could hit the bear if it bolted out of a bush,” he recalled during a recent interview at the zoo on the outskirts of Utsunomiya, describing the mission as highly dangerous and potentially life-threatening.

“I said I would pull the trigger, but I couldn’t guarantee I would hit the bear,” he said.

The media circus around the incident only added pressure to Iso’s big moment.

“There were all kinds of onlookers and YouTubers, and media helicopters buzzing overhead.”

Iso looked for a position from where he could aim the tranquilizer gun safely. He fired two shots, but both missed and hit the ground.

Tetsuo Iso carries a tranquilizer gun to sedate a bear as hunters and officials search for the wild animal in Utsunomiya on June 9. | AFP-JIJI

Finally, he moved around to the parking lot behind the house and used his gun to create a small space between the fence’s metal sheets. He saw the bear’s head and the white crescent mark on its chest, and fired toward the chest from about a meter away, striking the bear and ending the chase.

“When I aimed my gun, he looked at me but didn’t growl,” Iso says, noting he routinely uses tranquilizer guns at the zoo when treating sick animals. “I know that look, when he accepted his fate, because animals in the zoos sometimes show that same expression when they know their end is near.”

The bear was later killed by authorities in line with prefectural policy. Once bears get an appetite for human food, they are likely to venture into human settlements again.

“I felt sorry for it. He was terrified for days — and killed in the end,” Iso said.

Regardless of the reason that bear turned up in Utsunomiya, he won’t be the last.

Bears in Tochigi, which had long lived almost exclusively in the lush forests in northeastern areas such as Nikko and Nasu, have gradually expanded their habitats westward over the years, according to Tetsuya Maruyama, leader of wildlife damage control group at the Tochigi Prefectural Government.

This time, the officials were able to capture the bear without harming anybody. The fact that the city of Utsunomiya had compiled an emergency bear culling manual with a detailed flow chart in March helped, he says. But the incident has highlighted the need for local authorities to step up their preparedness.

“We realized that we should have more shields and bear sprays ready, and improve coordination between police, the prefecture and local municipalities,” he says. “There are municipalities in the prefecture that still don’t have emergency manuals made. They should create them soon to better prepare for contingencies.”

World.title: Not so cozy? Japanese bookstore fiction gets real.
World.content:
Lately, the titles of Japanese books released in English translation are starting to blend into each other.

“Every Bookshop Needs a Cat,” “The Nine Lives of a Bookshop Cat,” “The Friday Bookshop,” “Matcha on Monday,” “Dreamers of the Full Moon Coffee Shop,” “Welcome to the Kokoro Cat Clinic,” “The Calico Cat at the Chibineko Kitchen.”

That’s a lot of bookshops and cats, and quite a few cafes, too.

World.title: Firefighters battle hill fire near residential area in Tuen Mun
World.content:
Hong Kong firefighters continued to battle a hill fire near a residential area in Tuen Mun on Sunday afternoon, several hours after it broke out.

No injuries were reported, but the flames were spreading along the hillside near Shan King Estate, not far from two secondary schools, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing into the air.

The blaze, reported at about 1.30pm, broke out in a patch of grass measuring about 10 metres by 20 metres (108 square feet to 215 square feet) on Por Lo Shan near a freshwater service reservoir off Wong Yin Street. As of 5pm, emergency crews were still battling the blaze.

Plumes of smoke rise up the hillside behind one of the schools. Photo: Facebook / tuenmunlocals

Authorities also deployed a Government Flying Service helicopter to drop water on the fire.

World.title: Upgrade or eyesore? Why Hong Kong’s Peak light display has hit a snag
World.content:
A controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak is in doubt following mounting complaints that the installations damage Hong Kong’s natural beauty.

Designed as one of several new attractions meant to replace a retired light show, the initiative has been criticised by local residents and visitors as counterproductive.

The South China Morning Post looks at what has gone wrong with the project.

1. What is the project about?

The Tourism Board planned small light installations for selected points along the walking trail near Lugard Road and Harlech Road to add new features to The Peak’s attractions.

The installations feature a soft, low-glare lighting design and were scheduled to operate from 7pm to 10pm on a 12-month trial basis, according to the board.

World.title: Veteran Hong Kong stock commentator Louie Shum dies aged 66
World.content:
Veteran Hong Kong stock commentator Louie Shum Chun-ying has died aged 66, with a police source revealing he had a history of heart disease and diabetes.

His twin sister confirmed on Sunday that he died on Saturday night at Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai, sharing the news in a post on his social media page.

Shum, also known as “Master Shum”, was chief executive of stock brokerage Sincere Securities until his retirement two years ago. He remained active on internet radio shows over the past two years to share market information and investment tips.

World.title: The Weeknd wows Hong Kong fans with tribute song sampling Faye Wong classic
World.content:
Canadian singer The Weeknd surprised concertgoers in Hong Kong on Saturday with a new song inspired by the city, evoking nostalgia among local music fans.

Abel Tesfaye – the Canadian singer, songwriter, record producer and actor known professionally as The Weeknd – performed “Hong Kong” to tens of thousands of fans at Kai Tak Stadium on Saturday night. It was his first of four concerts in the city as part of the “After Hours Til Dawn Tour” world tour.

The crowd reacted with awe and cheers.

“Hong Kong” sampled heavily from the Cantopop song titled “Seasonal Wind” or “Monsoon” in English, a melancholic ballad released in 1993 by Faye Wong.

World.title: AIIB keen to fund projects in Northern Metropolis, Hong Kong finance chief says
World.content:
The China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) has expressed interest in financing projects in the Northern Metropolis mega development, Hong Kong’s finance chief has said.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also told the media on Sunday that global finance leaders had set aside their political differences during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Finance Ministers’ Meeting held in Hong Kong last week and reached a consensus on promoting digital infrastructure, employment and youth exchanges.

“Speaking of the AIIB, it is very interested in infrastructure development in the Northern Metropolis, as this is its own expertise,” Chan said on a radio show, referring to the government’s plan to turn 30,000 hectares (74,130 acres) of land bordering mainland China into a technology and housing hub.

“They told us that … if there are any Northern Metropolis projects open for co-investment, [they will be] very interested. When there are any specific projects, we will explore ways for cooperation.”

World.title: 1 million Hong Kong employees to get ‘full portability’ of MPF funds in December
World.content:
About 1 million employees in Hong Kong will be allowed to move their entire Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) balance to a different provider once a year under the “full portability” arrangement, effective from December 21 for the first phase of implementation.

The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority, which manages the city’s mandatory pension plans, said on Sunday that the “full portability” arrangement would be carried out in two phases to ensure a smooth and orderly implementation.

In a blog post, authority chairwoman Ayesha Macpherson Lau said the new arrangement would allow eligible members to transfer both the employer and employee contribution portions to their preferred MPF scheme once per calendar year.

World.title: What’s next for Hong Kong developers in mainland China?
World.content:
Hong Kong’s major property developers are shifting investment in mainland China from residential projects to commercial assets, including hospitality, as weak home sales and fewer attractive investment opportunities prompt them to focus on existing properties, recurring income and debt reduction.

“In recent years, after we recycled the capital from our projects, we haven’t really found many good opportunities on the mainland,” Stephen Ng, chairman and managing director of Wharf Holdings, said at its interim results press conference in August.

Wharf’s experience reflects a broader change in how Hong Kong developers are approaching assets in the world’s second-largest economy.

Once an important growth market for Hong Kong’s major developers, mainland China offers opportunities to expand beyond their home market through residential projects and established local connections.

World.title: Law enforcement alerted to firm offering LGBTQ surrogacy services in Hong Kong
World.content:
Hong Kong’s regulator for in vitro fertilisation (IVF) has referred a case to law enforcement agencies after a mainland Chinese influencer was suspected of offering to bring non-local surrogate mothers of LGBTQ parents to give birth in the city.

Tan Zubiao, also known as berlinsun, had set up a company in the city and advertised on social media commercial surrogacy services for LGBTQ couples, according to Hong Kong media.

Tan and his foreign husband, who have two children through surrogacy, were deported from Taiwan’s Kaohsiung last Thursday after being fined NT$200,000 (HK$48,109) for breaching Taiwan’s Medical Care Act by offering assisted-reproductive services.

In a written reply to the South China Morning Post on Sunday morning, Hong Kong’s Council on Human Reproductive Technology said commercial surrogacy arrangements and the distribution of related s were prohibited under the city’s Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.title: China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.content:
Chinese scientists have developed the world’s lightest wireless mesoscope, a miniature microscope weighing just 1 gram that can record 25 times as many neurons in mice as comparable devices.

The device, named Airscope, was unveiled in the prestigious journal Nature on Oct. 19, and developed by a team led by Tsinghua University professor Dai Qionghai and Chinese PLA Medical School professor Dai Pu, in collaboration with researchers from other institutions.

When installed on a mouse’s head, the Airscope can record activity from over 8,500 neurons as it freely explores, climbs, and interacts with other mice.

Previously, microscopes designed to image large areas of the brain at high resolution often required cables or the subject to be restrained, making it difficult to study natural behavior. Meanwhile, head-mounted microscopes that let animals move freely could observe only limited areas.

In contrast, the Airscope combines wireless operation with mesoscopic imaging, allowing scientists to observe large areas of tissue while still distinguishing individual cells. This enables researchers to “understand how large numbers of neurons interact and work together to produce complex functions,” Wu Jiamin, an associate professor in Tsinghua University’s Department of Automation and one of the study’s corresponding authors, said in an article published Tuesday by Tsinghua University.

The device weighs just 1 gram without its battery, more than 30% less than the latest head-mounted mesoscopes, according to the researchers. It has single-cell resolution of 4 to 6 micrometers, and a 6-millimeter field of view compared with typically less than 1 millimeter for conventional head-mounted devices. A magnetically attached battery can be replaced in two seconds.

With the Airscope, the team conducted several experiments that were previously difficult because of cables or equipment weight.

For example, in a simulated natural habitat with ramps, tree hollows, and shelters, mice could explore freely while researchers recorded their cortical activity. The team could also use neural signals to predict which portion of the habitat a mouse was in.

In another experiment, researchers placed two mice at opposite ends of a narrow tube and used their neural activity to predict which would force the other to retreat, achieving over 80% accuracy.

Other experiments included mounting one Airscope on a mouse’s head and another on its back to compare spinal cord and cortical neural activity, as well as tracking mice exploring a large maze in search of water rewards.

The team has also publicly released several datasets collected from their experiments.

Zhang Yuanlong, one of the study’s first authors and an assistant professor at Tsinghua University’s Center for Life Sciences and Artificial Intelligence and Department of Automation, said the team used AI to help optimize the optical design. The technology also uses a 2-megapixel image sensor, whereas previously published wireless systems had not exceeded 1 megapixel, allowing higher resolution.

Dai Qionghai said the Airscope could enable “more precise neural detection” and potentially expand into fields such as immunology and cancer research.

Zhang added that the device could be used to track the progression of Alzheimer’s disease, brain injuries, cardiovascular diseases, depression, and other conditions in animal models, and gain insights into disease mechanisms, prevention, and treatment.

In 2023, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed two head-mounted microscopes using a new optical design: one optimized for a larger field of view, measuring around 4 millimeters and weighing 1.4 grams, and another optimized for lower weight, with a 1-millimeter field of view and weighing just 1 gram. Both devices required wires for power and data collection.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from the WeChat public account of Tsinghua University, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.title: In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.content:
For her vacation to China’s southern province of Hainan during this year’s weeklong National Day holiday, Chang Yajie bought five new pieces of clothing: a beach skirt, a floral halter top, a straw hat, a swimsuit, and a pair of loose rainbow pants.

She wore them all on the trip, relishing taking photos in her new outfit on the resort-laden island’s beaches and posting them to social media.

But when she got home, she stuffed the clothes into her trash can.

Chang, an office worker in Xinxiang, a city in the central Henan province, used to spend thousands of yuan on vacation outfits. Unsuitable for work and out of place in everyday life, they ended up at the back of her closet after her trips.

“You can’t possibly wear a plunging, neon-colored beach dress to a corporate desk job,” the 37-year-old told Sixth Tone. “Spending so much on clothes I might wear only once or twice just isn’t worth it.”

In contrast, the five items she packed in early October had cost a total of just 200 yuan ($28). Known as cipaoyi, or disposable outfits, these clothes typically cost under 50 yuan per item and are designed to be worn once for holidays, photo shoots, or social media posts, and then discarded or resold.

The trend, which took off this National Day, comes amidst fast fashion and influencer-driven consumer culture, as well as the phenomenon of haoyangmao, or buying clothing, wearing it for travel, photoshoots, or events, and then returning it for a full refund.

On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, posts under the topic have drawn over 60 million views. On e-commerce platforms, sellers offer clothing ranging from coats and snowpants for use in the northeastern city of Harbin to red dresses designed for photos in the desert. The trend is particularly popular among young women.

Proponents of disposable outfits argue that they’re an inexpensive way to look and feel good while matching scenery and holidays. But others, including environmental advocates and medical professionals, have raised concerns about their potential impact on the planet and people’s health.

Cutting costs

Despite having always loved dressing up, Chang said her clerical desk job leaves little room for it, so she keeps an understated, practical wardrobe. Disposable outfits, then, are a way to “boost her mood.”

“When I go to work, I just wear whatever helps me blend into the crowd,” she said.

But travel, and embellishing her outfits, have helped her reconnect with a more energetic, youthful version of herself. “After months of the same dull routine, dressing up for a trip feels like a shot of adrenaline,” she said.

Chang wasn’t initially looking for disposable clothes. But as she scrolled online for holiday looks, she found it hard to choose among those that caught her eye. In the end, she opted for cheaper versions of similar styles so she could buy more.

A brand dress can easily cost 300 to 500 yuan, she said. “For the same amount of money, I could buy seven to 10 cheaper outfits — enough to wear a different look each day of the trip.”

Chang said the appeal of disposable outfits lies partly in their novelty, helping her match a destination’s look and feel. The clothes let her try styles she rarely wears in daily life — brightly colored pieces with bold, saturated hues, more revealing cuts, or designs that push the boundaries of her usual wardrobe.

For 20-year-old Wu Xiangmeng, a college student in the southern Guangdong province, disposable outfits help her travel money — saved from her university’s monthly living allowance — go farther, leaving more for train tickets, accommodation, food, and activities. So far, she has visited almost 10 cities across China this way.

Before each trip, she researches her destination to pick disposable outfits that fit the scenery. When she’s done with her clothes, she lists them on secondhand platforms like Xianyu and Xiaohongshu instead of throwing them away, pairing the listings with photos of herself wearing the outfits on holiday to attract buyers.

“I can recoup some of the cost while making room — and saving money — for my next trip,” she said.

Outside impact

Though disposable clothing can be a cost-effective way to dress for specific destinations, Wu said she spends hours finding clothes she considers suitable, shopping, sorting through poor-quality purchases, and returning those that don’t make the cut. “The shopping experience is very draining,” she said.

While preparing for a trip to Hainan’s city of Sanya, for instance, Wu ordered several dresses, only to find the fabric flimsy, ripping at the slightest pull. She ultimately kept only two pieces from the pile and returned the rest.

Zhang Bingquan, who operates a garment factory in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, said disposable outfits cost so little partly because of their simplified designs and production process. With fewer patterns and straightforward sewing techniques, as in beachwear, he said production costs per garment can be kept in the single digits in yuan.

But the low prices have also intensified competition among manufacturers. To cut costs, some factories use lower-quality fabrics, reduce fabric weight and thickness, or take risks by using fabrics and dyes that fail to meet quality standards, he added.

“The biggest health risk with disposable clothing lies in the materials used,” Zhong Jianbo, deputy chief physician of the dermatology department at Hangzhou First People’s Hospital, told local media. “Cheap garments often use low-quality fabrics and dyes that may contain high levels of chemical residues.”

Sun Weiling, a dermatologist at Jiangsu People’s Hospital, told domestic media that disposable clothing is often made from stiff fabrics that can irritate the skin and cause damage, particularly in more delicate areas, such as the underarms, chest, waist, abdomen, and inner thighs.

The trend has also drawn criticism over its environmental costs. China is the world’s largest producer, consumer, and exporter of textiles, and generates vast amounts of textile waste. According to the China Association of Circular Economy, discarded clothing in the country is expected to reach 50 million metric tons a year by 2030, with each person throwing away an average of 16 garments annually.

During this year’s National Day holiday, the volume of textiles collected by Shanghai-based recycling platform Feimayi nearly doubled from the same period last year, Deng Qihua, the company’s head of marketing and sustainable development, told Sixth Tone.

“Some of the clothes we collected still had their original tags attached,” Deng said.

But recycling disposable outfits can be difficult and costly, as they are often made from blends of synthetic fibers, she added. “A garment bought cheaply and worn only a handful of times may therefore leave behind a much longer problem once its owner is ready to discard it,” Deng said.

A growing number of users are noticing the problem. A September commentary by state-run media outlet People’s Daily called on regulators to steer the market toward more sustainable alternatives, such as clothing rental. A Douyin hashtag promoting alternatives to “disposable fashion,” with tips on styling existing clothes and buying clothes with long-term use in mind, has garnered more than 32 million views.

But for many, health and environmental concerns take a back seat to looking good on vacation for minimal cost. Chang, the office worker, said that when she posted pictures of herself in her disposable outfits, friends praised her looks and “girlish charm.”

“At least it helps me feel better about myself,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.title: China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.content:
China has approved its first auditory brainstem implant for clinical use among deaf patients amid a national push to commercialize brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies.

Approved Oct. 19 by China’s National Medical Products Administration, the implant — dubbed Nurotron WH-01A — is classified as a Class III medical device, the highest-risk category under the country’s medical device classification system.

The device was developed by a team led by Wu Hao, a surgeon and professor of otolaryngology at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Ninth People’s Hospital, in collaboration with Zhejiang Nurotron Biotechnology, headquartered in the eastern city of Hangzhou.

It is designed to restore hearing in patients who cannot benefit from conventional cochlear implants because of severe inner-ear malformations or an absent cochlear nerve, which normally carries auditory information from the inner ear to the brain.

Unlike cochlear implants, which stimulate the nerve via the inner ear, the auditory brainstem implant bypasses both the cochlea and the cochlear nerve, delivering electrical impulses directly to the cochlear nucleus, a brainstem structure through which all sound information enters the brain and where sound processing begins.

The system consists of six components, including a stimulator and a receiving coil. Used with Nurotron’s cochlear speech processor, located outside the patient’s body, it converts digital signals into electrical pulses that directly stimulate the cochlear nucleus.

Eligible patients include children aged 2 to 6 with “nonsyndromic deafness,” or deafness without other associated medical conditions or physical abnormalities, as well as those whose deafness was not caused by tumors or who cannot benefit from cochlear implants.

By 2024, the team had completed the implant surgeries and follow-up procedures for its clinical trial. The device achieved an overall treatment effectiveness rate of almost 97% after 12 months of activation, they told domestic media.

The approval comes as China ramps up efforts to advance its BCI industry toward clinical use and commercialization. China’s national development plan, part of its most recent five-year plan (2026–2030), identified BCI as one of six future industries. In July 2025, seven national ministries jointly set guidelines and targets for fostering a globally competitive BCI industry by 2030.

National regulators have also accelerated BCI device approvals for patient populations including those affected by stroke, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and spinal cord injuries. In March, the country approved its first BCI kit, designed to help patients with quadriplegia caused by cervical spinal cord injuries regain limited hand function.

China’s BCI market is expected to exceed 6 billion yuan ($900 million) by 2028, with a compound annual growth rate of roughly 18% between 2024 and 2028, according to domestic research agency CCID Consulting.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Left: Professor Wu Hao’s team during an auditory brainstem implant surgery. Right: The auditory brainstem implant recently approved for market release. From the website of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.title: Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.content:
In 2022, I spoke with Emma, a 22-year-old Chinese student in the UK, about her experiences with dating apps. Recalling one particularly disappointing encounter, she let out a sigh. Emma had matched with a man whose profile explicitly stated that he was looking for a long-term relationship. But the day after their third date, he texted her to say he had only ever wanted casual sex, then ghosted her. Feeling betrayed and emotionally drained, Emma changed her dating profile to say she was “Not Sure” what she wanted.

Emma’s experience was far from unusual. More than two-thirds of the 40 heterosexual Chinese students I interviewed in the UK reported similarly ambiguous dating intentions — findings drawn from a longitudinal study conducted between January 2022 and March 2023 that examined how their experiences with dating apps evolved while studying abroad. Many initially joined dating apps with clear goals, whether to pursue romantic relationships, make friends, or engage in language and cultural exchange. Yet over the course of the study, 27 of the 40 interviewees became less certain about what they wanted, increasingly adopting a “go with the flow” or “I’ll just see what happens” attitude.

For some, this ambiguity opened up new possibilities. For many others, however, it became a way to protect themselves after disappointing dating experiences. Beneath their apparent uncertainty, many still longed for a stable, long-term relationship.

For some young Chinese students arriving in the UK, keeping their dating intentions ambiguous is a deliberate strategy to leave their options open. In China, traditional dating culture places considerable emphasis on long-term commitment and marriage. Expressing vague or noncommittal intentions on Chinese dating platforms can carry a social stigma, with users sometimes labeled zhanan or zhanü, derogatory terms for men and women perceived as dishonest or irresponsible in romantic relationships.

Moving abroad can change these expectations. In the UK, students encounter a dating environment where a wider range of relationship arrangements is socially accepted. Living far from their parents and the social expectations of home also gives them greater freedom to experiment. For some, dating apps offer an opportunity to explore different kinds of relationships without committing to any particular one.

This “go with the flow” mentality was particularly common among postgraduate students enrolled in one-year degree programs.
