Analysts point to two factors driving the US thaw: efforts to combat online scam operations run by junta-aligned militias that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars, and the scramble to secure rare earth resources.

India has also joined the race for Myanmar rare earths as global supply chain competition heats up. In July, Ambassador Abhay Thakur outlined growing bilateral collaboration during a mining forum hosted by the Indian Embassy in Mandalay, where officials from both sides discussed joint ventures and investment opportunities. The talks reflected New Delhi’s growing interest in Myanmar’s mineral deposits as part of its broader “Act East” strategy and its push to divert supply chains away from China.

Myanmar military sympathizers argue that rare earths offer a crucial bargaining chip for the isolated and embattled regime. Yet as rare earth competition reshapes foreign policy, global superpowers face a glaring irony in courting the military regime: the junta controls virtually none of the mines.

World.title: A Fitting Conclusion to an Intellectual Life: James C. Scott on the Irrawaddy
World.content:
James C. Scott (2025). In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life Brings. Yale University Press. 220 pp.

In Praise of Floods, puts the Irrawaddy River itself—not generals, kings, peasants or revolutionaries—at the center of Myanmar’s history, and in doing so establishes principles for how river basins are best understood.

James C. Scott (Shwe Yoe) was one of the most important social scientists of the last 50 years. He began his international career in Burma in 1958 but was unable to return after Ne Win’s 1962 coup until 2012. His affection for Myanmar, however, did not diminish, and he then went back regularly until 2021. He was even known to give lectures in Burmese in the 2010s. He died at the age of 87 in 2024, and In Praise of Floods is his final book.

What Scott is most famous for is descriptions of how farmers resisted exploitation by feudal lords and politicians who sent armies and police to tax them. His research led to provocative books like The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak and The Art of Not Being Governed. Their creative tension was always between the cunning of the “weak” peasantries and the simplifications powerful governing elites make to squeeze surpluses from them.

In Praise of Floods is a departure in focusing instead on rivers and floods. Scott believes that they are “alive” in the sense that they are born, develop and shrink across millennia. In the Irrawaddy’s case, it created the fertile plains of central Burma at the end of the last Ice Age 12,500 years ago.

Scott’s point is that rivers emerge at particular times, support different types of life, shift channels and courses, and eventually disappear. He calls this process the river’s “pulse.” For the Irrawaddy, the low-water point is usually in February, and as the rains resume, about eight times as much water flows out of the highlands above Mandalay by September, bursting out of the meandering channels formed in previous years.

For thousands of years, perhaps from 10,000 BCE until about 5000 BCE, this meant that migratory people avoided the floods by annually moving their camps to higher ground. Life came from the rich topsoil the floodwaters laid down across the flat plains stretching from Mandalay, which is only 80 m above sea level, to the Andaman Sea some 1,000 km to the south. Early humans harvested the bounty of the river by fishing, netting birds, hunting game, collecting mussels, and gathering fruit and roots. The flood pulses determined what the people ate, and where they lived and settled.

By about 3000 BCE people began creating new ways to use the temperamental river and sought to bend the Irrawaddy’s surges to their own needs. They started by scattering seeds along the shoreline as the flood waters receded. After tending the crop of grain for a few months they could harvest more food than ever before, but this type of food needed to be processed and stored in granaries, to be eaten while waiting for the next harvest to mature.

This is also when they began managing water flows with weirs, fish traps, drainage canals and dikes, and eventually developed the engineering capacity to flatten fields with animal-drawn plows and other tools needed to harvest paddy rice. Human societies came to see the living river as a tamable resource, whose annual surges could be engineered, so people confidently settled into permanent villages near the rivers. There, the arts, markets, religion, literature, architecture and other human pursuits flourished. By about 2,200 years ago, the Pyu states began to emerge, building permanent cities, markets and worship centers.

And when the river behaved as planned, it was a great thing and populations flourished. But there were new dangers too for people living in fixed villages and cities, because the river pulses did not always rise and fall as humans intended—after all, Scott writes, the river was also alive, and perhaps even had a mind of its own. So when the monsoons arrived late or not at all, there would be a drought. Or when they arrived early and in force, there were floods.

Humans and the rest

A particularly creative touch in Scott’s book is his concluding chapters about non-human life, which includes fish, animals and plants, as well as the ubiquitous Burmese spirits, the Nats. A charismatic character, the Irrawaddy river dolphin organizes the other creatures of the river to comment on the algae, molluscs, worms, larvae, zooplankton and microbes, most of which are ignored by homo sapiens, who is only interested in the river as it applies to human endeavors.

As Scott admits, these chapters fit awkwardly with the overall tone of the book. But surely in his final book he can be given some leeway. He is correct, moreover, that social science needs to acknowledge the spiritual life that is important to the ecology of places like the Irrawaddy valley and delta.

Flooding is a catastrophe for humans, but the “infrastructure” of non-human life, including plants, fish, mammals, birds, and of course the river itself are perhaps more ambivalent, or at least have a different perspective on the river pulses. So, for that matter perhaps do the Nats.

Scott’s emphasis on these spirits reflects stories that his research associates Maung Maung Oo and Naing Tun Lin collected while travelling along the Irrawaddy seeking to understand what locals knew. They travelled from the headwaters of Kachin State through the dry zone of Magwe and Sagaing. The spirits must be placated because they are believed to cause both those disastrous floods and the good fortunes of farmers, fishers and hunters. And then there are the dangers of the surrounding forests, which are also effected by the Nats.

Scott soon segues into more modern descriptions of the Irrawaddy watershed, in which the hydrodynamics of the water surges are highlighted in the context of modern social problems like deforestation, mining, and rebellion. All such activities disturb the ecological balance, and the capacity of humans to manage the Irrawaddy.

Full circle

Scott’s lifetime of creative scholarship is impressive. He started in Burma, studied in Vietnam, went to Malaysia, and ended up studying the economics, politics and psychology of the oppressed, and how highlanders respond to attempts to control them. In Praise of Floods brings this career full circle; he is back in Burma and writing about geography. As he writes in his preface, he planned two more years of field research, following the stories of farmers, river dolphins, spirits and flooding himself, but was prevented by the 2021 coup. His own public activism supporting the Spring Revolution made a return even less likely.

But even without these field data, the book pushes social scientists yet again to consider the perspectives of beings they typically ignore. Scott spent a lifetime searching for what he once called “hidden transcripts“—the voices of people overlooked by rulers and states. In this final book he tries something still more audacious: hidden transcripts of dolphins, spirits, forests, floods and the river itself. It is an appropriately unruly ending to the provocative intellectual life of James C. Scott.

Tony Waters is a professor of sociology at Leuphana University, Germany. His most recent book is The Socio-Political Systems of Highland Burma and the Art of Governance.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Pushes on Four Fronts in Southern Chin State
World.content:
Thousands of regime troops are advancing on four fronts across southern Chin State as they push to seize the gateway to Rakhine State, according to resistance sources.

On Wednesday, the military claimed its forces had secured Hlaingdoke and nearby villages in Kanpetlet Township along the Rakhine border after clearance operations along the Laung She-Hlaingdoke-Kyindwe road.

The regime’s counteroffensive to retake Chin resistance strongholds spans from Magwe Region’s Tilin and Saw townships, across the border into Mindat, Kanpetlet and Kyindwe townships.

Intense clashes have erupted in Magwe’s border villages of Shweaungthar and Kyee as regime forces advance to cut off supply lines to Mindat, according to resistance sources.

“The regime has deployed roughly 3,000 troops across all the fronts,” Yaw Meng, spokesperson for the Chin People’s Army (CPA), told The Irrawaddy.

Regime forces began massing for a southward push five months ago after securing the northern Chin towns of Tonzang, Falam, and Thantlang. The southern Chin campaign launched in May, when around 1,500 troops advanced on Kanpetlet and Mindat from Magwe’s Saw and Kyaukhtu townships respectively, according to the CPA.

“During five months of clashes, resistance forces repelled regime troops and defended the Chin State and its people,” Yaw Meng wrote in an October 20 Facebook post.

He declined to comment on the current battlefield situation in southern Chin, where the regime’s ground offensive is accompanied by indiscriminate airstrikes.

On Sunday, a bomb struck the Paletwa jetty, killing nine civilians including a six-month-old child and injuring four others. A regime airstrike on the same site killed another person the following day, according to the Chin People’s Union, the CPA’s political wing.

World.title: Myanmar Ranks Worst in World for Internet Freedom
World.content:
Myanmar has scored just 9 out of 100 on the Internet Freedom Index for the third consecutive year in 2026, making it the world’s worst environment for internet users as the military regime continues its aggressive crackdown on media freedom and online expression, U.S.-based rights group Freedom House said.

Under the group’s rankings, Myanmar has long been categorized as “Not Free” for internet freedom, but its score dropped significantly from 36 in 2019 to 17 in 2021 after the military staged a coup, and finally to 9 from 2024 onward.

It said the military maintains control over all major service providers to enforce mass censorship, localized shutdowns and digital surveillance.

Following the coup, the Myanmar military regime stepped up suppression of internet freedom and digital rights by enforcing shutdowns, blocking social media and news platforms, and criminalizing virtual private network (VPN) use to crack down on political dissent.

As a result, Myanmar netizens have lost access to information and had their freedom of expression curtailed.

During December-January elections, authorities intensified the blocking of news platforms and the use of anti-censorship tools while arresting individuals for online expression under restrictive new laws.

“This is a very concerning situation,” Thit Nyan, a digital rights analyst from the Myanmar Internet Project, told The Irrawaddy. “This is a life-and-death matter for the public.”

He added that the people of Myanmar, whose lives are seriously affected by conflict, rely heavily on mobile and internet connections for information about airstrikes and to facilitate basic services such as health, education and money transfers.

Myanmar internet users require digital literacy for their own safety, he said.

More than 2,000 netizens have been detained as of September since the 2021 coup for sharing posts or comments criticizing the regime and supporting anti-regime movements, mostly on Facebook, according to Data for Myanmar, a monitoring group.

The regime relies mostly on the Penal Code’s Section 505A outlawing “incitement”, the counter-terrorism law, and the telecommunications law to arrest online critics, including artists and celebrities.

Data for Myanmar said, however, that in 2026 the regime has expanded its scope of action to target individuals who merely express their political views online, rather than just those who are deemed to pose a security threat.

At the same time, experts point out the regime has shut down or restricted mobile and internet networks to control information flow, in an effort to prevent military information from leaking and to conceal its human rights violations.

A total of 140 out of 358 monitored townships are facing communication shutdowns, according to Athan, a group that focuses on freedom of expression. Most of the affected townships are experiencing fighting between regime and anti-regime groups.

Meanwhile, users require VPNs, whose use the regime has criminalized, to access the most-used social platforms such as Facebook.

“I have to swallow my own feelings and control myself not to share them online,” a Yangon netizen told The Irrawaddy. He said he was using his real name for his social account and was aware of many people in major cities who had been arrested for sharing their views in favor of the anti-regime resistance.

“This is a violation of our rights to express ourselves freely and to live safely,” he said.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy—Consistent but Fundamentally Flawed
World.content:
Observers are often baffled by China’s outright support for Myanmar’s criminal military regime in the face of global opprobrium. But Beijing has been remarkably consistent in terms of where it believes its interests lie. During a visit to Naypyitaw in August 2024 that followed the Myanmar military’s unprecedented battlefield defeats in northern Shan, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi outlined what he called Beijing’s “three bottom lines”. Myanmar must not descend into civil strife, drift away from the ASEAN family, or be infiltrated or interfered with by external forces.

The position, in other words, was support for resolving Myanmar crisis within the ASEAN framework, with a warning that escalating civil war, state collapse, or intervention by other countries—especially of course Western countries—would directly harm Chinese interests. Stability comes before everything else.

Military first

China’s Myanmar policy has consistently centered on the Myanmar military. Since the late 1990s, Beijing has treated Myanmar military as the decisive force in stabilizing the country.

After the popular pro-democracy uprising in 1988 toppled the then-regime and the China‑backed Communist Party of Burma collapsed the following year, Myanmar’s military broke with the Western powers. With that, the assistance they had given it under the pretext of a counter‑narcotics campaign came to an end. Facing sanctions, the military turned instead to China and became Beijing’s trusted partner in assuring border security.

Beijing concluded that only the military could hold the country together. Despite its brutality, China viewed it as the sole practical guarantor of the status quo, aligning with Chinese interests and counterbalancing Western hostility.

Strategic energy interests

In 2003–2004, then President Hu Jintao highlighted the risks posed by great‑power competition over the Malacca Strait to China’s energy security. To reduce dependence on that chokepoint, Beijing proposed building oil and gas pipelines across Myanmar into Yunnan. Than Shwe’s regime obliged, and relations improved as a result.

Through these pipelines, China now imports about 22 million tons of crude oil annually—worth roughly US$16 billion—bypassing the Malacca Strait. Beijing’s recognition of Than Shwe as a trusted ally further entrenched its military‑centric policy.

The position today

China continues to prioritize the Myanmar military, treating ethnic armed groups along the border as secondary entities it must keep in check and largely ignoring forces farther afield such as the National Unity Government (NUG), People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and Spring Revolution alliances.

It was only natural, then, that when the military was on the verge of collapse after losing the northern Shan capital of Lashio in 2024, Beijing propped it up rather than let it fall.

To be sure, China’s policy on Myanmar has delivered some success, leading to the junta’s bogus elections and cosmetic transformation into a civilian government, and now ASEAN governments’ re-engagement with Myanmar. Their dealings with the putschist regime are motivated not only by trade, migration, drug trade and online scam concerns, but also by China’s political and economic influence.

It is an entirely pragmatic, interest‑driven diplomacy, prioritizing national interest over moral principles, and of course that is not unique to China. The U.S. is increasingly open about the transactional nature of its own international policies, and ASEAN has been taking note.

Drawbacks

Yet the core problems remain unresolved. The war has not abated. Myanmar is not stable. Min Aung Hlaing’s elections led to worsening airstrikes and intensified military campaigns, mass killings and war crimes.

Unlike the Thein Sein government, the rebranded regime has offered no political reforms of any kind. It rejects inclusive peace, aiming instead to divide resistance forces.

In practice, the regime remains keen on military solutions alone—retaking lost territory with Chinese backing. Since China intervened, hostilities ceased in northern Shan but the regime escalated fighting in the rest of the country, forcibly recruiting 100,000 young people under Conscription Law since 2024 for use as cannon fodder. The resulting brain drain has left the country poorer in human resources than ever.

Two years of heavy Chinese support have only allowed the regime to recapture 21 townships out of more than 100 lost. Over 80 remain under resistance control. And now its gains are slowing dramatically, with rural areas and key routes beyond its control.

China’s goal of stability in Myanmar, in other words, is further out of reach than ever. By trusting the military to deliver it, Beijing has handcuffed itself to failure. Is it too late to change course?

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Son of Aung San Suu Kyi Says He Has First Call With Her in 5 Years
World.content:
YANGON—The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.

Aung San Suu Kyi is detained at a “designated residence” in the capital, Naypyitaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

AFP could not immediately reach Aris—who lives in the United Kingdom—and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.

However, images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar Embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.

“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.

But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyitaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing—who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup—was earlier this year installed as civilian president.

Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

World.title: Japan’s Sasakawa Renews Myanmar Peace Pledge as Regime Battles Arakan Army
World.content:
Yohei Sasakawa, honorary chairman of Japan’s Nippon Foundation, met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Monday, pledging once again to assist Myanmar’s “internal peace process.”

Sasakawa made a similar promise during his last visit in August. This time, regime media said only that he offered to help strengthen Myanmar’s “human resources,” without elaborating on what that would entail. No details were released on what progress had been made since his earlier pledge to support peace efforts.

Sasakawa’s latest visit comes amid fierce fighting in Rakhine, where the regime is struggling to defend the state capital, Sittwe, from the ethnic Arakan Army (AA)’s attacks. Sasakawa previously mediated a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and the AA in 2021, though fighting resumed in late 2023 after Operation 1027. The regime has since lost 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine.

The regime claims to be open to peace talks with ethnic armed organizations (EAOs), but has excluded the AA from talks so far. It has demanded that the People’s Defense Force, the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government, surrender.

Sasakawa’s latest meeting follows the regime’s self-styled “peace talks” with several EAOs that were not actively fighting the regime, having maintained earlier ceasefire deals with the Myanmar military even after the 2021 coup—an event that led other EAOs to resume fighting.

Separately, two EAOs that had been fighting the regime—the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army—agreed to ceasefires with the regime under direct pressure from China.

The regime insists that EAOs, after signing ceasefires, must transform themselves into Border Guard Forces under the Myanmar military’s command or disarm.

The Nippon Foundation on Wednesday declined to comment on the details of Sasakawa’s latest meeting with Min Aung Hlaing. The organization believes the most useful contribution it can make in Myanmar is through “quiet, practical engagement rather than public commentary,” its executive director, Takashi Arikawa, told The Irrawaddy.

“It is not helpful to discuss the substance of ongoing efforts before there are results that can be shared publicly,” he said.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye noted that multiple countries and organizations are currently exploring ways to address Myanmar’s crisis, including attempts to open dialogue between the regime and resistance forces.

“Japan and Sasakawa may be among those countries and organizations. But they haven’t released details about their plans, so it is hard to gauge what measures they will take and what impacts they could have,” he said.

In recent weeks, Japanese lawmakers Hiromichi Watanabe and Shunsuke Takei visited Naypyitaw and met with Lower House Speaker Khin Yi. Meanwhile, Tokyo hosted meetings between U.S. officials and Myanmar regime representatives this month, leading to speculation that Tokyo is considering a shift in its policy toward engagement.

Japan suspended official development assistance to Myanmar after the 2021 coup. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reiterated in July that relations would only improve if the junta halts violence, releases detainees including jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, and pursues genuine political dialogue.

Months ago, the regime publicly appealed for previously agreed aid to be restored.

World.title: Denis Ten Memorial Challenge: How Tournament Keeps Olympic Champion’s Legacy Alive
World.content:
ALMATY – When Denis Ten became Kazakhstan’s first Olympic medalist in figure skating, winning bronze at the 2014 Winter Games in Sochi, he showed a generation of young athletes that they could compete with the world’s best. More than a decade later, a tournament established in his memory is helping turn that ambition into opportunity, bringing international competition to Kazakhstan and giving emerging skaters a chance to develop on home ice.

The Denis Ten Memorial Challenge was created to carry forward the work of one of Kazakhstan’s most celebrated athletes. Beyond commemorating his achievements, the tournament seeks to strengthen professional figure skating in the country, support young athletes and foster connections within the international skating community.

The event is organized by the Denis Ten Foundation, a public foundation established in 2018 to preserve the skater’s legacy, continue his projects and support young athletes and creative talent. Since 2019, the foundation has organized the memorial tournament, with Denis’s mother, Oksana Ten, serving as its president.

“On behalf of Denis’s dream, this international tournament was organized. Its goal is to develop professional figure skating in Kazakhstan and popularize this wonderful sport,” Oksana Ten said in 2025.

From an Olympic breakthrough to a platform for young skaters

Denis Ten’s achievements helped put Kazakhstan on the international figure skating map. He won his first major international title at the 2008-2009 ISU Junior Grand Prix event in Belarus, becoming the first Kazakh skater to win an International Skating Union competition. He was 16 at the time.

His progress had begun even earlier. At 12, he competed against senior skaters at the Kazakhstan Championships and won. In 2013, he earned silver at the World Figure Skating Championships, followed by bronze in 2015. His Olympic bronze medal in Sochi in 2014 was a historic first for Kazakhstan.

Ten was also known beyond the rink for his artistic interests, language skills and commitment to learning. His career demonstrated how an athlete from Kazakhstan could reach the highest levels of international sport while building a broader cultural and intellectual life.

His death in 2018 was a profound loss for Kazakhstan and the international figure skating community. The memorial foundation was established that year to ensure his projects and ambitions would continue beyond his lifetime.

The tournament that followed became one way to put that commitment into practice. Rather than limiting the memorial to an annual tribute, the foundation created an event where young skaters could compete against international opponents, gain experience and develop their skills without having to travel abroad for every major opportunity.

Why the tournament matters for Kazakhstan

International competitions play an important role in developing athletes. They allow skaters to test their preparation against competitors from other countries, perform before international judges and audiences, and build the experience needed to progress through the sport’s competitive levels.

The Denis Ten Memorial Challenge is part of the ISU Challenger Series, an international circuit for senior skaters that offers competition between national events and the Grand Prix series. Results from eligible competitions contribute to the ISU World Standings, helping athletes build their international rankings.

The series also gives Kazakhstan an opportunity to host high-level skating and bring the international figure skating community to the country. Challenger events must meet ISU requirements for participating countries and disciplines, placing them within a broader international competition structure.

According to the organizers, the growth of the memorial tournament has coincided with the development of new figure skating schools and the establishment of a figure skating academy in Kazakhstan. Domestic competitions with international participation have also given Kazakhstani athletes more opportunities to earn ISU ranking points on home ice.

The significance of that development became especially visible with Kazakhstan’s success at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where Mikhail Shaidorov won gold in men’s singles. His achievement marked a major milestone for the country’s figure skating community and brought renewed attention to the importance of sustained athlete development.

Oksana Ten reflected on that progress, noting the growth of the sport in Kazakhstan and the country’s Olympic success.

“I realized how necessary this tournament is for Kazakhstan. You can see how much the number of figure skaters in our country has grown, both in quality and quantity. We finally have Olympic gold. This is a huge achievement not only for our country; the whole world admires it. That is why I think holding this tournament is worthwhile,” she said during a press conference ahead of the tournament’s 2026 edition.

The memorial has also welcomed skaters who later achieved international recognition. Over the years, its winners have included Shaidorov, Russian skater Petr Gumennik, Belarusian skater Viktoria Safonova and Japanese figure skating legend Daisuke Takahashi. Their participation has helped connect younger competitors with athletes at different stages of their careers.

Held in Almaty and Astana over the years, the tournament has featured singles skating and ice dance, as well as pair skating in some editions. Its broader purpose remains consistent: to create opportunities for athletes to compete internationally while strengthening Kazakhstan’s figure skating community.

The 2026 edition brings together more than 20 countries

The eighth Denis Ten Memorial Challenge took place at Halyk Arena in Almaty from Oct. 7 to 10, bringing together around 150 athletes from more than 20 countries. Senior and junior athletes competed in six categories: Junior Men, Junior Women, Women, Men, Junior Ice Dance and Ice Dance.

In women’s singles, Alexandra Ignatova won gold with 226.01 points. South Korea’s Kim Yu-jae took silver with 209.20 points, while Kazakhstan’s Sofia Samodelkina claimed bronze with 204.36 points. Vladislav Dikidzhi won the men’s competition with 312.79 points, followed by Gleb Lutfullin with 277.23 points and Petr Gumennik with 261.76 points.

In ice dance, Finland’s Juulia Turkkila and Matthias Versluis took gold with 191.32 points. Vasilisa Kaganovskaya and Maxim Nekrasov finished second with 187.20 points, while the United States’ Caroline Green and Michael Parsons won bronze with 180.37 points.

For Samodelkina, the atmosphere in Almaty was an important part of the experience. The participant in the 2026 Winter Olympics and silver medalist at the ISU Grand Prix event in Osaka said the crowd’s support gave skaters an additional source of energy.

“The audience applauds so loudly that you feel as if you’re on a whole different level. They give you incredible energy and strength, and that helps you skate,” she said.

Remembering Denis Ten through sport and art

The memorial’s purpose extends beyond competition. Each edition also creates space to remember Ten’s personality, artistic interests and influence on those who knew him. The highlight of the 2026 event was the gala show, “The Ice That Remembers,” which brought together competition medalists, invited skaters and athletes from the Denis Ten Academy. The program combined figure skating with music and aerial acrobatics.

Marie-Pierre Leray, a French figure skater and longtime friend of Ten, took part in the show. She had also performed in the “Denis and Friends” program in 2013. Vocalists Daniil Yun and Sanat Asuat presented songs dedicated to Ten’s memory. The evening also featured a specially composed tournament anthem, an AI avatar of the skater and excerpts from his poetry.

The Denis Ten Memorial Challenge continues to serve two connected purposes: honoring an athlete whose achievements changed the history of figure skating in Kazakhstan and creating opportunities for the next generation to pursue their own ambitions.

The event is organized by the Denis Ten Foundation, with the assistance from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Tourism and Sports, the Almaty city administration and Samruk Kazyna.

World.title: Republic Day Is Reminder That Kazakhstan Belongs to Its People
World.content:
Every year, as Kazakhstan marks Republic Day on Oct. 25, we return to a moment in our history that is easy to describe in legal terms but harder to appreciate in its broader meaning. On Oct. 25, 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic laid the foundations for the country’s future statehood, establishing principles of territorial integrity, political self-determination and national identity that would become central to independent Kazakhstan.

Yet this date’s significance extends beyond the document itself. It invites us to consider what it means to be a republic, not simply as a form of government, but as a country whose future cannot be separated from the people who inhabit it.

In June 2022, at the first meeting of the National Kurultai in Ulytau, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed restoring its status as a national holiday. Parliament passed the relevant amendments on Sept. 29, 2022, and the country celebrated Republic Day again that October.

For much of Kazakhstan’s post-independence history, the story of the state was closely tied to the figure of its first president. This made sense in a country undergoing profound political and economic transformation, where building new institutions and seeking stability became defining priorities. But a state is larger than any individual’s political career, however consequential that career may be. Leaders come and go, political narratives change, and the durability of a country ultimately depends on its institutions, shared values and the strength of its civic life.

Seen in this light, the return of Republic Day means more than restoring a holiday. It brings the idea of the republic itself back into focus: the country as a shared political space, rather than an extension of any one person’s legacy. Perhaps Tokayev was guided by precisely this understanding when he proposed restoring the holiday, recognizing that the idea of statehood must ultimately rest on something greater than the legacy of an individual leader. A republic derives its strength not from any one political figure’s permanence, but from the people who sustain it, the institutions they build and their commitment to a common future.

This also carries deeper historical resonance. The steppe that shaped Kazakh society was vast, and survival across it required more than individual strength. Communities depended on agreements, customary law, mutual obligations and an understanding that disputes had to be resolved within a shared social order. These traditions should not be romanticized as a history without conflict or inequality, but they do remind us that collective life has always required rules, negotiation and an ability to find common ground.

Modern Kazakhstan is, of course, a very different society. Its citizens live in cities and villages, work in a highly connected economy, participate in institutions and increasingly engage with the world beyond their borders. Yet the underlying question remains familiar: what holds a community together, and what makes its members feel that the place they inhabit is genuinely theirs?

Patriotism is often expressed through symbols, ceremonies and declarations of loyalty, but its more meaningful test lies in everyday choices. It is reflected in whether we respect the law when doing otherwise would be easier, whether we demand accountability from public institutions, whether we treat public property as something we share rather than something that belongs to nobody, and whether we contribute to the communities in which we live. It also requires us to recognize that we cannot delegate the country’s future entirely to the government, just as we cannot simply blame those in power for every problem.

This does not diminish the role of the state. On the contrary, public institutions must create the conditions for citizens to participate meaningfully, exercise their rights and see that their voices matter. The relationship between the state and society cannot be one-sided: a government may set priorities and introduce reforms, but their success depends in large part on whether people trust institutions, take part in public life and believe that their actions can make a difference.

Republic Day also reminds us that sovereignty has a geographical dimension. Kazakhstan’s territory, stretching across the steppe and connecting different parts of Eurasia, is not merely a feature on a map or an economic asset. It is the space within which a political community can determine its own future. Preserving that sovereignty requires capable institutions and sound strategic decisions, as well as a shared sense of belonging and an understanding of what is at stake when the country’s long-term interests are discussed.

National identity, meanwhile, should not be understood as something fixed or inherited without question. It is shaped by the way we understand our history, preserve our cultural heritage, relate to one another and imagine the country we want to leave to the next generation. It can accommodate different backgrounds, languages and experiences without losing its central commitment to a common future.

Perhaps this is the most important meaning of Republic Day today. The 1990 declaration marked a decisive step toward sovereignty, but the work of building a country did not end with independence, nor can any single generation or political leader complete it. Statehood endures through functioning institutions, communities that support one another, and citizens who understand that the country’s future is not something that happens to them, but something they help shape. On Oct. 25, we celebrate not only a defining moment in Kazakhstan’s journey toward independence, but also the idea that this country belongs to all of us.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Recycling Problem Is Not Lack of Willingness
World.content:
Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience.

Kazakhstan has entered 2026 with an ambitious new plan for dealing with its waste. The government’s Waste Management Concept for 2026–2030 calls for less landfill disposal, more recycling and better monitoring of where waste ultimately goes. The timing could hardly be better. In 2025, Kazakhstan collected 4.1 million tonnes of municipal waste — 7.7% more than the year before. The country is producing more waste, and the question is no longer whether recycling matters. It is whether the system makes recycling easy enough for ordinary people to participate.

The central problem is surprisingly simple: Kazakhstan’s waste system still places too much responsibility on individual citizens and too little on the infrastructure surrounding them.

I see this problem in Astana. At home, I separate plastic, paper and cans instead of throwing everything into one bin. But doing so is only the first step. I often have to take recyclable materials myself to private collection points. For someone already motivated to recycle, this is possible. For a family rushing to work, taking children to school and dealing with daily responsibilities, it becomes a lower priority. This is why telling people to “be more environmentally responsible” will never be enough.

Kazakhstan is not starting from zero. Astana already operates a two-fraction collection system separating “dry” materials such as paper, plastic, glass and metal from “wet” waste such as food. The city has thousands of waste containers and collection sites. Nationally, progress is also visible: 1.5 million tonnes of municipal waste were sorted in 2025, 16.3% more than in 2024. Astana alone accounted for 377,000 tonnes of sorted waste.

Yet sorting statistics tell only part of the story. Waste must be separated correctly, collected separately, transported without being mixed again and eventually reach a recycler that can use it. If any step in that chain fails, a carefully separated plastic bottle may ultimately have the same destination as ordinary household rubbish.

A more effective waste system therefore has to make separation convenient, rewarding and accountable. Convenience comes first. Residents should encounter the same simple system wherever they live: clearly marked containers, consistent colours and straightforward instructions showing what belongs where. Collection schedules should ensure that separated waste remains separated throughout transportation. Organic waste deserves particular attention because food mixed with paper and other recyclables can contaminate material that might otherwise be reused. Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code already assigns local authorities responsibility for organizing environmentally safe municipal-waste systems, including separate collection. The challenge is turning that principle into an everyday routine people can trust.

Incentives can reinforce that routine. Deposit-return systems for bottles and cans, discounts or rewards for recycling, and convenient collection points can give recyclable materials visible value. The objective is not to pay people simply for behaving responsibly. It is to design a system in which throwing valuable materials into a landfill becomes the least attractive option.

Finally, accountability matters. Residents are less likely to spend time separating waste if they suspect everything is mixed together later. Municipalities and waste operators could publish simple data showing how much waste was collected separately, how much was actually recycled and how much went to landfill. Digital tracking, one of the priorities in Kazakhstan’s new waste strategy, could help make those flows more transparent.

Kazakhstan’s new waste policy sets a target of reducing the amount of municipal waste sent to landfills by 10% from the 2025 level by 2030. Meeting targets like this will depend not only on new recycling plants or government strategies, but on millions of small decisions made every day in kitchens, apartment courtyards and workplaces.

The important lesson extends far beyond Kazakhstan. Governments often treat recycling as a question of environmental awareness: educate people, run campaigns and hope for behaviour changes. But awareness works best when infrastructure makes the responsible choice the easy choice.

People should not have to be environmental enthusiasts to recycle. A successful waste system is one in which an ordinary resident can separate a bottle, a cardboard box or food waste without giving the process much thought. That is when recycling stops being an individual effort and starts becoming normal urban infrastructure.

The author is Samat Tulepbayev, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: UN Exhibition in Astana Highlights 30 Stories of Sustainable Development
World.content:
ASTANA – A young inventor turning air pollution into printer pigments, a teacher inspiring students to rediscover the joy of reading and an entrepreneur harnessing solar energy to extract drinking water from the air are among 30 people featured in a United Nations exhibition that opened in Astana on Oct. 21.

The photography and multimedia exhibition, titled “GLOCAL: Global Goals. Local Lives,” highlights people whose work is helping turn the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into practical solutions for communities across Kazakhstan.

The exhibition, which takes place in the National Museum of Kazakhstan, features stories from Astana, Almaty, Shymkent and Kyzylorda, as well as the Karagandy, Akmola, Turkistan and Mangystau regions. Those profiled include young innovators, educators, health care professionals, environmental activists, entrepreneurs working to address local challenges and expand opportunities for vulnerable communities.

From global commitments to global actions

Speaking at the opening ceremony, UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaaragchaa stressed the importance of involving local communities in sustainable development efforts.

“Sustainable development is not something we deliver to people. It is something we build with people,” she said.

The exhibition focuses on five pillars of the UN’s 2030 agenda — people, planet, prosperity, peace and partnership, highlighting local efforts to address challenges ranging from environmental protection and education to health care and economic opportunity.

“The theme of today’s exhibition underscores the importance of connecting this global agenda with national priorities and action in our regions, cities and rural communities,” said First Deputy Foreign Minister Yerzhan Ashikbayev.

Chinwe Ogbonna, United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) country representative in Kazakhstan, said the exhibition underscores the importance of aligning global goals with local priorities.

“This event signifies what can happen when we translate global goals to local priorities,” she said, describing the 30 featured stories as examples of transformative change.

Ogbonna noted that Kazakhstan has made progress toward the SDGs but emphasized that further work still remains. She highlighted persistent inequalities, climate-related challenges, the need for a more inclusive economy and the importance of strengthening partnerships and peace.

“Kazakhstan can do more across each of the five goals that we are demonstrating here today,” she said. Kazakhstan’s work on sustainable development also forms part of its broader agenda at the UN General Assembly, where the country has highlighted priorities ranging from water security to peacekeeping and nuclear disarmament.

Kazakhstan’s partnership with the UN

The exhibition also reflects the broader cooperation between Kazakhstan and the UN under the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for 2026–2030. The framework identifies four strategic priorities: empowered people and strong institutions, a resilient and inclusive economy, a sustainable environment, and strengthened social cohesion. Kazakhstan also used the UN General Assembly’s high-level week in September to strengthen international partnerships. The country’s foreign minister held bilateral meetings with international counterparts, discussing cooperation on issues of mutual interest.

Ashikbayev also pointed to the establishment of the UN Regional Center for Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty as an important milestone in cooperation between Kazakhstan and the UN.

Water security, he said, remains a priority for the region. Ashikbayev also highlighted the country’s initiative to establish an international water organization under the UN aimed at strengthening coordination in global water governance.

These national and regional priorities connect with the exhibition’s central message: sustainable development takes shape through concrete action in people’s everyday lives.

The exhibition will run until Nov. 4.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Direct Flights to New York in 2027 as Air Astana’s Dreamliner Undergoes Testing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan could launch direct flights between Astana and New York in 2027, following the expected completion of a United States’ aviation safety assessment and the planned introduction of Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft, Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said.

Speaking on the sidelines of an International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) security week event, Lastayev said a team of auditors from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had visited Kazakhstan several weeks earlier and given a positive preliminary assessment of the country’s civil aviation system and its compliance with international standards. The final official report is expected in November. Kazakhstan aims to obtain authorization to operate flights to the U.S. by the end of this year, Lastayev said.

Lastayev added that launching the route would also depend on aircraft readiness and the completion of required flight hours for crews and technical staff.

“A Dreamliner capable of operating these flights is expected in December. Before it enters service, crews and technicians need to complete a certain number of flight hours. I think that, provided these conditions are met, we expect to launch a direct flight next year,” he said.

Air Astana’s Dreamliner undergoes flight testing

Air Astana’s first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, registered as EI-KZA, began factory flight testing in Charleston, South Carolina, on Oct. 1. Boeing is conducting the necessary certification procedures before delivering the aircraft, reported the Air Astana’s press service.

The first three Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners are expected to enter service with Air Astana in 2027. The aircraft will be a major step in the airline’s fleet modernization, gradually replacing its Boeing 767-300ER aircraft, improving operational efficiency and creating opportunities to expand its international route network.

Air Astana expands international network from Astana

Air Astana Group is also expanding its international network from Kazakhstan’s capital, adding new routes and increasing flight frequencies on existing services.

In 2026, the group launched eight new scheduled and charter destinations from Astana: Guangzhou, Bangkok, Larnaca, Dalaman, Batumi, Issyk-Kul, Salalah and Yining. Seven additional destinations were introduced in 2025: Sanya, Jeddah, Medina, Nha Trang, Da Nang, Alanya and Kutaisi.

The group’s network from Astana now covers 32 destinations, including announced routes. The expansion targets major business and economic centers, such as Guangzhou and Bangkok, as well as popular tourist destinations.

Air Astana Group is increasing weekly flights on existing international routes from Astana from 99 to 116, including services to Beijing, Seoul, Frankfurt, Istanbul and Dubai. Compared with 2025, capacity on the Astana-Beijing route has risen by 55%, while capacity on routes to Seoul and Istanbul has increased by 20%.

The group is also expanding its operational presence in the capital. The number of aircraft based in Astana rose from 13 in 2024 to 16 in summer 2026 and is expected to reach 22 in 2027.

The expansion is accompanied by growth in technical, training and administrative teams, as well as passenger services at Astana International Airport. The company said its increased presence also supports local businesses through a growing number of partners and higher procurement of goods and services.

World.title: NVIDIA CEO Proposes Kazakhstan as Global Hub for Physical AI
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with NVIDIA co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang in Astana on Oct. 23 to discuss cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies, highlighting Kazakhstan’s ambition to become an AI-driven nation.

During the meeting at Akorda, Tokayev emphasized the importance of Huang’s visit in strengthening bilateral cooperation and expressed gratitude for his personal contribution to the development of Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem.

“This visit is of great importance to us in terms of giving serious momentum to our cooperation with NVIDIA. I would like to personally thank you for your contribution to strengthening our partnership and for what you are doing for Kazakhstan,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev identified AI development and digitalization as national priorities, noting that 2026 has been declared the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence in Kazakhstan.

Tokayev also welcomed NVIDIA’s partnership with Higgsfield, saying Kazakhstan was proud to see the company involved in a domestic technology project.

Huang praised Kazakhstan’s strategic ambition to become an AI nation, describing it as a goal set at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.

He also proposed positioning Kazakhstan as a global hub for physical AI, a field that combines artificial intelligence with physical systems, including robots, autonomous machines and industrial equipment.

“AI development requires, first and foremost, energy resources, as well as people with knowledge in science, mathematics and technology. Kazakhstan has significant potential to develop each of these areas,” Huang said.

The NVIDIA chief also highlighted progress in the company’s cooperation with Kazakhstan over the past year, particularly in building ties with local technology businesses.

He praised the work carried out jointly with Kazakhstan and expressed gratitude for the country’s decision to partner with NVIDIA, describing the cooperation as the beginning of a long-term journey.

Following the meeting, Tokayev awarded Huang the Order of Dostyk (Friendship) in recognition of his contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Republic Day Weekend: What to See and Do in Astana and Almaty
World.content:
ASTANA – As Kazakhstan prepares to celebrate Republic Day on Oct. 25, Astana and Almaty are offering a packed weekend of cultural events, from theater performances and concerts to art exhibitions. The Astana Times has rounded up some of the highlights to help readers make the most of the long holiday weekend.

Astana

Ethno Festival, Oct. 24

Spend time immersed in Kazakh traditions with horseback shows, kokpar, traditional games and local food. Visitors can also explore craft stalls and a market featuring national products, making it a great opportunity to enjoy the country’s rich cultural heritage with family and friends.

Venue: BalQaragai recreation area. Tickets are available here.

“Heritage of the Great Steppe” concert, Oct. 24

Celebrate the beauty of Kazakh dance through a program of folk choreography created by Aigul Tati. The performance brings together expressive movements, colourful costumes and traditional music, highlighting the richness of Kazakhstan’s dance heritage.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Swan Lake,” Oct. 24

Enjoy “Swan Lake,” one of the best-known works of classical ballet, set to Pyotr Tchaikovsky’s timeless music. The story of love, magic and the struggle between good and evil unfolds through graceful choreography and expressive dance.

Venue: Zhastar Palace; 34 Republic Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Abai-Togzhan” musical drama, Oct. 25

Explore the early life of Abai through a musical drama about his first love, Togzhan, and the experiences that shaped his worldview. Inspired by Mukhtar Auezov’s work, the production brings together romance, poetry and Kazakh cultural traditions.

Venue: 47B Zhakyp Omarov Street; Musical Theater of Young Spectators. Tickets are available here.

“Living Paintings” exhibition, Oct. 24-26

Discover the famous seascapes of Ivan Aivazovsky through a multimedia exhibition that combines classic art with immersive visual technology.



Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Almaty Open, Oct. 24-25

Tennis fans can watch top international players compete in the ATP 250 tournament. Beyond the matches, the event offers live music, entertainment and interactive activities, creating a lively atmosphere for sports fans and visitors alike.

Venue: Almaty Arena; 7 Nurkent Microdistrict. Tickets are available here.

Outlandish concert, Oct. 25

Relive the sounds of the 2000s with the Danish group behind popular hits such as “Aicha,” “Guantanamo” and “Callin’ U.” The concert offers a chance to hear familiar songs live and revisit the music that defined an era for many listeners.

Venue: Bla Bla Bar; 1A Satpayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Layla Qobyz Live concert, Oct. 25

Experience the distinctive sound of the qobyz in a live musical performance. With its rich, expressive tone and deep roots, the instrument offers a memorable way to connect with the country’s cultural heritage.

Venue: Caspian University; 85A Dostyk Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Marc Chagall: Beyond Gravity” lecture, Oct. 24

Step into the imaginative world of Marc Chagall through a lecture exploring the artist’s life, inspirations and distinctive style. Discover the stories behind his colourful imagery, his relationship with his muse Bella and his place in 20th-century art. The program also includes a visit to the exhibition dedicated to his work.

Venue: Oylau Space; 15 Gogol Street. Tickets are available here.

Ethno-cultural tour, Oct. 24 – Nov. 30

Discover the traditions and lifestyle of the Kazakh nomads through an immersive cultural experience. The tour offers an opportunity to learn more about the country’s heritage and explore customs that have shaped life on the steppe.

Meeting place: 100 Baityrsynov Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: World Wrestling Championships 2026: Entries Announced for Astana
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 320 wrestlers are set to compete in wrestling at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships, which will take place at Barys Arena in Astana from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1.

The entry list features athletes from around on the world across 10 weight categories, ranging from 57 kilograms to 125 kilograms. Eight returning world champions are expected to defend their titles at the championships.

Kazakhstan will be represented by wrestlers across all 10 weight categories, including Meirambek Kartbay at 57 kg, Assyl Aitakyn and Nurdanat Aitanov at 61 kg, Ossimzhan Dastanbek at 65 kg, Sanzhar Doszhanov at 70 kg, Nurkozha Kaipanov at 74 kg, Shamsat Tair at 79 kg, Bolat Sakayev at 86 kg, Azamat Dauletbekov at 92 kg, Rizabek Aitmukhan at 97 kg and Yedige Kassimbek at 125 kg.

The entry list includes several prominent international wrestlers, among them American Spencer Lee at 57 kg, Russian Zavur Uguev at 61 kg, Iranian Amirmohammad Yazdani at 74 kg, American Kyle Dake at 86 kg, Iranian Hassan Yazdani at 97 kg and American Wyatt Hendrickson at 125 kg.

The championships will bring together competitors from established wrestling nations and countries across multiple continents, with athletes entered from Europe, Asia, the United States and Africa.

According to the organizers, entries remain subject to change until 72 hours before the draw for each wrestling style.

The championships will be held in Astana over nine days, with freestyle wrestling among the events featured at the international competition.

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi “against oligarch Ivanishvili’s rule”. ‘Protests in Georgia’ video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than 700 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: “Don’t like it? Too bad”: third day of Constitutional Court hearings on opposition ban in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban case

On 23 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the third day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream argues that the parties have violated Article 23 of the constitution, which prohibits political parties whose objectives include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited in the lawsuit is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The party is held responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the allegations.

Hearings will resume on 26 October and continue throughout the week. The court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Key events and statements from third day of Constitutional Court hearings

The day focused on motions submitted by Gakharia for Georgia, all of which were rejected by the court.

No opposition motion has been granted during the three days of Constitutional Court proceedings in the case.

Court rejects request to postpone hearings by a month

Berdia Sichinava, representing Gakharia for Georgia, asked the court to postpone the hearing by one month. He argued that procedural rules allow that much time to prepare a response, but his party had only seven days from the announcement that hearings would begin. The United National Movement, Lelo and Coalition for Change joined the motion.

Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee and one of the MPs who filed the lawsuit, argued that neither the procedural rules, the organic law nor the constitution stipulates that failure to submit a response prevents the court from hearing the case.

The judges deliberated and unanimously rejected the motion. Court president Revaz Nadaraia said the request should have been submitted earlier, as proceedings had already been under way for three days. He added: “If you don’t like it, you don’t like it. What can I do about that?”

Judge Eva Gotsiridze noted that the proceedings would take a long time, adding: “You will have the month provided for in the procedural rules.”

Request to recuse judge Sergo Metopishvili rejected

Gakharia for Georgia’s legal team filed a motion seeking the recusal of judge Sergo Metopishvili. The full bench rejected this request too.

Court rejects request to summon Bidzina Ivanishvili and Irakli Kobakhidze as witnesses

Berdia Sichinava asked the court to summon senior Georgian Dream figures as witnesses, including the party’s founder and honorary chair, billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili; Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze; prime minister Irakli Kobakhidze; and current and former senior officials Archil Talakvadze, Mamuka Bakhtadze, Vakhtang Gomelauri and Grigol Liluashvili.

He said their testimony was relevant to the criminal case against party leader Giorgi Gakharia.

Criminal proceedings against Giorgi Gakharia, Georgia’s former prime minister and current leader of the For Georgia party, began on 12 November 2025 and relate to two separate incidents. Gakharia has left the country and is currently abroad. One case concerns events in 2019, when Gakharia was interior minister. He is accused of unilaterally deciding to set up a police post near the village of Chorchana, in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, triggering a sharp escalation of tensions. Prosecutors say Tbilisi subsequently lost control of another section of its territory. The second case relates to the dispersal of a mass protest in Tbilisi on 20 June 2019. Police used force, including rubber bullets, without prior warning. Two people lost an eye and five others sustained serious injuries. Gakharia is accused of ordering the police operation in his capacity as interior minister.

Berdia Sichinava said that under direct questioning, Ivanishvili, Kaladze and others would not be able to evade responsibility for the 2019 decision to establish a police checkpoint in the village of Chorchana.

He also argued that the events of 20 June 2019 in Tbilisi could not be used as grounds for banning the party. “This is an issue on which society cannot reach a consensus,” Sichinava said, adding that “the protest was genuine, but the attempt to storm parliament was unacceptable”.

In response, claimant Archil Gorduladze reminded the court that Giorgi Gakharia was currently wanted and argued that the evidence in the two criminal cases against him should not be considered by the Constitutional Court.

The court rejected this motion too.

Georgian Dream’s position

Before the hearing, claimant Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee, told journalists that the opposition’s statements “only strengthen the case filed with the Constitutional Court”.

Asked about the opposition’s request to invite experts from the Venice Commission to take part in the proceedings, Gorduladze replied: “The opposition apparently believes that a foreigner knows Georgia’s constitution better than the Constitutional Court judges.”

Responding to criticism that a single lawsuit had been filed against all five parties, Gorduladze said: “They are all just the same National Movement.”

Tengiz Sharmanashvili, another Georgian Dream MP who filed the lawsuit, also told journalists that “the opponents want to drag things out”. He said he was concerned that the opposition was deliberately submitting motions in a form that made it impossible for the court to grant them.

“The opposition is collecting rejected motions for the Strasbourg court, and none of the five parties intends to engage seriously with the proceedings at the Constitutional Court,” Sharmanashvili said.

Outside the court

Opera singer Paata Burchuladze, who was convicted over an attempt to seize the presidential administration on 4 October 2025, has sent a letter to the Constitutional Court offering to testify if the events of 4 October are discussed during the proceedings.

Burchuladze argues that opposition parties are being unfairly accused of organising the events. “I was the organiser of those events, and I alone,” he said, urging the opposition to file a motion to have him summoned for questioning.

Sopio Khorguani, an MP from the opposition party Gakharia for Georgia, told journalists that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s statement that “the days of this opposition are numbered” was unacceptable. Khorguani described the remark as a direct instruction to the Constitutional Court on the verdict the government expects it to deliver.

Another representative of the party, Giorgi Sharashidze, said that “the whole process resembles a theatre of the absurd”. He said Gakharia for Georgia had been added to the lawsuit at the last minute, calling its inclusion “entirely artificial”. The claimant, he added, had still been unable to specify which article of the constitution the party had violated.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Buying Czech aircraft is part of Armenia’s air force modernisation’ — military expert
World.content:
Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase

Armenian Defence Minister Suren Papikyan is on an official visit to the Czech Republic. He began his visit with a trip to Aero Vodochody, a Czech defence industry company. According to reports, he discussed the possibility of further cooperation with the company’s management. He also examined Aero Vodochody’s products in detail.

“These marvels will soon take to the skies over Armenia,” the defence minister wrote in a caption accompanying a video he posted shortly after visiting the company.

Papikyan also shared photographs, captioning them: “One of the landmark days in the history of the Armenian Armed Forces’ aviation.”

Experts have speculated, based on the video and photographs he posted online, that Armenia is preparing to receive Czech-made L-39 Skyfox aircraft. These are a new generation of jet trainers.

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan believes that Armenia, which has a limited fleet of aircraft, could use the L-39 Skyfox not only for training but also for certain operational tasks:

“As a result, the purchase could become a practical step towards modernising the air force. However, its scale does not yet justify claims that it would significantly change the combat capabilities of Armenian aviation. For training purposes, four aircraft could serve as the first batch in a transition to a new training system and curriculum. If the Skyfox purchase forms part of a broader restructuring of the air force, expanding the fleet further would be the logical next step.”

The L-39 Skyfox is a new-generation jet trainer designed for advanced pilot training. It features modern digital avionics, multifunction displays and an integrated virtual training system. These capabilities allow pilots to simulate various tactical scenarios during training flights. According to Defense Mirror, one Skyfox costs less than $10 million. The final price depends on the aircraft’s configuration and delivery terms. Depending on its configuration, the aircraft can carry air-launched weapons, reconnaissance equipment and additional external systems. This allows it to perform limited military and reconnaissance missions.

What we know about the defence minister’s visit

The defence minister arrived in the Czech Republic on 20 October. During his visit, Suren Papikyan attended the opening ceremony of the Future Forces Exhibition & Forum. He toured the exhibition halls and viewed the latest technologies and advanced military equipment on display.

The Armenian minister also held talks with Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna.

Armenia’s Defence Ministry said the two ministers discussed:

Armenian-Czech defence cooperation, including military-technical cooperation;

reforms in the Armenian Armed Forces and cooperation in military education.

“Both sides stressed the importance of cooperation in multilateral formats, including within the EU and NATO,” the statement said.

Papikyan also discussed bilateral military-technical cooperation with Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlíček.

Commentary

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan noted that a Czech defence industry source had reported a month earlier that AERO Vodochody Aerospace was producing four L-39 Skyfox aircraft for Armenia. Specialist publications had also circulated the information, but none identified the customer or disclosed the terms of the deal.

Meanwhile, Arakelyan said, the Armenian Air Force already operates Czech-made L-39 Albatros trainers. Armenia acquired these second-hand aircraft in 2004 and 2010–11. It purchased some of them from Ukraine.

“However, the exact number of aircraft that remain in service with the Armenian Air Force and can still fly regularly is unknown,” the expert said.

In Arakelyan’s view, the Skyfox purchase fits Armenia’s strategy of diversifying its arms suppliers and expanding cooperation with European defence manufacturers:

“An Armenian-Czech agreement on military-technical cooperation, which has been in force since 2023, provides an additional basis for collaboration.”

Arakelyan believes the Armenian defence minister’s statement signals that the Skyfox acquisition has reached a practical stage.

“Nevertheless, until the parties officially disclose the terms of the deal, questions remain about the actual cost, delivery schedule, configuration and maintenance. These include technical support from the manufacturer and specialist training.

“The delivery of four Skyfox aircraft would represent a generational shift in Armenia’s training platform rather than a numerical expansion of its air force. The deal’s significance will depend on whether it remains a standalone purchase or marks the first stage of a broader overhaul of pilot training and air force capabilities. In the latter case, the Skyfox could bridge the gap between existing training aircraft and future combat platforms, with the four aircraft serving as the first batch in an air force modernisation programme.”

Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase

World.title: South Ossetia’s new government takes shape, with Russian officials in top posts
World.content:
South Ossetia has appointed a new prime minister after parliament unanimously backed 44-year-old Soslan Margiev, a former chairman of the Moscow Region Court.

Addressing MPs, Margiev said the region needed reforms. His priorities include making high-quality healthcare more accessible, improving South Ossetia’s investment appeal, developing its tourism potential and expanding social benefits.

“We have every opportunity to deliver these changes through our strategic partnership with the Russian Federation. We need to build an effective system of public administration that will help us develop our economy and social sector and, ultimately, improve living standards in our country,” the new prime minister said.

Clarify Margiev’s previous judicial roleMake the Russian partnership wording more neutral

Soslan Margiev

Soslan Margiev was born in Tskhinval and studied law in North Ossetia before working in various Russian courts. He has now made the unlikely career move to become South Ossetia’s prime minister. Some people in South Ossetia see him as a protégé of influential businessman Anatoly Margiev, head of the Ossetian diaspora in Sochi, and suspect the two men are related.

However, the new president, Marat Kambolov, who personally selected Margiev for the post, justified his choice by arguing that a legal professional would find it easier to restore law and order in South Ossetia.

“When I arrived here, I was certain that the head of government would definitely come from Moscow. He didn’t necessarily have to be an administrator. But after working here, meeting people and speaking with many of you, we made the only right decision. He is a lawyer in the fullest sense of the word. We are building a state governed by the rule of law,” Kambolov said.

Unlike Kambolov himself, Margiev at least comes from South Ossetia. So he is not entirely an outsider.

Kambolov previously signed decrees appointing several ministers and a first deputy prime minister before parliament had officially confirmed the prime minister in office, thereby breaching the procedure for forming a government.

Ekaterina Tolstikova

Last week, he appointed local officials to head the interior ministry, emergency situations ministry, defence ministry and other departments. However, he named another Moscow-based official, Ekaterina Tolstikova, as first deputy prime minister. She is a former colleague of Kambolov, with whom she worked in Russia’s federal government.

The cabinet is still incomplete. The posts of economy, agriculture, justice, and education and science ministers remain vacant.

Kambolov has also made appointments at the State Security Committee (KGB). He dismissed an appointee of the former president and replaced him with Yevgeny Romanov, whom he also brought in from Russia.

Thus, the top three positions in South Ossetia’s government — president, prime minister and deputy prime minister — are held by Russian officials who had no previous experience in politics as such. Two of them have never had any connection with South Ossetia.

However, judging by social media and opinion polls, the people of South Ossetia do not seem to find this unacceptable, provided the “imported” government does its job and delivers on its many ambitious promises. Only time will tell.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

South Ossetia appoints new prime minister

World.title: Behind the scenes at COP17: where thousands of delegates are staying in Armenia
World.content:
How Armenia housed COP17 delegates

The sports and concert complex hosts the so-called Green Zone at COP17. Anyone can take part in discussions here, including civil society representatives, scientists and environmental activists. The venue also hosts debates, exhibitions and cultural events.

The 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) has opened in Yerevan. Delegations from around the world, including scientists, representatives of international organisations, civil society, the private sector and the media, will take part in events in the capital of Armenia until 30 October.

Since 19 October, the conference has hosted extensive discussions and negotiations with international partners on biodiversity conservation.

The government says around 15,000 international visitors have arrived in the country for COP17.

Organising an international conference of this scale requires not only thorough preparation and the delivery of the planned programme, but also coordination of security, transport and services for participants.

For a small country, accommodating thousands of visitors in comfortable conditions was, of course, a particular challenge. The Ministry of Environment told JAMnews that it had offered visitors a range of accommodation options, including hotels and other types of lodging in Yerevan and nearby settlements.

A guesthouse whose first guests were European experts

This year, Sofia Gabrielyan converted her parents’ house in Nork-Marash, an upscale administrative district of Yerevan, into a five-bedroom guesthouse. Its first guests were two groups of experts from European countries who had come to attend COP17.

“They booked our guesthouse back in August, while renovations were still in full swing. I was confident we would finish everything on time and welcome COP17 guests. First, we registered on the system, and our guesthouse passed the required checks. Soon afterwards, conference participants chose it as their accommodation,” Sofia says.

Sofia Gabrielyan’s guesthouse

She considers it symbolic and significant that her guesthouse opened during the conference and welcomed European experts as its first guests. She believes she has done everything possible to convey the spirit of Armenian culture and create the right atmosphere.
