“I hope to continue welcoming international visitors in the future. I bought some beautiful carpets with traditional patterns, hand-embroidered curtains and tablecloths. I carefully planned the breakfast menu. I decided to serve linden honey and local fruit, and selected herbs from the mountains for tea.”

In the evenings, she plans to play works by renowned Armenian composers, including Khachaturian, Babajanian, Forsh and Akhverdyan, for guests in a specially equipped small gazebo. She has also prepared a short guide in English suggesting things to do in Yerevan and the surrounding area in the evenings and at weekends.

“We exchanged emails with our guests. On one of their days off, we offered to take them on a tour in a seven-seater car. We thought we could show them the pagan temple at Garni and the medieval Geghard monastery complex. They were delighted. They probably weren’t expecting such an offer. We want to show them not only our country, but also how hospitable Armenia and its people are,” the guesthouse owner says.

As for prices, she offered her first guests a 30% discount.

Yerevan’s major hotels are also hosting conference delegates

Best Western Plus Congress Hotel confirmed that it has been hosting COP17 participants since 14 October, with bookings opening three months earlier. Most guests come from Europe and the Middle East.

“We have welcomed high-ranking guests from participating countries. Some have come for a few days, while others will stay for two weeks. We are delighted to host conference guests, just as we traditionally welcome all our visitors.

“Most of the bookings for this period come from COP17 participants. We are also hosting a group of media representatives. They know the conference venues and entertainment programmes very well. They probably researched the available information thoroughly before their visit.

“We met guests at the airport and prepared Armenian wine and sweets for them in their rooms. However, we serve a classic breakfast menu,” the hotel said.

How COP17 delegates found accommodation

A dedicated team worked to ensure that COP17 participants found suitable accommodation.

The organisers reserved hotel rooms at agreed rates for large delegations. They specifically designed this group booking option for delegations of 25 or more participants. Other delegates chose and booked their own accommodation through online platforms for hotels and guesthouses.

Although Yerevan hosts the main conference events, the organisers also considered hotels and guesthouses in other regions as alternative options.

However, the full picture of how the organisers distributed guests across different accommodation options will only emerge from official figures after the conference ends.

COP17 has undoubtedly marked an important moment for Armenia’s engagement with the international environmental agenda. At the same time, the conference has put the country’s infrastructure, tourism industry and service sector to the test.

Discussion in the Green Zone

Welcoming thousands of international visitors requires coordinated work across multiple organisations. It also gives Armenia an opportunity to strengthen its reputation as a country capable of hosting major international events.

“Based on the first few days of COP17 and our experience hosting the European Political Community summit, which took place in Yerevan this May, we can say that Armenia is positioning itself as a country capable of hosting high-level international events to a high standard,” Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said.

Another session of the conference in the Blue Zone at the Meridian Expo Centre

All delegates have found accommodation and are satisfied with it

Ani Hakobyan, spokesperson for the environment minister, told JAMnews:

“All COP17 participants have accommodation. Guests are staying in hotels, guesthouses and flats available for short-term rent. We also offered delegations accommodation options in settlements near Yerevan.”

According to Hakobyan, the ministry has received no statements, letters or complaints from participants who were unable to find accommodation. She noted that such problems sometimes arise at COP conferences, but no incidents of this kind have occurred in this case.

The accommodation team listed available options on official online platforms. Alternatives included hotels, guesthouses and rental properties not only near Yerevan but also in Gyumri, Vanadzor, Dilijan, Tsaghkadzor and Jermuk. There is no precise information yet on whether conference participants took up these offers.

Hakobyan also said that international visitors are covering their own accommodation costs.

Blue Zone foyer

How Armenia housed COP17 delegates

World.title: Georgia opposition party ban case: Day two of court proceedings
World.content:
On 22 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court continued hearing a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party in Batumi, seeking to ban (declare unconstitutional) five opposition parties: the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Below are the key developments from the second day of hearings. The proceedings remained at the preliminary motions stage, with none of the opposition’s motions granted.

The hearings continue today, 23 October, and are being broadcast live by the Georgian Public Broadcaster.

The court has until 24 June 2027 to issue its final ruling, meaning it still has plenty of time.

Unprecedented case

The main issue raised by the opposition on the second day of hearings was that the lawsuit sought to ban all five parties in one go.

Lelo leader Badri Japaridze told the court that the case was unprecedented, as the parties had no links to one another. He argued that this was particularly true of Lelo, which was founded in late 2019.

Badri Japaridze described a statement by a Georgian Dream leader that the parties would be dissolved within days as disrespectful to the court. He argued that this meant the “verdict had already been delivered”. Presiding judge Revaz Nadaraya responded that the court could not comment on statements made by politicians and that no-one would be able to exert any influence over it.

Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze partially agreed with Japaridze’s argument. He acknowledged that there was indeed no precedent for dissolving five parties in a single proceeding, but argued that there was equally no precedent for five closely linked parties jointly violating Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits parties aiming to forcibly change the constitutional order.

Venice Commission

The Lelo party asked the court to invite three experts from the Venice Commission to the hearing to assess whether banning the parties would comply with European democratic standards. Other opposition parties supported the motion, while Georgian Dream opposed it.

However, Revaz Nadaraya dismissed the motion as unfounded, saying that the European legal experts could be heard elsewhere. Nika Gvaramia, co-chair of the Coalition for Change, argued that the Venice Commission was an association of European constitutional courts and that the right to consult it was enshrined in the Organic Law.

The court’s full bench then held consultations and rejected the motion.

The court also rejected another motion by Lelo, requesting that its lawsuit No. 1907, filed on 28 October 2025, be admitted for consideration on its merits. The lawsuit challenges provisions of the Organic Law on Political Associations of Citizens which, according to the party, restrict freedom of association, freedom of expression and political pluralism.

“Lack of trust is not enough reasoning”

Another Lelo representative, Giorgi Sioridze, requested that the Constitutional Court seek an advisory opinion from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) on five questions: the criteria under which a political party may be banned, the evidence required, whether a party’s stated objectives or its actual actions should carry greater weight, whether less restrictive measures are available, and what standards should apply when examining a case involving several parties simultaneously.

One of the arguments put forward in support of the motion was a lack of trust in the Constitutional Court. Revaz Nadaraya dismissed this argument as unfounded. He said that although the case was important and unprecedented, this was not sufficient grounds for seeking an advisory opinion from the ECtHR. Nadaraya also added that a national court should not have to ask the European Court whether five parties could be named as co-defendants in the same proceedings.

Evidence and one month to review case materials

The Coalition for Change, meanwhile, requested that evidence be obtained from the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Government Administration, that witnesses be identified and that consideration of the case on its merits be postponed.

The coalition also requested that the defendants be given one month to review the case materials. The court’s full bench unanimously rejected the motion. Nadaraya explained that, at this stage, the court was not convinced of the need to obtain additional evidence, as the requested materials relied on the same opinion already included in the case file.

Georgian Dream representatives accused the opposition of attempting to delay the proceedings. According to Archil Gorduladze, the defendants were filing motions that had no legal basis or relevance to the case. Tornike Cheishvili argued that the parties were expressing the same arguments using different terminology and that their motions were virtually identical.

Meanwhile, outside the courtroom…

– Georgia’s Public Defender (ombudsman) has yet to submit a legal opinion (amicus curiae) to the Constitutional Court, despite Lelo calling on him to do so on 19 October. According to First Deputy Public Defender Tamar Gvaramadze, the ombudsman’s office is holding internal discussions and no decision has yet been made.

– Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili said it was unacceptable for international actors to make statements intended to put pressure on the court. He argued that such statements served harmful political purposes.

Reactions after the hearing

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, compared the proceedings to Franz Kafka’s novel The Trial, saying that no-one really knew who was being accused of what. Badri Japaridze also said that, by the end of the second day of hearings, none of the parties understood exactly what Georgian Dream was accusing them of.

Ana Tsitlidze, a representative of the United National Movement, accused the judges of behaving like Georgian Dream activists. According to Lelo representative Irakli Kupradze, the proposed ban would affect not only the parties but also nearly a million Georgian voters.

Ana Buchukuri, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, suggested that the third day of hearings would also begin with procedural motions. She argued that the court’s refusal to grant any of the motions indicated that a decision had already been made.

World.title: Should state have right to ban political parties? Tbilisi street poll – Video
World.content:
Ban on Georgian opposition

Should the state have the right to ban political parties? Tbilisi residents answered reporters’ questions.

Context

The Constitutional Court of Georgia began examining a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 21 October, seeking to ban five opposition parties.

The lawsuit was signed by 88 Georgian Dream MPs, who claim that the parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits the establishment and activities of political parties aiming to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order.

The proposed ban on opposition parties is no ordinary constitutional case. The court’s ruling could determine what kind of country Georgia ultimately becomes. The case has therefore attracted widespread attention.

How respondents reacted to the question

Most Tbilisi residents interviewed by reporters said that banning political parties was unacceptable in a country that claims to be a democracy. They stressed the importance of a multiparty system and people’s right to choose.

Many said the current developments reminded them of a slide towards dictatorship, drawing comparisons with Russia, North Korea and even the Soviet Union.

One respondent echoed claims made on Georgian pro-government propaganda channels that the opposition had attempted to set fire to parliament and stage a coup, and should therefore be banned.

Another respondent said that banning political parties could be open to discussion, but only if the process was fair and transparent.

Many passers-by declined to comment and tried to avoid appearing on camera. This was hardly surprising, given that people approached on the street generally tend to avoid politically sensitive questions.

World.title: Vanity Fair: Trump son-in-law received $750m from Azerbaijani bank
World.content:
Kushner’s links to Azerbaijani bank

Reports have emerged of hundreds of millions of dollars being transferred through Azerbaijan to a secret bank account that Jared Kushner, the son-in-law and former senior adviser to US President Donald Trump, allegedly had access to.

However, no evidence has been presented that the money belonged to the Azerbaijani state or that Azerbaijani authorities were involved in arranging these transactions.

The name of the Azerbaijani bank through which the transfers were allegedly made has also not been disclosed.

According to an investigation published in Vanity Fair, Dutch intelligence, while monitoring Kushner’s phone, discovered that a large sum of money had been transferred from an Azerbaijani bank to an account in the United Arab Emirates.

The claims were detailed in an article by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole, published on 22 October. The article is an excerpt from his new book, Princes and Thieves.

The investigation refers to a bank account holding approximately $750m, as well as an additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan. The author links these financial transactions to unofficial diplomatic negotiations involving the United States, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel.

How did Dutch intelligence gain access to Kushner’s phone?

According to Matthew Cole’s investigation, the Netherlands’ Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) gained access to data from Kushner’s phone in late 2017 through a hacker linked to Russian military intelligence.

Dutch intelligence officers initially discovered screenshots from Kushner’s iPhone on Russian military intelligence servers. Then, exploiting the same technical vulnerability, they were able to monitor activity on his phone screen in early 2018.

The intelligence officers’ attention was drawn to Kushner’s use of a bank account in the UAE. According to the investigation, hundreds of millions of dollars had previously been transferred to this account from an Azerbaijani bank.

Dutch intelligence initially suspected that the bank account from which the funds originated might have been linked to the Azerbaijani government. However, the article does not provide any banking documents confirming this connection.

$750m and possible intermediary role of Azerbaijani bank

The account, referred to in the investigation as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, one of the UAE’s largest banks.

According to the author, the Saudi and UAE leadership transferred around $750m into the account from 2017 onwards. The funds were allegedly intended to finance unofficial foreign policy initiatives.

The account did not legally belong to Kushner. It was held by Watani Al Emarat, a charitable organisation funded by the UAE government. However, according to the investigation, Kushner had signing authority over the account, allowing him to carry out certain banking transactions.

The section of the investigation concerning Azerbaijan focuses particularly on the mechanism used to transfer the funds.

According to Cole, all the funds deposited into the account monitored by Dutch intelligence arrived in US dollars from an Azerbaijani bank.

The author claims that some Azerbaijani banks acted as intermediaries in transferring large sums of money abroad. They accepted funds in Saudi riyals and UAE dirhams before transferring the equivalent amounts overseas in US dollars, charging a commission of 6–7%.

Under the arrangement described, a client would transfer funds in local currency to an Azerbaijani bank, which would then send the equivalent amount in US dollars to a recipient abroad from a separate internal account. The author notes that such transactions could make it more difficult to trace the original source of the funds.

Additional $1bn allegedly transferred to Israel

The investigation also describes a second major financial transaction allegedly carried out through Azerbaijan.

According to the author’s sources, by spring 2018, UAE leader Mohammed bin Zayed had transferred around $1bn to Israel through Azerbaijan, allegedly intended for Kushner.

The second account, referred to by Cole as Beta, was reportedly held at the Bank of Israel.

The article claims that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was to be informed of any potential transfers from this account. According to the author, former US ambassador to Israel David Friedman acted as an intermediary between Kushner and Netanyahu.

Friedman categorically denied these allegations. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client was unaware of the accounts in question, had no involvement with them and had not broken any laws.

Kushner’s financial ties have previously come under scrutiny

The new allegations come amid ongoing debate in the US over Kushner’s business ties with Gulf states.

In March 2026, US Senator Ron Wyden and House Representative Robert Garcia launched an investigation into Kushner’s continued efforts to raise funds from foreign governments for his investment firm while simultaneously engaging in diplomatic activities.

The members of Congress sought to establish whether investments received by Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, from Middle Eastern governments could have influenced his involvement in US foreign policy.

An investigation published by The New Yorker in September reported that Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund had invested $2bn in Kushner’s firm in 2021. The UAE and Qatar also invested in Affinity Partners.

These were separate financial arrangements, not directly linked to the alleged secret banking transactions of 2017–2018 described in the Vanity Fair article.

In addition, on 1 October, CNN published an investigation into investments made by Kushner’s firm in Israeli financial group Phoenix Financial. According to CNN’s analysis, Phoenix Financial had invested in at least nine companies supplying equipment to the Israeli military.

However, CNN said it had found no evidence that Kushner’s diplomatic decisions had directly influenced these investments. Kushner’s lawyer also stated that his client had not been involved in the companies’ investment decisions.

On 8 October, Kushner published a detailed response on his website to the earlier New Yorker article, rejecting allegations that he had used his diplomatic activities for personal financial gain.

Which previous investigations have implicated Azerbaijani banks?

Azerbaijan’s role in international financial transactions has previously been the subject of journalistic investigations.

In 2017, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), together with its partners, published a major investigation titled The Azerbaijani Laundromat.

The investigation documented financial transactions totalling around $2.9bn, carried out between 2012 and 2014 through various companies and bank accounts.

According to OCCRP, around $1.4bn of this amount was transferred through Baktelekom LLC, a company that held an account at the International Bank of Azerbaijan.

The investigation highlighted the role of Azerbaijan-linked financial entities in international money transfers. However, there is no confirmed link between this scheme and the recently reported accounts allegedly connected to Kushner.

Meanwhile, in January 2026, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Experts on the Evaluation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures and the Financing of Terrorism (MONEYVAL) reported progress by Azerbaijan in this area.

The committee upgraded Azerbaijan’s compliance ratings against international standards in seven areas, including money transfer controls, identification of the ultimate beneficial owners of legal entities and banking supervision.

However, the country remained subject to enhanced monitoring.

World.title: Another peaceful rally by Azerbaijani families of missing persons held in Brussels (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. On October 22, another peaceful rally by Azerbaijani families of missing persons was held at the historic Place de l’Albertine, one of the well-known tourist spots in Brussels, the capital of Belgium. The rally was organized by the “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union.

The rally continued a series of demonstrations held on October 20 in front of the European Parliament at Place du Luxembourg and on October 21 at Schuman Square, where the main institutions of the European Union are located.

As part of the rally, a special installation featuring photographs, clothing, and envelopes belonging to Azerbaijan’s missing persons was displayed. The envelopes contained poignant messages written from the perspective of the missing, including: “I am not just a number. I have a name, I have a family,” and “I am still someone’s child. How long must my family wait?” Through these letters, missing Azerbaijanis whose voices have gone unheard for more than 30 years seemed to break the silence themselves and appeal to the world.

Visitors who learned about the installation expressed solidarity by writing messages of support to the families of the missing, tying ribbons in remembrance, and laying flowers.

Visitors were informed that 4,010 Azerbaijanis had gone missing during Armenia’s occupation of Azerbaijani territories, including 71 children, 288 women, and 319 elderly people.

Konul Behbudova, Chairwoman of the “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union and sister of missing martyr Abbas Behbudov, said Armenia’s silence regarding missing Azerbaijanis was unacceptable and called for information about the fate of the missing to be provided to the Azerbaijani side.

Farida Jabbarova, wife of missing person Azad Jabbarov; Reyhan Janiyeva, wife of Sakhavat Janiyev; Sevinj Hajiyeva, daughter of Ahmad Mammadov; Mahuru Shahin, mother of Shahin Aliyev; Nazani Aliyeva, wife of Abulfat Aliyev; and Parvana Mammadova, wife of Ogtay Mammadov, also shared with visitors the void left in their families by the absence of their loved ones, as well as the years of uncertainty and anguish they had endured.

The families’ appeal to the international community remained unchanged: “We do not simply want to remember our loved ones; we want to know the truth about their fate. No family should have to wait forever!”

At a meeting held on October 21, 2026, in Brussels with Okke Bouwman, Political Adviser to the EU Special Representative for the South Caucasus and the crisis in Georgia, and Marco Cardinali, Coordinator for Relations with Azerbaijan, at the European External Action Service (EEAS), the families of missing Azerbaijanis reaffirmed that they would continue their international rallies until the fate of their relatives was clarified.

The “Garabagh Missing Families” Public Union is a winner in the 2026 grant competition organized by Azerbaijan’s Agency for State Support to NGOs. Its project is titled “Echo of Absence” (“Yoxluğun sədası”).

World.title: Strait of Hormuz will no longer be managed according to previous model – Iranian FM
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. The Strait of Hormuz will no longer be managed according to the previous model, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said at an event held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Tehran.

“The Strait of Hormuz has remained open for decades. Neither Iran nor Oman, as the two coastal states, has imposed any restrictions on the passage of vessels. On the contrary, they have ensured security and protected the environment,” he noted.

Araghchi said that talk of a possible resumption of war has resurfaced in recent days. According to him, Iran’s policy remains unchanged, regardless of whether war breaks out. Given the logic of the situation, a military attack on Iran should not happen again.

“Iran and the countries of the region must live in peace without external interference. Iran maintains relations with the countries surrounding the Persian Gulf and seeks to reach a common understanding on a new regional security mechanism. This is the only way to restore peace and stability in the region,” he noted.

The Iranian minister added that in all discussions with the U.S. side, mediated by Pakistan, Qatar and other countries, Iran had emphasized the need to end the war on all fronts. Otherwise, there would be no stability in the region.

“Peace and stability in the region must be pursued in a way that reduces the involvement of forces from outside the region to zero,” he said.

It should be recalled that the latest escalation in relations between the United States and Iran began on July 8. On that day, the U.S. Armed Forces launched several waves of strikes on Iranian territory for the first time since the signing of a memorandum between Washington and Tehran, claiming the strikes were in response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking U.S. facilities located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Oman.

As a result of the conflict, maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz was brought to a standstill.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev sends congratulatory letter to President of Kazakhstan
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. President Ilham Aliyev has sent a congratulatory letter to Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

This was reported by the press service of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Kassym-Jomart Kemelevich,

On my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan, I sincerely congratulate you and, through you, the people of your brotherly country on the national holiday of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Republic Day, and convey my best wishes.

Today, as a result of the deliberate policy pursued under your leadership, the Republic of Kazakhstan has achieved comprehensive development, made progress in all spheres, strengthened its economic potential, and gained considerable prestige on the international stage. As a brotherly country, we sincerely rejoice in Kazakhstan’s year-after-year progress and its continued achievements.

Our regular mutual visits, meetings, and active dialogue at the highest level play an important role in accelerating the development of our bilateral relations, strengthening our strategic partnership and alliance, and enriching them with new content. I highly appreciate your recent visit to Azerbaijan to participate in the 7th CICA Summit.

I am confident that Azerbaijan–Kazakhstan intergovernmental relations, drawing strength from our rich moral values and the brotherhood of our peoples, will continue to develop steadily and grow stronger through our joint efforts.

On this festive day, I wish you robust health, happiness, and success in your responsible state activities, and the brotherly people of Kazakhstan lasting peace, well-being, and prosperity," the letter reads.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva attends premiere of opera “Turandot” (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. The grand premiere of the opera “Turandot” took place at the Heydar Aliyev Palace. The Azerbaijan State Academic Opera and Ballet Theatre presented a new staging of Giacomo Puccini’s famous opera to a standing ovation. World-renowned tenor and People’s Artist of Azerbaijan Yusif Eyvazov performed in the production.

Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation Leyla Aliyeva attended the premiere.

Staged in Azerbaijan for the first time in 98 years, the new production of “Turandot” was specifically created for the Baku stage.

The production designer is Mustafa Mustafayev, the executive designer is Honored Cultural Worker Tehran Babayev, and the director is Elnur Ismayilov. The production director is Mikayil Mikayilov. Honored Artist and choirmaster Sevil Hajiyeva led the choral preparation. The choreographers are People’s Artist Madina Aliyeva and Honored Artist Anar Mikayilov.

The production features three different casts. Across the three premiere evenings, the roles of Turandot and Calaf will be performed by different soloists, with different conductors taking the podium.

On October 24, the famous role of Calaf was performed by People’s Artist Yusif Eyvazov, director of the Azerbaijan State Academic Opera and Ballet Theatre and one of the most renowned Azerbaijani opera singers on the international stage. The role has become a signature part of Yusif Eyvazov’s repertoire. At the same time, this marked the famous tenor’s first performance in the role in Azerbaijan. That evening, the role of Turandot was performed by Italian soprano Carmen Giannattasio, with Italian maestro Beatrice Venezi conducting.

At a press conference held before the performance, Yusif Eyvazov called the premiere of “Turandot” a historic event. The People’s Artist noted that, after 98 years, “Turandot” had returned to the Azerbaijani stage. He said that the new staging, presented by director Mikayil Mikayilov and production designer Mustafa Mustafayev, was of a very high standard. International opera soloists are also performing alongside Azerbaijani artists in the production.

Production director Mikayil Mikayilov added that the theatre troupe had made an immense effort. “We hope the audience will appreciate our efforts and enjoy the performance. This is a very remarkable event of great value to our theatrical culture,” he stated.

“Turandot” is one of Giacomo Puccini’s most famous operas. The three-act production is based on Carlo Gozzi’s play of the same name. The libretto was written by Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni. The world premiere of the opera took place on April 25, 1926, at La Scala in Milan, under the baton of Arturo Toscanini.

Baku audiences first saw the opera in 1928, just two years after its world premiere. The Baku production was the first performance of “Turandot” in the Soviet Union.

Puccini worked on “Turandot” from the summer of 1920 until his death in 1924. However, he did not live to complete his famous masterpiece. The final part of the opera was completed by Franco Alfano based on Puccini’s sketches.

The plot of the opera revolves around the romantic story of the cruel Princess Turandot and Prince Calaf. As in Gozzi’s fairy tale, Turandot tests all her suitors with three riddles, declaring that she will marry whoever answers them correctly, while anyone who answers incorrectly will be executed. After a series of trials, Calaf solves the riddles and ultimately marries Turandot, who surrenders to the power of his love.

World.title: Iran says resumption of war with US would not change its mind
World.content:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks on Sunday came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28.

Mr Araghchi said a fresh attack would not yield a different outcome.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," Mr Araghchi said during a televised event in Tehran.

" They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past. "

A plume of smoke rises after a US strike in Tehran in March. (AP: Vahid Salemi)

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the US put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.

Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation, moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.

In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the US to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.

Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

"The current war has changed everything," Mr Araghchi said.

"We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same.

"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Ten ballistic missiles intercepted over Riyadh

The Houthis have warned they could again target Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh's airport "a military target". (Reuters: Mohammed al-Mahdi)

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over its capital Riyadh and southern areas on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, as fighting with the Iran-aligned Houthis persisted.

The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising front in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

On Sunday, Saudi civil defence authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait, before announcing minutes later that the danger had passed.

The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait.

Travellers were told that the King Khalid International Airport was again operating normally. (AP Photo)

It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis warned they could again target Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after a deadly attack earlier this month.

The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and warned all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Hand-delivered death threat, being spat at among abuse ACT politicians cop
World.content:
A hand-delivered death threat, being spat at and misogynistic abuse are just some of the incidents ACT politicians say they've experienced.

Several members of the ACT Legislative Assembly have spoken out about the abuse they've been subjected to, following the attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines outside her Victorian electorate office on Monday.

It's not yet clear what motivated Brendan Nugent, 43, to allegedly run her down in the incident that led to both her legs being amputated.

But the incident has renewed concerns about the safety of elected representatives across Australia, and highlighted the risks that come with their jobs.

Canberra Liberals MLA and former ACT opposition leader Elizabeth Lee said she has had to contact police twice over "very serious threats" she received.

"I had a death threat that named my daughter and my partner, and it was actually dropped at my front gate, so it came to my house," Ms Lee recalled.

"That was a pretty scary moment, and it does actually question, to me, as a parent especially, whether it's worth it.

"I have got this duty to ensure that I am prosecuting the issues that are really important to the community, but does that come at the cost of safety to my family?"

Elizabeth Lee says threats against her family have left her questioning whether to stay in politics.

The incident came on top of the many sexist and racist comments she has received online over the past decade of representing her community.

"Belittling criticism on a personal level. Criticisms on my weight and my body shape as well, what I'm wearing sometimes," she said.

The mother of two daughters, Ms Lee said she tried to find the balance between ignoring the comments and calling them out to show her girls that such behaviour was unacceptable.

"I try and ignore it on the whole, but at the same time I know that there are people who need to know that it's not okay," she said.

"So, every now and then I will take that and make an example out of it to call it out."

'Disturbing part of the job'

ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson has also had some "pretty horrible" encounters with constituents.

"Yelling abuse at you, names at you," Ms Paterson said.

" I've been spat at; I've had things like that happen, standing outside the front of the shops and I've had people make violent threats to me face-to-face. "

Marisa Paterson says that while most of her interactions with constituents are positive, some recent encounters have been "pretty horrible". (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie )

Ms Paterson said she enjoyed meeting and greeting Canberrans at local shops and community events, and that "97 per cent of interactions" were "amazing".

But she said the abuse she received, both in person and online, was a "disturbing part of the job" that made her "feel very vulnerable".

"It's predominantly men. In fact, all of my examples are men," she said.

" And I don't know … why they feel they can say these things to me and speak to me like that. But that is what happens. It's really disturbing. "

Online, Ms Paterson said the abuse had "ramped up" over the past 18 months "very, very significantly", particularly with misogynistic, violent and hateful comments.

"The online world is a very unhappy place at the moment, I think," she said.

"Aside from having this job and needing to be there, other than that, I would have no part of it.

"It is a pretty awful environment with the online comments."

'Tough being a woman in politics'

For Greens MLA Laura Nuttall, it's her sexuality, gender and appearance that are often targeted on social media.

"You'll get some pretty nasty comments, which are often nothing to do with the debate [of the social media post], and everything to do with your appearance, your political leanings," Ms Nuttall said.

"I have had my sexuality speculated on and then sort of taken through the mud. I've copped a bit of queerphobic abuse, which is never fun.

"It is tough … being a woman in politics, particularly right now."

Laura Nuttall says that while most of her interactions with the public are positive, some encounters have been genuinely frightening. (ABC News)

Ms Nuttall said the comments she received could be demoralising and that she "would be lying" if she said the attack on Ms Haines hadn't scared her.

"I have occasionally … felt the impact of that in my personal life in terms of just a loss of confidence," she said.

"And at times, even though it's momentary, a little bit of loss of faith in humanity, that people could be so mean and so remorseless about it."

'Rage gets clicks'

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said he had seen his female counterparts cop far more abuse, particularly online, than he and his male colleagues did.

"Some of the men get criticised as well, but I think criticism on the basis of policy or disagreeing is really critical, that's part of our democracy and that's what a good, vibrant democracy looks like," Mr Emerson said.

"We should be able to disagree and disagree respectfully, debate those ideas. But when that flips into just abuse that's got nothing to do with the issue at hand, it is concerning."

Thomas Emerson acknowledges that his female colleagues are having "very different experiences as politicians" to his own. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

He said there was a lot more political leaders could do to lead by example.

"Every time we allow policy disagreement to devolve into denigrating the people we're disagreeing with, we're basically saying to the people we're supposed to be representing, and leading in some ways, that actually this is the right way to conduct yourself," he said.

"So there's some blame there for politicians.

"We know that rage gets clicks and it gets picked up in traditional media, on social media, and that can lead to some pretty perverse incentives for politicians themselves and for people out in that community."

Ms Lee agreed that "we all need to take responsibility as a society".

"Political leaders particularly have a role, but it's anyone who has a public voice including the media and the big companies that obviously are responsible for social media," she said.

"Anyone who has the opportunity and the privilege to be able to shape public discourse and debate has a responsibility."

Laura Nuttall says she wants to continue meeting with Canberra constituents at local shops. (ABC News)

As politicians across the country review their security measures, these ACT MLAs are determined to remain publicly available to constituents as part of a healthy democracy.

"It is absolutely the key part of my job that I love," Ms Paterson said.

"It is my job to be out and about talking to people, listening to people, listening to what their concerns are."

Ms Nuttall agreed that she did not want the pockets of aggression, venom and vitriol to detrimentally impact the way she did her job.

"The whole point of being a representative is to be as accessible as humanly possible," she said.

World.title: Fishermen racing crocs for crabs in Wadeye as new industry emerges
World.content:
Before dawn, the sea farmers are already on the water.

As the fishermen steer their boat along the mangrove-lined banks, they know they must move fast so they can load their catch onto a light plane bound for the Darwin Fish Market by the afternoon.

For Theo Dooling, these waters feel familiar. He has fond memories of catching crabs from mud holes with his family as a child.

Loading

"You can put in a stick and just take the crab out," he says.

Back then, the biggest challenge was avoiding a pinch on the finger.

Now, the sea farmers compete with crocodiles for their bounty. Mr Dooling says the reptiles have crushed five of his crab pots in their jaws, desperately trying to poach the fleshy crustaceans.

In Wadeye, a small mud crab venture has grown into a full commercial operation. (ABC News: James Elton)

As the pots are hauled in, it is easy to see why. Nearly all contain mud crabs, with the biggest weighing two kilograms.

A remote community

Sitting on the west coast of Australia's Top End, Wadeye is one of the NT's most unique Aboriginal communities.

Traditional culture thrives here through music and dance, and both adults and children speak the Aboriginal language Murrinh-patha fluently.

Wadeye's main ceremonial groups performed traditional dances during the 2025 Yidiyi Festival. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Its approximately 2,500 residents are cut off for half the year when the rugged Port Keats Road washes out.

But in recent years, the community has also been one of the NT's most troubled.

Wadeye is one of the largest Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory. (ABC News: James Elton)

It has made headlines for large-scale street fights involving weapons such as spears and crossbows.

Standard three-bedroom houses have as many as 20 people living in them, and black-market liquor is widely available but cripplingly expensive.

Desmond Longmair says a group torched his car using a Coke bottle filled with petrol in a recent round of fighting. (ABC News: James Elton)

Yet, nearly everyone in town points to the lack of jobs as the biggest problem.

At the 2021 census, only about one in five adults had a job.

The lack of jobs is a major issue for the residents in Wadeye. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

It is against this backdrop that the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have used Aboriginal coastal licences to grow their modest operation into a larger commercial venture that could change outcomes for the Wadeye community.

The acquisition of a full commercial licence means the fishermen can have up to 60 crab pots in the water, and they have expanded their team from three to nine workers within a year.

On average, they send 35 to 50 kilograms of mud crabs to Darwin each week.

Sea farmer Maurice Bitting with freshly caught crabs. (ABC News: James Elton)

"The people we brought on to the team, they are really very good," says Johnson Katuura, the sea farmers coordinator.

"They're people who have fished all their lives."

Joel Martin, one of the team's youngest members, said the sea farmers had already inspired local schoolkids.

Joel Martin is one of the youngest members of the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We go out to school sometimes, talk to the students, let them know that they're going to have to graduate, then they can find a good job," Mr Martin says.

" We want more young boys to come in so they can have a good life, good job. "

Sustainability a top priority

The NT's largest crab licence holder, the Aboriginal Sea Company, says Wadeye is the only "community-run" commercial fishing operation in the NT.

The operation is getting mentoring and training from Humpty Doo Barramundi, one of Australia's biggest aquaculture players.

The Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have grown to a workforce of nine. (ABC News: James Elton)

Elsewhere in the NT, concerns about mud crab numbers led to a pause on commercial licences so stocks could recover.

It came at a bad time for the sea farmers, who were about to begin commercial operations.

But once they negotiated with authorities, the licences were temporarily converted back to Aboriginal coastal licences, then returned to commercial when the pause ended.

Tracey Leo, the deputy CEO of Thamarrurr Development Corporation, backed the way the sea farmers do business.

Tracey Leo is the deputy CEO of the Thamarrurr Development Corporation. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We fully support sustainable harvest strategies," Ms Leo says.

She says the crew keeps detailed records of where they fish and how many crabs they take, "so that we're not over-harvesting in one … location".

The corporation is also lobbying for the Territory's fishery management zones to be reviewed, arguing that rules designed for more heavily fished areas don't necessarily make sense in the relatively "un-fished" waters around Wadeye.

Mr Katuura says the industry's sustainability is the top priority.

Johnson Katuura hopes the commercial operation will be sustainable and long-lasting. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We want it to be long-living," he says.

" We are focused on making a stronger foundation [rather] than rushing to numbers. And I believe that will be the game changer. "

Slow and steady investment

Ms Leo previously worked with Humpty Doo Barramundi and helped establish a two-way training relationship between the operators.

She believes a fully-fledged seafood industry could emerge in Wadeye within a decade, employing about 100 people across mud crabs, a black-lip oyster farm, and some other fisheries.

The black-lip oysters are yet to reach commercial production. (ABC News: James Elton)

"When we first invested in the Sea Farmers, there was a lot of capital infrastructure required, with a big shed and the boats and crab pots and oyster cages, but that's not going to translate to 100 jobs in a short period of time," Ms Leo says.

"We need government to recognise … those employment outcomes [are] going to take a long time.

"[Humpty Doo] were [running] 14 or 15 years before they were even profitable. And they've been going 30 years or whatever it is now … extremely successful."

The impact of 100 jobs to Wadeye would be significant, boosting family incomes in a town where only about 300 adults are currently employed.

But it's also about the type of work. Ms Leo says most of the existing jobs in Wadeye are "very service-based", staffing places such as the local supermarket or the family centre.

"Client-focused jobs, they don't meet the aspirations of local people … there's a lot of kinship complexities, and you might not be able to serve someone if there's relationships in the kinship system," Ms Leo says.

" Working on Country is what everyone wants to do. "

Mr Katuura says it is important to grow the industry sustainably and carefully.

There are hopes the crabbing operation could go on to provide 100 jobs for the local community. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We talk to the people who run [Humpty Doo] all the time," Mr Katuura tells 7.30.

" They train us. They inspire us. And what they tell us is 'take baby steps'. "

While most of the mud crabs go to the market in Darwin, some are going direct to seafood restaurants. (ABC News: James Elton)

Mr Dooling says working with his hands on his traditional Country has given him peace and purpose.

He also wants customers to know where the mud crabs came from, and that they were caught with pride.

"It makes me feel happy when I go out where my sea Country is," he says.

"I'm not an inlander. I'm a seaman."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Another Perth beach closed as more whale remains found
World.content:
Whale remains have closed another Perth beach today, as authorities warned of possible shark activity in Sorrento after removing the tail of a carcass found just off the shore.

This is the second whale carcass to wash up on the city's beaches this week, and the third in the past month, raising concerns about a further increase in shark activity just as beaches are about to become more crowded ahead of summer.

Sorrento Beach was closed about five weeks ago when Perth father Greg O'Neill was attacked and killed by a large great white shark as he was swimming close to the shoreline.

Sorrento Beach was closed last month after the fatal shark attack. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

He was the third person killed by a shark in Western Australia this year.

Greg O'Neill, left, was killed by a shark while swimming at Sorrento Beach. (Supplied)

The City of Joondalup removed the whale remains from Sorrento Beach a few hours after surf lifesavers reported seeing them, but said the beaches in the area remained closed as "residue from where the whale carcass was beached may attract sharks to the area".

AI-powered drones on cards for WA shark monitoring Western Australia's shark-tagging program will be expanded and the use of AI-powered drones investigated as new funding is announced.

The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD), along with staff from other agencies, is monitoring the situation, according to the government's SharkSmart app.

On Thursday, a 3-metre, significantly decomposed partial whale carcass washed up at South Cottesloe beach, triggering the closure of all beaches in the area.

The remains were buried at the Red Hill Waste Management Facility.

Council staff remove the whale carcass from South Cottesloe. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

On September 27, a 13-metre, 72-tonne humpback whale carcass washed up on South City Beach, requiring an excavator to remove it.

The state government is expanding its shark-tagging program and may use AI-powered drones as part of a suite of measures aimed at keeping beachgoers safe.

World.title: Darwin pregnant patients' medical information posted to Instagram in breach
World.content:
Royal Darwin Hospital has issued an apology for a privacy breach that led to confidential medical information belonging to about a dozen pregnant patients being shared to 28,000 followers on Instagram by a "medical observer" associated with the hospital.

In the letter sent to affected patients, RDH management said NT Health had been informed an overseas trained doctor attached to the hospital's obstetrics and gynaecology unit had posted to social media images and videos where "patient details were visible".

The information exposed included patient names, their presenting condition or any diagnoses they had. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"The information visible about you from our handover sheet included your name, your hospital record number, the ward and bed number, the name of the consultant, the presenting problem, medical history, investigations, and plan of management," the letter said.

"I recognise that learning of this incident may cause distress, embarrassment or concern about your privacy and your trust in our service.

" You should not have had to experience this and we are deeply sorry. "

The content, which has been seen by the ABC, was posted to the Instagram account of Dr Neda Mogharehabed and also included a video from a staff meeting, where health professionals can be heard discussing a woman's care.

Screenshots of the posts featured on the Instagram account @dr.neda.mogharehabed (Supplied)

In a statement to the ABC, Dr Mogharehabed said she "cannot confirm how these images were posted" or "whether they originated from the account I currently control", noting "there may be other accounts using my name".

Dr Mogharehabed added she "did not intend to disclose any patient information" and that she takes "patient privacy seriously".

"I am sorry for the concern this situation has caused. At this stage, however, I cannot verify the origin or circumstances of the images," she said.

In their statement, RDH management noted the doctor as a "medical observer" who was not permitted to undertake any patient management and that her attachment to NT Health had since been terminated.

Dr Neda Mogharehabed is no longer associated with NT Health. (Supplied)

'Shocking' and a 'violation'

One of the women whose information was exposed was ABC Radio Darwin producer, Shanelle Tobin, who is 17-weeks pregnant with her second child.

Ms Tobin said when she went for her appointment at RDH two weeks ago she was asked if she consented to a "medical observer" being present.

"I didn't give it a second thought, I was like 'yep, they're here to learn, to get exposure, whatever it is, I'm comfortable', and now I guess I'm reflecting on that [choice]," Ms Tobin said.

Shanelle Tobin is expecting her second child in April-May next year. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

The expectant mother said the information shared in these medical appointments was detailed and highly sensitive.

"You go through everything from previous pregnancies, whether or not you've had terminations, they talk through your mental health generally and how it was with your last pregnancy," she said.

"Every facet of physical health, so that goes into STIs [sexually transmitted diseases], any issues with your reproductive organs ... your fertility journey, whether that's with IVF or not, and your experience of domestic violence.

" So, yeah it is a very vulnerable space ... and you're just putting your trust in them that this is the cone of silence. "

When Shanelle Tobin saw the screenshots of the images posted showing private informaiton she was shocked. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Ms Tobin said she discovered her personal information had been shared online when a member of the public reached out to her saying they had seen the post and her name featured.

"It was obviously shocking," she said.

"I then received a phone call from Royal Darwin Hospital from the head of obstetrics who outlined that this breach had happened."

Ms Tobin said when she realised the account had 28,000 followers the "feeling of violation really set in".

Shanelle Tobin says the exposure of her information made her feel "violated". (ABC News: Grace Atta)

'Major wake-up call' for RDH

In a statement, the vice president of the NT Branch of the Australian Medical Association Dr Dayna Duncan said "any breach of patient confidentiality is unacceptable in all situations".

"There are very clear laws and guidelines about patient privacy in Australia, including social media," Dr Duncan said.

"All patients should expect that everyone in their treating team keeps their personal information confidential, with no exceptions."

Dayna Duncan says all patients should expect confidentiality from their treating medical professionals. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Tobin said she hoped the incident would be a "major wake-up call" for RDH about how it manages patient privacy and educates its staff, including international medical observers, about this principle.

The ABC asked Dr Mogharehabed if she had received any training from RDH about expectations around social media use and patient confidentiality.

Dr Mogharehabed said did not receive any specific training about "photography, video recording or posting content on social media" and that she was "not specifically informed during my observership that posting such content on social media was prohibited".

She added: "To my knowledge, the content I became aware of did not tag or mention Royal Darwin Hospital by name."

NT Health was contacted for comment.

Shanelle Tobin gave birth to her toddler at Royal Darwin Hospital almost three years ago. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Despite her recent bad experience, Ms Tobin said she still planned to access care and give birth at RDH.

"My birth at RDH with my first baby was a really amazing experience, thanks to the people that work there.

"They are some of the hardest workers you could ever imagine and ... I will put my trust back into those people because I know this is one individual who's decided to act in a certain way."

World.title: Final MotoGP race at Phillip Island washed out
World.content:
The MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled as heavy rain and poor visibility washed out what was the final race at the island circuit.

All races at the track, including the Australian Superbikes race three and both the Moto2 and Moto3 races, were cancelled earlier on Sunday, with hopes that fans would see the MotoGP take a final turn around the iconic circuit fading as the day passed.

The race will move to a street circuit in Adelaide, South Australia in 2027, after three decades at the circuit on the Bass Coast.

The wet weather derailed plans for a final lap of the Ventnor circuit, with the announcement made at 3:30pm that the MotoGP race had been called off after motoring fans sat in the stands for hours in the rain.

Jack Miller farewells fans after the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

The race had been delayed from its original 2pm start time, with hopes it would begin at 4:30pm.

A MotoGP riders farewell lap was being held at 3:45pm.

Racing fans braved the wet and windy conditions at the track before the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

In a statement, the Australian Grand Prix Corporation said poor visibility that prevented the medical helicopter from flying was behind the cancellation.

"We know this is an incredibly disappointing outcome for fans, teams and everyone who has contributed to the event," it said.

"Safety must always come first, and racing cannot take place without the medical helicopter able to operate."

The corporation said it would provide full refunds for Sunday ticketholders and partial refunds for multi-day ticketholders.

The official morning warm up was also cancelled, along with track side entertainment such as the monster trucks and a celebratory legends lap with world champions Mick Doohan, Casey Stoner and Wayne Gardner.

World.title: Deadly measles spread hitting US state's Amish hard amid White House row
World.content:
In a rural corner of the US state of Pennsylvania, crop fields, maple trees and colonial-era barn farmhouses dot a patchwork landscape of rolling grassy hills.

At the foot of the Appalachian Mountains, Lancaster County is less than 300 kilometres from New York City and home to the country's oldest and largest Amish community.

But it has also become the focus of a heated political row amid a scramble to contain one of the US's worst measles outbreaks in recent history.

Amish communities are caught in the state's fight to curb rising measles cases. (Reuters: Mark Makela)

The most vulnerable infiltrated

Measles is a highly contagious illness that can lead to the hospitalisation or death of a person, with up to nine out of 10 people who are not vaccinated likely to fall sick, the Australian Centre for Disease Control says.

Authorities in Pennsylvania say the outbreak there began in late April, west of one of the state's largest cities, Philadelphia.

Cases have since ballooned above 1,300 in what has become Pennsylvania's largest spread of the disease in more than three decades.

At least six people have died, including two infants — one of which was a newborn — and a 20-year-old from Lancaster County, an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County and a 39-year-old female from Franklin County.

The Pennsylvania Health Department said none of the victims was vaccinated, and Franklin County officials reported the 39-year-old had a previous measles diagnosis and "several underlying conditions".

Authorities say the disease has mostly impacted people aged between 18 and 49, who account for about 800 of the state's cases, and at least 251 people — or about one in every five — have been hospitalised.

Low vaccination rates, mostly in vulnerable Amish communities, remain the biggest challenge according to officials.

At least five who died were from Amish communities, local media reported.

The Amish traditionally reject modern-day medicine and technologies in favour of communal living. (Reuters: Mark Makela)

The Amish are insular, religious people who associate piety with surrendering to strict rules for the greater good of their community, and reject modern-day technologies.

They came to the US from Europe in the 1700s, and more than 410,000 still live across the country, including at least 40,000 in Lancaster County.

Braxton Mitchell, co-director of the University of Maryland's Amish research program, says their communal way of life creates a unique risk of rapid virus spread.

"Amish are very social. The Amish families have a lot of kids — the average [has] seven or eight, so a lot of people in the household," he said.

"The Amish get together with their neighbours, with their relatives; they have church services on Sundays which tend to be at somebody's house and the whole church district shows up."

The measles outbreak has also impacted Amish children in parts of Pennsylvania, including some infants who died as a result of their illnesses. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

He said they were sceptical of government intervention and do not see the need to engage with modern medicine.

"They don't like governments telling them what to do … Amish don't subscribe to the national health insurance," Professor Mitchell said.

" With some diseases, the Amish [believe] 'if we get sick, if God's will is that we're meant to survive, we'll survive'. "

Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College, has lived in Lancaster County for most of his life and said he loves the area's reputation for diversity, manufacturing, picturesque nature and pleasantness of local life.

"There's a strong sense of Lancaster heritage and Lancaster identity … [The county] is special, especially in the minds of people with deep roots here," he said.

Steve Nolt (left) says Lancaster County boasts a lifestyle and nature that make it attractive as a potential place to retire. (Supplied: Steve Nolt)

But he said while the majority of the non-Amish population live with them harmoniously, there is still concern about the spread of measles.

That worry has extended to non-Amish residents warily monitoring transmission alerts naming schools, stores or other popular locations where the virus has spread outside of Amish areas, Mr Nolt said.

Fears of deadly under-reporting

In the neighbouring Chester County, 93 cases have been reported this year, but there is concern around unreported infections.

Jeanne Franklin, the county's public health director, said officials were aware of people who fell ill and did not feel the need to access medical care or alert authorities.

She said by the time some patients present to hospitals or other medical clinics, they were significantly ill.

"What we're seeing is the worst of the worst," she told the ABC.

" It is definitely bigger than we are able to report because it is moving very quickly … Statistically speaking, we're likely going to see more deaths. "

In Chester County, and parts of the neighbouring Lancaster County, door-to-door and community outreach efforts are underway to spread vaccination awareness. (AP: Matt Rourke)

Ms Franklin described the Amish as "vaccine hesitant", but does not treat them as unique from the non-Amish who choose not to be vaccinated according to political or religious beliefs.

"What we want to remind people is, regardless of whether you're Amish or an anti-vaxxer … reassess the decision in the light of today," she said.

"Thirty years ago you may have said: 'Why do I need that? Measles isn't an issue.' Well, guess what, it's an issue."

Measles and other diseases are making a comeback A recent outbreak of measles in Adelaide has sparked concern from health authorities, but it's not the only infectious illness where cases are rising once again.

She said Chester County adopted a word-of-mouth approach to promoting vaccination and dispelling common myths about measles.

"We have a whole team … painting the picture [of the disease's spread]. Where is it? Is it in our adults? Is it in our youth?" she said.

"We're a health department; we can't be everywhere, but we know the church on Main Street, the food pantry on South Street, and the hardware store are trusted business owners and community members.

"We are going out to meet them, educate them, so if they get questions, they know how to direct to us … Some of them are like, 'give me 100 [flyers], I'm going to put it in everyone's grocery bag.'"

Pennsylvania health authorities say more than 6,000 MMR vaccines have been administered at 212 pop-up clinics in affected communities since April. (AP: Matt Rourke)

White House clash clouds vaccine efforts

With more than 4,500 reported cases, the US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said.

Rural Pennsylvania is not the only area under strain — large outbreaks have been reported in Texas, Utah, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Florida.

In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul this month declared a disaster emergency because of rising cases in neighbouring states.

The US eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates.

But the CDC said rates have fallen recently to below the 95 per cent coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

Following Pennsylvania's first two deaths, a political clash erupted between the state's vaccine-promoting Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro and the Trump Administration's Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr — known for raising alarms about vaccines.

Can anyone Make America Healthy Again? Robert F Kennedy Jr vowed to Make America Healthy Again, but his alliance with Donald Trump has left some true believers jaded.

Mr Kennedy suggested Mr Shapiro's office may have "altogether fabricated" the deaths and accused the governor of "fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponisation of infectious disease fears for political gain."

For weeks, the CDC did not record the measles-related deaths on its public disease-tracking dashboard, saying it was seeking more information to prove their validity.

Mr Shapiro condemned Mr Kennedy for those comments, and other claims he made that the US's MMR vaccine — which protects people against measles, mumps and rubella — included traces of fetal tissue.

Josh Shapiro accuses Trump administration authorities of allowing misinformation to spread, hampering his state's efforts to fight off measles. (Reuters: Hannah Beier)

"Unfortunately at a time where I needed the top 'health expert' in the nation to responsibly work with us to deal with this outbreak, he instead chose to go down a rabbit hole of conspiracy theories and false claims," Mr Shapiro said in a post on X.

" The correlation is clear: Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others — and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases. "

Robert F Kennedy Jr has routinely questioned the efficacy and safety of medically proven vaccines. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The Pennsylvania Health Department said at least 6,500 MMR vaccines have been administered at 226 pop-up clinics in affected communities since April.

Paul Griffin, the director of infectious diseases at Mater Health Services, said that while the vaccine was "incredibly effective", Mr Kennedy's comments undermine public health efforts.

"We need the advice to come from people that have a very good understanding of what [measles] is and what we need to do to address it," he said.

Loading...

Ms Franklin said she had seen no evidence of Mr Kennedy's comments impacting how frontline CDC health staff, who were aware of the urgency of addressing the outbreak, operate.

"They are still core passionate public health professionals … They're not misleading; they're being told what they can and cannot publish [and] how they define things," she said.

She says the outbreak is now a race against time.

"It's either how many people can get vaccinated and protected, or how many people are going to get the disease," she said.

" Pennsylvania is too far into this, by the numbers only, to outrace it. Now it's, how do we stay the course with as many people as we can in the hopes of minimising the impact and deaths? "

ABC/AP

This Halloween (C8), David Morrison of Springwood can do no other: “Years ago, I started calling 31st October ‘Martin Luther Day’ honouring the momentous historical event that occurred at that date in 1517. At Halloween, I put on an academic hat and provide chocolate for our young visitors. I get repeat customers every year, and they all seem to love the little printed summary of Martin Luther’s deeds, or the chocolate, or both.”

Speaking of chocolate, Coral Button of North Epping is “relieved to learn that bad weather in the cocoa bean producing countries, Ivory Coast et al, is the cause in the astronomical rise in chocolate prices. And here I’ve been thinking it was just the usual bastardry of the supermarket cartel.”

“Following on from Meri Will (C8), it sounds like Moses may have invented the protein shake,” posits Nick Walker of Suffolk Park.

“I just purchased a packet of two tap washers,” announces Don Leayr of Albury. “Among the benefits of said replacement parts, such as diameter, copper for durability, suits hot and cold water, was the fact that they are ‘Ideal for families of all ages’. I can’t imagine the fun that all-age families would have with this item!”

For Warren Howlett of Blackheath, Friday morning’s online reportage of Australia’s defeat in South Africa and in particular “a cricket journalist’s vibrant reporting, would probably fit well into John Howard’s idea of a citizenship test for migrants: ‘But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland’s marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder … producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate … for a new Test best of 40’.
