Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. MENTAL HEALTH The Victorian Government’s $1.5 billion promise to expand emergency departments to reduce waiting times is like trying to fix a blocked sink by installing a bigger sink. It might provide temporary relief, but it doesn’t address the blockage.

After nearly 30 years researching health services, particularly in rural and regional Australia, I have seen little evidence that expanding emergency departments alone provides sustainable solutions to overcrowding. The solutions lie largely outside emergency departments.

First, we must understand who is attending, why, and where they come from. Emergency department data provides a window into unmet community healthcare needs. Whether the problem is inadequate primary care, youth mental health services or support for older people, investment should target the local circumstances driving demand.

Second, we must address the barriers preventing patients from leaving emergency departments. Too often, patients cannot move into hospital beds because other patients cannot be discharged safely into appropriate community care.

Importantly, any investment must also address geographical inequity. Rural and regional Australians have fewer alternatives to emergency departments and must receive a fair share of funding.

Professor Leigh Kinsman, Rural Health Research chair, La Trobe University Violence is never a sign of strength

Many of our leaders have said that we need to “turn the temperature down″⁣ since Bondi, and the horrendous attack on Dr Helen Haines. But they don’t say how.

Over a long medical career, I’ve seen many angry and aggressive people and I think they are all suffering with anxiety, depression or other rarer mental health disorders.

I think a lot of men, and boys particularly, think that they need to appear to be tough by exhibiting verbal aggression and physical violence. I suspect that is the message received from social media algorithms or their own families.

I believe we need to change the narrative: violence is never a sign of strength, but rather a sign of mental health weakness.

The strongest men, women, and adolescents know to ask for help when they need it. Admitting that you may need help may be the bravest thing you ever do and accepting that help makes you a stronger more resilient person.

Non-violent people are the truly strong ones. They succeed by using their kindness, thoughtfulness and fairness, to improve the lives of us all, just as Helen Haines has always done.

Dr Jo McCubbin, Sale



Problem of untreated mental illness

The horrific attack on Helen Haines has raised a host of issues, not the least of which is mental health, especially the mental health of people living in isolated regional areas. But we need to be careful not to further stigmatise Australians with mental health problems.

The issue isn’t mental illness, but untreated mental illness. It is commonly said that governments can’t afford to provide adequate services to treat those with mental illness, but the truth is we can’t afford not to.

Paul Arnott, Ringwood East Inadequate community-based support

Regardless of the factors that have contributed to the alleged attack on Helen Haines, this horrendous event has once again raised the issue of the under-resourcing of mental health services.

Many years ago, when long-term psychiatric hospitals were being closed, we were informed that adequate community-based care and support would be provided to a group of vulnerable people. It was never adequate then, and with the growing numbers of people who need support, it is very far from adequate now.

Rita Thorpe, Coburg THE FORUM Homicide patterns

The horrendous attack on Helen Haines has provoked much discussion about why such attacks are happening. Most of the focus has been on the impact of social media and violent commentary in public forums.

This distracts from the major cause in this and many other violent attacks on innocent civilians. People with severe mental health illnesses are not being managed effectively in our current health system.

Forty five people with psychotic disorders were charged with homicide from January 2024 to December 2025. Half were not under active treatment at the time (″⁣Psychiatrists wanted to understand homicide patterns. They found a deadly warning″⁣, 25/10).

Freedom of choice about treatment and freedom to wander unmonitored is resulting in a rising death toll of innocent victims. These people need close monitoring, compulsory medication and safe places to stay where they can be monitored.

Increases to mental health funding in recent years have focused on programs that cater to anxiety and depression in young people. Important as these are, there needs to be a different response to those with psychotic mental illness.

This is an urgent problem that needs a major change in how these people are treated and managed.

Katherine McGrath, Toorak Care, kindness deficit

The Age news report (25/10) on the danger signs of the increasing psychotic behaviour of so many mentally disturbed Australians is relevant to the worrying attacks on MPs. It is also important that the well-being of Australians in everyday life is given maximum protection.

This will obviously be a momentous task needing far more thought than ″⁣lowering the temperature″⁣ in our immaturely conducted political system.

The news report shines a light on a hidden world of people who will randomly take lives.

Other news reports cover the despair of those who take their own lives. On average, over 3100 males and females suicide each year in Australia.

Care and kindness could be said to have been lacking in the past but is now an overdue priority.

Des Files, Brunswick



I’m one of the lucky ones

In 1995, I ran down my street naked. This unusual behaviour was caused by a manic episode of bipolar disorder, an illness that I have had since I was 18 years old.

The crisis assessment team was called and I was taken to Larundel, a government-operated psychiatric institution, where I was sectioned and treated with anti-psychotic medication.

Larundel closed in 1999, as part of the Victorian government’s policy of ‘deinstitutionalisation’ in which mental health services were incorporated within the general health sector.

While ostensibly driven by humanitarian intentions, deinstitutionalisation was in reality driven by the neo-liberal ideology of cost-cutting rather than patient well-being. Deinstitutionalisation required adequate investment into primary health care, social supports and housing, which wasn’t forthcoming.

The policy of deinstitutionalisation thus shifted care of people with psychosis to prisons, charities and families, who are often in no position to cope with the demands of mental illness.

I am one of the lucky ones. I have stayed well since my discharge from Larundel thanks to medication and an effective ‘stay well plan’. Unfortunately, many others don’t have access to the right treatments and supports.

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha How to spend it

I am sure I am not the only person holding this opinion: at a state level and federally, conditions are chronic, with health services overwhelmed and understaffed. We have a housing crisis, a mental health crisis, our state schools are crumbling, and more and more people are struggling financially. I think of the $368 billion plus that has been allocated to AUKUS, and it is open and shut what my decision would be.

Julie Stafford, Ivanhoe East It’s you who’s changed

Based on the responses of many recent Letters correspondents, at least some of the blame for the rising hostility in the community towards politicians can be attributed to the behaviour of the politicians themselves.

Such a view presupposes that political behaviour has somehow worsened over time. However, to reflect on the words and actions of politicians over the last 30 years reveals that little has really changed. There’s still the same theatrical name-calling. The same ad-hominem attacks. I would propose that what has actually changed is not the behaviour of the politicians but the attitudes of the public in terms of what we expect, or more accurately, demand, from these elected officials.

Rather than view politicians in terms of how they can serve the community as a whole, now we tend to view them in terms of how they can serve our own specialised interests. And when these people invariably fail to meet these expectations, their high-profile, public visibility makes them the perfect focus for our anger.

Instead of asking how politicians can improve their own conduct to reduce community anger, perhaps we should be asking how we ourselves can improve and modify our expectations for what these public servants can do for us.

Justin Shaw, Ringwood East Don’t deregulate cannabis

Record numbers experiencing psychosis are being admitted to public hospitals (25/10). At the same time, Libertarian MP David Limbrick has recently espoused the legalisation of “recreational cannabis” with the addition that the state monopolises the trade to improve the budget bottom line.

The proposal is deeply flawed on a number of grounds.

Recreational usage can lead to long-term addiction and have catastrophic effects on users, their families, and society in general. The AMA has long warned against deregulating recreational cannabis. Overseas jurisdictions that have legalised cannabis are now trying to reverse these decisions due to crime and mental health issues that have subsequently arisen.

A state monopoly would inevitably attract a black market run by criminals supplying a cheaper product. Cannabis wars would join the tobacco wars.

Martin Newington, Aspendale Melbourne is what it is

Yes, the Melbourne Assembly was a talk fest (Age editorial 24/10), and I agree that independent views from those less liveable and sustainable cities were perhaps questionable, but hey, it’s part of the chip-on-the shoulder mentality we carry as a penal colony.

The combination of visions (grid layout and Collins Street grandeur), later champions such as Rob Adams (Melbourne City Council), and yes, blind market forces (someone has to take the risk), have delivered a city which oscillates between the most liveable, and one which struggles with its true identity (hence the Assembly).

There is nothing wrong with the structure of Fed Square that re-activation of its commercial offer could not fix. When implemented, it was unique in city design, and eclipsed the urban spaces of other Australian cities. But as with all things these days, let’s just start again because someone says we should.

It’s really not about sprawl vs. high rise; it already is. A Paris-height opportunity is long gone, and that’s why we like going to Paris, when it is not setting itself on fire.

At the end of the day, it is Melbourne, and if two million visit the place each year, it must be pretty good.

Marc Bartsch urban planner, Wandin



Council steal

Re ″⁣The council that stole Christmas: Permit change kills beloved neighbourhood party″⁣, 25/10.

In recent decades there has been a general decline in local councils’ comprehension of the fundamental importance of helping local communities function well, especially important during times of hardship or rapid growth.

As much as The Age featured many cute stories of neighbours supporting each other during the tough COVID times we also know there were many dark days of desperate isolation for too many people.

Street parties are difficult to start during these difficult days but are needed to foster a sense of belonging and social connection, without which we humans go barmy pretty quickly.

It’s an inept decision for any council to impose financial imposts on residents trying to foster that social connection during the annual secular season of goodwill.

Bernadette George, Mildura A little light cleaning

Ben Groundwater in ″⁣My Airbnb host said I ‘trashed’ her flat. Why? I left some crumbs″⁣ (Traveller 24/10), compared the costs of multiple rooms in a hotel to staying in a holiday let, claiming equivalence, and using this as justification for guests not doing any “heavy lifting”.

However, even if equivalent in price, we love staying in a holiday let because of the extra space and facilities.

Few hotel rooms would offer a large deck to congregate on, a big dining table for shared meals, a garden to relax or play in, a kitchen with all you need to cook in, comfortable couches and logs for the fire, a washer and dryer.

Holiday lets also allow you to feel part of a community, even for a short time, rather than being in the centre with a mass of tourists like yourself.

I think the benefits are good enough to justify a little light cleaning, taking the bins out and simply wiping the kitchen benches down.

It doesn’t have to be slave labour, just showing some care and respect for someone else’s property.

Jan Williamson, Essendon AND ANOTHER THING Elections

The cat is out of the bag (″⁣Lib candidate advises One Nation vote in upper house″⁣ 25/10). Liberal candidate Simmone Cottom was caught encouraging people to vote for One Nation in the upper house. It is time for Jess Wilson to be clear about any One Nation Liberal coalition agreement.

David Baker, Parkdale It matters little that Simmone Cottom regretted saying that vote One Nation in the upper house. The fact is that she said it, and found it quite acceptable.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick



The Greens are the only party that takes climate change seriously. Why isn’t that stated proudly on every corflute, flyer, and how-to-vote card?

Geoff Cumming, Woodend Now that Pauline Hanson has discovered satire (particularly when it comes to cartoons mocking her colleagues), I think it’s time for Pauline Pantsdown to re-release Back Door Man. It was an absolute banger.

Elizabeth Long, Fawkner Trumpworld

We know that to repeat the same behaviour and expect a different result is insanity. AUKUS is insanity. It’s time to swap out the US and welcome our Canadian friends. It’s a CAUK-er!

Lee Guion, Portarlington Donald Trump digs himself into another hole claiming release of Stephen Hubbard had nothing to do with reward. I would say purchase of Russian oil had a lot to do with it.

Dan Drummond, Leongatha Furthermore

Are Tesla drivers becoming the new Volvo drivers? Their lack of awareness is mind boggling.

Craig Tucker, Newport



I decided to organise a street party and see if we could close a road. What a nightmare of paper work and insurance. So I decided to have the party at our house. I letter boxed the invitations and asked all who attend to bring a plate and something to drink.

Christine Hammett, Richmond The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington
World.content:
Blinkers On SportRacingVictorian racing The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington Danny Russell October 25, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ladies and gentlemen of the Flemington members’ stands, start your engines. A coveted place at one of the most prestigious tables in this country’s sporting landscape is up for grabs – a seat on the Victoria Racing Club board – and the contest is shaping somewhere between a demolition derby and a boat race. The Victoria Racing Club board is set for change following this year’s Melbourne Cup week at Flemington. Getty Images Nominations to join the board opened last week, and if trackside chatter is to be believed there will be some robust jostling, and behind-the-scenes campaigning, to get to the front of the queue. At least one seat will be filled by a new face. Club chair Neil Wilson announced his resignation last month and will be stepping away from the role at the annual general meeting in December.



Related Article Victorian racing Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift But adding spice to the mix is the fact that Wilson’s anointed successor, director Vin Cox, as well as club treasurer Glenn Carmody and fellow committee member Michael Saadie are all up for re-election. That’s four seats up for grabs. This throws up some startling possibilities. If more than one nomination is ratified, and there is behind-the-scenes talk of up to five interested parties, it will lead to an election that could change the composition of a long-stable VRC board. The director with the most to lose, or gain, is Cox.



Firstly, he needs to be re-elected before accepting the chair’s role from Wilson at the coming AGM - a controversial succession plan decided by a secret ballot last month. The Age quoted an inside source two weeks ago who claimed Cox was given the nod 6-5 – in a vote involving 11 directors – over vice-chairman Michael Ramsden. VRC chairman Neil Wilson, left, at the Cox Plate with Racing Minister Anthony Carbines and Moonee Valley chairman Adam Lennen. Wayne Taylor Secondly, if Cox is re-elected, he then needs to quickly reaffirm numbers at the boardroom table to quell speculation of a coup. In theory, a 6-5 vote in favour of Cox is easily reversed with at least one director being replaced.



But there are even wider ramifications than Cox’s potential rocky ascension to the throne, including the future direction of the VRC, which governs Flemington and runs Melbourne Cup week. Wilson has long been loyal to the VRC’s history and need for independence. He has continually shut down merger talks, as racing looks for new ways to make Melbourne’s three major clubs more efficient, and recently opposed changes to government legislation because he felt it would strip autonomy from his club. Only time will tell whether a Wilson-less VRC board will offer the same resistance. Nominations close on Oaks Day. Sheza Alibi gaps the field in the Doncaster Mile in April. Getty Images





It is a question that historically would have had an answer. In the trouble-free years before New South Wales’ self-serving creation of a $10 million pop-up race – the Golden Eagle – the country’s best four-year-olds ran in the country’s best weight-for-age race. Anamoe won at four in 2022, Winx in 2015, So You Think in 2010, Sunline in 1999 and Saintly in 1996. Not any more. History is being rewritten and Australia’s racing pattern (fixture) is in disarray. As the Cox Plate shows, we no longer have the best horses competing against each other in our grand final races. Instead, we have split the pack and become racing’s version of LIV Golf.



Sheza Alibi, trained by Peter Moody and Katherine Coleman, is a case in point. Her connections have bypassed the $6 million Cox Plate, and a clash with Cosmic Crusader, to chase greater riches. She will start odds-on favourite in Saturday’s $10 million 1500m Golden Eagle at Randwick – a race restricted to four-year-olds that was surprisingly awarded group 1 status by the Asian Racing Federation this year. Or, it should have been surprising had Racing Australia not been so impotent while the landscape was being reshaped – we say for the worse – by NSW in recent years. Cosmic Crusader wins the first Cox Plate run at Flemington. Getty Images Cosmic question No,2



The second question to emerge from Saturday’s Cox Plate meeting is also unanswerable, but equally worthy of debate. Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington Would Cosmic Crusader have beaten the same Cox Plate field on the tight-turning circuit of Moonee Valley instead of the long, wide straight of Flemington? No one will ever know, of course, but will next year be any different? Because if a rebuilt Moonee Valley is to reclaim its standing as the race’s spiritual home in 2027, as most believe it should, it needs to have its house on order to become a worthy host.



That’s no easy feat when a crowd of 30,000 punters are clicking through your turnstiles, and you don’t have a grandstand. In comparison, Flemington has three. The pressure is on the Valley hierarchy to get it right. Their promise of hosting members and dignitaries in elaborate Birdcage-like structures that line a new, longer straight is one thing, but catering for the rank-and-file punters, the backbone of the sport, is another. They will need somewhere to sit, like a mega temporary grandstand. Without it, Cosmic Crusader could be defending his crown back at Flemington. Heaven forbid.



Punters cheer home a winner at Flemington on Cox Plate day. Justin McManus Odds against punters. Again Flicking through the World Pool tote dividends continues to make for depressing reading. Those who placed a TAB tote bet on Flemington races on Saturday were once again sold short. Cox Plate winner Cosmic Crusader paid $9.50 TAB fixed odds and just $8.20 on the TAB’s World Pool tote; Moonee Valley Gold Cup winner Juja Kibo paid $8 fixed compared to $6.35 World Pool; and Crystal Mile winner Surfin Bird paid $2.80 fixed and $2.35 world pool.



That’s a significant difference, and all nine races at Flemington had a negative price discrepancy. The problem, as this column has raised before, is the takeout. Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing Racing’s big gambling problem, and why it’s hurting punters The World Pool tote, which merges with the Australian tote for big race days, continually operates above 120 per cent. This means for every $120 bet, it keeps $20, meaning a poorer return for punters.



When the Hong Kong-based World Pool merges with our tote for Australian races, it creates a bigger cash pool and a bigger turnover by attracting international punters, which then increases returns to the industry and rebates for professional syndicates, but leaves the grassroots punter worse off. Leek jumps for joy Despite its many detractors, the shaky future of jumps racing must be given new consideration following the profound impact it has had on Melbourne’s spring. The jumps jockeys have reigned supreme, and there has not been a hurdle in sight. Consider these achievements.



Caulfield Cup winner Kingswood is trained by former jumps jockey Gavin Bedggood and ridden by part-time jumps jockey John Allen. Trainer Andrea Leek poses with the trophy. Getty Images Cox Plate winner Cosmic Crusader is trained by former jumps jockey Andrea Leek, the first female trainer to win the race in 32 years. And that is before we even start on Ciaron Maher – the one-time farm boy from Warrnambool who cut his teeth by tackling the jumps. As career moves go, Maher’s decision to become a trainer has proven a masterstroke.



Not only is he neck-and-neck with Chris Waller as the country’s leading stable, he ran the trifecta in Saturday’s Moonee Valley Gold Cup with rising stayers Juja Kibo, Kings Valley and Mr Monaco. Maher could have an unprecedented nine starters in next week’s Melbourne Cup, including Point Of Law, Saint George, Middle Earth, Shockletz, Zahrann and Royal Supremacy. “A lot of jump jockeys are hands-on, where maybe the flat jockeys aren’t as hands on,” Leek said of her ability to train a horse. “The flat jockeys are sort of on and off (the horse), where we do the background work as well. “Everyone loves to get their horses fit, but we just do it that little bit differently. And I think having a jumping background, like Ciaron Maher is showing that and Gavin Bedggood, it really helps you know the differences in your horse.”



How does the racing industry place a price on that? Bad day for Ballarat Interesting to see the jockey fraternity vote with their feet on Friday, forcing the abandonment of the Ballarat meeting because of concerns over the surface. The riders first raised the issue with trackside stewards after a runner slipped near the 1000m mark during the second race. Quick repairs were ordered, but they did not do the trick.



The jockeys voted 14 to three to call the meeting off. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain October 25, 2026 — 7:33pm

October 25, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Early in my career, I learned that when things weren’t going my way, bemoaning my luck got me nowhere. I had to change my approach. The same lesson applies to Test cricket today, and the first change we need is how we read the evidence. This follows the second Test between South Africa and Australia at St George’s Park in Gqeberha, where rain did not save Australia from a humbling defeat. It was grim stuff for Pat Cummins and Australian in Gqeberha. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Worryingly, the familiar chorus has started: sparse crowds, the critics say, prove the longest format is dying. I don’t think they prove that. But the game’s administrators should feel distinctly uncomfortable because the real threats to Test cricket are less visible than empty seats, and they can fix them.



What the empty seats tell us A thin weekday crowd is a scheduling result, not a verdict on the format. This series sits in a shoulder window: after the peak of the rugby and soccer seasons, before the domestic summer begins, and across school and university exams. Asking families, students and young professionals to give up several consecutive weekdays at that time of year is asking the impossible, and that is before we count the cost of tickets, transport and food for households under real financial pressure. Fans hardly flocked to the first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban. AP Put the same contest in the middle of summer and the picture changes. Boxing Day, New Year’s Test and Ashes Tests still fill grounds. Demand for the best Test cricket, played when people can attend, has not disappeared. So the gate is a poor test of the format’s health. Better questions are:



Do the best players choose to play Tests?

Do broadcasters and streamers pay properly for them?

Can smaller nations afford to host and tour? On those questions, the news is more worrying. The real threat is collision T20 is not Test cricket’s executioner, but I won’t pretend it is a harmless neighbour. When the SA20 overlapped with South Africa’s tour of New Zealand in early 2025, the Proteas had to send a squad featuring seven uncapped players, led by a captain (Neil Brand) who had never played a Test match. With stars such as Virat Kohli, the Indian Premier League has gone from strength to strength. AP



That is the ultimate indignity when franchise leagues and international cricket overlap in the same weeks and one pays far better. I don’t blame players for choosing to secure their families’ futures. The failure belongs entirely to administrators who built (and tolerate) a calendar that forces that choice. Right now, Test cricket is thriving—but only if you belong to the “Big Three” of India, Australia and England, who pass a profitable revenue bucket back and forth in five-match marquee series. For the rest of the world, hosting a Test match is a fast way to go broke. Yet T20 also pays the bills Both things are true. The IPL, the BBL and the SA20 generate the broadcast and sponsorship revenue the sport relies on. Boards outside the wealthiest nations cannot fund Test hosting and touring from Test revenue alone. The answer is neither to fight T20 nor to hope it will be generous. Make co-existence a condition of doing business.



The one-way street Any serious settlement has to begin with the IPL because it is the world’s biggest league yet, paradoxically, the least reciprocal. It already occupies more than two months of the calendar, and it is reportedly set to expand further in 2028. For nearly two decades, it has drawn on the best players from every other country. Yet Indian players under BCCI contracts are barred from every other franchise league. I understand the case for that: workload and protecting the IPL brand. But a league cannot systematically strip the world’s asset pool while keeping its own off-limits and then expect everyone else to bend their Test calendars to fit its ever-expanding footprint. That cost falls on the other boards and on the players, who are left to choose between country and contract. Leagues need sanction from national boards and the ICC, and their players need release from their home boards. That gives the game leverage, and it should use it. I would write four conditions into every single league sanction:



A Test levy and guaranteed match fees: A fixed share of domestic league revenue must go into a global Test fund. This fund should serve two purposes: subsidising hosting costs for smaller nations so they can afford three-Test series instead of hollow two-Test jokes, and establishing a competitive global minimum Test match fee. If a young West Indian, Kiwi or South African cricketer knows that pulling on the creams guarantees a premium, reliable income, the temptation to abandon a Test tour for a short-term franchise contract evaporates.

A fixed share of domestic league revenue must go into a global Test fund. This fund should serve two purposes: subsidising hosting costs for smaller nations so they can afford three-Test series instead of hollow two-Test jokes, and establishing a competitive global minimum Test match fee. If a young West Indian, Kiwi or South African cricketer knows that pulling on the creams guarantees a premium, reliable income, the temptation to abandon a Test tour for a short-term franchise contract evaporates. Protected windows: The Future Tours Programme must ring-fence each host nation’s peak summer for Test cricket. The domestic leagues must schedule around international windows, not the other way around. Series should also be long enough to matter. A two-Test series is a cipher. Barely a story, forget an event.

The Future Tours Programme must ring-fence each host nation’s peak summer for Test cricket. The domestic leagues must schedule around international windows, not the other way around. Series should also be long enough to matter. A two-Test series is a cipher. Barely a story, forget an event. Full-strength squads: No sanctioned franchise window can overlap an ICC-scheduled Test series. Selectors must be free to pick their absolute best XI without forcing a player into an agonising contract dispute between country and club.

No sanctioned franchise window can overlap an ICC-scheduled Test series. Selectors must be free to pick their absolute best XI without forcing a player into an agonising contract dispute between country and club. Absolute reciprocity: Any league that draws on international players must accept the same rules as everyone else. The IPL has completed 19 seasons, drawing on global talent throughout its existence while barring Indian players under BCCI contract from participating in overseas leagues. Player release must work both ways. A league that wants the world’s best should be willing to share its own. English and Australian administrators, in particular, need to be tougher. We must stop being pusillanimous collaborators and sycophants when the future of Test cricket is at stake. Australia is one country where Test cricket isn’t a financial impost. Getty Images Scarce, not exclusive Some argue Test cricket should become a luxury product, like the majors in tennis and golf. I take one lesson from that: fewer, better-placed Tests, each treated as an event. I reject the price tag. The majors are annual showpieces. Tests are how most of us first fell in love with the game. In a country where cost-of-living pressure is real, pricing families out would be self-defeating. Make Tests premium in the calendar and accessible at the gate: cheap weekday tickets for schools and students, affordable family days and broadcasts that tell the contest’s story and the score.





That is a management failure, and leadership, not appeasement, must fix it. I learned long ago that bemoaning your luck changes nothing. The custodians of the game should stop wringing their hands over empty seats in Gqeberha and write rules that let the longest format thrive alongside the shortest. After all, it demands more of a player than any other form of the game: skill, patience and character – just ask Kohli or Starc. And that is worth protecting. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Why some educators think Labor’s $14 billion kinder promise won’t work
World.content:
NationalVictoriaChildcare Why some educators think Labor’s $14 billion kinder promise won’t work Nicole Precel October 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A network of sessional early educators says more consultation and funding is needed, warning the minimum 15 hours of free kindergarten rolling out across the state won’t suit everybody. The Metropolitan Melbourne Community Kinder Network (MMCKN), which represents at least 25 sessional community kindergartens, said that while Victoria’s lauded $14 billion rollout – which will offer parents 15 hours of free kinder for three-year-olds, and between 15 and 30 hours for four-year-olds by 2029 – would be instrumental in children’s early learning, the one-size-fits-all model is impractical for some communities and schools. Sophia and her son Alessio, 4, from the Chelsea kindergarten. Sophia sees benefits in having shorter days at kinder. Joe Armao A sessional community kindergarten is a part-time, teacher-led program for three and four-year-olds with fixed, short sessions during school terms. They are often not-for-profit and led by a community board, and may offer as little as five hours a week per program. University of Melbourne’s Educational and Developmental Gains in Early Childhood (EDGE) Study, released in September, found children who receive two years of funded kindergarten were five months ahead in language development and two to three months ahead in memory and problem-solving skills by the time they started school compared with those who had a single year. The greatest benefits were among those who attended 15 hours a week.



Amy Merrick, president of the Chelsea Heights Kindergarten committee, said she started the MMCKN because she felt sessional kindergartens weren’t being represented. Related Article Education Childcare upheaval stokes family pressure, but experts say there’s a solution “The community kinders that are around are very individual and different in terms of some of them are only one room, so it’s just literally not possible,” she said. “We’re not going to get any more community kinders … We’ve got to keep the ones we have going because they are going to be shut down with these reforms.” Merrick said some one-room services offering both three and four-year-old kinder would also require facility upgrades to offer more hours. Sessional kinders would also need funding for a full-time administration or operations position for continuity, governance and compliance support.



In metropolitan Melbourne, kindergartens can scale up to a maximum of 30 hours of free kindergarten a week by 2036. There is concern among some educators, however, that this could become a minimum requirement. “I don’t think 30 hours a week is education. I think it’s care, but just sort of tarring every service with the same brush is just not appropriate, not sustainable,” she said, adding, “It turns qualified teachers into carers.” Sophia and Alessio. Joe Armao Sophia Nardone said spending time and having adventures with her four-year-old son, Alessio, before he started school was an important reason she chose sessional kindergarten. The mother-of-three currently works part-time and sees the benefits of having shorter days at kindergarten.



“It can be pretty taxing for the kids,” she said. For families with a parent or carer working part-time or not in paid work, Nardone said fewer hours gave them the opportunity to have a free day together with their children and enjoy extracurricular activities. “When they are at school, you don’t get that opportunity,” she said. While attending kindergarten is not mandatory in Victoria, services failing to offer the minimum hours risk losing funding. Cara Armstrong Kindergarten director and educational leader Ella Slattery said many services were already struggling to offer the 15 hours, and would struggle with further increases without having to reduce enrolments, combine ages or make changes to class sizes.



“It’s a fantastic idea, everyone is in support of it, but the implementation has to recognise the practical realities of delivering the reform,” she said. Related Article Jobs Spoonfuls of sugar: $280,000 nannies for the ultra-rich are in high demand Slattery said her Hawthorn East kindergarten runs the three-year-old program over two days, at 13.5 hours a week, and the four-year-old program over three days at 15 hours. They also offer an extended hours program that families can pay for. Next year, they will increase their three-year-old hours to 15 per week. “We were talking about family choice. It really is eliminating that choice. Some families that opt in to that community approach because they opt into that shorter approach,” she said.



She said there were about 13 sessional kindergartens in her council area of Boroondara that were single room. “In terms of socio-economic scaling, there are communities that are really in need of new hours, but I don’t foresee how single-room not-for-profits will be able to sustainably move forward without some serious overhaul or serious funding from the government.” Slattery said if her kindergarten scales up to 30 hours, they would have to look at splitting educators’ shifts. “If we are expecting families to feel as though they have to access 30 hours of four-year-old kinder, that’s eliminating that choice for families,” she said. “There are families who say three, four or five day programs are too much for their children,” she said.



“Eliminating the option for a two-day program is not in favour of their child.” A Department of Education spokesperson said they valued the important role community kindergartens play in delivering quality services for their community, and worked closely with providers and local governments to understand demand and support access. Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘Can’t keep kids safe’: Inherent risks in market-driven childcare The 2026-27 state budget provides $548.3 million for early childhood education programs, infrastructure, and regulation. Jane Austen, executive director of The Front Project, an independent early childhood organisation, said the EDGE study was a “promising sign that participation in high quality early childhood education and care can reduce inequality, giving every child a fairer start to school”.



“The evidence shows that children did best when they turned up consistently, for the funded hours, in a program run by experienced teachers, backed by a needs-based funding system,” she said. Early Childhood Australia chief executive officer Samantha Page agreed, and said for more vulnerable children that extended to 30 hours. “I think we can’t necessarily have unlimited flexibility. We need to have some guardrails around what public investment is used for. That includes quality regulation as well as minimum hours,” Page said. Even with a parent at home, Page said, children learn in group settings and with families having fewer children, the opportunity to learn empathy, communication, co-operation and self-regulation alongside other children was important. “You don’t want your children to miss out on that,” she said.

World.title: How K-pop, Robbie Williams and Foo Fighters ruined the NRL’s Samoan and Tongan plans
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How K-pop, Robbie Williams and Foo Fighters ruined the NRL’s Samoan and Tongan plans Christian Nicolussi October 25, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of the biggest K-pop bands in the world, along with Robbie Williams and Foo Fighters, forced the NRL to abandon plans of shifting Sunday night’s World Cup epic between Samoa and Tonga to Accor Stadium where a crowd of 60,000 was expected. The two popular Pacific league powerhouses will play at a sold-out CommBank Stadium. Concert season at Accor Stadium, including Robbie Williams and The Foo Fighters, meant the NRL could not move Samoa and Tonga to the bigger venue. Michael Howard/SMH Capacity at the Parramatta venue is 30,000 – but Cup organisers were confident they could have doubled that number by moving to nearby Sydney Olympic Park. The NRL had the option to shift the game to Allianz Stadium, where an extra 10,000 fans could have been accommodated, but did not want the Samoan and Tongan fan bases to have to leave their western Sydney base.



ARL Commission executive chairman Peter V’landys confirmed there had been discussions about moving the one-off game to Accor Stadium, where the Samoans and Tongans would have been joined by neutral fans eager to enjoy the singing and respective pre-game Siva Tau and Sipi Tau performances. Samoa fans cheered their nation against France earlier this month. Getty Images But V’landys and Cup organisers were told Accor Stadium had begun “concert season”, with K-pop sensation BigBang set to perform this weekend. The three-piece boy band are expected to draw more than 70,000 fans, and there was no way the playing surface could have been prepared in time for a rugby league game just 24 hours later. Once BigBang perform, the ground staff will then be busy preparing for UK sensation Robbie Williams and US rockers Foo Fighters, who both perform in the coming weeks. The fact V’landys was prepared to entertain playing a Cup game at Sydney’s biggest venue, which did not feature host nation Australia, is proof of how much hype there is in the star-studded Pasifika teams.



Tickets being priced as low as $19, and families of five paying just $90, is a key reason decent crowds have supported the Cup. “We were keen to go to Accor, but we quickly found out it was not available because of concert season,” V’landys said on Sunday. “I was also mindful of inconveniencing fans who had already bought tickets to CommBank. “I’m confident we would have got around 60,000 fans at Accor had we gone there. “It just goes to show you how popular future Pacific Championships will be. We’ve established the international game again. That’s the beauty in all this.”



Tonga have beaten England and Lebanon, while Samoa thumped France 78-4, then Papua New Guinea 64-6, on the weekend. Tonga are already assured a semi-final berth, while if Samoa triumph on Sunday night, at 8pm – or 10pm for those tuning in on the islands – they will also qualify. Even if Samoa lose, they would still require England to beat Papua New Guinea by a big scoreline. Woolf confirmed halfback Isaiya Katoa would return after he missed the Lebanon clash to help nurse an ankle injury. As for the interest in the Samoan showdown, Woolf said: “I think back to that first night in Penrith when the NRL put on the first mid-season Pacific Test, the crowd was about 10,000, they were certainly not any less enthusiastic, it was a great crowd; it’s definitely grown since then.



“You only have to look at the 45,000 people we had last year at Suncorp Stadium … we’re now in a World Cup, which is a bigger event, and both teams are travelling really well at the moment. “It’s a huge occasion and I’ve got no doubts it would have brought in a really big crowd if it was able to [relocate to Accor Stadium].”

World.title: Large scrub fire threatens telecommunications towers in Southland
World.content:
Strong gusts of up to 100 km/h are expected to keep a scrub fire in Southland burning overnight into Monday.

Six helicopters have been combating the blaze in the Centre Hill area with monsoon buckets since shortly before 4pm Sunday in an effort to protect two nearby telecommunications towers.

In a social media post, Southland Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said there was no risk to people or homes and flames were likely be visible in northern parts of the region, particularly the Mossburn area.

"Pilots have done an excellent job in challenging conditions to protect the telecommunications infrastructure on Centre Hill.

"We expect a change in the weather overnight will bring more favorable conditions for containing the fire tomorrow, with rain forecast."

The crews had been stood down for the night and FENZ would re-assess the situation at first light.

World.title: Five people rescued after boat sinks near Auckland
World.content:
Five people have been rescued after a boat sank near Ponui Island east of Auckland on Sunday.

Police were alerted to a boat sinking east of the island in the Hauraki Gulf about 5.30pm.

An eagle helicopter located the group in the water before signalling a nearby boat to come and assist.

World.title: Hundreds gather to demand end to bottom trawling in Hauraki Gulf
World.content:
Hundreds of people gathered on Waiheke Island today to call for an end to bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf.

The conservation organisation Forest & Bird said the fishing method was contributing to the gulf's ecological decline.

More than 80 percent of people living around the gulf want it to be banned, according to national conservation advocate Bianca Ranson. She said the event, which was held on Oneroa Beach, reflected their frustration at the continued decline of the gulf.

"Bottom trawling is widely recognised as one of the most damaging fishing methods, dragging heavy nets across the seabed and destroying vital habitats that are slow to recover," she said.

"There is no future for sustainable fisheries without ending destructive fishing practices and transitioning to methods that can sustain our ocean's life, long term".

Hundreds of people gathered on Waiheke Island for the Ban Bottom Trawling event. Supplied

Ranson said it had become an election issue, with Forest & Bird calling on all politicians to listen to the vast majority of New Zealanders who want a living, thriving gulf.

"Overfishing, sedimentation, pollution, and climate impacts, combined with bottom trawling, are pushing species towards local extinction. We need strong action to restore the gulf."

Ranson hoped that the turnout had shown political parties how much support there was for stronger protection of the ocean.

"The people are on the side, and we just need the political will to make this a reality.

"The Hauraki Gulf is a microcosm for the rest of Aotearoa. If we can get this issue right in the gulf, and that's commitment to ending trawling, that starts with a phase-out and moving away from bottom-impact fishing, which destroys the benthic habitat and seafloor, and moving towards new technology, which is already available, and making sure that industry is brought along so that we can end trawling, but also have sustainable fisheries."

The event also included the unveiling of New Zealand's largest-ever Ban Bottom Trawling banner, measuring 15 by nine metres.

"It took many, many of us to unfurl it. And then we walked it out into the ocean, where we were surrounded by people on waka ama and kayaks who were also holding Ban Bottom Trawling signs. And then all of the boats in the bay behind us. So, yeah, just a really powerful kind of visual statement of the message from the people, not only here on Waiheke, but people who have sailed over here to be here with us today and people who have come over on the ferry.

"So the message could never be clearer with this banner, but also the voice of over 80 percent of people who live around the Gulf who want to see this destructive fishing method banned. So we hope that all politicians can see that loud and clear with the photos that we'll be sending through to you. And, yeah, let's get on with it.

"Our future generations are depending on this, and also the well-being of our ocean, with all of the pressures that it's facing at the moment."

World.title: Police issue amber alert for missing 11-year-old in Hawera
World.content:
Police have issued an amber alert, after an 11-year-old went missing in Hawera on Sunday afternoon.

D'Havland Phoebe Jade Laupama left her home on Koromiko Avenue in Hawera about 4pm on Sunday.

The young Māori girl was last seen wearing a charcoal-coloured short sleeve shirt with a guitar logo on the front and leopard print inside. She was also wearing light grey trackpants and black sneakers.

She has neurological disabilities including restless leg syndrome, which causes extreme fatigue in her legs.

Police say she is likely to lie down somewhere and fall asleep or hide.

World.title: Child critically injured in assault at central Auckland park
World.content:
A child is critically injured after being assaulted by a man at a central Auckland park on Sunday afternoon.

Hato Hone St John said two people were taken to hospital after the incident in Myers Park at 4.45pm.

One has been taken to Starship Children's Hospital with critical injuries.

An area around the children's playground was cordoned off by multiple police officers following the incident.

Police said a 20-year-old man was taken into custody over the assault.

Police erect a cordon around the playground in Myers Park in central Auckland after a serious assault. RNZ/Pretoria Gordon

Inspector Jim Wilson said the man was not known to the victim.

Wilson said both the victim and offender required medical treatment.

"This was an isolated incident, and there is no ongoing risk to the public."

St John sent two ambulances to the scene, as well as a rapid response vehicle and an operations manager.

In a social media post, Auckland Central MP Chlöe Swarbrick said she had been in touch with local police about the serious assault.

World.title: Kiwis crush Aitu to cap dominant day for NZ at Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
After a brief scare, the Kiwis have crushed the Cook Islands 82-16 to pick up their first win of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

The tone was set early with a fierce pair of challenges, but it was the Kiwis firing the first shots with two quick tries.

But the Aitu shocked the Kiwis with three of their own to take a lead and briefly send tremors through the Kiwis coaching box.

Esom Ioka's quickfire hat-trick gave the Cook Islands a surprise lead, but it wouldn't last long as the Kiwis clicked into gear and blew the Aitu away.

It took just three minutes for the Kiwis to get on the board, a crisp series of passes through the backs sending Jamayne Isaako away for the opener.

Just moments later, the Kiwis were in again through their other winger Ronaldo Mulitalo off a great ball by Casey McLean and it looked like things could get ugly quick.

But with the Kiwis looking set for a third, the Aitu, struck against the run of play, Ioka plucking a pass out of the air and streaking 90 metres away to send Rarotonga into raptures.

The Cook Islands went back to back in quick succession, Brad Takairangi putting it on an absolute platter with a cross kick to Ioka for his second.

Another stunning moment followed for Ioka, this time a 40 metre intercept to put his side in front.

With a sense of panic and urgency creeping in, the Kiwis reclaimed the lead through Isaako, converting his own try from out wide with a superb in-swinging strike.

Relief replaced the unease as Scott Sorensen ran onto a prefect Jahrome Hughes ball to restore an eight point advantage.

Tanner Stowers-Smith scored a double on debut for the Kiwis. Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz

More breathing space came after Tanner Stowers-Smith, on debut in his home city, rumbled his way over for the Kiwi's fifth.

With halftime approaching, the Kiwis struck again through McLean to take them to 36-16 at the break.

Usually known for his slick footwork, fullback Keano Kini instead took the direct route as he bust his way through the Cook Islands line to kick off the Kiwis scoring in the second.

Taking the ball flat footed 10 out from the line, Tanner-Smith displayed his dogged determination to bulldoze his way over for a double on debut.

Kodi Nikorima brought up the half century, before McLean showed why he is regarded as one of the best centres in the game right now, effortlessly weaving past two defender for his second.

With the result assured the Kiwis brought the razzle dazzle, Isaako completing his hat-trick after some enterprising attack.

Isaako capped off his fruitful afternoon with a third try to go with 13 conversions before replacement Te Maire Martin dotted down in the act of copping a high shot.

Driving in one final nail to the brave Cooks Island side, Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad ended the Kiwi's try scoring spree in the 79th.

A brave effort by the Aitu, but the Kiwis just a class above in Christchurch.

The double header with the Kiwi Ferns saw the two teams rack up 174 points and 32 tries in a dominant day for New Zealand rugby league.

World.title: Silver Ferns secure Constellation Cup after final quarter fightback over Australia
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have won the Constellation Cup for just the fourth time after beating Australia 52-49 in Sydney, and are now just a win away from the number one world ranking.

The Diamonds dominated the first three quarters, putting New Zealand under real pressure for the first time in the series, but the Silver Ferns pulled out a massive fourth quarter effort.

The Silver Ferns entered the Australian leg of the Constellation Cup leading 2-0 after claiming the first test 56-50 in Auckland, and the second test 62-50 in Christchurch.

Despite that, their recent record suggested it would not be easy beating the Diamonds in their own backyard, having only won two of the past 12 Constellation Cup matches on Australian soil, dating back to 2018.

New Zealand started with the exact same seven that lined up in the gold medal match at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, which the Silver Ferns won.

Despite an impressive game from Peta Toeava in test two, Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua left the specialist wing attack out of the Sydney clash, to bring Kimiora Poi back in, who was just as effective in the opening test.

Within the first minute Kate Moloney had to leave the court with a finger issue, which meant Australian captain Liz Watson had to step into centre again, and Sophie Dwyer came on at goal attack.

The Diamonds came out of the blocks strong to win the first quarter 15-11, for the first time in the series.

Grace Nweke of the Silver Ferns and Courtney Bruce tussle for the ball. John Davidson / www.photosport.nz

The Diamonds upped their defensive efforts and rare misses came early from Georgia Heffernan and Grace Nweke, and the Silver Ferns trailed by as many as six.

Te Paea Selby-Rickit replaced Heffernan near the end of the first quarter and the Silver Ferns inched their way back in the second quarter.

The quick movement between the Australian shooting pairing of Sophie Garbin and Sophie Dwyer, caught the Silver Ferns defenders off guard at times.

Selby-Rickit nailed a long-range shot on the half-time whistle to level it 26-all.

Poi came on at wing attack at half-time, which pushed Maddy Gordon, back to centre. Kate Heffernan went into wing defence halfway through the third spell, after starting at centre.

Australia started reasserting themselves again in the third quarter and rookie goalkeeper Jessie Grenvold continued to make life difficult for Nweke, who had been almost untouchable in the first two tests.

But the Silver Ferns reined them in to trail by just two heading into the final quarter.

The in-circle defensive pairing of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger didn't get the amount ball they did in the first two tests but starting having more impact as the game wore on.

Incredibly it took the Australian Diamonds six minutes to score in the final quarter but when they did, they started building momentum and took a two-goal lead with six minutes left.

Kelly Jackson (middle) fights for the ball. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Gordon, who brought up her 50th test cap, had to go to the bench not long after a heavy fall, which led to another New Zealand midcourt shuffle.

Nweke finished the game with 41 goals, and Garbin with 37.

The Diamonds, who barely won any ball on defence in the first two tests, finished with 10 gains, the same number as New Zealand.

After a whopping 85 penalties committed by Australia in the second test, the Diamonds finished with a more respectable 54 to the Silver Ferns 45.

The Silver Ferns can clean-sweep the series for the first time ever if they win in Melbourne on Wednesday.

They are also expected to dethrone Australia from their number one world ranking for the first time since 2013, with a win.

World.title: Diamonds great says coach 'safe for now' after Constellation Cup loss
World.content:
Australia has lost game three of the Constellation Cup 52-49 to New Zealand to hand the trophy back to the Silver Ferns in Sydney.

After leading 41-39 heading into the final quarter of a gripping contest, the Ferns rattled off seven straight goals after three-quarter-time to establish a five-goal lead.

The Diamonds went on their own run to square the ledger at 47-47 as the Test headed into its final five minutes, but costly turnovers and penalties by Australia allowed New Zealand to win the final quarter 13-8.

After falling behind 3-0 in the four-game series, the Diamonds will be playing for pride at Melbourne's John Cain Arena on Wednesday.

The Diamonds are also a chance of losing their world number one netball ranking to New Zealand after the Ferns won gold at the Commonwealth Games in August, while Australia claimed bronze.

Head coach Stacey Marinkovich now has just a 50 per cent series winning record in the Constellation Cup.

Sophie Garbin shot 47/63 in game three. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Before she took charge in 2020, the Silver Ferns had claimed the trophy once in 10 series. In the six series since, the Kiwis have claimed it three times.

Marinkovich is contracted through to the end of 2027. This is the last time her team will be together before next August for the Netball World Cup in Sydney.

The result looks ominous for the Diamonds' chances.

However, former Diamond Bianca Chatfield believes Marinkovich's role is safe, alluding to the challenges of the unlimited import rule in Australia's Super Netball league.

Loading Instagram content

"I think she's safe for now … unlike male sports there's not the money just to pay out coaches and get rid of them, and you do that in the heat of the moment," Chatfield told ABC's Offsiders.

"She deserves a chance to go through to the World Cup … She's facing different pressures to what other Australian coaches have in the past."

New Zealand head coach Noeline Taurua said the victory was a massive result for the Ferns after a challenging 12 months.

Taurua was suspended from coaching her team this time last year by Netball New Zealand and missed tours of Australia, England and Scotland before being reinstated.

Jessie Grenvold nabbed the Diamonds' only two intercepts of the game. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The New Zealand Premiership has also been in fast decline due to poor broadcast deals and management by the national body. Most Silver Ferns jumped ship and signed with Australian teams to ensure they could earn a full-time wage.

"This is our opportunity to write the next chapter of our book," Taurua said.

"Commonwealth Games gold was obviously the start of that and now backing that up with the Constellation Cup.

"Whether the world number one [is next] or not, we're within cooee of Australia and getting closer, knowing that we're building towards the World Cup.

"We're just riding the wave and enjoying the moment."

Look back at all the action in our live blog of game three.

World.title: Antonelli on pole as he eyes record-setting world F1 title
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has blasted to pole position for the United States Grand Prix on a weekend when he could claim his place as Formula One's youngest world champion.

The 20-year-old Italian turned the tables on Ferrari as the Scuderia, who had led the way for all three practice sessions, again fell flat when it came to the crunch on Sunday AEST.

Antonelli pipped Max Verstappen, winner of the past two races, to first spot on the grid by 0.179 seconds, with Isack Hadjar third in the second Red Bull.

Australia's Oscar Piastri and his McLaren teammate Lando Norris managed seventh and eighth respectively.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli can secure his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship with victory at the United States Grand Prix.

For Antonelli to claim the crown in the Lone Star State is a tall order; he would need to win Monday's race (AEST) and hope that George Russell finishes lower than ninth and Lewis Hamilton lower than fifth.

But he did the first part of his job in supreme fashion, delivering a stellar lap to blow away his rivals and underline why he is the champion-in-waiting.

Russell struggled and will line up sixth, while Charles Leclerc and Hamilton managed only fourth and fifth as Ferrari's pace disappeared when it mattered.

The race represents 20-year-old Antonelli's first shot at clinching the crown, but with a 102-point lead and only a maximum 150 left up for grabs, it appears merely a matter of when the Italian becomes champion.

Ferrari have not been on pole since Leclerc in Hungary in 2025, while Hamilton's wait for top spot in qualifying extends to that same race two years earlier, 1,190 days ago.

Hamilton is a five-time winner around the Circuit of the Americas and an upgraded Ferrari appeared to have put him in the mix to end his long wait for a pole position.

Ferrari president John Elkann was watching on from the garage, with pressure on the team to finally deliver in qualifying after a difficult run of races and increased speculation over the future of team principal Fred Vasseur.

This weekend could be bigger than Texas for Kimi Antonelli if he can clinch the world title. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

But Hamilton, 41, whose sole Ferrari win came in Barcelona in June, and Leclerc were again unable to pull it out of the bag.

Meanwhile, both Williams were among the stragglers knocked out in Q1 as their miserable season continued, with Alex Albon fuming "what a s***show".

Norris topped Q1 but McLaren chief executive Zak Brown told Sky Sports that Ferrari were "in a league of their own".

Leclerc hit back to lead Q2 but Antonelli and Russell had also come to the fore to suggest the battle for pole would be a tight one.

Antonelli soared to the top of the charts after the first run in Q3 and the Italian's challengers fell by the wayside.

AAP/PA

World.title: Volkanovski underscores UFC greatness with record ninth title win
World.content:
Australian Alexander Volkanovski has underlined his greatness with a stunning second-round TKO of previously unbeaten Russian Movsar Evloev in a record-extending ninth UFC featherweight title fight win.

Headlining the UFC 333 card in Abu Dhabi, Volkanovski was considered the underdog in some quarters, but the 38-year-old proved too good for his younger opponent, the number one contender.

He got Evloev down to the ground with some precise, hurtful punching and landed some brutal ground and pound to force referee Marc Goddard to stop the fight with six seconds of the second round remaining.

Volkanovski, from Windang on the NSW South Coast, landed with some good kicks and punches in the first couple of minutes.

Elite wrestler Evloev (20-1) took Volkanovski down three times in the last couple of minutes of the first round, but the Australian quickly bounced back to his feet each time.

The champion had a cut on his face in the second round, but in the last few seconds he bloodied Evloev's face, as his crisp, accurate punches found their mark.

It was his first stoppage win in six fights stretching back to 2023.

"It feels good to get a finish," said Volkanovski, who improved his MMA record to 29-4.

"I actually promised the missus, it was our wedding anniversary on Wednesday, I promised her a quick one (win) so she wasn't stressing on the sidelines."

It was a second successful defence of his second reign and Volkanovski indicated he wasn't ready to retire yet.

"I said if I didn't take too much damage, we'll probably keep going, so maybe we keep going," Volkanovski said.

Movsar Evloev had no answer to Volkanovski's attacks. (Getty Images: Zuffa LLC/Jeff Bottari)

Evloev landed some good strikes but couldn't maintain the pressure on the wily champion.

"He's like good wine; older, stronger, better, he's truly a legend," Evloev said.

In a thrilling co-main event, Russia's Petr Yan retained the bantamweight world title with a unanimous points decision over Georgia's Merab Dvalishvili, beating him for the second time in three fights.

In the prelims, Australians recorded a win and two losses against Russian opponents.

Volkanovski's stablemate, bantamweight Colby Thicknesse, scored a third straight win and a big upset with a split-decision victory over previously unbeaten Asaf Chopurov.

Middleweight Cam Rowston's run of seven straight wins ended with a first-round guillotine-choke-submission loss to 12th-ranked Abus Magomedov of Russia, and middleweight Jacob Malkoun's three-fight win streak was snapped by a unanimous-points loss to Abubakar Vagaev.

AAP

World.title: Sam Konstas cracks yet another century
World.content:
Sam Konstas has struck his second century in the space of a week to send national selectors yet another reminder he is ready for a Test recall.

Just days after posting scores of 71 and 151 not out in New South Wales' Sheffield Shield draw with Western Australia, Konstas cracked 149 off 131 balls on Saturday to lead his side to a 78-run victory over the Warriors in the One-Day Cup at the WACA Ground.

NSW posted 8-371 on the back of the monster knock from Konstas combined with handy contributions from Josh Philippe (51), Jack Edwards (45) and Lachlan Shaw (44).

In reply, Sam Whiteman plundered 116 from 113 balls to give WA a faint hope of chasing down the mammoth victory target.

But with spinner Ashton Agar (43) and Ashton Turner (41) the only other WA batters to pass 40, the home side fell well short of what was required, bowled out for 293 in 46.3 overs.

The result left WA with a 0-3 record, all but ending its title hopes just three games into the season.

NSW moved into second spot with a 3-1 record.

But it remains to be seen how much longer its will have Konstas in its Shield and one-day ranks given his rich vein of form.

The 21-year-old burst onto the international scene in December 2024 when he made a memorable Boxing Day Test debut against India, scoring 60 in his maiden knock.

Konstas failed to pass 25 in his next nine Test innings, with his most recent appearance in the baggy green coming in July last year against the West Indies.

Awkward questions linger after Australian loss It is a case of the same old problems leading to the same old questions as Australia squanders a series lead, setting up a grandstand finale in South Africa next week.

The talented opener has worked hard on his game over the past 15 months, and it was on full display on Saturday as he cracked 15 fours and four sixes in a masterful display.

And with Australia still crying out for an opener to make his mark ahead of a busy Test schedule, it seems just a matter of time before Konstas is donning the baggy green again.

Whiteman was brave in WA's run chase, but he simply lacked the support needed.

Jack Nisbet snared 3-47 for NSW, including the key scalp of Whiteman in the 46th over, while Bryce Jackson chipped in with 2-58.

One rare highlight for WA came earlier in the day when Agar leapt high into the air to pull off a stunning one-handed catch at backward point to remove Ben Dwarshuis for 20.

AAP

World.title: Valkyries shut down Borlase's Dream to square WNBA Finals
World.content:
Gabby Williams scored 17 points on Saturday (Sunday AEST) to help the visiting Golden State Valkyries post a 67-62 victory over the Atlanta Dream and even the WNBA Finals at two games apiece.

Tiffany Hayes and Veronica Burton each scored 13 points for Golden State, which won despite making just four of its 25 3-point attempts. Cecilia Zandalasini had 10 points and Kiah Stokes pulled down 16 rebounds for the Valkyries, who return home for Game 5 ‌on Monday.

WNBA Finals Golden State Valkyries vs Atlanta Dream Game 1: Golden State wins 68-64

Game 2: Atlanta wins 79-65

Game 3: Atlanta wins 97-71

Game 4: Golden State wins 67-62

Game 5: Tuesday Oct 27, 11am AEDT

Game 6: Friday Oct 30, 11am AEDT

Game 7 (if required): Sunday Nov 1, 11am AEDT Series tied 2-2

Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19 points while Jordin Canada and Australia's Izzy Borlase chipped in 10 apiece. Angel Reese (eight points) and Allisha Gray (five points) shot a combined 3-for-19 from the field.

Atlanta sliced its 16-point ‌half-time deficit to 46-40 when Borlase made a 3-pointer with 4:27 left in the third ⁠quarter.

Hayes scored four straight points to extend the visitors' lead to ‌11 before two Canada free throws narrowed the margin to 54-45 after ‌the third.

Consecutive baskets by Howard and Borlase pulled the Dream to within six, but Burton responded with a 3-pointer to make it 64-55 at the 4:23 mark of the fourth.

From there, two Howard foul shots and Reese's lay-up cut the deficit to five with 1:36 left. Atlanta had ‌chances to inch closer, but Gray and Borlase missed 3-point attempts before Burton hit a runner on the other end to give the Valkyries a 66-59 advantage with 34.6 ⁠seconds remaining.

Howard converted a 3-point play, but Burton ‌split a pair of free ‌throws to give Golden State a 67-62 lead.

Howard and Canada missed 3-point tries on the next possession ‌to seal the Valkyries' massive win.

Australia's Izzy Borlase had 10 points for Atlanta in Game 4. (Getty Images: Colin Hubbard)

Borlase made a driving lay-up to give the Dream a 7-2 edge just over four minutes in. Golden State scored the next ‌12 points and grabbed a 14-7 ⁠lead on Zandalasini's 3-pointer with 2:09 left in the opening quarter.

Aussie Borlase having dream WNBA Finals Australian basketballer Izzy Borlase is one step closer to a WNBA title as her Atlanta Dream side beats Golden State Valkyries to lead 2-1 in the best-of-seven WNBA Finals.

The Valkyries held a 16-11 advantage entering the second quarter despite missing nine of their 10 3-point attempts.

After Reese's basket pulled the Dream within four, Golden State rattled off a 9-0 run ⁠to extend the lead to 33-20 on Burton's bank with 2:46 left in the half.

Kayla Thornton drilled a 3-pointer to push ‌the lead to ‌16. Williams closed the first half with a lay-up to put the Valkyries up 42-26.

Golden State attempted 40 first-half field goals to Atlanta's 19 as the Valkyries forced the Dream into 14 turnovers in the opening 20 minutes.

Reuters

World.title: Infantino claims support of 'vast majority' of soccer ahead of FIFA elections
World.content:
FIFA's embattled president Gianni Infantino says he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of soccer despite his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Infantino is seeking re-election next year in the face of attempts to force him to stand down following the divisive plan.

He infuriated soccer leaders in Europe, North America and Asia over the proposal to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary.

But in an interview released on Saturday with the BBC at the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, Infantino brushed off calls for him to step down.

"Well, you know, I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world," he said.

"I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA there can be different views, different points of view.

"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority."

Challengers to Infantino for the FIFA presidency have until November 18 to nominate. (Getty Images: Robert Hradil)

Infantino is standing for a final term in office in March. The deadline for opposition candidates is November 18.

His latest comments came after he apologised to FIFA's ruling council last week for "mistakes" in his secretive investment plan for the World Cup.

Despite his apology, European delegates said they left the meeting disappointed about what they saw as a lack of clarity.

On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation endorsed Infantino for another term in an apparent turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised him for a breach of trust.

AP

World.title: Usman Khawaja reveals illness he kept secret his entire Test cricket career
World.content:
Usman Khawaja was just 22 and revelling in being part of the New South Wales cricket team when he was diagnosed with a potentially crippling disease that he would keep secret his whole career.

Only now, having retired from international cricket after Australia's Ashes win in January, is Usman revealing that he lived with rheumatoid arthritis while playing 88 Tests for Australia.

Usman Khawaja in hospital with his mother Fozia Khawaja by his side when he was first diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

Even good friends such as his childhood cricket buddy David Warner and Test teammate Michael Hussey were unaware of the diagnosis that Usman thought would end his cricket dream before it really took off.

In fact, Usman says that when doctors initially battled to diagnose the cause of debilitating pain in his left knee, he feared he had a terminal illness.

"I genuinely thought I was going to die," Usman, 39, tells Australian Story. "I went from this athlete who was playing professional cricket to not being able to walk 10 metres to the bathroom."

Left out of the Australian team eight times, Usman Kahwaja was one of the most dropped players in Australian Test cricket history. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

It's another remarkable story to add to Usman's eventful career that saw him score 6,229 Test runs, including 16 centuries, as well as two one-day international tons for Australia.

He was the first Pakistani-born person to play Test cricket for Australia, and the first Muslim.

He was one of the most dropped players in Australian Test history, losing his place in the team eight times but always finding his way back, most notably in Sydney in 2022 when he scored twin centuries at the age of 35.

His experience of racial and religious vilification would lead him to speak out about discrimination, in cricket and more broadly, contributing to a greater cultural awareness within the Australian squad.

Says Todd Greenberg, Cricket Australia's CEO: "He's broken the mould in so many different ways. He'll leave the culture of Australian cricket in far better shape than what he found it."

Loading...

Now, Usman is keen to give hope to those living with an autoimmune disease, detailing his health battle in his soon-to-be-released autobiography, Sabr.

"If a person can play at the top level … as a professional cricketer with rheumatoid arthritis, then I think a lot of other people can achieve a lot, too," he says.

Given the cricket rumour mill, Usman admits it's surprising the secret he's kept since the 2009 off-season never got out. He told medical and coaching staff and cricket administrators but not a single player because he did not want special treatment, or for the disease to be used against him.

Usman manages his condition with regular injections of a drug which he calls a "godsend" and credits with getting him back to the crease about six months later.

"Without that drug," Usman says, "I would never have played cricket ever again or even lived a normal life again."

By January 2011, he had become the 419th Test player to be handed a baggy green, and the tumultuous and influential international career of Usman Khawaja was on its way.

Usman Khawaja had an emotion-filled final Test match at the Sydney Cricket Ground on January 8, 2026. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar/Eurasia Sport Images)

Breaking the 'typical' cricket player mould

As a cricket-mad immigrant boy growing up in Sydney, Usman found it hard to relate to the Australian cricket team.

Its beer-drinking and larrikin culture felt foreign to the way he was being brought up by his parents, Tariq and Fozia Khawaja, who had immigrated from Pakistan when Usman was four.

A young Usman Khawaja (left) plays cricket in the park. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

He wasn't keen on the sledging, either, having copped racial abuse on the sporting field — mostly from parents.

"As great cricketers as they were," Usman says of the Australian team of the early 1990s, "it kind of felt like that bogan vibe, that same vibe [from those] parents."

Usman Khawaja, pictured with his father Tariq Khawaja, was cricket-obsessed from a young age. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

That vibe changed for Usman in 1999, when players he could relate to — Adam Gilchrist, a left-handed batsman like him, and fast bowler Brett Lee — arrived on the scene.

"They're the ones that dragged me over to the Australian cricket team … I started supporting Australia way more and then eventually after that it was just Australia, Australia, Australia."

Usman and Tariq Khawaja hanging out at the cricket fields. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

But despite his obvious skills, the Pakistani/Indian community told him he would never make the Australian team.

"They're like, 'Oh yeah, you're good but you'll never play for Australia because they don't pick our kind, they don't pick brown people to play for Australia, there's too much racism. You'll never get there.'"

But then, Ricky Ponting broke his finger in December 2010.

And Usman got his big break.

"I was a Pakistani boy debuting for the Australian cricket team," Usman says. "It's a big deal."

The crowd applauded as the debutante made his way onto the Sydney Cricket Ground in January 2011. Usman was nervous, hoping not to get a duck. His father Tariq recalls sitting in the SCG stands with Fozia, praying.

Usman Khawaja chats with Ricky Ponting at an Australia training session just before his debut. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)
