Tech.title: 12 Absolutely Banging Proper Watches Under $400
Tech.content:
The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.

Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.

To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.

Caravelle Sea Hunter

Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.

Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm

Courtesy of Orient Bambino

Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.

Brew Metric Lite Retro

This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.

Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound

Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.

Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”

Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.

Baltic HMS

Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).

Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.

Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”

Bulova A-11 Hack Watch

As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”

Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”

Citizen Tsuyosa

Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).

Tech.title: Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
Tech.content:
I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated October 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations after testing all the new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops, as well as the new Googlebooks. The Surface Laptop Ultra has replaced the Dell XPS 14, and I've added back the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 at its discounted price.

The Laptops I Recommend Most

When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

While the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.)

Speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

If you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well-worth it.

Cheap Laptops That Are Actually Good

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU at under $700. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I'll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Photograph: Luke Larsen Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Apple MacBook Neo $697 Amazon $699 Apple

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work at a computer all day.

Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that's why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I've tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they're so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, as the chassis is nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks, as you can't download applications from the web and are forced to rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it comes in the cheapest at $899. Even that isn't exactly what I'd call a “budget laptop,” though.

Photograph: Luke Larsen Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 $749 $599 (20% off) Best Buy

That's why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it's on sale for under $700 (which is frequent). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn't recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook because if you're paying more, you should consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook's limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you're paying for.

Truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I'd recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

Powerful Laptops for Those Who Need It

While the laptops above are great for most people, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, though, and the competition from the Windows side is finally heating up.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Photograph: Luke Larsen Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra $2,600 Amazon $2,600 Microsoft

I'm talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia's new RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia's involvement, these aren't gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they're designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That's not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing the on-device AI performance. So, if you've been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra's Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

Perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you plan to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

That’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it's still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d currently buy, given where prices are.

There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s new Panther Lake chips and should have vastly improved battery life.

Other Good Laptops I’ve Tested

If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

Tech.title: iPhone Duo Owners: Your Apps Will Look Better Soon
Tech.content:
For some lucky Apple superfans, today is the day they get to unbox their iPhone Duo. (Others may have to wait until January.) But after formally transferring all their software, they’ll discover a troubling truth: Some of their favorite apps look bad, with awkwardly unused space.

Yet the message from CNET phone reviewers over the decades is reassuring. If precedent is anything to go by, updates will be coming to adjust apps to the iPhone Duo’s novel screen ratios, from the squat and wide front screen to the 4:3 inner display. Don’t worry — your apps will get better (and some are already tuned to the device’s dimensions).

That may be little comfort for Duo owners looking forlornly at Android foldables, which have had the better part of a decade on the market for app makers to adjust to the new formats. Despite having a similar passport-sized format to Apple’s foldable, most apps are sized correctly for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8.

But that wasn’t the case with the first Samsung Galaxy Fold, which launched in early 2019, as CNET Editor at Large Andy Lanxon recalls.

“I had exactly the same experience when I used the first Samsung Galaxy Fold on the day it came out, with many apps appearing to be oddly squashed into that larger inner display,” Lanxon said. “Over time, both Android and foldable makers like Samsung and Google developed better software to accommodate foldables, and I’m confident that Apple won’t take long to patch up any shortcomings in this area.”

Indeed, it’s easy to forget that as the world’s first mainstream foldable, the original Galaxy Fold launched with plenty of display, hinge and other hardware problems that were ironed out over the years. Apple’s first foldable benefits from that refinement, launching with a minimal crease, a smooth and seemingly durable hinge, internal software suited to a folding screen (with FOMO-inspiring animations), IP68 dust- and water-resistance and other qualities that ease use.

The Duo also benefits from being a single design, as opposed to the various screen sizes and formats across all the Android foldables. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, for instance, both have 6.5-inch outer screens and 8-inch inner screens, but the former is slightly wider yet shorter than the latter.



The iPhone Duo’s inner and outer screens have the same ratio. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

But it’s the Duo’s specific design that might also accelerate app adjustment, Lanxon notes: The outer display has the same aspect ratio as the larger inner display, something Apple highlighted during its Sept. 9 presentation launching the device. So developers only need to design one app size for the Duo that will work perfectly well on both displays.

Compare that to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which pairs a tall and narrow 21:9 cover screen with an almost square 10:9 inner screen.

That’s somewhat reassuring, but what iPhone Duo owners likely want to know is: When will my apps get updated? To predict that, we look to the past — both the development of other foldables and the radical changes in Apple’s own iPhone line.

The iPhone X, revealed on stage in October 2017, shifted to an all-glass front panel and the notorious notch at the top, requiring apps to adjust. Apple / Screenshot by Sarah Tew

Remembering when apps had to adapt to new screens

Given how long smartphones have had all-glass front panels, it’s understandable that it takes time to adapt apps to foldable displays. But it’s easy to forget that app makers had to go through the same process before when phones finally ditched physical buttons below screens for the all-glass front to begin with.

“I remember when the iPhone X came out, and apps that hadn’t been optimized had black bars above and below,” said CNET Editor at Large Scott Stein, who reviewed the device back in 2017. “It meant all apps didn’t initially make the most of the new phone’s size.”

The Duo will have the same growing pains until more apps get optimized, Stein added — it takes time, and it’s part of what it means to be a hardware early adopter.

The original Samsung Galaxy Fold, launched in Feb. 2019. Sarah Tew/CNET

It’s important to remember how complex it is to make software for a foldable, as explained by Jessica Dolcourt, CNET Group and CNET Labs vice president of content operations and commerce. When you open and close a foldable device, you’re asking your app to perform acrobatics, instantly leaping between internal and external displays while simultaneously expanding or contracting the view window and rearranging all the pixels.

Dolcourt spent over a decade reviewing phones for CNET, including the original Samsung Galaxy Fold in 2019, where she got her first taste of apps rendering badly.

“Native apps could be slow to load, but brought the vision of a foldable future to life. Third-party apps — which were most of them — struggled to catch up quickly and smoothly to the demands of a folding screen,” Dolcourt said. “At the outset, some were barely usable.”

Nowadays, most apps are designed for Android foldables, in part thanks to years of Google software updates specifically addressing flexible displays. The Duo will have to play catch-up.

But as Lanxon pointed out, Apple has deep relationships with developers of its apps, which sometimes launch on iOS first before heading to the Google Play Store. Apple will surely be working closely with its software partners to ensure they’re using the Duo’s proportions to the best advantage, Lanxon said.

When your apps, like Instagram, will be updated to fit the Duo’s screens is hard to gauge (especially given it took 15 years to get an iPad-native Instagram app), but developers have many more advantages than they did when adapting to the first Android foldables’ displays. Over time — and hopefully soon — the Duo will be even better to use as apps catch up with it.

Tech.title: Man Destroys $2,000 iPhone Duo With Dirt, Fire, Knives and Medieval Chainmail
Tech.content:
It might seem obvious, but try not to sit on your iPhone Duo when you leave it open.

That lesson comes a day after Apple’s foldable iPhone hit stores with lines of people queued up to buy the new device. Tech reviewer Zach Nelson dropped an iPhone Duo video on his YouTube channel, JerryRigEverything, testing the scratch resistance and bendability of the new $2,000 phone.

Let’s just say that Nelson’s measured, soothing voice didn’t keep me calm as he meticulously destroyed the Duo.

More from CNET

He subjected it to numerous scratch tests on both its cover and inner screens. Nelson praised Apple for the cover screen’s Ceramic Shield 2 glass and noted that the inner screen, even with its nano-texture finish, scratches as easily as the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s nonmatte folding display.

But why stop there?

Nelson used medieval chainmail (no proof it was actually from the Middle Ages), dirt, dust and pebbles to test the Duo further. Surprisingly, the new phone handled the chainmail easily. Nelson partly credits that to the Duo’s matte finish on the inner screen, which seems to hide imperfections.

He then opened the Duo’s inner screen and tried to bend it backward a few times. As you might expect, the frame flexed, which led to cracks showing up on the main 7.6-inch screen. So if you set your Duo down with its main screen open on a chair or couch, just don’t sit on it.

In a review by CNET senior technology reporter Abrar Al-Heeti, Al-Heeti recommends protecting the Duo, saying, “You should probably still get a case and AppleCare, or be prepared to pay a pretty penny for repairs.”

You can watch Nelson’s video to see the entire nearly 15-minute video. Warning: the dust and dirt portion against the Duo’s hinge is psychologically difficult to witness (because of all the dust and dirt). Also, if you’re wondering more about the iPhone Duo’s durability, CNET has designed and constructed a custom machine called the Fold-a-Phone that is currently hard at work testing how many times Apple’s foldable can be open and closed.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Just Passed 20,000 in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
Tech.content:
Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched Friday and was met with long lines and product sellouts. We braved three hours at the Apple Store on Friday to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

Now the big question? How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 1:30 p.m. ET on Saturday, we’ve just passed 20,000 folds.

The goal is simple. On Friday afternoon, my team and I loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube on Monday from 1-5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and ask questions about our iPhone Duo testing process.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: Apple’s iPod Turns 25: The Song Catalog That Rode Wit You
Tech.content:
In 2001, some of the top songs included Fallin’ by Alicia Keys, Ms. Jackson by Outkast and Nelly’s Ride Wit Me. When people wanted to listen to those songs but weren’t near a car stereo or their home audio equipment, most carried music with them on skip-prone portable CD players, boomboxes or maybe even a homemade mix cassette.

Sure, some early adopters were already carrying a small collection of songs on a portable MP3 player (MP3s: the new-new thing!) like the Diamond Rio or Creative’s Nomad Jukebox. But these weren’t common, and you didn’t see them that often. There was no ubiquitous sign yet that the times were changing musically in a digital direction.

Enter Apple with its original iPod, a small hard drive encased in smooth white plastic that could stash between 1,000 and 2,000 songs, a sum that seemed godly at the time.

More from CNET

Who would ever need to listen to 1,000 songs (or have access to that many) at their fingertips? What mortal would dare?

The iPod, which was announced on Oct. 23, 2001, and released on Nov. 10, 2001, had a starting price of $400. It heralded the smartphone era before smartphones were a thing, making portable electronics more tactile, user-friendly and information-forward. The white earbuds that were bundled with the device were the beacon of that era. Before long, it seemed everyone had white cables coming out of their ears.

For the 25th anniversary of Apple’s game-changing music player, the device’s creators are getting nostalgic about its silver anniversary. On Apple Music’s website, you can find at its 404 Not Found page a playful mockup of the OG iPod with its pleasing-to-use scroll wheel and a selection of songs you might have had in your iPod at some time or another.

Apple Music’s website has an Easter egg: a first-generation iPod that works and can play music in your browser. Apple

CNET writers and editors had a good time playing around with the fully functional iPod online, sharing favorite hits from its music library and enjoying some nostalgia ASMR.

We also looked back at CNET’s earlier write-ups, including one from CNET’s former Editor-in-Chief Connie Guglielmo, explaining what it was like to watch Steve Jobs introduce the iPod. There’s also a great 2021 piece by CNET’s Scott Stein on the iPod’s evolution, and a commentary by CNET’s Ty Pendlebury on how the iPod captured and held the throne for so long, surviving music streaming and rival players.



As Tony Fadell looks back, collectors and new fans are still listening

If the iPod can be primarily credited to one person — leading a team of many — it’s widely acknowledged to be Tony Fadell, who came to Apple as a contractor and went on to head one of its most successful product divisions. These days, Fadell is thinking a lot about the future of AI assistant devices, but he took time on his LinkedIn to acknowledge the iPod anniversary this week.

“We took it from approval to shipping in less than eight months,” he wrote. “There wasn’t time for endless refinements. We had to make decisions, trust our experience and stay focused on one clear promise: 1,000 songs in your pocket.”

While Fadell says that the iPod took a few generations to really take off and eventually come in iterations like the Nano and the Touch, some music fans who still love the original iPod design have been using the device for decades. If you have any hard drive-based gadget that lasts that long, count yourself lucky.

In addition to those old enough to remember what a Hoobastank is, iPods are also getting popular again with younger generations on a nostalgia kick, many of whom would rather carry around a separate physical device for their music than stream their Spotify accounts on their phone for the millionth time. Axios reports that iPods and MP3s are back in a big way in a trend called “friction-maxxing.” You don’t have to use that term to indulge, we promise.

Old iPods, new life

Getting into the hobby isn’t cheap: Working iPod models can cost several hundred dollars on eBay. And one that’s never been opened? Try $25,000 to $60,000.

A cheaper route may be to keep the familiar outside trappings but replace the guts with a new motherboard. A group called Crowd Supply promises in a YouTube video a new way to bring nonworking iPods back to life. It hasn’t launched yet, but you can keep an eye on the project at Crowd Supply’s website. Other tinkerers have had years and years to work up hundreds of iPod hacks; you can find many of them on Hackaday.

Alternatively, it may be the function that a modern MP3 enthusiast seeks, not necessarily the Apple branding or hardware. Other companies, such as Fosi Audio, have their own takes on the modern music player, like the $80 DAP Neo. CNET has a list of the best MP3 players of 2026, with devices like the Shanling M0s and the Android-based HiBy R4 coming out on top.

Lastly, if you want to relive the iPod glory days, you don’t necessarily need new (or old) hardware at all; your phone can do it with iOS apps such as RetroPod, My Classic – Retro Console or, if you’re feeling saucy on Android, ClassiPod.

Tech.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends Next Week. Here’s When the Clocks Go Back
Tech.content:
Daylight saving time ends next weekend, with the clocks officially changing at 2 a.m. on Sunday. While it’ll still be light enough for trick-or-treating on Halloween, the time change will hit the day after, when most of the US adjusts back one hour.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March.

More from CNET

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time Sunday, Nov. 1. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates.

Daylight saving time vs. standard time

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located. Time.gov/Screenshot by CNET

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.



Sleep experts seek year-round standard time

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Will we ditch these time changes for good?

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

"You're in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally." Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation

Adjust your body clock to daylight saving time

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

Tech.title: My iPhone Wouldn’t Charge but My Simple Trick Fixed It Easily
Tech.content:
If you’ve had your phone for some time, a blocked charging port might well be a problem. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

A common fault with your iPhone or Android phone is that it might not start charging when you plug the power cable into the USB-C port. From damaged plugs or power cables to broken pins in the port, there are a number of things that could be causing it and not all of them are easy to diagnose. Some of them are easy to troubleshoot — try a different plug or cable and see if that fixes the issue. Others may be more difficult to resolve.

A very common reason for faulty charging is that your phone’s charging port is clogged with fluff, dirt and other debris from inside your pocket, preventing your cable from connecting properly.

This can easily happen with any charging port, whether that’s Lightning on the iPhone 14 Pro or older iPhones, or USB-C on the more recent iPhone 18 Pro lineup and Android phones such as the Google Pixel 11 Pro or Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.

More from CNET

However, this is one of the simplest and cheapest charging problems to fix. Here’s how you can do it at home.

Why is my charging port blocked?

There are no covers on your phone’s charging port, meaning it’s exposed to every bit of dust, dirt and debris it encounters. Every time you slide your phone into your pocket, your phone will be susceptible to pocket fluff, and if, like me, you’ve got pockets filled with detritus from accidentally washing your jeans with old receipts in the pockets, then that’s asking for trouble. And that’s to say nothing of the cookie crumbs. Do not ask me why I have cookie crumbs in my pockets.

Day by day, this won’t be much of a problem, but those tiny bits of dust and fluff will build up inside your charging port over the months or years you have your phone, compacting and building up each time you plug in your charging cable until it forms a solid barrier that stops your charger from going all the way in and allowing it to connect and charge.

A wooden cocktail stick is a great tool for the job as the wood won’t damage the internal parts. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

If you’ve had your phone for more than a few months and you’re gradually finding the charger becoming less and less stable (particularly if you have to wiggle it around to get it to begin charging or if the cable won’t go in all the way) then it’s highly likely that dirt in your port is the culprit.

How to clean out your phone’s charging port

Unclogging your phone’s port is simple. You’ll need a cocktail stick, toothpick or other thin item that you can poke into the port to scrape out the grime. Wood or plastic is better, as it’s less likely to scrape against anything inside and potentially cause harm. I’ve done this using a metal SIM removal tool, a sewing needle and the pin on the back of an earring, and while it worked well, it’s not always the safest option for your phone.

Insert your tool of choice into the charging port until it won’t go further and gently start scraping away. With an older iPhone’s Lightning port you can scrape back and forth, but with USB-C you’ll need to scrape around the charging connector, which sits in the middle of the port.

Get it in there. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Eventually, you’ll start to work the compacted debris loose and then remove it from the port. It’s a satisfying process, and you might be surprised at how much stuff actually comes out. Gently work on the sides of the port, too, but be careful not to scrape hard against any of the metal charging connectors.

Soon, you’ll have pretty much all of it out. It’s difficult to check for sure if you’ve gotten rid of it all, as it’s tricky to see inside the port, even if you have a good light handy. But once you’ve got a good amount of debris out, you can try your charging cable again.

It’s satisfying to remove debris from your phone’s charging port. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Hopefully, it’ll plug in more securely and begin charging. If not, keep trying to extract more dirt and then test the charger again. If that still doesn’t solve the issue, it’s time to consider other solutions like a new cable or charger.

Tech.title: America, You Can’t Get This Powerhouse Phone. It’s a Shame
Tech.content:
If the only two names that pop into your head when you think about the best phones on the market are Apple and Samsung, frankly, you’re thinking too small.

Chinese phone-makers aren’t just making phones that rival those from Apple and Samsung; in some respects, they’re surpassing the iPhones and Galaxys — in batteries and fast charging, and especially when it comes to cameras.

On Wednesday, Oppo launched its latest photography-focused high-end phones, the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro, on the sun-bleached Spanish island of Mallorca. A finca covered in bougainvillea and surrounded by gnarled olive groves and roving wild goats might at first glance seem like an offbeat choice for a Chinese tech giant to stage a global launch event, but the decision is far from random. Spain is Oppo’s biggest European market, and it’s only getting bigger.

More from CNET

It’s a story we’re seeing repeat itself around the world. According to researchers Counterpoint and Omdia, Oppo was the fourth-largest phone-maker globally by shipments in the first half of this year. Already well established in China, the company is now seeing growth across the globe, and in Europe in particular.

It’s an impressive feat given that growing a smartphone business is harder than it’s ever been. It’s no secret that RAMageddon, the ongoing memory shortage, is pushing up phone prices and causing a massive drop in shipments.

Phone-makers might be putting on a brave face as they release new devices to the world, but behind the scenes they’re scrambling to draw up new strategies that will hopefully see them through in both the short and long term.

Growing sales of flagship and premium phones will be key to their survival, said Runar Bjorhovde, principal analyst at market research firm Omdia, during a briefing at the Oppo event. Compared with the budget and midrange segments, the high-end segment is relatively resilient.

You might think that means more exciting (if expensive) phones everywhere – witness the launch of Apple’s folding iPhone Duo, which starts at $1,999 – particularly in wealthy countries such as the US. But that’s not exactly the case.

Bad news for US phone buyers

When it comes to premium phone markets, none is larger or more profitable than the US. And yet Oppo and other Chinese smartphone-makers are steering well clear.

There are several reasons for this. Firstly, they don’t have Apple’s and Samsung’s long-standing carrier relationships that would facilitate their phones being presented as solid options to buyers. Together with the geopolitical roadblocks affecting Chinese tech companies, this makes the US simply too tricky and precarious right now to make that investment worthwhile.

“The barriers to enter make it almost impossible to go in and actually scale there unless you have lots of money to invest,” said Bjorhovde. Instead, the money they do have to invest is being poured into Europe. (Oppo said it will increase its investment in its European business by 30% over the next three years.)

This is bad news for Americans, who simply don’t and won’t be able to benefit from the full array of choices on offer to people in Europe and beyond, including the Find X10 Pro. In CNET’s review of the device, Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon described it as “a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title,” praising its cameras as the best on the market alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Xiaomi’s Leitzphone.

Oppo has nailed its camera system. Katie Collins/CNET

Of these three, only one is on sale in the US, but Europeans can take their pick.

“It definitely feels like US consumers are missing out by not having the latest and greatest smartphones from the leading Chinese manufacturers,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS. It’s especially noticeable when it comes to some of the cutting-edge foldable phones from companies like Honor, Oppo and Xiaomi, he added.

Breaking the duopoly

The Apple-Samsung duopoly that dominates the American market also exists in Europe, albeit to a lesser extent. But Elvis Zhou, Oppo’s European CEO, wants to see it broken completely.

“People deserve more exciting options,” he said in a briefing with journalists. When it comes to picking a premium phone, he thinks people should have a choice between three or four brands, rather than just two.

This reflects the more diverse array of successful phone brands in China, he added. In his company’s home country, there are only a few percentage points difference between Huawei, Apple, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi and Honor.

Xiaomi, Honor and Vivo are all now vying with Oppo for a slice of the European pie. One sign of intensifying competition is the shrinking gap between products being launched in China and Europe, which has historically spanned months. Zhou says that’s changing — the Find X10 series launched in China only a month ago.

When it comes to choosing a premium phone, Omdia’s research shows that buyers place more importance on camera quality than do people buying budget and midrange devices, but also “softer” values, including preferred brand, perceived status and aesthetics. Oppo has nailed its camera system, but the same isn’t necessarily true of the latter values.

Zhou isn’t worried, though. Oppo is squarely targeting Gen Z with the Find X10 series (Omdia research shows that people under 35 are most likely to buy premium phones), and he thinks they’re savvy enough to look beyond ads to first-person recommendations and chatbots that will provide specs-based advice to discern which product will offer the best value.

Oppo is targeting savvy young Europeans with the Find X10 Pro. Katie Collins/CNET

“We want to focus on the young generation because … they know how to make the decision very logically – they will not make the decision only following the brand name,” he said. “Young people really care about the product itself, and they can get all the information they want from AI and from social media. It’s a good opportunity for me.”

The company has already found success using this strategy for the Find X9 series, which saw its share of the premium European market quadruple between 2025 and 2026, according to Omdia.

But while Oppo might have made headway in Europe, it might be difficult to sustain this effort over time, said Wood — especially given that all of its Chinese rivals are adopting a very similar strategy at the very same moment.

Competition might be fierce, but Oppo is ready to play the long game. “We’re very patient,” Zhou said with a wry smile. “We’re not rushing here in Europe.”

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Oppo. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Review: A Dolphin Dive in the Right Direction
Tech.content:
The Call of Duty series needed a win this year. Last year’s Black Ops 7 was a clown car of bad decisions, featuring an always-online campaign mode with ridiculous zombie bosses and open-world Warzone. Worse still, the multiplayer mode (the only reason that many people buy the game) was entirely forgettable. Developer Treyarch was tasked with putting out Call of Duty games two years in a row — that crunch was a recipe for disaster.

On the other hand, that means Modern Warfare developer Infinity Ward had plenty of time to cook up the fourth and final entry in its own series. Thankfully, the studio used that extra runway to its advantage. Modern Warfare 4 may not have returned Call of Duty to the highest highs of the original trilogy that ended in 2009 (and which Infinity Ward rebooted over the last decade), but this is a leap in the right direction for a series that has become increasingly sloppy in recent years.

Players will find plenty of cinematic action in the single-player campaign, and the multiplayer mode has slowed down just a touch, which I think the game largely benefits from.

More from CNET

More importantly, Modern Warfare Zombies has been completely dropped in favor of DMZ, an accessible player-versus-player-versus-AI extraction shooter experience. The experimental swing feels like a lifeline for the series, and DMZ is the standout mode for the game.

The campaign identity crisis is (mostly) resolved

Modern Warfare 4 is a tighter game than Infinity Ward’s previous project, and it’s leagues better than Black Ops 7.

At the same time, it has a complicated campaign to crack open (and not because the plot is hard to follow). Players flit back and forth between the perspective of Captain John Price, longtime protagonist of the series, and South Korean soldier Park Hyun-Jun, a newcomer whose squad is fighting for his homeland. A battle rages against a united coalition of Russian and North Korean ultranationalists, who are blazing a path into other territories.

Russian bad actors have been the primary antagonists of every Modern Warfare game, and it’s actually really cool to see South Korea’s positive representation in a Call of Duty title. But the propaganda is laid on thick — Russia and North Korea are presented as sneering colonialist powers, while the Western world’s soldiers are a shield on every front.

Americans spearhead the fight against imperialism; forget about the Strait of Hormuz and gun down these unambiguously bad guys. The whole plot hinges on a somehow less-subtle Red Dawn-type of scenario, and the gung-ho military politics are absolutely nauseating this time around. Sure, Price is framed as morally gray — he’s working with a cartel to achieve his goals, and there’s boring melodrama where he comes to blows with his former allies — but he’s vindicated in the end because he is the type of Call of Duty leader that prevents global conflict.

Captain Price’s arc feels like a vague indictment of Western military overreach, but it ultimately amounts to nothing. Activision-Blizzard

Modern Warfare 4 also features an obligatory shockingly graphic mission, which is something of a tradition for the series. In it, you play as a North Korean soldier rounding up and executing the occupants of a small village for hiding a defector. During my playthrough, I earned an achievement for successfully interrogating a villager without beating them down. The whole affair is gratuitous, gross and gamified in a problematic way, exacerbated by the bizarre decision to continue making this kind of mission a mainstay in each game.

It’s a shame that the story is so trite and icky because the tentpole action is really good. The best mission takes place early in the campaign, when Price infiltrates a New York nightclub to search for a Russian oligarch. Bright lights and pulsing music contrast with brutal fistfights and gunplay — it’s like playing through the climax of a John Wick film. From there, the highlights keep coming: There’s a fight in a train yard where the cover moves on rails, a chase scene across Mumbai rooftops, a high-stakes nighttime penthouse raid and a full-out assault on a dictator’s compound.

But the worst mission in the campaign repeats the mistakes of other modern Call of Duty games. When the player’s squad initially counterattacks North Korean airspace, they’re shot down and have to survive behind enemy lines with scavenged gear. It’s an interesting setup that is completely wasted on a Warzone-like, open-world mission with a checklist of more than 50 optional collectibles to seek out.

The few puzzles that exist are mind-numbingly easy — despite my best efforts, I checked out after completing around half of the activities. I focused on the main objective to end the mission as soon as possible, which is just about the worst feeling to have while playing a game.

I don’t know if there’s an edict from up top to put one of these open-world missions in each new game to funnel players into Warzone, but they don’t work at all and are the worst part of any campaign.

Still, the folks that play the campaign will probably have a good time here. Players can explore tons of cool locales, and the enemies are surprisingly difficult this time around. Still, if you care about the loose narrative implications of a Call of Duty campaign, it’s tough to wash the bad taste out of your mouth.

DMZ is full of the same thrills as other extraction shooters, but it’s much easier to jump into. Activision-Blizzard

DMZ is better than Warzone and a welcome reprieve from Zombies

DMZ, a fairly accessible extraction shooter game mode, returns with new content for the first time since its “beta” ended in 2023. Players have been mourning what could have been for years, but it seems like the developers at Infinity Ward have been tinkering with it in the background for quite some time.

And their hard work has paid off because I’m confident that DMZ is the standout mode for Modern Warfare 4.

This extraction shooter is perhaps simpler than even ARC Raiders, but that’s part of the appeal. Players drop into North Korea to loot, fight each other and take down key targets throughout the map.

Everything is streamlined and easy to understand, including the loot. During play, you will come across several types of scrap, an assortment of healing items and tons of weapons, so you don’t have to think too hard about what to grab. Just move, shoot and pull out high-value items, then run the loop again.

The enemy AI is surprisingly aggressive and fun to battle against, especially when you run into an overwhelming number of troops. Armored vehicles and helicopters will try to smear you into the dirt. It’s an adrenaline rush, and as far as I’m concerned, Infinity Ward nailed the really important part of DMZ. It’s tough to get the player-versus-AI balance right, but these enemies feel like a real threat.

Other players might also come for your loot, which is what sometimes puts folks off of the extraction genre altogether. But DMZ’s in-depth bounty system provides a foil to player-versus-player gameplay.

Folks who hunt down other players rack up a bounty and appear on the map, so pacifists have a better chance to steer clear while bounty hunters stalk them down. It’s a pretty genius compromise that encourages the player-versus-player enjoyers to butt heads while the player-versus-environment crowd hides away because the tension of a potential run-in with aggressors is never truly alleviated.

I’m concerned that the pared-down simplicity of the gameplay loop could hurt DMZ’s long-term success, but Infinity Ward seems committed to adding new world bosses. That could really shake up how matches play out, even if there’s nothing as over-the-top as Marathon’s Cryo Archive boss.

DMZ isn’t perfect, but I see the groundwork laid for one of the better extraction shooters I’ve played. Depending on how the development team builds on this game mode, I can see it becoming something special (and maybe even a Call of Duty mainstay for years to come).

New traversal options are available in Modern Warfare 4, but they’re tame compared to other modern Call of Duty games. Activision-Blizzard

Multiplayer remains quick, but it’s heavier and grounded

Call me an oldhead, I don’t care: Black Ops 7’s omnimovement system, which allowed players to run, jump and slide around while looking in any direction, was disastrous for Call of Duty game balance.

Treyarch’s update to the formula might work for massive Warzone maps where there’s plenty of open space and a higher time-to-kill for other players, but the smaller multiplayer maps become impossible to breathe on. Call of Duty is, first and foremost, an arcade shooter, but the multiplayer formula still works best when there’s time to recoup and recover, make tactical flanks and call in your scorestreaks.

Infinity Ward’s Modern Warfare 4 removes the omnimovement system, but it still allows players to sprint, slide and dolphin dive around at appreciably high speeds. The new mantling mechanic adds some traversal options, but everyone feels a little heavier.

The slightly slower six-versus-six matches feel great, and the larger modes are a bit less chaotic. The Modern Warfare games have always skewed closer to classic boots-on-the-ground Call of Duty, and the latest entry doesn’t disappoint in that regard.

Still, the fatal flaws of the modern Call of Duty formula have gone untouched. There remain more than 70 attachments for many weapons. Many modes have maps cut out of larger Warzone areas. The seemingly mandatory 24/7 Shipment playlist is being added soon to prey upon your nostalgia. Progression needs to synergize across a complete Modern Warfare 4 product, so unnecessary bloat exists everywhere you look.

This is a solid modern Call of Duty game, but the overall quality is still a far cry from the series’ heyday. In a post-Warzone world, this is about as good as it gets — but if that formula doesn’t work for you, it might be worth steering clear of Modern Warfare 4.
